title: October 23, 2026
description:
Cloud Database Migration Service

Security

On Saturday, October 17, 2026, Google received a report from a security researcher regarding the compromise of private keys associated with eight eMudhra subordinate Certification Authority (CA) certificates, including those cross-signed by AAA Certificate Services. Consequently, these CA certificates are no longer trusted and are being revoked.

To continue connecting to a source database after its CA certificate is updated, upload the new CA certificate to the Database Migration Service source connection profile:

  • Update the connection profile using gcloud database-migration connection-profiles update or the connectionProfiles.patch API method.
  • Modify the connection profile in the Google Cloud console:
    • MySQL connection profiles
    • PostgreSQL to Cloud SQL connection profiles
    • PostgreSQL to AlloyDB for PostgreSQL connection profiles
    • Oracle to Cloud SQL connection profiles
    • Oracle to AlloyDB for PostgreSQL connection profiles
    • SQL Server to Cloud SQL connection profiles
    • SQL Server to AlloyDB for PostgreSQL connection profiles

For more information, see security bulletin GCP-2026-071.

Cloud Monitoring

Fixed

Ops Agent version 2.73.0 includes patches for a Go vulnerability involving system root certificates, CVE-2026-111943. For more information, see Ops Agent 2.73.0 notes.

Cloud SQL for MySQL

Security

In response to GCP-2026-071, Google is updating Cloud SQL's managed components. No manual updates to the certificate store are required for Cloud SQL-managed instances. The fix is shipping in a new maintenance version that will be applied during scheduled maintenance. You can also apply the fix by performing self-service maintenance. An announcement will be published when the self-service maintenance fix is available.

What should I do?

  • If you use the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy, then upgrade the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy to 2.26.3 or later and the Cloud SQL Proxy Operator to 1.8.4 or later. If you run the standalone proxy binary, then also update the host's certificate authority (CA) certificates.

  • If you use a Cloud SQL Language Connector, then update the language runtime and operating system CA certificates used with the Cloud SQL Language Connector (for example, Go 1.26.10 or 1.27.3 or later, certifi 2026.10.19 or later).

  • If you're using the gcloud CLI to install the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy, then update the gcloud CLI to 590.0.1.

title: October 21, 2026
description:
Apigee X

Announcement

Apigee Emulator

Apigee Emulator v2.0.2

On October 21, 2026, we released Apigee Emulator version 2.0.2.

This release upgrades the Apigee Emulator runtime to Java 21 (Eclipse Temurin JRE 21) to align local proxy development and policy execution with the production Apigee runtime, while keeping the embedded Apache Cassandra datastore pinned to Java 8. It also addresses 46 security vulnerabilities across Netty, Jackson, Apache Log4j, BouncyCastle, Apache CXF, Eclipse Jetty, and the embedded Cassandra Go standard library health-check binary.

The emulator image is available at Artifact Registry.

To upgrade, update the emulator version in your Cloud Code for VS Code settings to 2.0.2. See Manage the Apigee Emulator for details.

Feature

Apigee Emulator

Changed in this release

  • Upgraded the Apigee Emulator runtime JVM to Eclipse Temurin JRE 21 (21.0.12.1.0+1-0, from JRE 11 11.0.31+11), adding JVM 21 compatibility flags (-Djava.security.manager=allow and --add-opens module flags) for JavaCallout, JavaScript (Rhino), and Python (Jython) policies while keeping the embedded Apache Cassandra 4.0.19 datastore pinned to Eclipse Temurin JRE 8.
  • Upgraded Netty to 4.1.137.Final (from 4.1.135.Final) and updated netty-tcnative-boringssl-static and netty-tcnative-classes to 2.0.81.Final (from 2.0.77.Final).
  • Upgraded Jackson (jackson-core, jackson-databind, and jackson-dataformat-yaml) to 2.21.7 (from 2.18.6 and 2.19.2) and jackson-annotations to 2.21.
  • Upgraded shaded Apache Log4j (log4j-api and log4j-core) in ConfigUtil.jar to 2.25.5 (from 2.17.1 and 2.25.4).
  • Upgraded BouncyCastle (bcprov-jdk18on, bcpkix-jdk18on, and bcutil-jdk18on) to 1.85 (from 1.84).
  • Upgraded Apache CXF (cxf-*) to 3.6.12 (from 3.5.11).
  • Upgraded gRPC to 1.82.3 (from 1.62.2), Protobuf (protobuf-java and protobuf-java-util) to 4.33.6 (from 3.25.5), and Guava to 33.5.0-jre (from 33.4.8-jre).
  • Removed unused org.eclipse.jetty:jetty-* (9.4.58.v20250814) and commons-collections:commons-collections (3.2.2) JARs from the emulator distribution.
  • Refreshed the Cassandra base image to pick up Go standard library 1.27.0 (from 1.25.11) in the embedded /opt/apigee/ready health-check binary.

Apigee hybrid

Announcement

v1.15.9

On October 21, 2026 we released an updated version of the Apigee hybrid software, v1.15.9.

  • For information on upgrading, see Upgrading Apigee hybrid to version v1.15.9.
  • For information on new installations, see The big picture.
Note: This is a patch release: The container images used in patch releases are integrated with the Apigee hybrid Helm charts. Upgrading to a patch via the Helm chart automatically updates the images. No manual image changes are typically needed. For information on container image support in Apigee hybrid releases, see Apigee release process.

Fixed

Fixed in this release

Bug ID Description
573622417 Fixed an issue where apigee-ingressgateway forwarded the x-envoy-decorator-operation header to upstream runtime and target backends.
571378258 The apigee-redis container now uses the Valkey engine (version 8.1.10). The RESP2 wire protocol and redis-server and redis-cli binary names are unchanged.
568860869 Fixed an issue in the RegularExpressionProtection policy where patterns starting and ending with .* whose middle section contained regular expression syntax were matched as literal text instead of regular expressions.
565072374 Fixed an issue where VerifyJWT policies using a JWKS uriRef could return steps.jwt.NoMatchingPublicKey on the first request after the 5-minute JWKS cache TTL expired when the identity provider rotated keys. The cache now refreshes synchronously upon expiration.
535395491 Extension Processor (ext_proc) denials now return the status and body that the policy or FaultRule produced, instead of always returning HTTP 500.
524115876 Fixed an intermittent HTTP 400 error in the OASValidation policy's strict parameter validation that rejected valid requests under load.
519729209 Fixed a SAML XML Signature Wrapping vulnerability in the ValidateSAMLAssertion policy.
502231886 Fixed an issue where the SanitizeUserPrompt and SanitizeModelResponse policies failed to extract content using default source templates when the <Source> element was omitted and <IgnoreUnresolvedVariables> was set to false.
432315283 Fixed an issue where changes to a multi-certificate truststore's trust anchors required a Message Processor restart when features.truststore.multi_cert_bundle.enabled was toggled at runtime; the outbound SSLContext now rebuilds automatically.
428750492 Removed the required validation constraint on the strategy and stages fields in the ApigeeDeployment CRD.

The AI.CHUNK_DOCUMENT function is a table-valued function that splits unstructured documents into semantically coherent text chunks optimized for vector embeddings and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) workflows.

This function is generally available (GA).

Cloud Billing

Feature

SKU attributes and granular usage units in pricing data export (Preview)

SKU attributes and granular usage units are now available in Preview in the Cloud Billing pricing data export to BigQuery.

  • SKU attributes: SKU attributes are key-value pairs that describe the SKU. For example, Key: model_name, Value: gemini_2_5_flash.
  • Granular usage units: Granular usage units are the usage unit of the SKU, such as tokens.

For more information about these dimensions, see the following:

  • SKU attributes
  • Granular usage units

For more information, see Streaming high availability.

Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform

Fixed

CodeMender updates (v0.16.0)

This release introduces updates to CodeMender:

  • Deep scan by default (cm find): cm find now runs a concurrent file-by-file deep scan (--deep) by default for higher vulnerability recall across repositories. To run a single-session quick scan instead, pass the --quick flag (cm find --quick). cm stats now breaks down scan usage by mode (--deep, --quick, and --diff).
  • Pre-flight health checks (cm health): Added the cm health command (with --json, --strict, and --timeout flags) to verify credentials, configuration, endpoint reachability, and project authorization before running scans.
  • Expanded file discovery: cm find now scans .hh, .hxx, .inl, and .ipp C++ headers, extensionless scripts with supported language shebangs (python, node, ruby, and php), nested build/, target/, obj/, and bin/ source directories, and production code under spec/, locale/, and i18n/.
  • Bug fixes:
    • Restricted cm verify file writes to .exploit/ inside the project root and skipped missing or out-of-scope session artifacts during workspace restore.
    • Capped single-turn file reads at 256 KiB with pagination hints, bounded unified diff generation on large files, and raised run_command default and maximum timeouts to 120 seconds and 300 seconds.
    • Fixed an issue where sandboxed sessions could not write tool call entries to ~/.codemender/audit.log.
    • Updated multi-file --deep and --diff scans to report INCOMPLETE status when one or more file scans fail.

For more information, see the CodeMender documentation.

description:
Agent Platform Workbench

M154 Release

Installed latest packages from upstream dependencies.

Fixed dataset and table search in the BigQuery panel, which sometimes failed to return results. Root cause is due to Datacatalog API being sunsetted in favor of Dataplex API.

Apigee X

Announcement

On October 20th, 2026, we began maintenance updates of Apigee instances configured for maintenance windows.

If you set a preferred window for maintenance for your instance, and your instance version is below 1-18-0-apigee-6, your instance will be updated to 1-18-0-apigee-6 within the next seven to 21 days. A notification containing the expected date of upgrade will be sent within the next two business days.

Note: Instances that meet either of the following two criteria will not be updated:
  • Your instance has a DNS misconfiguration, as described in Known Issue 445936920.
  • Your instance uses an Apigee Java Library that has been removed, as described in Apigee release notes dated October 16, 2025.

For more information on participating in scheduled maintenance windows, see Maintenance overview and Manage Apigee instance maintenance windows.

Cloud Workstations

Feature

Cloud Workstations supports automatic failover for boost configurations in Preview. When you enable automatic failover, Cloud Workstations automatically provisions a workstation VM using the boost configuration if Compute Engine lacks capacity for the default machine type during startup.

Gemini Enterprise

Feature

Gemini Enterprise: Antigravity Enterprise Gateway support

Antigravity Enterprise Gateway lets organizations route model inference requests from the Antigravity app, Antigravity CLI, and Antigravity for IDEs through a centralized enterprise gateway before forwarding them to Google Cloud. This deployment enables organizations to inspect and audit model traffic, enforce custom security and network egress policies, and authenticate developers through a gateway API key without requiring individual Google Account sign-in.

Requests routed through Antigravity Enterprise Gateway use a centralized Google Cloud service account and are billed on a pay-as-you-go (PAYG) consumption basis through the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform. This deployment model doesn't use your Gemini Enterprise seat-based subscription quotas (such as included Standard or Plus monthly allowances). You can't use a gateway and sign in with a Google Account at the same time. If you want to use your included subscription quota instead, disable the enterprise gateway and sign in with your Google Account.

This feature is generally available (GA).

For more information, see:

  • Deploy Antigravity Enterprise Gateway
  • Connect Antigravity to an Enterprise Gateway.

Breaking

Gemini Enterprise: Gemini 2.5 Pro discontinued in Canada and Japan

Gemini 2.5 Pro has been discontinued for in-country Gemini Enterprise app deployments in Canada and Japan. Agents and chat sessions in these regions that previously used Gemini 2.5 Pro automatically switch to in-country Gemini 3.5 Flash.

Gemini 2.5 Pro remains available in the global, us, and eu regions.

For more information, see Data residency for Gemini Enterprise and Manage web app features.

Feature

Spanner supports approximate aggregate functions for both GoogleSQL and PostgreSQL dialects. These functions produce statistical estimates of distinct counts, allowing you to compute results faster and save resources on large datasets compared to exact aggregation.

title: October 15, 2026
description:
Apigee Edge for Private Cloud

Announcement

Released Apigee Edge for Private Cloud 4.54.00.

Designated Apigee Edge for Private Cloud 4.54.00.00 a long-term support (LTS) release: 18 months of full support ending April 2028, then 18 months of maintenance ending October 2029. After October 2029, 4.54.00.00 receives no software updates, security mitigations, or technical support.

Installing a later 4.54 minor release or patch does not change those dates. To extend the support lifecycle, upgrade to the next LTS release.

For the support lifecycle phases, release cadences, and version numbering, see Apigee Edge for Private Cloud release and lifecycle policy.

Announcement

This release replaces Java 8 with Java 17 and Java 21, removes the Classic UI and the apigee-sso component, and updates the bundled Cassandra, Postgres, OpenLDAP, ZooKeeper, Qpid Broker-J, Nginx, and Consul versions. These changes are not backward-compatible.

For the 4.54.00 versions and the 4.53.01 versions they replace, see Supported software and supported versions.

Before upgrading, read Changes in Edge for Private Cloud 4.54.00, then Update Apigee Edge 4.53.00 or 4.53.01 to 4.54.00 or New installation overview. For known issues, see Known issues with Edge for Private Cloud.

Announcement

Replaced the Classic UI (edge-ui) with the New Edge UI (edge-management-ui).

The New Edge UI is the only management UI in 4.54.00 and is installed by default. Deployments running the Classic UI must transition to it before upgrading. Custom Classic UI properties do not carry over automatically. The default port also changes from 9000 to 3001, configurable with conf_uebe_port, so firewall rules and load balancer target ports that point at 9000 fail until they are updated.

For the migration steps and the supported feature list, see Migrate to the New Edge UI and What features are supported?.

Breaking

In deployments with Apigee SSO enabled, an integrated OIDC identity broker in apigee-openldap replaces the standalone apigee-sso component and Apache Tomcat 9.0.x. Before upgrading, take a complete and validated LDAP backup; existing apigee-sso configurations do not migrate automatically. Deployments not using Apigee SSO require no action.

For migration prerequisites, validation checks, and rollback constraints, see Option 2: Upgrade UI (with Apigee SSO).

Breaking

4.54.00 runs Java in mixed mode: Java 17 for Cassandra and ZooKeeper, Java 21 for the Management Server, Message Processor, Router, and Qpid Broker-J. Both Oracle JDK and OpenJDK are supported at those versions.

Oracle JDK 8 and OpenJDK 8 are no longer supported.

API proxies with custom JavaCallout policies or custom resource JARs can break on Java 21. For details, see Changes in Edge for Private Cloud 4.54.00.

Change

Upgraded Nginx on the Edge Router to 1.30.0.

If you are upgrading from Nginx 1.20.x, see Nginx 1.30 changes in Apigee Edge 4.54.00 for the full list of changes.

Change

Changed the TLS defaults on Message Processors to the Java 21 cryptographic baseline.

Message Processors run on Java 21, which enables TLS 1.3 by default (JEP 332) and prefers it for outbound backend connections, falling back to TLS 1.2. No configuration change is required if your target servers and load balancers negotiate TLS 1.3, or negotiate TLS 1.2 with forward-secret (ECDHE) cipher suites.

Java 21 also disables the non-forward-secret static RSA key-exchange suites (TLS_RSA_*). If you have overridden conf_http_HTTPTransport.ssl.cipher.suites.whitelist or conf_message-processor-communication_local.http.ssl.ciphers with static RSA suites only, backend calls fail with no cipher suites in common and the Router cannot complete a TLS handshake with the Message Processor. Replace the TLS_RSA_* entries with modern cipher suites and restart the Message Processor.

For the remediation path, see Legacy backend requirements and remediation.

Feature

Added Basic authentication to the New Edge UI, which lets you sign in without configuring an identity provider.

The New Edge UI supports Basic authentication without additional configuration. You can also configure Apigee SSO, or an external identity provider such as SAML or OIDC. This feature is generally available in 4.54.00.

Feature

Added automated pre-flight validation checks to apigee-setup and apigee-service, which surface environment configuration problems before a component is installed.

This feature is generally available in 4.54.00.

Security

Fixed multiple security vulnerabilities in Apigee Edge for Private Cloud 4.54.00.

These fixes ship as part of the component upgrades in this release; see Changes in Edge for Private Cloud 4.54.00.

Change

Changed the default garbage collector on Message Processors to the Garbage-First garbage collector.

Message Processors set useG1GC=true and useStringDeduplication=true by default in 4.54.00. In 4.53.01 neither was set by default. To configure garbage collection, see Configure the garbage collector for Message Processors.

Apigee Edge for Public Cloud

Announcement

On October 15, 2026, we began releasing Single Sign-On (SSO) updates for Apigee Edge for Public Cloud.

Fixed

Bug ID Component Description
560310696 SSO Fixed an issue where the Portal SSO endpoint inadvertently accepted deprecated TLS 1.1 connections. The endpoint now strictly enforces TLS 1.2+.

Apigee Integrated Portal

Announcement

On October 15, 2026, we released a new version of the Apigee integrated portal.

Fixed

Bug ID Description
560310696 Fixed an issue where the Portal SSO endpoint inadvertently accepted deprecated TLS 1.1 connections. The endpoint now strictly enforces TLS 1.2+.

Apigee X

Fixed

Bug ID Description
466116259 Updated the startup script for the managed instance group (MIG) that routes external traffic to Apigee. net.ipv4.ip_forward is now written to /etc/sysctl.d/, so an instance no longer stops forwarding traffic when a reboot or an OS update resets it. The script does not change unrelated iptables NAT rules. Instances pick up the change the next time they are restarted or recreated.

BigQuery

Feature

You can copy tables across regions. This feature is now generally available (GA).

Feature

You can now use reusable column aliases in GoogleSQL. This feature lets you define an alias for an expression in the SELECT clause of a SQL query and immediately reference that alias within the same SELECT list or in the WHERE clause of the same query block.

Reusable column aliases also streamline the migration of workloads from other data warehouses such as Snowflake and Teradata, by supporting their syntax.

This feature is generally available, and is opt-in only. To use reusable column aliases, you must first enable the feature.

Feature

You can export a conversational analytics agent's answer, including text, visualizations, tables, and citations, to a PDF or CSV file. This feature is generally available (GA).

Cloud Vision

Deprecated

Face detection model update

The emotion label response in the Cloud Vision API is deprecated. Going forward, the Cloud Vision API face detection (FACE_DETECTION feature) will return UNKNOWN for all emotion-related labels.

Compute Engine

Feature

Preview: You can create regional disks, including Hyperdisk Balanced High Availability volumes, by cloning a zonal boot disk.

For more information, see Duplicate a disk with clones.

Change

If you try to create an on-demand reservation or increase the number of reserved Compute Engine instances in a reservation when the zone has reached its reservation capacity limit for your requested machine family, then the request fails with a RESERVATION_CAPACITY_LIMIT_EXCEEDED error. For more information, see Reservation capacity limit exceeded.

Feature

Generally available: The storage-optimized Z4M machine series is generally available for Compute Engine. Powered by fifth generation Intel Emerald Rapids Xeon Scalable processors and Titanium offload processors, Z4M instances are purpose-built for workloads that require larger storage capacity, such as:

  • Parallel file systems to support AI/ML workloads
  • I/O intensive workloads such as SQL, NoSQL, and vector databases
  • AI/ML training and inference workloads such as checkpointing and distributed Key-Value (KV) cache

The Z4M machine series delivers up to 1,536 GB of memory and 168,000 GiB of local Titanium SSD capacity. Z4M also supports up to 400 Gbps of network bandwidth using two physical NICs. Z4M instances use Titanium and Cloud RDMA to help enable higher levels of networking performance, isolation, and security.

For more information, see Storage-optimized machine family.

Dataflow

Feature

Dataflow Auto VM Selection now supports 4th generation Compute Engine machine series. When Auto VM Selection is enabled, the service prioritizes these newer generation VMs for improved performance. If 4th generation VMs are unavailable at startup, the service automatically falls back to widely available 2nd generation machine families to ensure that your jobs can start without unnecessary delays.

For more information, see Auto VM Selection.

Gemini Enterprise

Feature

Gemini Enterprise: Anthropic models are available in the Gemini Enterprise app

Administrators can make Anthropic models—Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Sonnet 5.5—available to users in the Gemini Enterprise app. After an administrator turns on a model in the Enable third-party models section of the Feature Management tab, users can select the model in the model selector. Claude models are available in the global location and the us and eu multi-regions, and are charged on a pay-as-you-go basis.

This feature is generally available. For more information, see Enable third-party models.

Looker

Announcement

The latest versions in the Looker (Google Cloud core) release channels are beginning deployment as follows:

  • Latest version in the Rapid channel: Looker 26.20
  • Latest version in the No Channel channel: Looker 26.20

The latest version in the Regular channel remains Looker 26.18.

Note: This item was added on October 23, 2026.

Feature

The Looker 26.18 features have begun to be enabled for Looker (Google Cloud core) instances.

NetApp Volumes

Announcement

Google Cloud NetApp Volumes now supports the Flex Unified service level, including custom performance, in the following region:

  • europe-west8 (Milan)

For more information about available regions, see Supported regions.

Security Command Center

Feature

To increase the precision of attack path analysis and provide attack exposure scores that help you prioritize confirmed internet exposures, Risk Engine attack path simulations support the EXTERNALLY_EXPOSED_VM_INSTANCE External Exposure finding category (Preview). This finding category identifies Compute Engine or Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) resources with a direct public IP address that allows host OS access.

For more information, see Detect exposed resources, Risk Engine feature support, and Overview of attack exposure scores and attack paths.

Video Intelligence API

Deprecated

We are deprecating the emotion label response in the API. Going forward, the API will return UNKNOWN for all emotion related labels.

title: Create custom monitors in Vercel Observability
description:
You can now create custom monitors to get alerts based on your Vercel Observability query results.

For example, you can track signals such as AI Gateway costs, Core Web Vitals and other performance metrics, Workflow and external API failure rates, or Vercel Sandbox CPU time.

Each monitor tracks a single metric, such as response time, or a ratio of two metrics, such as errors divided by total requests. Choose statistical anomaly detection or a fixed threshold, then configure the detection window, filters, and grouping.

To create a monitor, inspect a chart’s query in Observability, start from a preset, or open Settings > Alerts for your team.

You can also define a custom monitor in a JSON file and create it with vercel monitors add in the Vercel CLI. Run vercel monitors schema --type custom for the schema and examples.

Receive alerts through email, Slack, Vercel Inbox, push notifications, or team-level webhooks. You can also add context for Vercel Agent to use when investigating an alert.

Custom monitors are available on Pro and Enterprise plans with Observability Plus, at $0.0035 per GB of data scanned. Built-in alerts remain included with Observability Plus.

Create a custom monitor or learn more in the configuration documentation.

Read more

title: Vercel Agent can now validate alerts before paging
description:
Vercel Agent can now investigate alerts from Vercel monitors before they reach your paging system. With validation enabled for a webhook destination, only alerts Agent classifies as Critical are sent to it.

To enable validation:

title: Making every harness durable
description:
Developers are familiar with running coding agents locally through harnesses like Pi, Claude Code, and others. They are reliable daily drivers for generating code, but keeping agents running around the clock requires your computer to be on and awake, which led to the laptop lid memes and Mac mini demand spike.

Running harnesses in the cloud

Harness workloads are moving to the cloud. Individual developers are deploying always-on coding agent workflows, projects like OpenWork and HanaAgent use open-source harnesses as the engines behind the apps, and engineers are building their own harness products.

These harnesses are designed for long-lived processes that keep the session in memory, and agent tasks commonly run for minutes or hours. Locally, a harness has direct, continuous access to the workspace and session history on the same disk, so resuming interrupted work only requires a simple prompt.

In the cloud, you can replicate that setup with a VM and persistent storage, but the VM doesn't automatically record which model and tool calls completed or resume interrupted turns after a crash. A failed turn or network error means lost work.

Also, not every agent task executed through a harness needs a sandbox. Database queries and API calls can run securely in functions, and that also means required credentials never have to enter the sandbox.

Making every harness durable

We built eve and fx to run durably in the cloud out of the box, and today we are introducing durable-harness, which extends that durability to any harness, including Pi, OpenCode, Codex, and Claude Code. It uses the same machinery that powers Workflow SDK to survive crashes and function timeouts.

With durable-harness, you can:

  • Run any of these harnesses durably on Vercel

  • Self-host a harness with your own Postgres instance

  • Make your local harness workflow durable

  • Build your own durable harness

Sessions that survive a crash mid-turn

Take the example of a coding agent adding a pricing page to an existing app. The agent reads the existing page, writes a new one, opens a pull request, and waits for CI to finish before reporting back.

What happens if its function times out while CI is still running?

Kill the function or drop the connection in the demo below to compare how the two agents recover and which work is repeated.

Without durability, the agent stops work until it is manually restarted, and completed work is repeated unnecessarily.

With durable-harness, a new function reads completed results from the log and resumes the turn. If the browser disconnects, the agent keeps running, and reconnecting catches up from the log.

Logs and queues

durable-harness is the newest package in our open source portfolio. It’s a set of adapters and utilities that let the harnesses you already use keep their sessions in a World, the Workflow SDK’s durable backend.

It writes each step of a turn to a durable log. Before a model call or tool call runs, it records an intent, and when the call finishes, it records the outcome. The turn itself is backstopped with a queue message, so if its function dies, the queue hands the turn to a new function that reads the log and continues where it left off.

After a crash, the log says what finished, what was running, and what never started:

  • Completed calls never run again because their results are read from the log, so you’re never billed twice for a finished model call’s tokens.

  • Models remember their previous calls rather than repeating them.

  • Interrupted tools marked replay: 'safe' run again. Any other tool comes back to the model as possibly run, and the model decides whether to check.

Harnesses that keep their own session files, like Claude Code's transcript, Codex's rollout, and OpenCode's event store, have every record mirrored into the log, so a new function or Sandbox rebuilds them from it.

Pick your harness

fx and eve are durable on their own. For the rest, durable-harness adds durability from the outside, without changing the harness.

For the full setup guide for each harness, check the docs.

Runs everywhere

Durable agents need a log of each step, a way to resume a turn when its process dies, and a stream for whoever is watching.

Workflow SDK ships all three behind one interface, a World.

durable-harness writes to that interface, so you can move the same agent from one World to another without changing its code:

  • On Vercel, it uses the Vercel World.

  • In development, it uses files on your machine.

  • On your own servers, it uses Postgres, MongoDB, Redis, or Turso.

Two variables move every agent using durable-harness to Postgres.

For more control, such as setting a namespace or recovering sessions when your server starts, create the World in code and pass it to your agent:

Check the self-hosting docs for more details.

See every session in Agent Runs

Agent Runs on Vercel shows the trace for every session, including each model call and tool call. Turns that resumed after a crash appear in the same trace, so you can see exactly where a turn stopped and picked back up.

Tools

An agent has only the tools you give it, and they run in your function. Each tool says what should happen if a crash interrupts it. A 'safe' tool, such as a lookup, can run again. A 'never' tool, such as a refund, never runs twice: the model is told the call may have happened, so it can check before it tries again.

Here’s how the coding agent from the demo above might define its tools:

  • A tool that reads a file or checks CI status is marked as 'safe' so it can run again automatically.

  • A tool that posts a PR comment is marked as 'never' so that comments aren't posted twice.

The following example defines a tool for each policy using the example of an agent processing a refund:

For each harness’s built-in tools, like its shell and file editing, read on.

Files

When a harness needs a shell and files, it’s not safe to run them directly on a shared serverless function host. Many sessions can share the same function, and its filesystem isn’t guaranteed to persist between invocations.

To address this, durable-harness gives you a few options:

  • virtual() keeps the files in the session’s log, with a bash-compatible shell that can’t reach your function’s files or the network. It suits short tasks and small workspaces without starting an entire sandbox.

  • virtual({ durable: false }) keeps the files in memory for scratch work and clears them at the end of every turn.

  • sandbox() gives the session its own Vercel Sandbox, with /workspace on a Drive that outlives every sandbox and every function. It suits real projects and long-running work.

Compare the three side by side in the docs.

Each harness’s built-in tools run on the workspace you choose. With Pi, CodingTools installs Pi’s own read, write, edit, and bash, and virtualEnv() or sandboxEnv() gives them a workspace:

For OpenCode, pass the workspace as workspace, and for fx, pass it to fxTools(). Claude Code and Codex always run in a Vercel Sandbox, since they expect a real shell and filesystem, and aren’t safe for multi-tenant use. Their built-in tools work on the session’s Drive once you turn them on with builtins: true. Each harness guide lists its built-in tools.

Documents

Some state belongs with the session but isn’t part of the conversation, such as a to-do list, a plan, or a form the agent fills in. A document is typed JSON that lives in the session’s log, so it survives a crash and moves with the session.

Tools can edit documents through io.docs, and each edit commits to the log alongside the tool’s result, so the document’s durable state stays consistent with the tool calls themselves:

Your app can read and edit the same document without a database of its own, and the chat route can even stream every change to your UI:

In fact, the virtual() workspace from earlier is built on documents: its file tree is a document in the session’s log, and each tool call’s changes commit with its result.

Learn more about tools, files, and documents and how to keep your agent secure.

Wrapping up

Developers choose a harness for the choices it makes about prompts, tools, and context. How it survives a crash shouldn’t be one of them. With durable-harness, a turn that loses its function partway through continues from the log on a new one, without a manual retry and without repeating what already finished. Self-hosting and portability work out of the box by building on top of the Workflow SDK’s World interface.

durable-harness is open source on GitHub.

Read more

title: AI Gateway logs now show session affinity
description:
AI Gateway logs now have a Sessions view that groups requests into sessions and shows how session affinity routed each one. Each row shows the coding agent or app that ran the session, such as Claude Code, Codex, or Cursor, along with its cost, models, providers, and how much of its input was cached across every turn.

Open a session to see its cache hit rate, duration, and path. The path lists each turn with its model and timing, and names the provider serving the session along with any earlier ones. Session affinity sends each turn to the provider that served the one before it, so the provider already has most of the prompt in cache. A session that stays on one provider reads more of each prompt from cache.

Filter sessions by turns, client, model, provider, authentication, or cost. Single-turn sessions are hidden until you clear the minimum turns filter.

Session affinity runs by default on text and chat requests. To group requests yourself, send the same sessionId in providerOptions.gateway, or the same x-session-id header, on every request in a conversation. Requests without one are grouped by a fingerprint of the conversation's opening and appear as fingerprinted sessions.

Read the session affinity documentation for more information on how AI Gateway identifies sessions.

Read more

title: Deleted deployments are permanently removed sooner
description:
Deployments deleted before they are 30 days old now have a shorter recovery period before permanent deletion. As developers deploy more frequently on Vercel, this reduces the buildup of old deployments on the Recently Deleted page.

For successfully built deployments, the recovery period is the time you have to restore them after deletion:

When the deployment is deleted

Time to restore after deletion

By retention policy before it reaches 30 days old

Same length as the policy. A 7-day policy gives you 7 more days.

Manually, less than 1 day after creation

1 more day

Manually, at least 1 day but less than 30 days after creation

Same as its age at deletion. Delete it 3 days after creation, and you have 3 more days.

Manually or by retention policy, 30 days or more after creation

30 more days, unchanged

After this time, deployments are permanently deleted and cannot be restored. Unsuccessful deployments may be permanently deleted sooner.

Learn more in the deployment retention documentation.

title: Findings from the $1M Vercel Sandbox challenge
description:
In August, we launched the $1M hacker challenge for Vercel Sandbox, inviting security researchers to try and escape Vercel Sandbox. We also coordinated with cybersecurity experts Trail of Bits to review the source code and security architecture.

Here is a summary of the challenge:

  • 1,285 reports over two weeks

  • $242,000 in bounties paid out

  • One Linux kernel zeroday vulnerability uncovered

No reports showed anyone accessing customer data in Vercel Sandbox. The most severe finding was the defect in the upstream Linux kernel.

The kernel zero day

The program's most important report arrived on day three.

Paulos Yibelo of pwn.ai, a HackerOne researcher working from a standard sandbox with no special access, found a defect in the Linux kernel's networking stack. Paulos discovered that specially crafted packets sent from within the microVM enabled three different attacks:

  1. Leak host memory over the network

  2. Crash the host machine

  3. Execute code on the host

Leaking host memory

In the first attack, memory from the host, the machine your sandbox shares with other tenants, shows up in packets the guest sends over the internet. This can happen continuously, for as long as the guest keeps sending.

This attack was demonstrated against Vercel production sandboxes.

Crashing the host and executing code on the host

The researcher also found that by sending specific packets, they could compromise the host.

First, by sending two packets, the researcher crashed the host machine, shutting down every sandbox running on it. Second, using the same flaw, they were able to run commands with full administrator privileges on the host, breaking out of the sandbox’s isolation boundary.

The packet-related crash and code execution attacks were demonstrated on the researcher’s own KVM and Firecracker machines matching Vercel Sandbox configuration.

Responsibly disclosing the kernel vulnerability

Almost every major cloud provider isolates customer workloads on this same layer of the Linux kernel, so any defect is shared-infrastructure risk.

Immediately after being notified, we collaborated with the researcher to understand and mitigate the vulnerability, working with AWS and other industry partners to prioritize a fix, and ensuring that Vercel customers and other developers using the kernel were safe.

The researcher also contacted the kernel maintainers and worked with them to create candidate patches. Fixes are under private review and CVEs are pending, so we are not publishing additional details until the patches are public. We are disclosing the existence of the vulnerability because it was separately disclosed in public.

Our approach to pressure-testing Vercel Sandbox

The HackerOne challenge made bounties available to any researcher, but we also extended our program to include internal evaluations and an independent investigation.

Before launching the public bounty, we performed live security assessments internally with full source access and support from the engineers who created and maintain Vercel Sandbox. We also engaged Trail of Bits, bringing on two engineers to evaluate our security architecture.

Not every finding came from the outside. Marcos Hernanz, a Vercel intern, found a cross-tenant data leak in the Linux device-mapper storage layer. This vulnerability let any sandbox read recycled disk blocks from previously deleted sandboxes.

The white-box deep dive

Trail of Bits spent four engineer-weeks inside our source code, with full access to the repositories and two enterprise test teams. They delivered 20 findings, and each was tested, confirmed, and referenced to the exact code.

They also performed an architectural review and concluded that our virtualization boundary is sound. Each sandbox runs on its own Firecracker microVM with a dedicated guest kernel, and the device model is deliberately tiny. No guest shares a running kernel with the host, or with another tenant.

On top of that foundation, they gave us three structural recommendations, which we implemented:

  • Find and eliminate all trust in the guest. Our control plane accepted values returned by software running inside the microVM, and every one of those values is tenant input. Anything that crosses the boundary should be derived server-side or signed with a key the guest cannot reach.

  • One policy, one decider. Egress enforcement was split across subsystems that each parsed the same network policy independently, and they did not always agree. We now use one canonicalization routine per data type, one component per decision, and revalidate connections when policy changes.

  • Assume the next zero day. Keep host and guest kernels up to date, reduce the kernel attack surface via build and runtime configs, disable nested virtualization, and use Firecracker’s jailer to run each microVM process with restricted permissions and isolate it from the rest of the host.

Vercel Sandbox findings

We received 1,285 reports in two weeks. This volume is only possible because researchers now hunt at AI speed.

Here is a breakdown of reports by category:

  • 877 duplicates

  • 319 not applicable

  • 57 valid

  • 32 informative

In our report triage we have validated:

  • 1 Critical finding

  • 5 High findings

  • 9 Medium findings

  • 42 Low findings

  • 32 Informative findings

We have paid out $242,000 in bug bounties.

The medium, Low, and Informative findings are small policy-boundary gaps, like a firewall rule that behaved differently than documented and a field that trusted the guest more than it should.

The most severe finding was the Linux kernel zero day defect, and no reports showed anyone reading a customer’s files, secrets, or application data.

We were most impressed with the heterogeneity of the reports. It was clear that researchers used different setups and have different obsessions. Some clearly know Linux namespaces and steered their agents straight at the kernel boundary. Others went after the network policies, and many went after areas we didn’t think to put on the menu.

That variety is what you're funding with a public challenge. Here's one of the more interesting findings it produced.

Cross-tenant disk snapshot restore (with limits)

Filed on day one of the challenge, this report is our favorite example of why we run a public bug bounty, even after internal assessments and a white-box engagement.

When you snapshot a sandbox, the control plane has to record where the snapshot data landed: {storage_url, size, checksum}. The flaw the researcher found was subtle: that answer came from software running inside the guest, and services running on the host trusted it. That is a trust-boundary violation. The guest is where our customers (and hackers) run untrusted code, so the host can never take its word as authoritative.

The researcher combined a known, documented container-escape primitive with this trust flaw. They intercepted the snapshot response inside their own sandbox and rewrote it, swapping the storage objects of two snapshots belonging to two separate accounts they owned. That meant restoring "your" snapshot materialized the other account's entire filesystem.

The researcher demonstrated that each account could read and modify the other’s files, verified the results using hashes, and preserved the test resources so we could independently reproduce the findings.

The limits of this attack matter. Aiming the swap at a specific victim required knowing that victim's internal snapshot storage key, a random 96-bit identifier the platform generates per snapshot and never exposes through the API. The only place that key appears is inside the victim's own sandbox. The researcher owned both accounts, which is what made the proof possible; there was no demonstrated path for a stranger to target another tenant. We still treated it as a priority fix, because a boundary that depends on a secret staying secret is not a boundary.

Trail of Bits independently flagged the same root cause in their assessment, which told us the finding was real, important, and discoverable from two completely different angles.

The fix shipped within a week, and the control plane now binds every snapshot object to the project that created it and rejects anything else. Snapshot creation moved out of the guest-reachable environment into a host-side service, and storage paths are project-scoped with strictly validated URLs.

Thank you to the research community

We would like to thank every researcher who filed a report, whether their finding was a zero day or a duplicate. Every technique discovered in the challenge informs how we protect the workloads running on Vercel Sandbox.

Thank you also to Trail of Bits for your comprehensive internal investigation and guidance.

Read the original challenge announcement and learn more about Vercel Sandbox in the documentation.

Read more

title: How v0 authenticates to Snowflake without exposing the user's OAuth token
description:
AI-generated applications often need to authenticate to external services on behalf of their users. That creates a problem: generated code shouldn't have access to the user's credentials.

We faced that decision when building the v0 Snowflake integration. It lets users connect Snowflake, inspect schemas, query data, and generate applications that run against their warehouses. That generated code has to authenticate to Snowflake, but it is written by a model and runs without human review, and prompt injection can steer it into exfiltrating whatever it can read, so the user's OAuth token should never enter the environment the code runs in.

We solved this with a Snowflake request proxy for v0 sandboxes, built on the Vercel Sandbox firewall. The sandbox can run normal Snowflake clients, but the real credential is resolved at request time in a server proxy outside the sandbox runtime. This lets existing Snowflake clients work inside the sandbox without exposing the user's credential to generated code.

The harder problem was deciding where the proxy could safely inject the credential. The obvious implementation, replacing a placeholder token wherever it appears, introduces another credential leak.

Isolation doesn't protect secrets

v0 runs generated applications in isolated sandboxes. Isolation protects the rest of the system from untrusted code, but it doesn't protect secrets inside the sandbox.

If a generated app can read a token from the filesystem, that token can be copied into logs, returned in an API response, embedded into generated client code, or sent to another host. Sandbox isolation limits what the application can access, but it does not help once the credential itself is available inside the sandbox.

For Snowflake, the credential represents the Snowflake role the user connected with. v0 should be able to help the user explore and build with data they are authorized to access, but generated code should not receive raw provider credentials just because it needs one.

Every Snowflake request goes through the proxy

The sandbox cannot talk to Snowflake directly. When code inside it sends a request to the user's Snowflake account host, the sandbox firewall forwards that request to the v0 Snowflake proxy:

The firewall terminates TLS with a certificate authority unique to each sandbox, which lets the proxy read and rewrite traffic that would otherwise be encrypted. The sandbox trusts that certificate authority automatically, so the Snowflake SDK and CLI run with their default certificate validation, OCSP included. The proxy then verifies the sandbox's OIDC token, looks up the v0 chat the sandbox belongs to, restores the user session bound to that chat, and retrieves a fresh Snowflake credential for that user.

The sandbox does not choose where a token-bearing request is sent. The proxy derives the Snowflake account host from the server-side credential and rejects invalid account URLs, keeping the credential scoped to the connected Snowflake account rather than trusting host information supplied by generated code.

Compatibility without credential exposure

As a stopgap, the first version of the integration wrote the user's real token into the sandbox's Snowflake token files. The proxy replaced that approach. Ideally, we would remove token files from the sandbox entirely, but Snowflake clients expect credentials in different locations depending on the authentication flow.

Some requests, such as Snowflake SQL API calls, authenticate with an Authorization: Bearer header. Other client flows read local token files and send the token as part of a login request. Once the client has authenticated, subsequent requests use Snowflake-issued session tokens, and the proxy passes those requests through untouched.

To preserve compatibility, v0 still writes a token-shaped placeholder into the sandbox. The placeholder is a fixed, public, 72-byte string that grants no access, and its only job is to let existing Snowflake SDK and CLI flows behave as if a token exists. The proxy never authorizes a request based on the placeholder itself. Instead, the proxy authorizes the request using the sandbox's server-side identity and its binding to the user's chat.

The real OAuth token, the reusable credential that represents the user, is never written into the sandbox. Snowflake does issue session tokens that live inside the sandbox after login, but each of those belongs to a single authenticated session.

Those sessions are short-lived in practice. The Snowflake helper in generated apps destroys its connection after each query, which ends the session right away. Closing the chat does not end a session on its own, but tearing down the sandbox takes the token with it, and Snowflake expires the session server-side after four hours of inactivity by default. When a request reaches the proxy, it decides whether and where to attach the credential.

Why blind replacement fails

The first version of the proxy searched each request for the placeholder and swapped in the real token wherever it appeared:

The problem is that generated code controls parts of the request, including where the placeholder can appear. A SQL statement, for example, is caller-controlled data. If a query contains the placeholder as a string literal, blind replacement turns that query into one containing the real OAuth token. If the database then returns that string, the real token comes back into the sandbox as query output, and the proxy would have leaked the token it was built to keep out.

Stricter matching does not close the hole. The proxy shouldn't inject a credential based on attacker-controlled text. Instead, it needs to know which field in each Snowflake request carries authentication.

Injecting credentials only into authentication fields

Snowflake requests reach the proxy in three shapes, and each shape puts authentication in a different place.

For Snowflake SQL API requests, the proxy sets the OAuth token on the Authorization: Bearer header. The body remains caller-controlled SQL and is not rewritten. If the placeholder appears in the SQL payload, the proxy rejects the request before it reaches Snowflake and logs it as placeholder misuse.

For Snowflake login requests, the proxy parses the JSON request body, sets the token structurally at the login token field, and serializes the body again. If the placeholder remains anywhere else in the request body, the proxy fails closed.

Post-login session requests authenticate with Snowflake-managed session tokens, so the proxy has nothing to inject.

Failing closed

The proxy rejects any request where:

  • The sandbox is not bound to a chat

  • No user-scoped credential can be obtained

  • The Snowflake account host cannot be derived

  • The placeholder appears outside an approved authentication field

  • A structured login body cannot be parsed safely

Requests are also bounded before inspection so that compressed or oversized bodies cannot turn the proxy into an unbounded parser. Every proxied request emits an observability event with the upstream outcome, status, duration, and injection location. This surfaces misuse and integration failures without exposing secrets.

Handling refresh and deploy

Token refresh cannot depend on an ambient browser cookie, because proxy requests originate from the sandbox, not from the user's browser session. v0 binds the user session to the sandbox instead, and the proxy mints and refreshes OAuth credentials from that binding.

The publish path uses Snowflake CLI flows with the same credential boundary. Deploy can write the placeholder into credential files, but never the real token.

After deployment, the application runs in Snowpark Container Services and authenticates as its own service user, with a token that Snowflake manages and rotates automatically, mounted at /snowflake/session/token. The user's OAuth token and the v0 proxy are no longer involved.

The resulting security boundary

For users, none of this is visible. Connect Snowflake, ask v0 to inspect schemas or build an app, preview the result, and deploy when it's ready.

The security model rests on five rules:

  • Credential injection happens only at each endpoint's authentication fields

  • Requests that use the placeholder outside an authentication field are rejected and logged

  • Token-bearing requests go only to the connected Snowflake account host

  • Credentials are minted and refreshed server-side

  • Generated code uses Snowflake without ever reading the user's OAuth token

In its first 15 days in production, the proxy attached credentials server-side for roughly 13,000 requests and recorded zero placeholder-misuse rejections.

Although we built this proxy for Snowflake, the same problem applies to other integrations: generated code often needs to authenticate without receiving the user's long-lived credential. The important part is to inject credentials only into protocol-defined authentication fields, rather than rewriting arbitrary request data.

title: Vercel Agent is now available in Slack code channels
description:
Vercel Agent now works in Slack code channels, a new kind of channel launched today for working with a coding agent. Anyone in the channel can follow the work, give Agent new instructions, and review the code it writes.

Choose Create a code channel from the Slack sidebar, select Vercel as the agent, and describe what you need to get started. You can also ask Agent to create one from an existing channel or thread. It brings that context with it to the new channel.

Use code channels to investigate incidents, write and review code as a team, or manage ongoing work such as dependency upgrades and migrations.

Inside a Vercel Agent code channel:

  • Follow the work: Agent posts relevant deployments, logs, errors, and diffs in the channel as it works.

  • Talk without repeated @Vercel mentions: Agent follows the conversation, recognizes which messages are for it, and continues when the team gives it more work.

  • Review pull requests: Ask Agent for a PR review and it posts its findings in the channel. It can find bugs outside the diff, and explain failing checks and their root causes.

  • Approve every change: Agent is read-only by default and never exceeds the requester's permissions. Before making a change, it drafts a plan and waits for approval. For every action, Vercel records who requested and approved it and what Agent ran.

  • Stop work at any time: The person who created the code channel can cancel an active task.

Vercel Agent in Slack code channels is available in public beta for Pro and Enterprise teams. Add Vercel to Slack, learn about Slack Code, or read the docs.

Vercel Functions now support the new Bun 1.4 release, a rewrite of Bun from Zig to Rust, with over 2,900 issues resolved, more than 1,500 additional Node.js compatibility tests passing, and new features and performance improvements.

Algolia is a hosted search platform. You send it your content, it builds an index, and your app queries that index instead of your database. Results come back in milliseconds, with typo tolerance, synonyms, and facet counts built in.

title: Introducing Vercel for Slack
description:
Vercel Agent now works in Slack. Mention it the way you'd pull a teammate into a thread, and it reads the discussion, answers with the context of the platform running your app, and turns the team's decisions into changes you approve. Vercel for Slack is available today in Public Beta for Pro and Enterprise teams.

Work starts in conversation. An alert gets noticed in a channel, a fix gets agreed on in a thread, and then someone leaves Slack to do the work. With Vercel Agent, you can tag it in for answers about your infrastructure or hand it the work, all without leaving the conversation.

What is Vercel Agent?

When we introduced Vercel Agent, we called it an AI teammate for your development workflow. Today it's the first responder for your production apps. When something changes, it investigates your logs, metrics, and deployments, finds the root cause, and proposes a fix, often before anyone's opened a laptop. Give it a PR and it flags the regressions and risky changes that a passing CI run won't show.

In Slack, that agent joins the conversation itself. It is a core part of Vercel, so your deployments, build statuses, logs, metrics, code reviews, and PRs are in front of it before you've typed anything. Mention @Vercel in a channel, a thread, or a DM, and it answers like a teammate with every tab already open. And answering is only half of it, because once you know what's wrong, the agent can go fix it:

  • Diagnose issues: Investigate incidents, trace errors to the deploy that caused them, explain a cost spike, and answer questions about your codebase.

  • Code alongside your team: Fix failing builds and CI, review PRs with knowledge of how the code runs in production, and turn a thread's decision into a tested pull request.

  • Operate your projects: Roll back deployments, update configuration, manage feature flags, and resolve unusual usage before it becomes a bill.

The agent is read-only by default, and anything that changes code or configuration goes through a plan that you approve. Vercel for Slack brings that whole loop into the threads where you and your team are already discussing work.

Accelerating development with a conversation

Teams form decisions through collaboration. Incidents get triaged in a channel, code reviews are hashed out in threads, and features get scoped between standups. But once a thread settles on what needs to be done, the actions still need to be translated into tickets, terminal commands, and PR descriptions. Every handoff drops context, and the conversation that held the full picture becomes the thing everyone summarizes from memory. Vercel for Slack gives the agent the full context of the original conversation for every turn.

Answers in one place speed up the whole team

A deployment goes out at 1:42pm. By 1:51, checkout error rates are climbing and an alert lands in the platform engineering channel.

What used to happen next was a scatter. One responder opens logs to see how bad it is, another asks their coding agent to line up the anomaly up against the deploy timeline, a third starts reading the diff of the suspect PR. Each person investigates alone, in their own view of the same system, and the thread is where they reconcile by pasting screenshots, summarizing agent findings, and correcting each other as they establish the actual state of the situation. The minutes that matter get spent assembling the picture before anyone can act on it.

With Vercel for Slack, the first question goes to the agent, right in the thread.

"@Vercel, checkout errors spiked after the 1:42 deploy. What's going on?"

It sizes the blast radius, correlates the spike with the deployment, identifies the PR that shipped in it, and explains which change, in which file, caused which behavior. The answer arrives in the channel, where the whole team reads the same diagnosis at the same time.

Nobody has to re-run a teammate's investigation or wait for the recap, because everyone is looking at the same report. The engineer who knows the checkout code speaks to the change itself, the on-call weighs how many users are hit against how long a fix would take, and what's left for the thread is the decision, whether to roll back or fix forward.

Vercel Agent understands how your team already talks

The thread, channel, or DM is the beginning of the prompt itself. You don't have to re-explain anything that was already said, or pass in any context from your app or codebase. Bring it into a conversation like any other team member and it reads the room, picks up what the team has been discussing, and can act on it when asked.

One example of this was our iteration on Vercel Agent's plan card, the message it posts in Slack to request approval for the work it wants to do. The first version we tested internally was a wall of text, but when one of our engineers noticed that people were often approving actions without reading all of the details, we had a redesign thread that ran 47 replies deep on what a person needs to see before confirming an action on the group's behalf. Tagging Vercel Agent in at the end of that thread is what resulted in the card you see today.

By the time a PR from a conversation like this lands in a thread, the tests have already run and the preview deployment is live, so the team can start reviewing it in the conversation that kicked off the feature in the first place.

Vercel Agent reviews pull requests in the thread

Ask Vercel Agent for a review in the thread where the PR is being discussed, and the conversation is passed along with the request. What your team has been raising becomes context for what Vercel Agent checks, and its findings land back in the same thread, so discussing them, deciding, and fixing them is one loop instead of a trip to another tool.

One example from one of our own PR discussions was a review someone requested mid-thread. The agent came back with a bug sitting just outside the diff, the same title rendered twice in the UI.

A finding doesn't have to end as a comment. If the team agrees it should be fixed, the agent can patch the PR itself, and that change arrives the same way everything else does, as a proposal waiting on an approval.

Changes always go through a plan your team approves

When a thread lands on a change, Vercel Agent replies with a plan that says what will happen, in which project, and at what scope. Decisions in a channel form in fragments, across people and hours, and nobody types "DECISION:", so the plan is where all of that becomes one explicit thing to say yes to. Once approved, the agent does the work under its own identity, and the audit trail shows who asked, who approved, and what ran.

One example from our own threads was a cached page showing stale data after we shipped an update. Someone called for a cache purge scoped to just the specific pages, since it was peak hours, and asked the agent to set it up. The plan that came back matched the ask exactly, a purge of the specific path and its sub-paths with the rest of the site's cache left warm, and nothing ran until someone approved it.

Whether a thread ends in a diagnosis, a pull request, or a cache purge, the last step belongs to a person.

Getting started

The easiest way to get started is to simply ask Vercel Agent questions. Ask about the error you're chasing or the build that just failed, see what comes back, and let your team decide over time how much of the work the agent takes on. Until someone approves a plan, it's only ever reading.

Vercel for Slack is available in Public Beta for Pro and Enterprise teams. To start using Vercel Agent in Slack:

  • Open the Slack app in the Vercel Marketplace and click Connect Account.

  • Choose the Slack workspace to connect, then click Allow.

  • Mention @Vercel in a channel, a thread, or a DM.

  • Sign in to your Vercel account when it prompts you the first time.

See the Vercel for Slack docs for setup and permissions.

title: $1 million hacker challenge for Vercel Sandbox
description:
Agents need to run untrusted code, and the microVM has become the standard way to do it: a dedicated guest kernel per workload, isolated from the host and from every other workload on the same machine.

But recent security research and real-world incidents have revealed that agents running untrusted code do not need to cross a VM boundary to escape containment; they only need one network path the security model failed to account for, which we explained in our post A sandbox without a network boundary is only half a sandbox.

Isolation only holds if both sides of it hold: the Firecracker microVM and the host-side network controls. Recently our CTO pointed an open-weight model with no safeguards at Vercel Sandbox. It did not escape, but it mapped the guest kernel, built a VM to reproduce its ideas, and wrote a fuzzer.

Defenders have first-mover advantage, but it won't last forever, and the choice is when to test the boundaries (we strongly encourage building a scanning program, which you can do on any budget with an open-source tool like deepsec and AI Gateway).

We are proactively choosing to test Vercel Sandbox on our own schedule, not an attacker's, and we are doing it in the open, with the best researchers in the world.

So for two weeks, we are paying up to $1,000,000 USD to the researchers who can escape a Vercel Sandbox.

The challenge

Starting today, Vercel is running a two-week public HackerOne program focused on Vercel Sandbox isolation.

  • Program: Public HackerOne program, open to all eligible researchers

  • Window: Tuesday, August 18 to Tuesday, September 1, 2026, or earlier if the reward pool is exhausted

  • Max per report: $50,000 USD, for a vulnerability that lets a threat actor read or modify another Vercel tenant's data

  • Total pool: Up to $1,000,000 USD in total payouts

Bounties are paid per report, scoped to a single root cause, and assigned by Vercel triage based on the maximum demonstrable impact. The full bounty table, detailed scope, and the list of known-duplicate classes are on the HackerOne program page.

How Vercel Sandbox is built

Vercel Sandbox runs on bare-metal EC2 hosts. Each sandbox gets its own Firecracker microVM with a dedicated guest kernel, and inside that microVM a Linux container runs the operator's code. The microVM, not the container, is the security boundary, so operator-supplied code runs two layers removed from the host. We assume that code is fully hostile: root inside the container, full kernel access inside the microVM, and motivated to reach the host or another tenant.

The network side of the boundary is enforced on the host, outside the microVM, where code inside the sandbox cannot modify or disable it. The sandbox firewall intercepts outbound TCP and DNS, checks each connection against the operator's domain and CIDR policies, and can inject credentials at the boundary so they never enter the microVM.

What we're looking for

In short: anything that breaks the sandbox boundary.

  • Compute boundary: Escaping the Firecracker microVM to the EC2 host, or reaching another tenant's sandbox through the compute layer (reading, modifying, or executing code in it), or crashing another tenant's sandbox from within another sandbox

  • Network boundary: Defeating the sandbox firewall without crossing the microVM: reaching destinations the operator did not authorize, exfiltrating data, or retrieving brokered credentials

Container namespace escapes that only reach the Firecracker guest OS are not in scope. Namespaces are a developer-experience feature, not the security boundary.

Bounties

Severity

Bounty

Critical

$25,000 – $50,000

High

$10,000 – $25,000

Medium

$5,000 – $10,000

Low

$1,000 – $5,000

The full bounty table, with example vulnerability classes for each tier, is on the HackerOne program page.

How to participate

The program is open now and closes on Tuesday, September 1, 2026, or earlier if the $1,000,000 USD reward pool is exhausted. Reports go through the HackerOne program page.

To reproduce a finding, boot a sandbox with the @vercel/sandbox SDK and demonstrate the impact with a live proof of concept. The default sandbox OS is enough for most reports; bring a custom image from the Vercel Container Registry only if your PoC needs extra tooling. We will not reward static-analysis-only findings; to issue a payout, we need to see the boundary break.

Full rules, eligibility, the complete scope and bounty table, and the submission process are on the HackerOne program page.

Results and payouts

We will triage reports from the day the program opens through one month after it closes. As findings are confirmed, we will pay bounties, ship fixes, and credit every researcher whose report holds up. The techniques discovered during this program will become permanent additions to the sandbox boundary, protecting every workload on Vercel long after the challenge ends. After the program closes, we will publish a follow-up writeup of the techniques and the fixes we shipped.

Thanks to HackerOne for standing up the program, and to the researchers who will spend the next two weeks trying to break what we built.

Read more

title: The Vercel Sandbox CLI is now more agent-friendly
description:
The Sandbox CLI version 4.0.1 ships four output and error improvements:

  • New sandboxes point users towards how to connect into them.

  • A sandbox not found error shows where to look for existing sandboxes.

  • Common mistakes, like typing a command after sh, redirect to the command that was intended.

  • Outdated installs show an update notice when they create a new sandbox.

Each of these messages now carries the action to take next instead of leaving you to work it out.

New sandboxes tell you how to connect

create and fork output now ends with a connect hint, so a fresh sandbox never leaves you wondering what to type next.

Not found errors point you to your sandboxes

When a command references a sandbox that does not exist, the error is quiet and actionable instead of a raw API dump. Setting DEBUG=sandbox:errors restores the request detail for debugging.

A misused command explains the right one

sh opens a plain interactive shell, so it takes no command of its own. The CLI can now return precise answers that rewrite the attempt into the command that does what you meant, whatever the command is.

Outdated installs warn you at creation time

create, sh, and run check for a newer published CLI and print an update notice when the install is behind. The check is cached to a file and refreshed at most once per hour; when a lookup does run it happens concurrently with the creation request, so it adds no latency. Creation defaults, such as the base image, are chosen client side, so an outdated global install silently keeps old defaults. Prerelease versions skip the check, and SANDBOX_SKIP_VERSION_CHECK=1 disables it.

Learn more in the Sandbox CLI documentation.

title: Sign JWTs from your Functions without managing private keys
description:
Vercel KMS lets you sign JWTs and arbitrary messages from your Vercel Functions using managed asymmetric signing keys, so private keys never live in your code or environment variables. Your function authenticates with its Vercel OIDC token, and the private key stays inside Vercel's key management service while verifiers use only the public key.

With Vercel KMS you can:

  • Create and rotate issuers and signing keys (RSA and ECDSA) from the CLI and dashboard.

  • Sign JWTs with custom claims and a configurable TTL, or sign raw bytes, using the @vercel/kms package.

  • Grant a project signing access per environment, including production, preview, development, and custom environments.

  • Constrain the claims a project can request per grant, and validate token claims against a JSON Schema.

  • Verify signed tokens anywhere. Each issuer publishes a public OpenID Connect Discovery document at https://kms.vercel.com/<issuerId>/.well-known/openid-configuration and a JWK set at https://kms.vercel.com/<issuerId>/jwks.json, so any standard OIDC or JOSE library can validate tokens without Vercel-specific code.

Sign a token inside a function:

Verify a token anywhere with a standard JOSE library, using the issuer's public JWKS:

Set up an issuer and grant a project access from the CLI:

As a best practice, create a separate issuer per project and environment. Isolating issuers keeps each token audience distinct, scopes signing access to exactly one project and environment, and lets you rotate or revoke keys for one without affecting the others.

To get started, read the docs or open Key Management in your team's dashboard.

title: Encrypted Client Hello (ECH) is now supported on Vercel CDN
description:
Vercel CDN now supports Encrypted Client Hello (ECH) for domains managed by Vercel DNS. ECH encrypts the Server Name Indication (SNI) in the TLS handshake, the last part of an HTTPS connection that revealed which hostname a client was connecting to. With ECH, network observers see a connection to Vercel's shared ECH hostname, vercel-ech.com.

ECH is managed at the platform level and automatically enabled selectively where supported, starting in the US for a limited number of TLDs, and expanding to more TLDs and regions over time.

Recent versions of Chrome, Edge, and Firefox support Encrypted Client Hello.

Learn more about ECH and how Vercel CDN protects your application in the CDN encryption documentation.
