title: Inside the Vercel intern experience
description:
The best way to learn is by shipping product to users in production, and that's why we don’t treat our interns as temporary guests. Every intern at Vercel is expected to operate like a core part of our engineering team from day one.

This past winter, we welcomed a small cohort of those interns to our headquarters in San Francisco. Over an intense four months, they contributed to some of our most important products: the CDN, v0, financial infrastructure, AI Gateway, and more. They shipped features used by millions, helped close the gap for enterprise deals, and in more than a few cases, left a mark that will outlast their time here.

Meet the Winter '26 intern cohort

Yash Kothari, CDN Team

University of Waterloo

What Yash shipped:

Yash's internship spanned the full CDN stack, from infrastructure to CLI to UI in the dashboard.

His first major project was Project-level routing, which is part of the new CDN tab in the Vercel dashboard. This feature lets customers update routing rules, including redirects, rewrites, and header transforms, from the dashboard, API, CLI, or SDK, without needing to redeploy their project or touch a single line of code. Yash built the underlying API endpoints (including a staging/publish workflow), the vercel routes CLI commands, and contributed AI-powered route generation. Right after launch, hundreds of teams immediately adopted it and created thousands of rules.

"One of my favorite things about my internship was that at Vercel you get a lot of autonomy and ownership," Yash said. "I hopped on calls with enterprise customers, saw my work featured on Vercel's changelog, and demoed my work in a live YouTube community session."

In the second half of his internship, Yash worked on Vercel's Firewall and Security products. He shipped the vercel firewall CLI command, enabling users and AI agents to configure custom rules, IP blocks, and firewall controls directly from the terminal. He also built an AI-powered Firewall Rule Builder that lets users describe a desired rule in natural language and generates a WAF custom rule automatically.

Kavin Valli, v0 Team

University of Waterloo

What Kavin shipped:

Kavin worked across the full v0 platform over four months, taking on projects that ranged from user-facing features to cost efficiency for the system’s backend infrastructure.

He started by building Folders and v0 Projects end-to-end: core CRUD operations, a library page redesign, favoriting, visibility controls (private/team/public), and folder sharing. He also closed a critical gap in v0's version history by shipping the manual commit button, which ensured that manual edits in the VM editor properly created commits and blocks, which closed the loop between manual edits and v0's iteration model.

His highest-leverage work came later in the term, when he focused on VM and sandbox infrastructure. By splitting VMs into tiered pools and routing smaller projects to a cost-efficient default pool, Kavin significantly reduced memory usage and infrastructure cost for roughly 80% of sandboxes.

"I worked on v0 and got thrown into the deep end pretty quickly, especially around the v1 launch," remembered Kavin. "It was a bit chaotic at times, but that's something I actually enjoyed."

His final and most involved project was taking ownership of the v0 Slack agent. He shipped Slack preview deployments for safe testing, rebuilt the router agent with improved thread history and SAML re-auth resume, redesigned project context tracking, and built out the full PR flow including v0 labels, Slack thread links, and merged/closed state tracking. The result was an agent that went from rough around the edges to something teams can genuinely rely on.

Mingchung Xia, Financial Infrastructure Team

University of Waterloo

What Mingchung shipped:

Mingchung pushed over 250 PRs in four months and became one of the top contributors on Vercel's central control systems monorepo.

His most externally visible project was the v1/billing/charges API endpoint and the vercel usage CLI command, which let users view their usage and costs in the standardized FOCUS v1.3 FinOps format. Originally scoped as a full-internship project, Mingchung completed it early and expanded its scope into a joint launch with Vantage. The work was subsequently adopted by Meta, Notion, Porsche, and other prominent companies to analyze their Vercel spend in a modern, compliant format.

His most technically complex project was designing and building Vercel's core entitlements system, which is the infrastructure that enables granting, revoking, and provisioning entitlements across project-based monetization, add-ons, enterprise, and marketplace work streams. The system architecture incorporated strong and eventual consistency guarantees, async and synchronous derivations, transactional outboxing, write-ahead logs, plan change manifests, stale-validation sentinels, and materializations. It was rolled out to production and backfilled across all active subscriptions.

"Most companies don't give interns or even existing engineers the opportunity to touch payment systems or billing infrastructure, let alone own it end to end," explained Mingchung. "Correctness is imperative when you're working with money, and I got to experience that firsthand at Vercel."

He finished his internship by shipping Vercel Buy, a new billing service supporting frictionless purchasing for agent credits, gateway credits, v0 credits, and pro subscriptions, complete with a CLI surface.

Mingchung will be joining Vercel full-time on the Financial Infrastructure team after completing his degree.

Kevin Thomas, v0 Team

University of Waterloo

What Kevin shipped:

Kevin's work spanned ML infrastructure, enterprise features, reliability engineering, and incident response, often simultaneously.

His most ambitious self-directed project was v0's auto model routing system: a full pipeline that automatically routes user prompts to the right model tier based on complexity. Kevin proposed the system, built the labeling pipeline, experimented with multiple classifier architectures (embedding-based MLP classifiers, TF-IDF baselines, fine-tuned TinyBERT), and integrated everything into TypeScript-only functions for production deployment. By launch, the system had processed over 1.4 million v0 messages and became the default for all non-enterprise users, reducing decision fatigue and latency for a very large share of v0's user base.

"From working on on-call incidents and vulnerabilities in month one to working directly with enterprise customers in April, I've gotten to work on an unusually wide range of meaningful problems," Kevin said at the end of his internship.

In the latter half of his internship, Kevin focused on enterprise work, most notably the v0 × Snowflake integration. He built enterprise admin controls for model access, RBAC for team skill management, resolved issues in SAML and isolated tenant environments, and shipped the integration itself. This work directly unblocked enterprise customers, supported renewals, and addressed live customer issues.

Kevin also served as a primary investigator for several incidents around signup, billing, auth, and account access, staying at the center of v0's reliability work throughout his term.

Sylvie Zhang, AI Gateway Team

University of Pennsylvania

What Sylvie shipped:

Sylvie worked across the AI Gateway service, contributing to everything from database and backend logic to observability, the frontend, and documentation.

Her first project was Price Strikethrough, surfacing provider MSRP as a strikethrough price alongside Gateway pricing, making provider discounts visible to end users. It touched the full stack and gave her a complete view of the AI Gateway product from the start.

"All that sounded daunting to a student like me with little experience," Sylvie said, "but it was the best learning experience I could have asked for."

Her most impactful and technically demanding project was the AI SDK v5 → v6 endpoint migration for AI Gateway's OpenAI-compatible and Anthropic-compatible endpoints. As the AI provider landscape had grown significantly more complex since v5 was designed, maintaining the legacy version had become a bottleneck, especially for handling token usage granularity differences across providers. Sylvie led the migration with a disciplined approach: deep cross-provider knowledge to catch incorrect AI-generated assumptions, systematic multi-turn and cross-provider testing scripts, concurrency testing to surface race conditions, proactive customer communication, and a deliberate fallback strategy that left legacy code in place until the migration proved stable.

The result was a cleaner, more maintainable Gateway service better equipped to handle the continued evolution of AI providers and models.

Advice for future interns

We asked these interns to share their top advice for future cohorts.

Take ownership from day one

Vercel gives interns real autonomy, but that means it's on you to use it well. Don't wait to be assigned work. Take initiative, identify what needs to be done, and start shipping.

Ask questions

Every intern said the same thing: no one at Vercel makes you feel like a burden for asking. The team genuinely wants you to succeed, so use that to your advantage and ask.

Work in public

Share your PRs in team channels. Post updates. Present at Demo Days. The feedback loop is fast, and the visibility helps you iterate and build trust faster.

Talk to people outside your team

Some of the best conversations happen across team lines with engineers, designers, finance, and people in roles you've never considered. Go to the office. Grab lunch with someone new.

Give yourself time to ramp up

The codebase, the culture, and the pace can be a lot at once. Don't rush. The first few weeks are for absorbing, not sprinting. Take time to ramp well, and you will be able to run fast.

Apply to become a Vercel intern

There are additional internship opportunities coming soon. If you want to join our next cohort, check our career site in September to apply.

Implement a harness by passing that package to createACP and configure basic harness mapping.

Then pass it to HarnessAgent like any other harness:

ACP is an abstraction over coding harnesses, but the AI SDK harness layer stays deliberately decoupled from it. Not every harness supports ACP, and for some, ACP limits or changes how well they expose their internal behaviors, so a direct adapter can produce a tighter integration.

For Claude Code and Codex, prefer the direct @ai-sdk/harness-claude-code and @ai-sdk/harness-codex adapters over an ACP-based implementation; reach for @ai-sdk/harness-acp when a harness has no direct adapter but ships an ACP-compatible package.

title: Building a software factory for AI SDK
description:
The AI SDK is one of the most popular open-source AI projects in the world. It serves over 20 million npm downloads a week and the repo has over 26,000 stars. Maintaining the codebase means tracking four moving targets at once:

  • Model providers: new providers, new capabilities, and new bugs

  • UI frameworks: bindings for React, Next.js, Svelte, Vue, and others

  • Sandboxes: the execution environments agents run code in

  • Harnesses: adapters for Codex, Claude Code, Pi, and others

After multiple years of growth, the repo was getting 100+ new issues every month, and when Anthropic's Opus 4.6 model was released, PRs hit an inflection point. By late June, that compounding had accumulated over 1,000 open issues and almost 800 pull requests.

That backlog is not a discipline problem. No maintainer, however good, can close that gap by working harder, and because generating code is cheap, it will only grow.

Instead of trying to scale ourselves, we built a software factory. Four weeks in, it authors between 25 and 35% of PRs we merge and closes 70-80% of issues.

Deciding what type of factory to build

Before we built anything, we had to answer three questions:

  • Why our existing approach using agents wasn't enough

  • What level of automation fit a project like the AI SDK

  • How to align automation and human effort to risk

Why not add more agents?

The best maintainers are already using agents aggressively. Mitchell Hashimoto runs Ghostty with the goal of an agent always working, and encodes every agent failure in AGENTS.md so it never repeats. Simon Willison runs four coding agents in parallel, and review bots like Vercel Agent and CodeRabbit sit on millions of repos. Other maintainers like Daniel Stenberg have opted to block AI-generated submissions to curl.

All of it helps, but none of it solves for the core constraint: every one of these solutions still routes every change through one human's attention. We believe that human accountability is still the core of trust in agentic engineering, so we knew our factory needed to solve for reviewer efficiency as a first principle.

What kind of automation fits AI SDK?

Software factories sit on a spectrum. At one end is full automation, where agents write, ship, and deploy without a human ever reading the code. In the middle are harnesses like Codex and Claude Code, where a person steers an agent or fleet of agents. At the far end is software you barely want to automate because the risk is too high, like firmware in a pacemaker or self-driving vehicle.

The AI SDK needs to operate closer to the careful end. It is foundational AI infrastructure with millions of applications built on top, so quality and security are non-negotiable, and a human needs to have control over what ships. We needed our factory to heavily automate the lifecycle around the human, without removing them.

How do we align automation and effort to risk?

For a given change, the depth of human review needed scales with risk.

Centralized roadmaps with detailed feature specs can define risk up front and directly shape the work going into a software factory. But open-source projects like AI SDK also get issues and pull requests from the community, and there is no guarantee they align with the goals of the project, or that changes are safe to make. Higher risk means human judgment is an even more critical part of the system.

To optimize our factory for that judgment, we knew agents had to go beyond generating code based on a request; they needed to evaluate full units of work in the context of the entire project.

Our goal was for the factory to generate a comprehensive assessment of each change for both fit and risk, including a full chain of documented evidence, making it easy for reviewers to apply the right amount of effort:

  • Docs fixes get a quick glance for verification

  • Well-defined provider changes get focused validation

  • A new public API gets deep review

What we built

ai-sdk-factory is a software factory that autonomously processes incoming issues and pull requests for AI SDK. Agents in the factory perform specific, reviewable tasks, like reproducing bugs, implementing features, and creating backports for older SDK versions. A human stays in control throughout the entire process, including merging every change.

We didn't ship the factory in one swing. We built it incrementally, starting at the beginning of the process with classification of issues as bugs, features, or documentation updates. That first step not only gave us more visibility into the shape of the backlog, but also passed helpful context to the other specialized agents we built later.

We prototyped multiple ways to build each new type of functionality, and in the process developed a set of guiding principles that shaped the architecture of the factory that went into production.

Build one agent per task

Once our classification agent reached a high level of accuracy, we focused on automating bug reproduction, fixes, and review of those fixes. We explored building a single agent equipped with skills for each step, but quickly realized that would come with a higher maintenance and troubleshooting burden over time.

Instead, we built a single agent for each specific task, making every new capability easier to reason about, test in isolation, and debug. Each one is scoped to a specific job, with its own prompts, context, and evals.

Today the factory has dedicated agents for every step in the flow:

  • Bug reproduction

  • Bug fixes

  • PR reviews

  • Backports

  • Documentation updates

  • Feature analysis

  • Feature implementation

Secure everything from the start

We implemented security with the second agent, because bug reproduction was the first step where the factory executed code based on content it didn't control.

A factory operating on a public repository has to assume attacker-controlled input: every issue, pull request, comment, and the links inside them are untrusted. Because successful open-source projects are high-value targets, threats range from malicious code changes and supply chain attacks to resource exhaustion, API key exfiltration, and prompt exfiltration.

Sandboxes are the foundation of our defense. Every agent in ai-sdk-factory runs inside an isolated Vercel Sandbox containing its code, its runtime, and only the secrets the agent's specific task needs. With those guardrails, untrusted content can shape what an agent proposes, but the damage any one task can do is contained to the sandbox.

We also built a shielding layer around the sandbox that controls what agents can reach over the network, blocking the paths an attacker would use to pull secrets out of the isolated environment.

The last line of defense is human review: nothing is merged without approval from a human on the AI SDK team.

Build value locally, then move to the cloud

The first several agents we built for the factory ran through a local CLI. That enabled our team to iterate quickly as we noticed inaccuracies, felt friction, and prototyped different ideas.

Once multiple steps were running reliably through the CLI, we were ready to move the system onto managed infrastructure. ai-sdk-factory uses:

  • Vercel Functions for the API, workers, and webhook ingress

  • Vercel Queues for task execution

  • Vercel Blob for logs

  • Vercel Sandbox for the agent workspaces

  • Neon Postgres for factory data

Today, GitHub webhooks feed the issue queue, and as soon as they arrive workers automatically pull them and kick off agent runs in sandboxes. We also built a monitoring UI that tracks every run in parallel, and visualizes the queue for the team of reviewers.

Shipping software through our factory

On July 24, a community member asked for blocked-domain support in OpenAI web search, and the request became issue #17898. The following section explains every step the software factory went through to process the issue, open a pull request with an implementation of the feature, and ultimately backport the merged feature to v5 and v6 of the SDK.

Classification

The first agent that runs in the factory classifies issues and pull requests. In this case, the ai-sdk-factory bot commented on the issue and applied a label, identifying the type as Feature with high confidence. The agent included its rationale for the classification in the comment.

Analysis

After classification, the analysis agent runs. Agents in the factory don't make any assumptions about the technical validity of a feature request or bug, so the analysis agent wrote a probe to confirm the absence of support for blocked domains. issue-17898-type-probe.ts was generated and run, and failed with an error when it looked for blocked-domains and didn't find it.

The failing probe proved the feature was missing on main, and the agent included it in the analysis as evidence.

The analysis agent then used the results of its investigation to build out a spec for the feature: add an optional blockedDomains filter to the existing web-search tool and map it to the provider's blocked_domains field.

The agent also confirmed the spec fit the SDK's provider-adapter architecture and was backward compatible, and even scoped documentation changes.

Implementation

Another agent then implemented the spec and opened a pull request. The implementation agent ran a live end-to-end test, executing an OpenAI web search with wikipedia.org blocked and confirming the domain wasn't reachable. The test was included as additional evidence on the pull request.

Automated review

Next, a review agent scored the change, and when it didn't find any concerns, approved it. The agent rated the feature as fully implemented, with:

  • Side-effect risk: low

  • Performance risk: none

  • Backwards-compatibility risk: low

Human review

Finally, Lars read the chain of evidence from the agents, reviewed the code changes, and merged PR #18033 into main.

Backporting

Once Lars merged the initial PR, ai-sdk-factory opened additional PRs for two backports, #18035 for v6 and #18036 for v5. The v5 backport did not apply cleanly, so the factory agent labeled and committed the conflicted state, identified and validated a fix, and pushed it seventeen minutes later. After review, Lars merged both backport PRs.

Results

We are just over four weeks into running the software factory in production. Here are the results:

PRs merged to main

Between 25-35% of the PRs we merge on a weekly basis are now authored by ai-sdk-factory agents.

Backports

Factory PRs are above 50% of weekly merges to the v6 release line, and v5 looks similar. Backports used to be work we skipped because dealing with merge conflicts wasn't worth the effort. v5 and v6 get far better support now.

Issues

In July, over 75% of closed issues were closed by the factory.

Open issues fell from a peak of 1,022 in late June to 844 by early August, and open bugs are down roughly 25%.

The ai-sdk-factory runs in public, so you can see every pull request it has authored on the repo.

Improving the factory becomes the job

The most interesting part of running the factory is what happens when it fails. Every run ends one of four ways: success, flawed, blocked, or manual. Only success ships, so the rest are signal that re-enters the system as feedback.

  • A flawed run means an agent produced the wrong thing, and the fix is better prompts, better context, or a new eval case so the same mistake gets caught automatically next time

  • A blocked run means the environment was missing something, like a credential, a service, or a dependency, and the fix is provisioning it

  • A manual run marks a boundary we drew on purpose, and forces us to ask whether improvements in the factory justify removing it

Each of those fixes expands the automation boundary, and every week the factory can handle work that it couldn't be trusted with before.

Running the factory is the same discipline teams already apply to their test suites and pipelines, but pointed at the system that does the work, instead of the system that checks it. In a world where agents define the SDLC, improving the factory will become the standard engineering job.

title: Go Explained: Simple Code That Runs Fast
description:
Introduction

Go was built at Google for a specific frustration: large programs that were slow to build and hard to read. The answer was a language that is deliberately small — fewer features, but the right ones, done well.

If you know one programming language already, Go will feel familiar within an hour. The interesting parts are not the syntax, but two ideas: goroutines and channels.

Goroutines: cheap concurrency

Most languages make running things at the same time feel heavy — threads, thread pools, and careful setup. A goroutine is Go's lightweight version: you start one by writing go in front of a function call.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "time"
)

func say(text string) {
    for i := 0; i < 3; i++ {
        fmt.Println(text)
        time.Sleep(100 * time.Millisecond)
    }
}

func main() {
    go say("hello")
    say("world")
    time.Sleep(500 * time.Millisecond)
}

The go say("hello") line does not wait — it starts a goroutine and moves on, so "hello" and "world" print interleaved. Goroutines are cheap enough that a program can run thousands of them, where thousands of operating-system threads would struggle.

Channels: how goroutines talk

Goroutines that never communicate are not very useful. A channel is a pipe between them: one goroutine sends a value in, another receives it.

package main

import "fmt"

func worker(done chan bool) {
    fmt.Println("Working...")
    done <- true
}

func main() {
    done := make(chan bool)
    go worker(done)
    <-done // Wait until the worker sends its signal
    fmt.Println("Done!")
}

The <-done line blocks until the worker sends true, which is how the main program waits without guessing how long the work will take. The famous Go saying sums it up: "Do not communicate by sharing memory; instead, share memory by communicating."

Why Go skips the features

Go deliberately leaves things out: no classes, no inheritance, no generics in the original design, no exceptions. Instead you get:

  • Structs and interfaces for organising data and behaviour, without class hierarchies.
  • Explicit error returns — a function returns its result and an error, and you check it, instead of exceptions jumping across the program.
  • A single formatting tool (gofmt) so all Go code looks the same, ending style arguments forever.

This can feel restrictive at first. The payoff is code that a new team member can read and understand quickly, even in a large codebase.

Where Go shines

Go is most at home in backend services, command-line tools, and cloud infrastructure — Docker and Kubernetes are both written in Go. If you need a fast API server, a small tool that compiles to a single binary, or a service handling many connections at once, Go is a strong default choice.

Takeaway

Go trades features for clarity: goroutines for cheap concurrency, channels for communication between them, and explicit errors instead of exceptions. Write a small program, add one goroutine, and you have felt the core of the language.

Originally published at https://practicaldevblog.blogspot.com/2026/10/go-explained-simple-code-that-runs-fast.html

title: Salesforce Org-to-Org Data Migration: Step-by-Step Checklist & Sequence
description:
Salesforce org-to-org data migration is the process of moving records from one Salesforce org to another, cleanly and in the right order. Done well, your data arrives complete, with every relationship intact. This checklist walks you through the steps and the sequence that make that happen.

Moving data between orgs sounds simple until you start. Records depend on each other, so the order you load them in matters a great deal. Load a contact before its account exists, and the link breaks. Skip a step, and you spend days cleaning up afterward. The difference between a smooth move and a messy one is almost always planning.

A clear checklist removes that risk. This guide gives you the full sequence for Salesforce data migration between orgs, step by step. Read on if you want your records to land in the new org accurate, connected, and ready to use from day one.

What Is Salesforce Org-to-Org Data Migration?

Org-to-org data migration means moving data from one Salesforce org into another. It covers records, relationships, and the order they move in.
This is more than a simple data transfer. A good migration preserves how records connect, so nothing arrives orphaned or broken.
The goal is a clean landing. Your data appears in the new org complete and correct, ready for your team to use.

Why the Sequence Matters So Much

In Salesforce, records are linked. The order you load them in decides whether those links hold.
Getting the sequence right prevents common problems:

  • Broken links between related records
  • Orphaned records with no parent
  • Failed loads that need redoing
  • Days of cleanup after the move

A planned sequence is the heart of any successful database migration. Load in the right order, and relationships stay intact.

Step 1: Plan and Analyze Your Data

Every strong Salesforce migration starts with a clear look at your data. You can’t move well what you don’t understand.

Before anything moves, map out:

  • Which objects and records you’re moving
  • How records relate to each other
  • What data to clean or leave behind
  • The field mapping between the two orgs

This planning shapes the whole project. Clear analysis is the cheapest insurance against a messy migration.

Step 2: Clean Your Data First

Moving messy data just spreads the mess to a new home. Clean it before the move, not after.

Good data cleanup covers:

  • Removing duplicate records
  • Fixing missing or wrong values
  • Standardizing formats
  • Archiving data you no longer need

Clean data moves faster and lands cleaner. This step saves real time later in the process.

Step 3: Map Your Fields

Fields in the two orgs may not match exactly. Mapping connects each field to its correct home.

Careful field mapping confirms:

  • Each field connects to the right target
  • Formats match for dates, numbers, and IDs
  • Required fields are accounted for
  • Custom fields carry over correctly

Good mapping prevents data landing in the wrong place. It’s a quiet step that makes a big difference.

Step 4: Load Data in the Right Order

This is the core of the whole process. Records must load in a sequence that respects their relationships.
A typical loading order looks like this:

  • Load parent records first (like Accounts)
  • Then load child records (like Contacts)
  • Then records that link to both
  • Finally, the records that depend on those

Following this order keeps every relationship intact. It’s the single most important part of a clean data transfer.

Step 5: Validate and Test

Never call a migration done without checking it. Validation confirms the move actually worked.

Test the results carefully:

  • Compare record counts between orgs
  • Check that relationships are intact
  • Spot-check key records for accuracy
  • Confirm no data was lost or duplicated

Thorough testing catches issues while they’re easy to fix. It’s how you move forward with confidence.

Step 6: Go Live and Confirm

With testing done, complete the move. Then confirm everything is in place before your team starts work.

A final check seals the job:

  • Run a last full validation
  • Confirm users can access their data
  • Watch for any early issues
  • Keep a backup until all is confirmed

A careful close means a calm go-live. Your team starts in the new org with data they can trust.

FAQ

What is Salesforce org-to-org data migration?

It’s the process of moving records from one Salesforce org to another, including their relationships, in a planned sequence so the data arrives complete, connected, and accurate.

Why does the loading sequence matter in a Salesforce migration?

Records in Salesforce are linked. Loading in the right order, parents before children, keeps those links intact and prevents broken or orphaned records.

How long do Salesforce data migration services take?

It varies by data volume and complexity. A small, clean migration can finish quickly, while large or messy data takes longer. Good planning and clean data speed it up.

Should I clean my data before or after migration?

Before. Cleaning first means only good data moves, which saves time and prevents spreading errors into the new org.

Do I need help with a Salesforce data migration?

Many teams benefit from expert help, especially with complex relationships and large volumes. Salesforce data migration services can plan the sequence and prevent costly mistakes.

Conclusion

A smooth org-to-org move comes down to planning and sequence. When you analyze your data, clean it, map it, and load it in the right order, your records arrive complete and connected. This checklist turns a risky move into a steady, repeatable process your team can trust.

That said, a complex migration takes real experience, and the stakes are high when business data is on the line. As a Trusted Salesforce Partner since 2006, the team plans every migration around your data and goals.

So if you want this done right, start with a clear plan and the right guidance. A strong migration partner maps your sequence, protects your data, and confirms every record lands correctly. Reach out for a short strategy call, and move your data with confidence.

title: ACH Return Codes Explained: R01–R85 and How to Handle Them in Production
description:
ACH Return Codes Explained: R01–R85 and How to Handle Them in Production

ACH Return Codes Explained: R01–R85 and How to Handle Them in Production

When you're building a payout system, ACH return codes are the language your bank uses to tell you "this transfer failed—here's why." Unlike HTTP status codes, ACH returns follow the NACHA ruleset and arrive days after you thought the payment succeeded. Understanding them isn't optional; it's the difference between a robust payout flow and one that silently loses money.

Why ACH Returns Matter to Your Code

An ACH debit entry (money leaving a customer's account) can be returned within five business days. Your system must detect the return, decode it, log it, and decide whether to retry, escalate, or route to a fallback rail. If you don't, you'll reconcile payouts that never landed and customers will file disputes.

The Major ACH Return Codes (NACHA R-Codes)

Here are the codes you'll encounter most often:

Code Meaning Cause Retry?
R01 Insufficient Funds Account has insufficient balance Yes, after 1–3 days
R03 No Account/Unable to Locate Account number doesn't exist or is closed No—use alternate payment method
R04 Invalid Account Number Structure Account number format is wrong No—validate input
R05 Unauthorized User/Consumer Dispute Payer claims they didn't authorize it No—escalate to support
R07 Authorization Revoked Payer withdrew consent No—update records
R10 Customer Advises Not Authorized Payer disputes the transaction No—investigate & document
R29 Corporate Customer Advises Not Authorized Business payer disputes it No—legal review
R31 Permissible Return Entry (PRNE) Payer requested return within window No—honor it

Reversibility note: R01 (insufficient funds) and R09 (uncollected funds) are temporary failures; R03, R04, and R07 are permanent.

Building Retry Logic

Here's a minimal handler:

def handle_ach_return(return_code, payout_id, attempt_count=0):
    """
    Decode an ACH return and decide next action.
    """
    temporary_codes = {'R01', 'R09', 'R16', 'R17'}  # Retry-able
    permanent_codes = {'R03', 'R04', 'R05', 'R07', 'R10', 'R29'}  # Don't retry

    payout = db.get_payout(payout_id)

    if return_code in temporary_codes:
        if attempt_count < 2:
            # Schedule retry in 2–3 days
            schedule_retry(payout_id, delay_days=2, attempt=attempt_count + 1)
            log_event(payout_id, f'ACH return {return_code}; retry scheduled')
        else:
            # Escalate after 2 failed retries
            escalate_to_support(payout_id, reason=f'ACH {return_code} — max retries exceeded')

    elif return_code in permanent_codes:
        # Route to alternate rail (Visa Direct, RTP, check)
        log_event(payout_id, f'ACH return {return_code}; permanent failure')
        route_to_alternate_rail(payout_id, preferred='visa_direct')

    else:
        # Unknown code—escalate
        escalate_to_support(payout_id, reason=f'Unknown ACH return code: {return_code}')

Settlement Timing and Return Windows

  • Standard ACH: 1–2 business days to settle; returns can arrive up to 5 business days later.
  • Same-Day ACH: Settles same day; returns still arrive within 1 business day.
  • Return window: NACHA allows 5 business days for most codes; R05, R07, R10, R29 allow up to 60 days.

Your reconciliation logic must account for this lag. Don't mark a payout "complete" until the return window closes or you've received explicit confirmation from your processor.

Logging and Monitoring

Always log the full return entry:


json
{
  "payout_id": "po_abc123",
  "return_code": "R01",
  "return_timestamp": "2024-01-15T14:32:00Z",
  "original_amount": 500.00,
  "customer_account": "****5678",
  "retry_count": 1,
  "next_action": "retry_scheduled",
  "next_retry_date": "2024-01-18"

---

*Decoding ACH return codes programmatically? The [ACH Return Codes API](https://rapidapi.com/payoutrail-ach-return-codes/api/ach-return-codes-api?utm_source=nichestream&utm_medium=devto&utm_campaign=payoutrail-ach-returns) returns the full Nacha R01–R85 set with plain-language descriptions and handling guidance.*

title: How I keep 13,000 kids' events fresh on Cloudflare Workers (and the 128 MB wall I hit)
description:
Grassy Knees is a directory of real things to do with kids across 42 US metro areas. Its rule is simple: every listing comes from the organizer's own page and shows the date it was last checked. This post covers the parts that turned out to be interesting to build.

The daily refresh plan

Re-researching 13k listings every day would be wasteful, so a planner runs over the database first. It picks a few "deep" metros to research from scratch and a list of recheck items: events close to their date, sources that changed, listings that failed a check. Research agents (LLMs with a browser and fetch) read the organizers' pages and return JSON records. A full pass across all metros took 32 agents and about 6.3M tokens, and added 2,415 public listings.

The import gate

Agents are confident even when they're wrong, so nothing goes live without passing a gate. A record needs a street address, an official URL on the organizer's domain, and a date in range. It must not copy from another directory. Records that fail are logged as DROPs with the reason, which helps tune the next brief.

Library feeds are a firehose

Library event systems (BiblioCommons, LibCal, Communico) expose clean feeds, and libraries run more free family events than anyone. Left alone, they took over whole metros (Seattle was 100% library one day). The plan now carries a per-metro mix with a cap on the library share.

The 128 MB wall

The site is Next.js-style React rendered on Cloudflare Workers, with D1 for data, KV for page caches and R2 for images. Loading the full catalog to render a list page OOM'd the 128 MB isolate. The fix was precomputed per-metro slices plus streaming. A side quest: an orphaned per-version page cache had grown to 356k keys (~15 GB) in KV before I noticed.

Markdown twins for AI assistants

Every page has a .md twin (append .md to the URL) and the site has an llms.txt, so assistants can quote real listings with their source links instead of inventing events.

It's free to browse. If you're a parent, I'd love to know what's missing in your city. If you're a builder, I'm happy to go deeper on any of this in the comments.

title: Human-in-the-Loop Validation for AI-Generated Financial Models
description:
AI can generate a financial model that looks coherent, contains valid formulas, and produces a plausible result while still being wrong in ways that matter.

A formula can reference the wrong cell. A cost assumption can be expressed in the wrong unit. A revenue schedule can omit a phase. A model can calculate correctly from an unsupported market assumption.

These are different failure modes, and they need different controls. For real estate feasibility models, the objective should not be to ask whether an AI-generated workbook looks correct. It should be to establish which properties can be tested automatically, which assumptions require evidence, and which decisions must remain with a qualified human reviewer.

A useful validation architecture has five layers:

  1. Structural validation
  2. Deterministic calculation checks
  3. Domain and consistency checks
  4. Evidence and provenance checks
  5. Human review and approval

No single layer is sufficient.

1. Separate the output from the evidence

Consider a hypothetical development model with the following inputs:

  • Site area and developable area
  • Permitted gross floor area
  • Unit mix or lettable area
  • Revenue assumptions
  • Construction and other development costs
  • Financing assumptions
  • Development programme
  • Exit assumptions

The model calculates development costs, revenue, cash flows, residual land value (RLV), and potentially internal rate of return (IRR).

For example, a model might calculate an RLV of £4 million. That output can be mathematically consistent with the workbook and still be commercially misleading if the revenue assumptions are unsupported or the construction cost basis is outdated. Validation therefore needs to test both the calculation and the justification for its inputs.

2. Layer one: validate the structure before the numbers

Before reviewing financial logic, validate the shape of the generated output. If an AI system is expected to return structured data before creating a workbook, define an explicit contract. JSON Schema is one established option for specifying required fields, data types, and constraints.

See the JSON Schema getting-started guide.
A simplified model input contract might look like this:
{
"project_id": "DEMO-001",
"currency": "GBP",
"site_area_sqm": 5000,
"gross_floor_area_sqm": 12000,
"construction_cost_per_sqm": 1800
}
This is illustrative data, not a market benchmark or a recommendation for a production schema.

A structural validator could check that:

  • Required fields are present.
  • Numeric values are actually numeric.
  • Areas and costs use declared units.
  • Currency is explicitly identified.
  • Values fall within defined technical bounds.
  • Unexpected fields are rejected or handled deliberately.
  • Missing values are not silently replaced with zero.

The last point is important. Zero and unknown are not equivalent. If a finance rate is missing, substituting zero can make a model appear more profitable. A missing value should normally trigger a validation error or an explicit unresolved status.

Structural validation establishes that the model can be interpreted. It does not establish that the model is economically sensible.

3. Layer two: use deterministic checks for deterministic rules

Rules that can be expressed precisely should not depend on an LLM's judgment. For example, if a model defines construction cost as gross floor area multiplied by construction cost per square metre, the expected calculation is:

\text{GFA}
\times
\text{Cost per sqm}
]
For the hypothetical inputs above:
[
12{,}000 \times £1{,}800 = £21{,}600{,}000
]
A deterministic test can independently calculate the expected result and compare it with the workbook output.
from decimal import Decimal

gfa_sqm = Decimal("12000")
cost_per_sqm = Decimal("1800")
reported_cost = Decimal("21600000")

expected_cost = gfa_sqm * cost_per_sqm

assert expected_cost == reported_cost

This test checks arithmetic for the stated formula. It does not establish that the GFA is permitted, that the cost rate is appropriate, or that the formula captures every relevant cost.

A production implementation should also define tolerances where appropriate, particularly when comparing rounded spreadsheet values or calculations involving floating-point numbers.

Other deterministic checks might include:
Revenue equals the sum of its components.

  • Total costs reconcile to their component schedules.
  • Cash flow totals reconcile across periods.
  • Unit counts and areas reconcile between schedules.
  • The reported output matches an independently calculated result.
  • A sensitivity case actually changes the intended input.
  • Required formula cells are not unexpectedly blank or replaced by constants.

Where possible, use independent calculations rather than simply checking that a formula cell contains a formula. A formula can exist and still be wrong.

4. Layer three: validate model relationships

Many serious errors are not syntax errors or arithmetic errors. They are inconsistencies between parts of the model.

Suppose a development model contains:

  • 120 residential units in the unit schedule
  • 116 units in the sales schedule
  • Revenue calculated using the sales schedule
  • Construction costs calculated using the unit schedule

Every formula may evaluate successfully, but the workbook contains a discrepancy that needs resolution.

Domain-level checks can flag conditions such as:

  • Unit counts that differ across schedules.
  • Areas that exceed a declared model constraint.
  • Revenue periods that do not align with the programme.
  • Cost totals that exclude a populated cost category.
  • An exit value that uses an inconsistent timing assumption.
  • A sensitivity scenario that changes revenue but leaves dependent calculations unchanged.
  • An IRR calculation using a cash-flow range that omits a period.

These checks should be encoded as explicit rules wherever the intended relationship is known.

Some rules require context. For example, whether a particular cost should be included in a development budget depends on the model's scope and conventions. A validator should not impose a universal rule where none exists.

Instead, it should identify the relevant condition, record the rule being applied, and send ambiguous cases for review.

5. Layer four: validate the provenance of assumptions

A financial model can pass every arithmetic test and still fail as an analytical tool.

The reason is straightforward: calculations cannot establish the truth of their inputs.

For every material assumption, a validation system should try to preserve:

  • The value and unit.
  • The source or origin of the value.
  • The source's date and relevant data period.
  • The geography and asset type, where applicable.
  • The transformation from source evidence to model assumption.
  • Any manual adjustment made by the analyst.
  • The model locations that depend on the assumption.

Consider a construction cost assumption of £1,800 per square metre. A validator might confirm that the figure is numeric, the unit is recorded, and the workbook uses it consistently. Those checks do not establish whether the figure is suitable for the location, asset type, specification, and cost period. That question requires appropriate evidence and professional interpretation.

An LLM may help extract candidate assumptions from documents or explain how a value is used in a workbook. The extracted result should still be checked against its source, and the resulting assumption should remain distinguishable from the underlying evidence.
A useful principle is:
Traceability makes an assumption inspectable. It does not make the assumption correct.

6. Layer five: make human review a defined state transition

Human review should not be an informal final glance after an automated process has already treated the model as complete.

A practical workflow can represent validation explicitly:

GENERATED
|
v
STRUCTURE_CHECKED
|
v
CALCULATIONS_CHECKED
|
v
DOMAIN_CHECKED
|
v
EVIDENCE_REVIEWED
|
v
HUMAN_APPROVAL_REQUIRED
|
+----> APPROVED FOR THE DEFINED PURPOSE
|
+----> RETURNED FOR CORRECTION
|
+----> BLOCKED: UNRESOLVED ISSUE

The states are illustrative, but the distinction matters. A successful automated test should not automatically mean that a model is approved. Approval should be scoped to a defined version of the workbook, its assumptions, its evidence, and its intended use.
A reviewer should be able to see:

  1. What was generated.
  2. Which automated checks passed.
  3. Which checks failed or were skipped.
  4. Which assumptions lack adequate evidence.
  5. What changed after a correction.
  6. Who approved the model and for what purpose.

If a material input or formula changes after approval, the system should identify which checks need to run again and whether the earlier approval remains valid. This is where versioning and change tracking become part of model governance rather than administrative overhead.

7. Design the exception path before the success path

Validation is often designed around a clean example: the model is generated, every check passes, and the user receives the output. Production systems need to handle less convenient outcomes.

A failed check should produce actionable information. “Validation failed” is less useful than “The unit count in the sales schedule differs from the unit schedule; review the linked inputs before approving revenue.”

Similarly, a warning should not disappear simply because a later stage of the workflow succeeds. For auditability, preserve the check identifier, the model version, the result, the relevant evidence, and the resolution.

8. Measure validation quality without inventing an accuracy score

A single “model accuracy” percentage can hide important distinctions. A workbook might pass every arithmetic test while containing several unsupported assumptions. Another may contain a harmless formatting issue but have fully reconciled calculations and well-documented inputs.

A more useful validation report separates categories:

  • Structural checks passed or failed.
  • Deterministic calculation checks passed or failed.
  • Domain checks passed, failed, or were not applicable.
  • Assumptions with verified, missing, or conflicting evidence.
  • Open exceptions and their severity.
  • Human review status.
  • The scope and version of the approved output.

If the system is evaluated over time, track false negatives and false positives for individual validation rules against a reviewed test set. Record the test cases, expected outcomes, rule versions, and known limitations.

Do not interpret a high pass rate as proof that the model is correct. It may simply mean that the checks cover only a narrow set of failure modes.

The purpose of validation is to make known risks visible and testable, not to manufacture certainty.

9. A practical implementation sequence

A team introducing validation around AI-generated financial models does not need to automate every review step at once.

A sensible sequence is:

  1. Define the contract. Specify the required inputs, output fields, units, and missing-value behaviour.
  2. Write deterministic tests. Start with totals, reconciliations, formula ranges, and independent calculations.
  3. Add domain checks. Encode known cross-schedule relationships and clearly defined constraints.
  4. Track provenance. Associate material assumptions with sources, dates, units, and transformations.
  5. Introduce exception handling. Make failures explicit and prevent unresolved material issues from being silently treated as passed.
  6. Define human approval. Record the reviewer, workbook version, purpose, and outstanding qualifications.
  7. Build a regression suite. Retain representative valid and invalid examples and rerun the checks when the generation logic or validation rules change.

The test suite should include deliberate failures, not only successful examples. Examples might include missing finance assumptions, inconsistent unit counts, a formula referencing the wrong period, and a source whose geography does not match the project.

This helps test whether the validation process detects the intended problem rather than merely accepting a plausible-looking output.

Conclusion

Human-in-the-loop validation is not a person checking an AI result after the important work is finished. It is a system design in which deterministic rules handle deterministic questions, domain checks expose inconsistencies, evidence is kept separate from assumptions, and a human reviewer remains accountable for unresolved judgments.

For financial modelling, that distinction is material. A workbook can be well-formed without being economically sound, mathematically consistent without being supported by market evidence, and ready for review without being ready for a decision.

The objective is not to make every AI-generated model look trustworthy. It is to make the model's logic, assumptions, limitations, and unresolved issues sufficiently visible that a professional can challenge it before relying on the result.

title: How a Kubernetes Database Migration Caused a 502 Production Outage
description:
Originally published on Naveed Ahmed's Engineering Blog.

A routine Kubernetes rolling update. A breaking PostgreSQL schema migration. And suddenly, a production API starts returning 502 Bad Gateway errors.

At 2:15 AM, an automated CI/CD deployment triggered what should have been a normal application update.

Instead, database queries started blocking, API latency increased, and PostgreSQL connections became exhausted.

The incident lasted around 24 minutes.

The real problem wasn't Kubernetes itself. It was a database migration that wasn't compatible with the old and new application versions running simultaneously.

Here's what happened and how to prevent it.

1. What Went Wrong During the Kubernetes Rolling Update?

Kubernetes rolling updates gradually replace old application pods with new ones.

During deployment, both versions can run at the same time.

Kubernetes Rolling Update

Application v1 (Old Pods)
        +
Application v2 (New Pods)
        |
        v
 Shared PostgreSQL Database

In this case, the deployment included a destructive database migration that removed a column still required by the older application pods.

Those pods continued querying the deleted column, causing database errors.

Key lesson: A Kubernetes rolling update doesn't guarantee zero downtime if your database schema isn't backward-compatible.

2. How PostgreSQL Lock Contention Caused 502 Errors

The schema migration also introduced PostgreSQL lock contention.

Operations such as dropping a column require an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock.

For example:

ALTER TABLE users DROP COLUMN full_name;

If existing transactions hold conflicting locks, the migration must wait.

New queries can then queue behind the waiting migration, causing a cascade:

Schema Migration
       ↓
Exclusive Lock Wait
       ↓
Blocked Database Queries
       ↓
Connection Pool Exhaustion
       ↓
Application Timeouts
       ↓
HTTP 502 / 5xx Errors

This explains why a database migration can disrupt API traffic even when Kubernetes pods appear to be running.

To investigate blocked PostgreSQL sessions:

SELECT
    pid,
    query,
    wait_event_type,
    wait_event,
    pg_blocking_pids(pid) AS blocking_pids
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE cardinality(pg_blocking_pids(pid)) > 0;

This helps identify queries waiting on other database sessions.

3. Why the Kubernetes Rollback Failed

Rolling back the application doesn't automatically reverse database schema changes.

For example:

kubectl rollout undo deployment/api

This restores the previous Deployment revision, but it doesn't restore deleted PostgreSQL columns.

If the older application still depends on the removed schema, errors can continue even after the rollback.

Key lesson: Application rollback and database rollback are separate operations. Both need a compatible recovery strategy.

4. The Solution: Expand and Contract Database Migrations

The safer approach is to introduce database schema changes gradually.

Phase 1: Expand

Add the new schema without removing existing columns.

ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN display_name TEXT;

Phase 2: Migrate

Deploy compatible application code and backfill existing data.

For large tables, use controlled batches rather than one massive transaction.

Phase 3: Switch

Update application reads and writes to use the new schema. Verify data consistency and wait until older application versions are no longer serving traffic.

Phase 4: Contract

Remove the old column in a later deployment.

ALTER TABLE users DROP COLUMN full_name;

This approach helps avoid breaking application compatibility during Kubernetes rolling updates. Destructive DDL can still require careful lock management.

5. Production Best Practices

A few safeguards can reduce the risk of database migration outages:

  • Use backward-compatible schema changes.
  • Run database migrations through a controlled CI/CD step or Kubernetes Job.
  • Avoid running migrations independently from every application pod.
  • Configure appropriate PostgreSQL lock_timeout values.
  • Monitor database connections, lock waits, API latency, and HTTP 5xx errors.
  • Test rollback compatibility before production releases.

For example, a bounded lock wait can prevent migrations from waiting indefinitely:

SET lock_timeout = '5s';

Choose timeout values based on your workload and migration strategy.

Read the Complete Kubernetes Database Migration Postmortem

In the full article, I break down:

  • The 24-minute production outage timeline
  • Kubernetes rolling update failure
  • PostgreSQL AccessExclusiveLock contention
  • Database connection pool exhaustion
  • Why the rollback didn't restore service
  • Expand and Contract migration strategies
  • Production troubleshooting and prevention

Read the Full Kubernetes Database Migration 502 Outage Postmortem

Final Thoughts

Kubernetes rolling updates can keep applications available during deployments, but they can't protect you from incompatible database changes.

The biggest lesson from this incident is simple:

Your database schema must support both old and new application versions during a rolling deployment.

Have you experienced database migration failures during Kubernetes deployments? How does your team handle zero-downtime schema changes?

Share your experience in the comments.

Written by Naveed Ahmed — Lead DevOps & Platform Architect

🌐 Engineering Blog | 🐙 GitHub | 💼 LinkedIn

🛠️ SRE Interview Scenarios | ☸️ Kubernetes Mastery

title: Content Security Policy: A Complete Implementation Guide for Modern Web Apps
description:
Content Security Policy (CSP) is the most powerful XSS defense available to web developers. When properly implemented, it prevents injected scripts from executing even if an attacker successfully injects HTML, because the browser only executes scripts from sources your policy explicitly permits.

The reason CSP has a reputation for being hard to implement isn't the directive syntax; that part is straightforward. It's that most web applications have legitimate inline scripts and styles, third-party embeds, and dynamic content that requires careful policy design to accommodate without weakening the security guarantees. Getting from no CSP to a strict policy that doesn't break your application requires systematic work.

This guide walks through that process end to end. It pairs well with our web accessibility and WCAG conformance guide, which covers the compliance side of front-end work, our front-end web security and attack mitigation guide, and our operational breakdown on Layer 7 web application firewall fundamentals. If you distribute logic across edge networks, our edge CDN architecture and security analysis shows where response headers fit in that model. For the formal directive definitions, the MDN CSP reference and the W3C CSP Level 3 specification are the authoritative sources.

How CSP Works

CSP is delivered as an HTTP response header. The browser reads the policy and enforces it for every resource loaded by the page: scripts, styles, images, fonts, frames, API calls. Any resource load that violates the policy is blocked and optionally reported. A basic policy looks like Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'; script-src 'self' https://cdn.example.com; img-src *.

The browser treats the policy as a whitelist: if a resource's source isn't explicitly permitted, it's blocked. The default-src directive serves as a fallback for any resource type not explicitly listed.

Core Directives

script-src

Controls where JavaScript can execute. The most important directive. Common values: script-src 'self' allows only same-origin scripts, script-src 'self' https://cdn.jsdelivr.net adds a specific CDN, and script-src 'none' disables JavaScript entirely.

style-src

Controls CSS sources. Inline styles require 'unsafe-inline' or hashes/nonces.

img-src

Controls image sources. img-src * (wildcard) is acceptable for images since external images cannot execute code.

connect-src

Controls which URLs can be reached via fetch(), XMLHttpRequest, WebSocket, and EventSource.

frame-src / child-src

Controls what can be loaded in iframes. Default to 'none' unless you specifically need iframe embeds.

base-uri

Controls what URLs can be used in <base> elements. Always set to 'self' or 'none': base injection attacks can redirect all relative URLs.

form-action

Controls where forms can submit. Often forgotten but critical.

Starting Point: Report-Only Mode

Never deploy an enforcement-mode CSP on a production site without first running in report-only mode. Report-only mode sends violation reports without blocking anything; you see what would break without breaking it. You enable it with the Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only header and point report-uri at a collection endpoint, for example report-uri /api/csp-report.

On the server, that endpoint accepts POST requests with a application/csp-report content type, extracts fields like blocked-uri, violated-directive, source-file, and line-number from the csp-report object in the body, and stores them for analysis. Group violations by violated-directive and blocked-uri to understand what your policy needs to accommodate, and collect reports for at least a week across realistic user traffic before enforcing.

The Nonce-Based Approach (Recommended)

The most common CSP mistake is using 'unsafe-inline' to allow inline scripts. This defeats the primary purpose of CSP; an attacker who injects <script>maliciousCode()</script> into your page will have it executed.

The correct solution is nonces (number-used-once). Each page response generates a fresh random nonce, includes it in the CSP header, and adds it as an attribute to every legitimate inline script:

app.use((req, res, next) => {
  const nonce = crypto.randomBytes(16).toString('base64');
  res.locals.cspNonce = nonce;
  res.setHeader('Content-Security-Policy',
    `default-src 'self'; script-src 'self' 'nonce-${nonce}'; base-uri 'self'`);
  next();
});

In your templates, every legitimate inline script carries the nonce attribute, like <script nonce="<%= nonce %>">const config = { ... }</script>. An injected script won't have the matching nonce, so the browser blocks it.

The nonce must be cryptographically random (not predictable), different on every page response (not static), and long enough to be unguessable (128 bits / 16 bytes minimum).

Next.js CSP with nonces

In Next.js, generate the nonce in middleware.ts using crypto.randomUUID() converted to base64, build the policy string with script-src 'self' 'nonce-${nonce}' 'strict-dynamic', and pass the nonce to the response via a custom request header such as x-nonce. In app/layout.tsx, read it back with headers().get('x-nonce') and pass it to the Script component, which applies the nonce attribute automatically. Collapse the multiline policy string with a whitespace replacement before setting the Content-Security-Policy header on the response.

Hash-Based Inline Script Approval

For truly static inline scripts (not generated per request), use hashes instead of nonces. Calculate a SHA-256 hash of the exact script content: echo -n "console.log('hello world');" | openssl dgst -sha256 -binary | openssl base64, then allow it in the policy as script-src 'self' 'sha256-RFWPLDbv2BY+rCkDzsE+0fr8ylGr2R2faWMhq4lfEQc='. The script whose content matches that hash byte-for-byte will be allowed to run.

Hashes work well for configuration scripts that don't change per request. Any change to the script content, even whitespace, invalidates the hash.

Handling Third-Party Scripts

Third-party scripts are the biggest CSP challenge. Analytics, chat widgets, A/B testing tools, customer success platforms: all require script execution from external origins, and many inject their own inline scripts.

Approach 1: Allow the CDN domain

Add specific origins to script-src, like script-src 'self' https://www.googletagmanager.com https://widget.intercom.io. This allows scripts from those origins but not arbitrary injection. The risk: if those CDN assets are compromised, your users are affected.

Approach 2: Use strict-dynamic with nonces

'strict-dynamic' is the right solution for trusted scripts that load other scripts. A policy of script-src 'nonce-{random}' 'strict-dynamic' works like this: only scripts with the correct nonce (those you explicitly included in your HTML) are initially trusted, those trusted scripts can dynamically create and append script elements which are also trusted, and domain allowlists are ignored in favor of nonce-verified entry points. This means Google Tag Manager (loaded with a nonce) can inject its own analytics scripts without needing their domains in your policy.

Approach 3: Proxy-loaded scripts

For maximum control, proxy third-party scripts through your own origin. Serve the third-party file from a route on your domain, fetch and cache it server-side, compute its SHA-256 hash on each fetch, compare it against a known-good hash, and refuse to serve it (with an alert to your logging system) if the hash mismatches. Now the URL lives under your own domain and is covered by your 'self' allowance, and you get integrity checking on top.

Dealing with Common CSP Challenges

Inline event handlers

Inline event handlers like <button onclick="doSomething()"> are blocked by CSP. Move the handler into an external or nonce-approved script and use addEventListener, for example document.getElementById('my-button').addEventListener('click', doSomething).

Inline styles

Inline style attributes require 'unsafe-inline' in style-src, which weakens your policy. For static styles, use CSS classes. For dynamic values, use CSS custom properties: set style="--user-color: red" on the element and reference var(--user-color) in a stylesheet class. Alternatively, allow inline <style> blocks that carry the nonce attribute.

eval() usage

eval(), Function(), and setTimeout('string') require 'unsafe-eval'. This is a significant security weakening, these features enable arbitrary code execution from strings. Audit your codebase with a search for eval, new Function, and string-argument setTimeout calls across your JS and TS files. Most eval usage in third-party libraries can be replaced with alternatives or eliminated by switching to a different library. If you genuinely need it, scope 'unsafe-eval' as narrowly as possible.

A Production-Ready CSP Template

Here's a starting policy that's strict enough to be meaningful while accommodating common requirements:

Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'; script-src 'self' 'nonce-{NONCE}' 'strict-dynamic' https:; style-src 'self' 'nonce-{NONCE}' https://fonts.googleapis.com; img-src 'self' data: https: blob:; font-src 'self' https://fonts.gstatic.com; connect-src 'self' https://api.yourdomain.com wss://realtime.yourdomain.com; media-src 'self' https://cdn.yourdomain.com; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'self'; form-action 'self'; frame-ancestors 'none'; upgrade-insecure-requests; report-uri /api/csp-report

The https: fallback in script-src (after strict-dynamic) provides backward compatibility for browsers that don't support strict-dynamic. Browsers that do support it ignore the fallback. Before shipping any policy, run it through the Google CSP Evaluator to catch bypassable configurations.

Using Helmet in Express

Helmet simplifies CSP header management in Express. Call helmet.contentSecurityPolicy({ useDefaults: false, directives: { ... } }) with camelCase directive names: defaultSrc: ["'self'"], scriptSrc including a function that returns 'nonce-${res.locals.cspNonce}' for dynamic nonces, plus 'strict-dynamic' and https:, imgSrc: ["'self'", "data:", "https:"], objectSrc: ["'none'"], baseUri, formAction, and frameAncestors all set to 'self' or 'none', and reportUri pointing at your report endpoint. Note the trade-off in most real apps: styleSrc often needs 'unsafe-inline' because UI libraries inject inline styles, and forcing nonces on styles breaks more than it protects.

Debugging CSP Violations

When violations occur in production, the report tells you what you need: document-uri shows the affected page, blocked-uri shows what was stopped, violated-directive names the policy line that fired, and source-file plus line-number locate the reference in your code. A blocked-uri of inline means an inline script without a matching nonce or hash, eval means an eval() call, and blob: means a blob URL. Browser developer tools show CSP violations in the Console panel with the blocked resource URL, the violated directive, and the line number of the blocked resource reference. Use the Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only header alongside your enforcement header to test policy changes without affecting users.

CSP is a defense-in-depth measure; it's not a substitute for input validation and output encoding, but it's the catch-all that stops injected content from doing damage even when those primary defenses miss something.

What Most Guides Get Wrong

Most CSP tutorials tell you to paste a strict policy into your server config and fix what breaks. That advice inverts the actual risk. The sites that suffer from XSS are rarely the ones with a slightly permissive policy; they are the ones that never deployed CSP at all because the strict version broke checkout on day one. A policy you actually ship with script-src 'self' https: beats a perfect nonce-based policy that lives in a ticket backlog for two years. Guides also treat 'unsafe-inline' in style-src as equivalent to 'unsafe-inline' in script-src. It is not. Style injection is a much smaller attack surface, and most component frameworks require inline styles to function, so fighting that battle costs you weeks for marginal risk reduction. Another common mistake: recommending hash-based policies for everything. Hashes silently break the moment a marketing tool edits one inline pixel, and a broken allowlist often gets "fixed" by someone adding 'unsafe-inline' back. Nonces fail loudly; hashes fail quietly. Finally, almost no guide tells you to budget for report triage. Violation reports from real traffic are noisy, full of browser-extension noise, and someone has to own reviewing them weekly or your report-only phase never ends.

Conclusion

Start every CSP rollout in report-only mode with a real report collection endpoint, and give the report-only phase a calendar deadline so it doesn't drift. Use nonces for inline scripts, reserve hashes for genuinely static blocks, and lean on 'strict-dynamic' instead of growing your domain allowlist every time a new vendor appears. Add third-party origins only after proxying or nonce-chaining fails, and validate the final policy with an automated evaluator before enforcement. Input validation and output encoding remain your first line of defense, CSP is the backstop that makes a missed vulnerability an annoyance instead of an incident. Ship the imperfect policy this month rather than the perfect one next quarter.
