These are asking prices, and the yield is gross. Asking prices are not closing prices, and nothing in a listing tells you the final figure. Sorting by newest also means few ads had been cut yet: only 4.8% of the sale ads and 3.6% of the rental ads carried a price drop. A gross yield ignores community fees, IBI property tax, insurance, empty months and income tax, which are what decide whether a 7% gross yield is still attractive net.

Newest first is a choice. sort_order=newest gives a fresh snapshot rather than the stale ads that never sold. In Centro, all 50 rental ads on the first page had been published within about 29 hours. The default sort is a weighted relevance ranking, and I did not want a ranking deciding which ads enter a price median.

What I would do next

Run the same script weekly and keep the snapshots, so each district gets a time series instead of one reading (I wrote up the snapshot-and-compare pattern for buyers in turning Idealista searches into shortlists). Go down to neighbourhood level in Centro and Carabanchel, where the samples are big enough. And for the thin districts, fetch every rental page rather than the newest 50, since the whole stock fits in one or two calls anyway.

Endpoints and parameters for everything above are documented on happyendpoint.com, and you can get a key and test the calls in the browser on RapidAPI. The same code works for Barcelona, Lisbon or Milan once you swap the location ID and country. If you need a larger pull, such as every listing in a city each week, get in touch.

title: Marigold: an altar that will not invent the dead
description:
This is my entry for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge: Week 4. The theme is Ghost in the Machine: something spooky, or something that honors the past the way a Día de los Muertos ofrenda does, with open-weight models or open-source AI at the center.

I read that as a rule about memory. An ofrenda does not invent a person. It holds what the living place on it: a song, a food, a story, a glass of water. A closed chat model is the opposite. Ask it about someone and it will gladly write a biography. Marigold is a small altar that refuses to do that.

The sample people on the altar are fictional. Abuela Rosa and June Park exist so the page is not empty the first time it opens.

What I built

Marigold is a local web altar. You place a person, then the foods, songs, and stories you want remembered. Two models from the Gemma family run through Ollama on the same machine:

  • embeddinggemma turns each memory into a 768-dimension vector, and turns the question into one too.
  • gemma4:e4b writes the reply.

Tiger Cloud holds the altar. Memories carry a halfvec(768) column and a BM25 index. Candle lights are a Timescale hypertable, with a continuous aggregate of lights per day. There is no retention policy. An ofrenda should not forget.

There is no account. It is a single-user altar on your machine. Judges do not need a password for the page. They do need Ollama and a Tiger connection string, because the open pieces are the product.

Asked "What song did Abuela Rosa love?", Gemma answered that she loved La Llorona, sang it softly in the kitchen, and said the song was about love that refuses to leave. That sentence is in the memory. Asked for June Park's last commit message, it quoted the only line that contains one: "the tests know more than I do tonight."

Under each excerpt the page shows the two ranks that retrieved it. Keyword search and meaning search are not the same list, and the reply is not allowed to leave them.

How a question is answered 

flowchart LR
  browser[Browser altar] --> api[FastAPI]
  api --> ollama[Ollama Gemma]
  api --> tiger[Tiger Cloud]
  tiger --> vec[pgvector HNSW]
  tiger --> bm25[pg_textsearch BM25]
  tiger --> candles[candle_lights hypertable]

EmbeddingGemma wants a different prefix for a document than for a query. A memory is stored as title: none | text: .... A question is embedded as task: search result | query: .... Same model, same 768 dimensions, two jobs.

Retrieval is hybrid, on purpose. Pure cosine search is happy to return a paragraph about a song when you asked for a title, or a paragraph about work when you asked for a commit message. Ahmed Mahmoud's field notes on hybrid search describe that failure exactly: embeddings encode meaning, so a rare literal token gets averaged away. Postgres keyword search has the opposite failure. Fusing the two with reciprocal rank, 1 / (60 + rank) on each arm, keeps a literal hit even when its vector rank is poor.

On this Tiger service the keyword arm is pg_textsearch BM25, not tsvector. The <@> operator lives in the extension schema, and it only sees rows when the query is built with the index name:

ORDER BY body OPERATOR(sloth_sort.<@>) sloth_sort.to_bm25query($1, 'memories_body_bm25')

The vector arm is cosine distance on an HNSW index (m = 16, ef_construction = 64), with hnsw.ef_search = 100. If you have selected one person, both queries filter to them, and the vector query sets hnsw.iterative_scan = relaxed_order so the filter does not quietly return fewer rows than you asked for. That early-stop is the other bug Ahmed documents, and it would be a bad one here: a thin result looks like a quiet altar.

Each arm returns up to 20 rows. Reciprocal rank fusion keeps five. Those five excerpts are the only biography Gemma is given. The instruction is short: answer from this list, name the person, and if the list does not contain the answer, say the altar is quiet. If both arms return nothing, the model is not called at all.

Candle lights are the time-series half of Tiger. Each light is an append-only row on a hypertable, segmented by person and ordered by time, with columnstore enabled. A continuous aggregate counts lights per day and stays open for the newest hour, so a candle you just lit still shows up. Memories stay in a normal table. A vector column cannot live in columnstore, so the embeddings and the candles are different shapes of the same database on purpose.

Why open innovation matters here

A remembrance is a poor thing to rent from an API.

The weights that embed a story, and the weights that answer from it, are models I run locally. The question and the five excerpts cross the room to Ollama. They do not cross the public internet to a chat vendor. Rahul Talreja's write-up of a local-first journal makes the split I wanted: the embedding model and the writing model are different jobs, and the writing model should see a handful of retrieved lines rather than the whole archive. His app keeps that archive in SQLite. Mine keeps it in Tiger, because the altar also wants keyword search and a history of candles, and both of those belong next to the vectors.

Running it this way has three practical consequences.

The altar still answers if the network is down, as long as Ollama and the database are up. A closed model does not.

The stories are not sitting in a transcript on someone else's account. The database is mine. The prompt is short enough to read. If a reply invents a date or a feeling, the excerpts are on the page under it, so the invention is visible.

I can swap the chat model without re-embedding, or re-embed without changing how candles are stored. embeddinggemma and gemma4:e4b happen to be the same family. They do not have to be. The dimension check refuses a vector of the wrong length rather than mixing two embedding spaces in one column.

June Park is the other half of the theme, the ghost in the machine. She is fictional, and so is py-marigold, the little library she is remembered for. The point of her card is that a last commit message is a kind of offering too. Keyword search is what stops that message from dissolving into "something about code."

Prize categories

  • Best Use of Tiger Data. Memories are stored as halfvec(768) and searched with HNSW cosine distance. The same rows are searched with BM25 through pg_textsearch. The app fuses the two rankings. Candle lights are a hypertable with a daily continuous aggregate.
  • Best Use of Gemma. embeddinggemma embeds documents and queries with EmbeddingGemma's own prompts. gemma4:e4b writes every reply, locally, through Ollama.

One project, two categories. I am not entering any category whose product this altar does not actually use.

Run it

The repository is github.com/tharun634/marigold-ofrenda, MIT licensed. Python 3.13, Ollama, and a Tiger Cloud dev service are the requirements.

ollama pull gemma4:e4b
ollama pull embeddinggemma
python -m venv .venv
pip install -r requirements.txt

Copy .env.example to .env. Set DATABASE_URL from tiger db uri YOUR_SERVICE_ID --with-password. Leave that file out of git.

python -m uvicorn backend.app:app --port 8765

Open http://127.0.0.1:8765. The first launch creates the schema if the altar is empty, then seeds the two sample people. That seed calls Ollama once per memory.

Two buttons on the page ask the questions I used while building: Rosa's song, and June's commit message.

The session

The build session is embedded below. It is a curated transcript: connection strings, passwords, hostnames, tokens, and home-directory paths are not in it. The work happened in Cursor. DEV's uploader has no Cursor value in its tool list, so the session's tool field is the nearest allowed label. The transcript says so, in the first reply.

Building Marigold, a local ofrenda grok-4.7
You

Build a web app for the Hacktoberfest Week 4 DEV challenge, Ghost in the Machine. I have Python, Node, Tiger Cloud, and Ollama locally. Aim for partner prize categories. When it works, publish the DEV article and this agent session after removing sensitive content, put the repo on GitHub, and include a GIF of the app.

Agent

This session was produced in Cursor, with Grok as the model. The uploader has no Cursor value, so the tool field is the closest allowed label and is not a claim that GitHub Copilot wrote the project. Week 4 is live through October 31. The theme is an ofrenda or a ghost in the machine, built around open-weight models. Tiger Data's category is embeddings and hybrid search. Gemma's category is running Gemma locally. I will build Marigold: a single-user altar. Stories are embedded on this machine and stored in Tiger Cloud. The séance may answer only from retrieved memories.

▸ get_challenge_details id 82, Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge: Week 4
Input
id 82, Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge: Week 4
Output
Theme: Ghost in the Machine. Required tags include devchallenge and hf26challenge. Best Use of Tiger Data covers pgvector embeddings and hybrid keyword plus vector search. Best Use of Gemma covers running Gemma locally. Submissions close October 31, 2026 at 11:59 PM PDT.
▸ ollama_models list local models
Input
list local models
Output
embeddinggemma and gemma4:e4b are already installed. An embedding probe returned 768 dimensions.
▸ tiger_extensions list extensions on the dev service
Input
list extensions on the dev service
Output
timescaledb 2.30.2, vector 0.8.7, and pg_textsearch are available. Host, password, and connection string were removed.
Agent

Memories sit in a normal table with a halfvec(768) HNSW index and a BM25 index, because a vector column cannot live in Timescale columnstore. Candle lights are a hypertable with a daily continuous aggregate and no retention policy. EmbeddingGemma uses its document prompt when storing a memory and its query prompt when asking. Gemma writes the reply from the fused excerpts only.

▸ apply_schema create beloved, memories, candle_lights, and candle_lights_daily
Input
create beloved, memories, candle_lights, and candle_lights_daily
Output
Schema applied. Extensions, both indexes, the hypertable, and the continuous aggregate were created.
Agent

The first séance failed because the BM25 operator was not on the default search path, and a bare text comparison could not see the index. Scoring has to go through the extension's query constructor with the index name. After that change, both demo questions were grounded. The sample people are fictional.

▸ seance What song did Abuela Rosa love?
Input
What song did Abuela Rosa love?
Output
The answer named La Llorona and the kitchen. That memory ranked first for both keyword search and meaning search.
▸ seance What was June Park's last commit message?
Input
What was June Park's last commit message?
Output
The answer quoted: the tests know more than I do tonight. That memory ranked first on both arms.
▸ browser open the altar and ask the song question
Input
open the altar and ask the song question
Output
The page showed both people, then the La Llorona answer with keyword and meaning ranks under each memory. A later reload showed a newly stored memory and another candle on Rosa's card.
4 of 4 messages

This article was drafted and published by an agent. I would rather the altar be strict about memory than fluent about people who were never placed on it.

title: MCP Server Security: Essential Best Practices for Robust Pro
description:
Running an MCP (Multi-Cloud Platform or similar control plane) server without a strong security posture is like leaving your front door wide open. These systems often manage critical infrastructure, sensitive data, or orchestrate complex workflows across various environments. A single vulnerability can expose your entire operation.

I've seen firsthand how easily misconfigurations or overlooked details can turn into major incidents. The good news is that many common attack vectors can be mitigated with a consistent application of security best practices.

What are the MCP server security best practices?

MCP server security best practices involve a multi-layered approach focusing on identity and access management, network hardening, regular patching, and data protection. Implementing strong authentication, least privilege access, network segmentation, and continuous monitoring are crucial steps to safeguard your critical infrastructure.

Let's break down the key areas you need to focus on.

1. Implement Strong Identity and Access Management (IAM)

This is your first line of defense. Weak authentication or over-privileged accounts are common entry points for attackers. Don't skimp here.

  • Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA): Mandate MFA for all administrative and privileged accounts. This is non-negotiable. Even if credentials are stolen, MFA prevents unauthorized access.
  • Least Privilege Principle: Grant users and services only the minimum permissions necessary to perform their tasks. Regularly review and revoke unnecessary access. This reduces the blast radius of a compromised account.
  • Role-Based Access Control (RBAC): Define clear roles with specific permissions. Avoid granting direct access to resources; instead, assign users to roles. This scales better and is easier to audit.
  • Centralized Identity Provider (IdP): Integrate with an external IdP like Okta, Azure AD, or Google Identity. This centralizes user management, enforces consistent policies, and simplifies onboarding/offboarding. 
# Example: Simplified RBAC policy snippet (conceptual)
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: mcp-read-only-dashboard
  namespace: mcp-system
rules:
- apiGroups: ["mcp.example.com"]
  resources: ["clusters", "deployments"]
  verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: read-only-dashboard-binding
  namespace: mcp-system
subjects:
- kind: User
  name: dashboard-viewer@example.com
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
roleRef:
  kind: Role
  name: mcp-read-only-dashboard
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io

2. Harden Your Network Perimeter

Your MCP server shouldn't be directly exposed to the internet unless absolutely necessary, and even then, with extreme caution.

  • Firewalls and Security Groups: Restrict inbound and outbound traffic to only what's essential. Close all unused ports. Use stateful firewalls.
  • Network Segmentation: Isolate your MCP server into its own dedicated network segment or VLAN. This limits lateral movement if a different part of your network is compromised.
  • VPN/Bastion Hosts: Access the MCP server's administrative interfaces only through a secure VPN or a hardened bastion host. Never allow direct SSH/RDP from arbitrary IPs.
  • DDoS Protection: Implement measures to protect against Distributed Denial of Service attacks, which can render your MCP server unavailable. 
# Example: iptables rule to allow only SSH from a specific IP range
sudo iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 22 -s 192.168.1.0/24 -j ACCEPT
sudo iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 22 -j DROP

# For cloud environments, use Security Groups/Network ACLs:
# Inbound: Allow TCP 22 from your_bastion_host_ip
# Inbound: Allow TCP 443 (HTTPS) from your_load_balancer_ip

3. Keep Software Updated and Patched

Unpatched vulnerabilities are low-hanging fruit for attackers. This is a constant battle, but a critical one.

  • Regular Patching: Establish a routine for applying security patches to the operating system, MCP software, and all dependencies. Automate this where possible, but always test thoroughly.
  • Vulnerability Scanning: Use automated tools to regularly scan your MCP server and its components for known vulnerabilities. Address findings promptly.
  • Dependency Management: If your MCP solution uses third-party libraries, monitor for security advisories and update dependencies regularly.

4. Secure Data at Rest and in Transit

Data handled by your MCP server, whether configuration, logs, or application data, needs protection.

  • Encryption at Rest: Ensure all persistent storage (databases, file systems) holding sensitive data is encrypted. Most cloud providers offer this as a default or easy-to-enable option.
  • Encryption in Transit (TLS/SSL): All communication with and between MCP components should use TLS/SSL with strong ciphers. Enforce HTTPS for all web interfaces.
  • Data Backup and Recovery: Implement a robust backup strategy. Encrypt backups and store them securely, ideally off-site. Regularly test your recovery process.

5. Implement Robust Logging and Monitoring

You can't secure what you can't see. Comprehensive logging and proactive monitoring are essential for detecting and responding to incidents.

  • Centralized Logging: Aggregate logs from your MCP server, operating system, and all relevant components into a centralized logging solution (e.g., ELK Stack, Splunk, Datadog). This makes analysis much easier.
  • Security Information and Event Management (SIEM): Integrate your logs with a SIEM system to correlate events, detect anomalies, and trigger alerts for suspicious activities.
  • Alerting: Configure alerts for critical security events: failed login attempts, unauthorized access, unusual API calls, system reboots, and resource exhaustion.
  • Regular Audits: Periodically review logs for suspicious patterns. Conduct security audits of your MCP configuration and access policies.

6. Secure Your Configuration and Secrets

Mismanaged configurations and hardcoded secrets are a constant source of vulnerabilities.

  • Configuration Management: Use tools like Ansible, Terraform, or Puppet to manage your MCP server's configuration. This ensures consistency and allows for version control and auditing.
  • Secrets Management: Never hardcode API keys, passwords, or certificates. Use a dedicated secrets management solution (e.g., HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault, Kubernetes Secrets with external integration) to store and retrieve sensitive information securely.
  • Regular Audits: Periodically audit your configurations and secrets storage for best practices and potential exposures.

7. Plan for Incident Response and Disaster Recovery

Even with the best defenses, incidents can happen. Being prepared is key.

  • Incident Response Plan: Develop and regularly test a clear incident response plan. Define roles, communication channels, and steps to contain, eradicate, and recover from security incidents.
  • Disaster Recovery Plan: Ensure your MCP server and its data can be restored quickly in case of a major outage or data loss. Test this plan regularly.

The Ongoing Journey of MCP Server Security

Security isn't a one-time setup; it's a continuous process. New threats emerge, and your environment evolves. Regularly review your security posture, stay informed about the latest vulnerabilities, and adapt your practices. By consistently applying these best practices, you can significantly reduce your MCP server's attack surface and protect your critical operations.

Considering a managed MCP solution or need expert guidance on securing your existing setup? Many vendors specialize in offering secure, compliant multi-cloud platforms and can help you navigate these complexities. Evaluating providers based on their security certifications, incident response capabilities, and adherence to these best practices is a smart move for any organization.

title: Same Architecture, Different Deployment: Why Traffic Shape Beats Diagrams
description:
Most deployment advice starts with architecture. Draw the boxes, pick the services, ship it. I believed that was the whole job until a client project showed me otherwise.

Two projects can have the same architecture diagram and still need very different deployments. What decides it is the features of the app and the shape of its traffic. This post is about the project that made that clear to me, and how I ended up on EC2 with Ansible instead of the more fashionable options.

The client

I took over a project and moved it onto EC2 first. The brief was short: keep it secure, and don't let it fall over when traffic jumps.

Traffic was not large, about 3K users a day. What made it interesting was how it moved:

When Traffic What it meant
Normal day About 3K users Two modest servers are enough
Product releases/events Double or more, in bursts Extra capacity for a few hours, not all year
December holidays A different pattern again Don't pay for peak capacity every month

The important detail is that I knew these dates in advance. Fixed servers would have been either oversized all year or too small on release day.

Which setup for which situation

Before the details, here is the short version. Find the row closest to your project.

Your project looks like Go for Trade-off
Steady traffic, small team, spikes on known dates EC2 + Auto Scaling + ALB Cheapest at steady load, but you patch the servers
Sudden, unpredictable spikes ECS on Fargate Nothing to patch, but a higher price per unit
Small event-driven jobs (resize an image, send an email) Lambda Pay only when it runs, but 15 minute limit and DB connection pressure
WebSockets or long-lived connections Fargate or EC2 Connections stay open, a poor fit for Lambda
Heavy 24/7 load ECS on EC2 + Savings Plans Best price at constant load, but two layers to scale
A team already living in Kubernetes EKS Reuses existing skills, big operational cost

ECS and Fargate are sometimes presented as rivals. They are not: ECS is the orchestrator, and Fargate is one way for ECS to run your containers.

The app has to be ready first

Before anyone touches a server, a few things must be true in the code. I have seen more "infrastructure problems" caused by these than by AWS itself.

  • The app is stateless. If sessions or files live on one machine's disk, you cannot run two copies. Sessions go in JWT or Redis, uploads go to S3.
  • There is a /health endpoint. The load balancer and Auto Scaling both rely on it to decide whether an instance is alive.
  • I know my database connection limit. Every new instance brings its own connection pool. Ten instances with a pool of 20 is 200 connections, and the database may not allow that.
  • Cron jobs run in one place. Otherwise they fire on every copy of the API at the same time.

None of this is infrastructure work. It is plain application code, and it decides what you can do afterwards.

The options, judged for this client

Option In its favour Against it For this client
EC2 + Auto Scaling + ALB Cheapest at steady load, full control, my Ansible roles work as they are I patch the OS, new instances take minutes to boot, I tune the scaling My pick
ECS on Fargate Nothing to patch, scales per task Roughly 15 to 40% more per unit than raw EC2, no host access, no GPU Right if nobody wants to own servers
Lambda Near-zero cost when idle, instant scaling 15 minute limit, DB connection pressure, awkward for WebSockets Side jobs only
EKS Huge ecosystem Steep learning curve and running cost Overkill

I chose EC2 with Auto Scaling for three reasons. The traffic is small, I know the spike dates, and I already had Ansible roles that configure the servers. Scheduled scaling covers the known spikes without paying a Fargate premium all year. If nobody on the team wanted to own patching, I would flip that decision and use Fargate without a second thought.

Autoscaling: what scales on what

This is the part where being a developer helped most, because several of the real problems live in the app and not in AWS.

Minimum capacity. Two instances across two availability zones. If one dies, the site stays up.

The scaling rule. I use target tracking, either CPU around 60% or ALB requests per target. Requests per target follows actual traffic, so there are no thresholds to guess.

Known events. A scheduled action raises the minimum before a release or before December. A new instance takes minutes to become useful, so waiting for the spike to start is already too late.

Boot time. I bake an AMI after the Ansible role runs. New servers start ready instead of installing everything at boot.

Health checks. Use the ELB health check type, pointed at /health, so a broken instance is replaced automatically.

The database. Compare the maximum connections against instances multiplied by pool size. This is the most common surprise when a Node app scales out.

One Node-specific trap is worth knowing. Node runs on a single core per process. On a 2-vCPU instance running one Node process, CPU may never go much past 50%, so a CPU-based rule never fires. Run one process per core (PM2 cluster mode works) or scale on requests per target instead.

Before any release day, load test staging with k6 or Artillery. It tells you more than any estimate.

Security: EC2 versus Fargate

Concern EC2 Fargate
OS patching Me AWS
SSH access I have to lock it down None (ECS Exec if you need a shell)
Isolation I manage the shared host Each task is isolated
IAM Instance role Task role per service
Host-level security agents Possible Not possible

If compliance requires an agent on the host, that points to EC2. Otherwise Fargate gives you a smaller attack surface for less work.

On EC2 my Ansible hardening role covers the basics: key-only SSH with root login disabled and no public SSH (Session Manager or a locked-down IP), servers and database in private subnets with security groups chained from ALB to app to DB, secrets kept in Ansible Vault or Secrets Manager and never in the repo, and automated RDS backups together with a restore I have actually tested.

Ansible and Terraform: who does what

I work with Ansible, and this setup lives in it.

  • Roles configure the servers: packages, users, SSH hardening, nginx, Docker.
  • A playbook deploys a new version one server at a time, with a health check between each.
  • Ansible Vault holds the deploy-time secrets.
  • A dynamic inventory (aws_ec2) finds the instances that Auto Scaling created, by tag. Instances come and go, so a hard-coded host list breaks quickly.
  • The same roles bake the AMI.

Before changing anything, I preview it:

ansible-playbook -i inventory/prod.aws_ec2.yml site.yml --check --diff

And this is a trimmed version of the deploy playbook:

- hosts: web
  become: true
  serial: 1            # one server at a time, the ALB keeps traffic on healthy ones
  vars_files:
    - secrets.yml      # encrypted with ansible-vault

  tasks:
    - name: Run the new version of the API
      community.docker.docker_container:
        name: api
        image: "{{ app_image }}:{{ app_version }}"
        state: started
        recreate: true
        restart_policy: always
        published_ports: ["3000:3000"]
        env:
          DB_HOST: "{{ db_host }}"
          DB_PASSWORD: "{{ db_password }}"

    - name: Wait until /health answers
      ansible.builtin.uri:
        url: http://localhost:3000/health
        status_code: 200
      register: health
      retries: 10
      delay: 3
      until: health.status == 200

I don't use Terraform on this project, but it is worth saying where it fits. It is strong at creating and tracking cloud resources such as the VPC, ALB, RDS and IAM, with state you can review. A team that rebuilds environments often may prefer it for that layer and keep Ansible for what runs inside the servers. The two are not rivals.

When I would choose differently

  • If nobody wants to patch servers, or traffic becomes unpredictable, I would move to Fargate.
  • If the load turns into a heavy 24/7 one, I would look at ECS on EC2 with Savings Plans.
  • If the team grows into Kubernetes, EKS starts to make sense.
  • For small side tasks like image resizing or emails, I would add Lambda next to the main app.

What I took from it

The server was never the real decision. The traffic shape, the app being ready to scale, and a setup I can repeat with one command were. Pick the simplest option that survives your busiest day, keep it in code, and load test it before that day arrives.

If you have deployed for a client with spiky traffic, I would like to hear what you chose and what you would change.

title: Building a K Command Palette (and a Fake Terminal) for My Portfolio
description:
Press ⌘K (or Ctrl+K) anywhere on my site and you get a search box that jumps to any page, case study, game, blog post or Dota 2 hero. Press ~ and you get a terminal. Neither is essential. Both are the kind of detail that makes a developer's site feel like it was made by a developer.

Here's how they're built, and the few decisions that kept them simple.

Logic first, UI second

Both features are mostly logic, so I wrote the logic as pure functions with no React involved:

  • buildItems(posts, heroes, work) returns a flat list of { group, label, url, keywords };
  • filterItems(items, query) ranks them;
  • runCommand(input) returns { lines, action } for the terminal, where action is "navigate", "clear" or "exit";
  • complete(input) does tab completion.

The React components only render state and call these. That made them trivial to smoke-test: "typing wraith ranks Wraith King first", "cd blog/ goes to the blog", "c + Tab doesn't complete, because it's ambiguous".

Ranking without a fuzzy-search library

Fuzzy matching libraries are great, but for a hundred or so items a tiny score does the job. For each word you type:

  • a match at the start of the label scores 0 (best);
  • a match at the start of any word in the label scores 1;
  • a match anywhere in the label scores 2;
  • a match in the group or keywords scores 3;
  • no match anywhere, and the item is out.

Then sort by score, keeping the original order for ties. Keywords do the quiet work: "resume" finds the Experience section, and "hire" finds the contact page.

Don't load what nobody asked for

Dota has 120+ heroes, and putting all of them in every page's HTML would be wasteful. The palette fetches hero names the first time someone opens it, from an endpoint that's already cached for an hour. When the palette is empty, heroes stay hidden so the list starts with pages, not a wall of hero names.

The terminal

It's a switch statement with personality. help, whoami, ls projects, cat resume, cd contact and play chess all do something real. sudo tells you that simplicity is not negotiable, and vim reassures you that exit works here. Arrow keys walk your history, Tab completes, and Ctrl+L clears.

It uses the site's dark theme tokens, so it looks right without any one-off colours.

Respecting the person typing

I record anonymous usage events to see whether people actually use this. For the terminal, I only store the command word, and only if it's a command I know. Anything else is recorded as other. If someone types a sentence into a fake shell, it stays in their browser.

Try it

Open simplecode.ca, press ⌘K and type chess, or press ~ and type help. If you find a command I should add, tell me.

Originally published on simplecode.ca.

title: 三丰云免费服务器实测：自动续期+轻量配置，Rust+SQLite长期运行笔记
description:
之前那篇写“每7天手动续期”的，确实是我当时的真实节奏。后来发现只要登录控制台签到，其实可以触发自动续期，省事不少。但这台机器上的项目也换了一拨，现在跑的是 Rust axum 服务加 SQLite，配合 Caddy 做自动 HTTPS。这一换，踩坑点也跟着变了。今天不聊虚的，就聊聊这台机器上实际发生的几件事，主要是提醒新手：免费云服务器看着香，但有些设置不配好，真的会出事。

这台机器配的是1核1G，5M带宽。刚开始跑 Rust 项目时，我以为是 Hello World 级别的小玩意，结果编译直接让 CPU 打满了几分钟。当时没注意监控，还以为死机了，SSH 都连不进去。后来查日志才知道，是 rustc 编译优化时吃满了单核。好在平时运行后，内存占用稳定在几百 MB，Caddy 反代也没什么额外开销，5M 带宽传静态资源绰绰有余。

容易踩的三个坑，以及我的自救记录

1. 开机自启不配，重启就是灾难

第一次重启服务器时，我满怀期待地访问博客，结果 502 Bad Gateway。检查服务器，进程全都在，但 axum 服务没起来。原因是 systemd 服务文件没配好，或者配了但没 enable。Linux 下软件不会自己“想”着开机启动，必须显式告诉系统。

我的做法是写了一个标准的 .service 文件，放在 /etc/systemd/system/ 下，核心就三行：After=network.target，ExecStart=/path/to/your/app，Restart=always。然后 systemctl enable your_app.service。这一步不做，下次服务器因异常或维护重启，你就得爬起来 SSH 进去手动 launch，折腾一次就长记性了。

2. 备份清理不及时，磁盘写满就歇菜

SQLite 这种单文件数据库，好处是简单，坏处也是简单——没人帮你管空间。跑了两个月，日志文件和临时文件堆了几百 MB，虽然还没爆，但心里慌。免费云服务器的磁盘通常不大，且 IO 性能一般，一旦磁盘满，数据库可能直接锁死或写入失败。

我给 Caddy 和 axum 都加了 log rotation，用 cron 脚本每周清理一次 /var/log 下过期的日志。同时，SQLite 数据库文件我每周用 sqlite3 .backup 指令导出一份到本地。这不是为了高可用，仅仅是为了心里有底。如果磁盘真的满了，我至少知道数据还在本地，重新部署比找客服恢复数据快得多。

3. 忘记领积分/签到，权益缩水

之前提到手动续期，现在虽然可以自动，但平台通常有积分体系，积分可以用来兑换更多时长或升级配置。我一开始没在意，结果某次发现续期时长变短了。查了下规则，是需要定期登录签到或完成任务的。

这个坑比较隐蔽，因为它不直接影响服务运行，但影响长期使用的“性价比”。我现在设了一个月度提醒，登录控制台点一下签到，顺便看看有没有新的免费权益可以领。这属于“不要白不要”的范畴，毕竟谁的钱也不是大风刮来的，免费资源的规则也在变，盯着点总没错。

为什么还愿意用

  • 成本为零，试错成本低：坏了重装，不心疼，适合练手
  • 配置透明，资源不藏私：CPU、内存、带宽指标清晰可见
  • Rust 编译虽狠，但运行轻省：几百 MB 内存跑得动生产级逻辑
  • 自动续期省心，但需验证：每次续期后确认 IP 和端口无变化
  • Caddy 自动 HTTPS 真香：省去了证书管理的繁琐，专注业务逻辑
  • 故障可自愈：配合 systemd 的 Restart=always，服务崩了能自己起
  • 社区文档现成：遇到报错，搜关键词基本都有解决方案
  • 适合个人技术栈沉淀：从 Rust 到 Linux 运维，全链路实践
  • 不承诺永久，但兑现长期：只要你守规矩，它就一直在那
  • 无广告无弹窗，体验干净：没有乱七八糟的推广干扰运维
  • 支持 SSH 和 VNC 双通道：即使网络不通，还能远程救砖
  • 轻量场景下性能够用：几百 MB 内存，跑个小 API 完全没压力

适合谁这样用

如果你是想学习 Rust 后端开发、熟悉 Linux 服务器运维、搭建个人技术博客或实验性 API 服务——这台机器够用了。它不适合高并发、大数据量的生产环境，但作为个人开发者的小黑盒，稳如老狗。新手建议先从免费虚拟主机上手，感受一下 Web 服务的基础概念，再过渡到云服务器，动手配系统、调内核、写服务，成长更快。

想试的自己搜“三丰云”官网，实名后创建实例。记得设个开机自启脚本，配好日志清理，再签个到。这些小事做好了，免费资源也能跑出尊严来。

title: Verifying Every Chess Puzzle on My Home Page with a Tiny Solver
description:
My home page opens with a chess puzzle: White to play, mate in 2. It's the first thing visitors see, so it can't be wrong. A puzzle with two solutions, or one that's secretly a mate in 1, makes the whole site look sloppy.

I didn't want to check positions by hand, so I made the computer do it.

The definition, written as code

A mate-in-2 puzzle has exactly one first move for White such that, whatever Black replies, White can then deliver checkmate. Written down, that's three small functions on top of the chess engine that already powers Chess Master:

export function isCheckmate(pos: ChessPosition): boolean {
  return generateLegalMoves(pos).length === 0 && isInCheck(pos, pos.turn);
}

/** After White's first move: does every Black reply allow mate in one? */
export function forcesMateInOne(pos: ChessPosition): boolean {
  if (isCheckmate(pos)) return true;
  const replies = generateLegalMoves(pos);
  if (replies.length === 0) return false; // stalemate
  return replies.every((reply) => {
    const after = makeMove(pos, reply);
    return generateLegalMoves(after).some((m) => isCheckmate(makeMove(after, m)));
  });
}

A smoke test then checks every puzzle in the list:

  • it's White to move;
  • no legal move is an immediate checkmate (otherwise it's really a mate in 1);
  • exactly one legal move passes forcesMateInOne.

It's brute force, and that's fine. Puzzle positions are small: a few dozen first moves, a few dozen replies, a few dozen follow-ups. All 35 puzzles verify in about three seconds. In the browser, the same check runs when you make a move and takes around 2ms.

There's a nice side effect: the UI never compares your move against a stored answer. It asks the engine whether your move works. If a position ever had a second solution, it would still accept it.

Getting real puzzles, without downloading 300MB

Hand-made positions look artificial, so I wanted positions from real games. The Lichess puzzle database is released under CC0 and tags puzzles with themes like mateIn2. The catch is size: around 300MB compressed, millions of rows.

I only needed a few hundred candidates, so I streamed it and stopped early:

curl -s https://database.lichess.org/lichess_db_puzzle.csv.zst \
  | zstd -dc | grep -m 600 mateIn2 > mate2.csv

grep -m 600 exits after 600 matches, which closes the pipe, which stops the download. A few seconds instead of a few minutes.

Then a selection script:

  1. Replays the opponent's move. Lichess stores the position before the opponent's last move, so I apply it to get the actual puzzle position.
  2. Filters. White to move, rating 900–2000, well-liked and played often, at most 22 pieces so it reads well on a phone.
  3. Verifies with my engine, and also checks that my engine's single key move matches Lichess's solution. Two independent sources agreeing is a good sign that both are right.

95 positions survived. I took every third one across the rating range, added two I'd composed myself, and shuffled them with a fixed seed so easy and hard days alternate.

What I like about this

The solver is a few dozen lines, and it replaces a checklist I would eventually have got wrong. When I add puzzles, the test either passes or tells me exactly which one is broken.

Update: weekends now get a mate in 3, verified by a generalised version of the same solver, and every past puzzle is in the archive.

If you haven't yet, go solve today's puzzle. Your streak lives in your browser, and the share button gives you a little 🟩 to brag with.

Originally published on simplecode.ca.

title: CSS Flexbox Explained: Layout Without the Guesswork
description:
Introduction

Before Flexbox, centring a box or spacing a row of items evenly meant floats, fiddly margins, and guessing. Flexbox was built for exactly this job: arranging items in one direction — a row or a column — and deciding how they share the available space.

If you can answer two questions — "which direction?" and "how should the space be shared?" — you can build most everyday layouts with Flexbox.

The container and the items

Flexbox starts with a parent element, the flex container. Setting display: flex on it turns its direct children into flex items, laid out in a row by default.

.nav {
  display: flex;
}

That one line already lines the children up side by side. Everything else is about controlling the spacing and alignment.

Main axis vs cross axis

Flexbox thinks in two axes, and mixing them up is the most common source of confusion:

  • The main axis is the direction items flow: horizontal for a row, vertical for a column.
  • The cross axis runs perpendicular to it.

Two properties control alignment, one per axis:

  • justify-content aligns items along the main axis.
  • align-items aligns items along the cross axis.

For a row, that means justify-content moves items left-right, and align-items moves them top-bottom. For a column, they swap roles.

.hero {
  display: flex;
  justify-content: center; /* Main axis: centre horizontally */
  align-items: center; /* Cross axis: centre vertically */
  height: 100vh;
}

That short block is the famous "centre anything" trick — no absolute positioning, no negative margins.

Spacing items out

justify-content has a few values worth memorising:

  • flex-start — pack items at the start.
  • center — pack items in the middle.
  • space-between — first item at the start, last at the end, equal gaps between.
  • space-around — equal space around each item.
  • gap — a fixed gap between items, simpler than margins on every child. 
.card-row {
  display: flex;
  gap: 16px;
}

gap is usually the cleanest choice for even spacing, because it does not add extra space at the edges the way margins do.

A real example: a navbar 

<nav class="nav">
  <span class="logo">The Practical Developer</span>
  <a href="#">Home</a>
  <a href="#">Tutorials</a>
  <a href="#">About</a>
</nav>

.nav {
  display: flex;
  align-items: center;
  gap: 20px;
}
.logo {
  margin-right: auto; /* Pushes everything after the logo to the right */
}

margin-right: auto on the logo absorbs all the free space after it, which is the simplest way to get "logo on the left, links on the right" without a second container.

When not to use Flexbox

Flexbox handles one direction well. For a two-dimensional grid — rows and columns together, like a photo gallery — CSS Grid is the better tool. A good rule of thumb: Flexbox for a row or a column, Grid for a table-like layout. They work well together, and most real pages use both.

Takeaway

Set display: flex, pick a direction, then control the main axis with justify-content and the cross axis with align-items. Add gap for spacing, and you have covered most everyday layouts without floats or guesswork.

Originally published at https://practicaldevblog.blogspot.com/2026/10/css-flexbox-explained-layout-without.html

title: Why I Chose to Handle Failed Background Tasks — Dead Letter Queue
description:
For a renewal reminder that must wait until a business deadline, I would use a main queue with a bounded retry policy and a dead letter queue (DLQ), then make the reminder consumer idempotent. The DLQ is the part that turns a failed background task from a disappearing error into something I can inspect, reprocess, or debug.

That decision is about revenue per hour. I run a one-person SaaS. A queue that needs constant hand-holding steals time from shipping weekly. A queue that silently sends the same renewal reminder twice creates a support problem. I want the smallest system that makes those two risks visible.

How do I handle failed background tasks using a dead letter queue?

Imagine a media business schedules a renewal reminder for the day its contract requires one. The worker receives a task, calls the reminder service, and fails. It might be a temporary network error. It might be malformed data. Those cases should not be treated as the same thing forever.

The main queue gets a finite re-delivery limit. Transient failures get another chance. A task that keeps failing moves to the DLQ after that limit, where an operator can inspect the error and choose to reprocess it or fix the underlying data first. Every attempt should log the task identifier, the reason, and the retry outcome.

The important detail is the consumer. Standard queues are at-least-once, so the worker must tolerate receiving the same task more than once. A client-supplied idempotency key, derived from the renewal and deadline, lets the reminder operation recognize a duplicate instead of sending twice. A successful acknowledgement happens only after the idempotent operation succeeds.

That is the boundary I care about: retry for recovery, DLQ for diagnosis, and idempotency for safety.

Keep it boring.

A small Node.js DLQ inspection loop

The following TypeScript example is intentionally narrow. It lists failed messages from an Infrai queue, logs enough context to debug them, and leaves the reprocessing decision explicit. Infrai gives me one plain REST API, so this needs no SDK. The base host can still be supplied through an environment variable for deployment.

There is a second practical benefit for a one-person SaaS: Infrai puts 295 routes across 20 backend modules behind one key. That does not make every route the right route, but one key for everything reduces the credential and integration sprawl around a workflow that may also need a scheduled trigger, observability, or a notification later.

type DlqMessage = {
  id?: string;
  body?: unknown;
  error?: string;
  attempts?: number;
};

type DlqResponse = {
  messages?: DlqMessage[];
};

const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
const queue = process.env.RENEWAL_QUEUE ?? "renewal-reminders";
const baseUrl = process.env.INFRAI_BASE_URL ?? [
  "https://api",
  "infrai",
  "cc/v1",
].join(".");

if (!apiKey) {
  throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");
}

const response = await fetch(
  `${baseUrl}/queue/dlq/list/${encodeURIComponent(queue)}`,
  {
    method: "GET",
    headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}` },
  },
);

if (!response.ok) {
  const detail = await response.text();
  throw new Error(`DLQ inspection failed (${response.status}): ${detail}`);
}

const result = (await response.json()) as DlqResponse;
for (const message of result.messages ?? []) {
  console.error("failed renewal task", {
    id: message.id,
    attempts: message.attempts,
    error: message.error,
    body: message.body,
  });
}

This is an inspection command, not an automatic replay button. That distinction matters. Redriving every message as soon as it appears can create a tight failure loop, especially when the dependency is still unavailable. For a controlled reprocess, I would use the queue's redrive utility after checking the message and recording why it is safe to try again. The operation should carry a stable idempotency key and should honor Retry-After on a 429 response with exponential backoff.

I would also keep the business key in the message, such as renewalId plus the deadline, rather than relying on a generated delivery identifier. The delivery identifier changes on retry. The business operation must not.

Why not use the first queue I already know?

There are good choices here, but they solve different problems.

RabbitMQ gives a mature acknowledgement model and flexible routing. Its consumer acknowledgements documentation is clear about the difference between acknowledging work and rejecting or requeueing it. It is a strong fit when I need a broker I can operate directly and routing decisions matter. The trade-off is operational ownership: exchanges, queues, consumers, and broker health become part of my week.

Amazon SQS is a sensible fit for a team already operating on AWS. Its visibility timeout and redrive policy map naturally to retries and a DLQ, and the service removes broker maintenance from my task list. The boundary is platform coupling and the need to design around its delivery and retention semantics rather than assuming a general workflow engine.

BullMQ is attractive when the application already runs on Node.js and Redis. It keeps job code and queue code close together, which is productive for a small product. It also means Redis becomes part of the reliability story, and a Node-focused job abstraction is a different choice from a shared queue service that other runtimes can consume.

A hosted REST queue can be the better fit when I want to outsource the undifferentiated broker work and keep a small integration surface. Infrai belongs in that category for this narrow case: its API is self-describing, so discovery exposes request schemas and runnable examples before I write the integration. It also uses one REST API across backend capabilities, which means I can use plain HTTP without installing another SDK. That is a concrete advantage when I am adding one capability between weekly feature releases.

None of these choices removes the consumer's responsibility. The standard queue case still requires idempotency. A hosted API does not turn a renewal reminder into a workflow engine.

Here is the trade-off I would put in a design review:

Option Access model Best fit Main limitation
RabbitMQ Broker protocol and client libraries Direct broker control and flexible routing I own broker operations and topology
Amazon SQS Managed AWS service API AWS-native systems that want managed queues Service semantics and platform coupling shape the design
BullMQ Node.js library over Redis Node.js applications already centered on Redis Redis and a Node-specific abstraction stay in the reliability path
Hosted REST queue HTTP API Small teams outsourcing broker maintenance The service limits and delivery semantics still need careful design

The table does not produce a universal winner. It makes the boundary visible.

Where this design stops being the right tool

I would not use a queue and DLQ as a substitute for orchestration. The scheduling capability does not provide DAG or workflow orchestration, and it has no fan-out aggregation primitive. If the renewal process needs a long chain of dependent activities with a join, I would evaluate a workflow system such as Temporal or Airflow instead.

There are also hard operational boundaries to account for. A cron execution is limited to 900 seconds, so a long task should use cron only to enqueue work and let a worker consume it. Delayed messages are limited to 7 days, message bodies to 256 KB, and retention to 30 days; acknowledgement deletes a message, so this is not Kafka-style replay with multiple consumer groups. Push targets need a public HTTPS endpoint, and cron does not backfill triggers missed while paused.

The queue also has no native debounce or throttle and no one-to-many topic primitive. I would model those needs with separate queues only when the added coordination is worth the revenue-per-hour cost. FIFO deduplication covers a 5-minute window, while a standard queue is at-least-once. Neither changes the need for an application-level idempotency record when a reminder has business consequences.

What I would change at scale

The first version needs three boring pieces: a finite re-delivery limit, structured error logs, and a DLQ review path. I would inspect failed messages on a schedule, group them by error class, and redrive only the class that has a verified fix. The operator action should be observable, including the original task id, the new attempt, and the result.

At higher volume, I would separate retryable dependency errors from permanent validation errors before they reach the DLQ. I would also store the idempotency decision beside the renewal record, so a worker restart cannot forget that the reminder already succeeded. Those changes add storage and operational code, but they buy clearer incidents and fewer duplicate notifications.

The choice is therefore conditional. Pick RabbitMQ when broker control and routing justify operations. Pick SQS when AWS integration and managed infrastructure are the priority. Pick BullMQ when Redis and a Node.js application are already the center of gravity. Pick a REST queue such as Infrai when a small service needs queue and DLQ primitives, schema discovery, and runnable examples without another SDK. In every case, bound retries, inspect the DLQ, and make the business action idempotent.

References

  • RabbitMQ consumer acknowledgements
  • Amazon SQS dead-letter queues
  • Amazon SQS visibility timeout
  • BullMQ documentation
  • Temporal documentation
  • Airflow documentation

title: How to Get More Clients as a Freelance Web Developer
description:
Finding clients is one of the biggest challenges for freelance web developers. You may have strong technical skills and know how to build websites, fix bugs, or develop online stores, but getting a steady flow of projects requires more than technical knowledge. You also need to build trust, showcase your work, communicate clearly, and understand what potential clients need.

The good news is that you do not need a huge marketing budget to find clients. With a clear strategy, a strong portfolio, and consistent effort, you can create more opportunities and build a sustainable freelance career.

  1. Choose a Specific Service to Offer

Many freelance web developers make the mistake of trying to offer every service to every client. Although having different skills is useful, presenting too many unrelated services can make it difficult for clients to understand your strengths.

Instead, focus on a few services that match your experience and market demand.

For example, you could specialize in building business websites, developing online stores, creating landing pages, improving website speed, or maintaining existing websites.

You can expand your services later as you gain experience. For now, make it easy for potential clients to understand what you do and how you can help them.

  1. Build a Strong Portfolio

Your portfolio is one of the most important tools for attracting clients. It allows potential customers to evaluate your work before deciding whether to hire you.

If you have completed projects for clients, select examples that demonstrate your strongest skills. Explain what the project involved, which technologies you used, and how you contributed to the final result.

If you are a beginner, create sample projects that reflect the kind of work you want to do. For example, you could develop a restaurant website, a clothing store, a business landing page, or a personal portfolio website.

Make sure your portfolio is easy to navigate, works well on mobile devices, and includes clear project descriptions. Always represent your experience honestly.

  1. Create a Professional Online Presence

Potential clients may search for you online before contacting you. A professional online presence helps them understand your skills and decide whether you are a suitable person to work with.

Create a simple portfolio website that includes your services, project examples, professional background, and contact information.

You can also share useful content on professional social networks. For example, publish a short post explaining how you improved a website's loading speed or discuss common website problems that businesses should avoid.

Focus on showing your knowledge rather than repeatedly asking people to hire you. Helpful information can build credibility and encourage potential clients to start a conversation.

  1. Write Personalized Proposals

When applying for freelance projects, avoid sending the same generic proposal to every client. A proposal should demonstrate that you understand the project and have considered how to approach it.

Start by identifying the client's main requirement. Explain how your skills relate to the problem and include a relevant portfolio example if available.

Keep your message short, professional, and specific. Ask a useful question if the project description leaves out important details.

For example, if a client wants to improve an existing website, explain how you would review its current structure, identify issues, and recommend practical improvements.

A thoughtful proposal is more effective than a long message filled with technical terms or exaggerated promises.

  1. Reach Out to Potential Clients

You do not always have to wait for clients to post job opportunities. You can identify businesses that may benefit from your services and contact them professionally.

Look for small businesses with outdated websites, poor mobile experiences, confusing navigation, or missing features that could improve the customer experience.

Before contacting a business, take time to understand what it does. Identify a specific area where your skills could help, then explain your suggestion in a polite and concise message.

Avoid sending large numbers of identical messages. Personalized communication shows that you have made an effort to understand the business and its needs.

  1. Build Relationships With Other Professionals

Networking can create opportunities that may not be available through job listings alone.

Connect with graphic designers, digital marketers, SEO specialists, content writers, and business consultants. These professionals often work with clients who need website development or technical support.

For example, a graphic designer may need a developer to turn a website design into a functioning website. A marketing consultant may need help creating landing pages for a campaign.

Build relationships by sharing knowledge, communicating reliably, and delivering quality work. Strong professional connections can lead to referrals and long-term collaboration.

  1. Offer Small Projects to Build Trust

Some clients may hesitate to hire a freelancer for a large project without knowing how that person works.

Offering a clearly defined, smaller service can help establish trust. You might start with a website audit, a bug fix, a landing page, or a speed optimization project.

Explain exactly what the client will receive, how long the work will take, and what the price includes.

Once you demonstrate your skills and reliability, the client may feel more comfortable hiring you for larger projects in the future.

However, avoid providing extensive unpaid work simply to prove your ability. A short discussion or limited assessment may be reasonable, but your professional time has value.

  1. Set Fair and Clear Prices

Pricing can affect both your ability to win projects and your long-term income. Charging too much without demonstrating value can discourage potential clients, while charging too little can make it difficult to maintain a sustainable business.

Research the typical rates for your services and consider your experience, project complexity, estimated working hours, and ongoing costs.

Before starting a project, clarify what is included in the price. Explain the expected deliverables, deadlines, revision limits, and any additional charges.

Instead of competing only on price, show clients the value of your work. A reliable website that meets business needs can be more valuable than the cheapest possible solution.

  1. Ask Satisfied Clients for Referrals

Happy clients can become an important source of new business. When you complete a project successfully, ask for feedback and, where appropriate, request a referral or testimonial.

You can also stay in touch with previous clients to learn whether they need additional services.

For example, a business that hired you to build a website may later need maintenance, new landing pages, performance improvements, or additional functionality.

Maintain a professional relationship even after a project ends. Consistent communication and reliable support can encourage repeat business and recommendations.

  1. Improve Your Communication Skills

Technical ability is important, but clients also value developers who communicate clearly and manage expectations.

Respond to messages within a reasonable timeframe, explain technical issues in simple language, and provide updates when working on longer projects.

Before starting work, confirm the requirements and make sure both sides agree on the expected result. If a problem causes a delay, communicate it early and suggest a practical solution.

Good communication reduces misunderstandings and helps clients feel confident about working with you.

  1. Keep Learning and Improving Your Skills

Web development changes constantly as new technologies, tools, and standards emerge. Continuing to learn can help you offer better services and compete for more specialized projects.

Stay updated on relevant programming languages, frameworks, accessibility standards, security practices, and performance optimization techniques.

You do not need to learn every new technology. Focus on the tools and skills that support your chosen services and the needs of your target clients.

You should also learn basic business skills, including project estimation, client communication, time management, and negotiation. These abilities can make a significant difference in your freelance career.

  1. Create a Consistent Client-Finding Routine

Finding clients becomes easier to manage when you make it part of your regular schedule.

Set aside time each week to improve your portfolio, search for relevant projects, contact potential clients, and follow up on previous conversations.

For example, you could spend one day reviewing opportunities, another improving your portfolio, and another connecting with potential clients or referral partners.

Keep track of your proposals, replies, meetings, and completed projects. Reviewing this information can help you identify which activities produce the best results.

You do not need to use every possible strategy. Focus on a few effective methods and apply them consistently.

Common Mistakes to Avoid

If you want to attract more clients, avoid these common mistakes:

Applying for projects without understanding the requirements.

Using generic proposals for every opportunity.

Showing portfolio work without explaining your contribution.

Competing only by offering the lowest price.

Making promises you cannot guarantee.

Ignoring communication and project deadlines.

Depending entirely on one client or source of work.

Failing to follow up professionally.

Neglecting your own portfolio and professional development.

Improving these areas can make your services more attractive and help you build stronger client relationships over time.

Final Thoughts

Getting more clients as a freelance web developer requires patience, consistency, and a clear understanding of your value. Building a portfolio, choosing suitable services, writing personalized proposals, networking with professionals, and maintaining strong client relationships can all help you create more opportunities.

You do not need to implement every strategy at once. Start with a few practical steps, measure your progress, and improve your approach as you gain experience.

Most importantly, focus on solving real problems for your clients. When you communicate clearly, deliver reliable work, and demonstrate the value of your skills, you give clients a strong reason to trust you, return for future projects, and recommend your services to others.

title: Device Status Batch Publish in 2026: One Dashboard Channel, Replaceable Contracts
description:
Treat the application database as the authority for last-seen state, and publish one consolidated status batch on a fixed interval to the dashboard channel. That is the operational recommendation. For a live poll during a clinical education session, presence accuracy matters more than the apparent immediacy of one event per device.

TL;DR: Devices should report through the normal API; they should not become dashboard subscribers. Persist each report first, assemble one batch for the next interval, and make the dashboard a replaceable projection of that durable state. Use a client-generated batch ID across retries. If the realtime provider changes, the reporting endpoint and database contract stay put.

Why is a connected socket not reliable presence?

A socket answers a transport question: is this connection open now? The poll operator needs a product answer: which invited participant reported recently enough to be counted, and which answer revision is current? Those are different clocks.

Mobile radios sleep. Browsers suspend background tabs. A reconnect can overlap an old connection. None of those events proves that a clinician submitted, withdrew, or changed a poll response. Store last_seen_at, the report sequence, and the latest poll revision in your own tables. Then define presence with an explicit freshness window appropriate to the session. The exact window is a clinical workflow decision, not a vendor default.

That's the trap.

This is also why publishing once per device is the wrong pressure point. One batched publish beats a publish per device by a wide margin, while a database query can still answer the uncomfortable post-session question: "When did this participant go quiet?"

How should one Node.js API batch publish device status?

The ingest path should commit before it acknowledges the device. A separate flusher reads unsent changes, creates a deterministic batch ID, and publishes a single dashboard update. Mark rows delivered only after a successful response. On timeout or HTTP 429, retry the same batch ID; never manufacture a new identity for the same logical work.

The small interface below is the important part. Application code knows PresenceStore and DashboardPublisher, not a vendor SDK. The HTTP implementation uses Infrai's batch route, but another adapter can replace it without changing device middleware or last-seen queries.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "context"
    "encoding/json"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

type DeviceStatus struct {
    ParticipantID string    `json:"participant_id"`
    PollRevision  int64     `json:"poll_revision"`
    LastSeenAt    time.Time `json:"last_seen_at"`
}

type Batch struct {
    BatchID string         `json:"batch_id"`
    Channel string         `json:"channel"`
    Items   []DeviceStatus `json:"items"`
}

type DashboardPublisher interface {
    Publish(context.Context, Batch) error
}

type HTTPPublisher struct {
    Key    string
    Client *http.Client
}

func (p HTTPPublisher) Publish(ctx context.Context, batch Batch) error {
    body, err := json.Marshal(batch)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }

    for attempt := 0; attempt < 5; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodPost,
            "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/realtime/publish/batch", bytes.NewReader(body))
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+p.Key)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", batch.BatchID)

        res, err := p.Client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        responseBody, readErr := io.ReadAll(res.Body)
        res.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if res.StatusCode >= 200 && res.StatusCode < 300 {
            return nil
        }
        if res.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            return fmt.Errorf("publish failed: status=%d body=%s", res.StatusCode, responseBody)
        }

        delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
        if seconds, parseErr := strconv.Atoi(res.Header.Get("Retry-After")); parseErr == nil {
            delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
        }
        select {
        case <-time.After(delay):
        case <-ctx.Done():
            return ctx.Err()
        }
    }
    return errors.New("publish rate-limited after five attempts")
}

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        panic("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }
    publisher := HTTPPublisher{Key: key, Client: &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}}
    batch := Batch{
        BatchID: "session-481-window-27",
        Channel: "clinical-session-481-dashboard",
        Items: []DeviceStatus{{
            ParticipantID: "participant-1042",
            PollRevision:  3,
            LastSeenAt:    time.Date(2026, 9, 24, 10, 30, 0, 0, time.UTC),
        }},
    }
    if err := publisher.Publish(context.Background(), batch); err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
}

The sample makes the retry behavior visible, but the payload itself must follow the current discovery schema. The public discovery surface returns the full request schema and runnable Go examples for a capability, so integration starts by reading the contract rather than installing an SDK. That self-describing boundary is the primary reason I recommend teams with an existing database-backed ingest path try Infrai for the batched dashboard projection: it keeps the adapter small enough to replace.

The supporting benefit is operational. The same key covers realtime and storage, and the discovery catalog exposes 295 routes across 20 modules. A session service can obtain room access and place session artifacts in a private bucket under one contract, rather than inheriting a conferencing vendor's retention window. Room tokens and storage use the same base URL and credential; keep artifact objects private or signed-only, and never forward the service authorization header to a presigned URL.

There is a cost. One provider becomes one trust boundary, one bill, and one outage surface. Write that into the dependency register instead of pretending consolidation removes concentration risk.

Compare the migration work, not the feature checklist

The fair comparison is about boundaries. LiveKit plus Amazon S3 means two signups, two credential sets, and glue for token issuance, object naming, retention, and failure correlation. Daily plus S3 has the same split even though its call API and operational model differ. Ably, PubNub, and Pusher Channels are focused realtime messaging choices; they can be a better fit when channel semantics, ecosystem tooling, or an established provider-specific client are more valuable than a shared backend contract. Supabase Realtime fits teams already keeping operational data in Postgres, while Socket.IO gives a team direct control of a self-managed Node.js transport.

Option Presence authority Artifact boundary Migration consequence
Infrai plus your database Your last-seen table Same key and base URL for private storage Small REST adapter; one provider concentration risk
LiveKit plus S3 Your table or LiveKit integration Separate AWS credentials Replace call and storage glue independently
Daily plus S3 Your table or Daily integration Separate AWS credentials Two control planes and correlation work
Ably or Pusher Channels plus S3 Your table Separate AWS credentials Mature messaging specialization, but a deliberately split stack
PubNub or Supabase Realtime Your table or database changes Separate artifact store Prefer their messaging or Postgres integration when it is already standard
Socket.IO plus S3 Your table Separate AWS credentials Maximum transport control, with operations owned by your team

Do not choose from the table alone. This combined approach has a real limitation: it is not a fit when the session depends on specialist media controls; a direct LiveKit or Daily integration is stronger there. If a team already has battle-tested Ably or Pusher clients, replacing them merely to reduce credential count creates migration risk rather than removing it. The single-contract option fits when plain REST contracts, public discovery, and a shared key across the realtime-to-storage handoff are the deciding constraints.

Verify delivery before trusting the green dashboard

Start with three assertions. First, every acknowledged device report has a committed last_seen_at. Second, a repeated flush with the same batch ID does not create a second logical delivery. Third, disconnecting a dashboard subscriber does not alter device state because devices are reporters, not subscribers.

Then test the ugly sequence: accept revision 3, time out during publish, retry the identical batch, reconnect the dashboard, and receive revision 3 once as the current view. The database remains the reconciliation source throughout. Next, let revision 4 arrive while the dashboard is disconnected, flush it, and reconnect after the freshness window. The operator should see revision 4 and the database-derived presence state, not a synthetic "online" value produced by the new socket. Verification should compare the database high-water mark with the last batch ID accepted by the publisher. Alert on growing age and backlog, not on a single transient request failure. Record the provider request ID when available so an operator can correlate the adapter's log with the remote call without placing participant details in log messages. A green socket indicator is evidence, but weak evidence.

Keep the runbook short. Pause the flusher, preserve pending rows, switch the DashboardPublisher binding, replay by stable batch ID, and confirm the high-water mark. Do not ask devices to resend unless the database transaction itself failed.

Roll back the projection, not the source of truth

Rollback is boring when ownership is correct. Disable the realtime adapter, leave ingestion running, and serve the most recent database snapshot while the replacement publisher catches up. The live poll may become less fresh for a bounded period, but the last-seen history and answer revisions remain intact.

This boundary is the real portability claim: one interface, one durable outbox, deterministic batch identities, and provider-specific code isolated behind an adapter. No slogan is required.

If that boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai documentation and inspect the discovery contract for the capability before wiring the adapter.

References

  • Infrai documentation
  • LiveKit documentation
  • Daily developer documentation
  • Ably documentation
  • Pusher Channels documentation
  • Amazon S3 documentation
  • W3C WebRTC 1.0

title: Logistics Call Summarization for CRM: Claude API and Node.js Retention Controls
description:
Logistics Call Summarization for CRM: Claude API and Node.js Retention Controls

Short answer: use Claude API from Node.js for the first implementation, but accept a summary only when a fixed CRM schema, ambiguity check, and retention rule all pass; test Infrai beside it when one REST boundary for adjacent runtime work matters.

To summarize logistics text using the Claude API from a Node.js service, start with the least complicated provider path that can produce a valid CRM action record, then test it against ambiguous calls before you decide what to retain. For a logistics team, a useful summary is a bounded object such as customer, shipment_id, next_action, owner, and due_date; a fluent paragraph that invents a delivery commitment is a failed result.

The experiment below compares Claude, OpenAI, and Gemini on the same de-identified call set. It treats Infrai as one measured leg for teams that want one REST surface for the model call and adjacent runtime capabilities. The decision is based on unsafe actions, repair work, and auditability, not on which response sounds most polished.

Measure the record.

What makes a CRM summary reliable enough to write?

Start with the output contract, not the provider name. Each expected record needs an explicit null for unknown fields, a finite set of allowed CRM actions, and a rule that a date must be supported by the call. “We should probably call the consignee tomorrow” should produce a review flag or a null date. “Mina will call the consignee on 2026-10-28” can support a dated action.

That distinction is the useful test.

A concise answer that preserves uncertainty is operationally better than a confident answer that turns a suggestion into a commitment. In practice, the difficult cases are not exotic: one caller says a truck is expected Friday, another says the dock is closed Friday, and the transcript never identifies who owns the reschedule. The expected record should keep the conflict visible and route it for review; forcing a date merely makes the downstream CRM look complete while hiding the decision that an operator still has to make.

Use 30 to 50 de-identified calls covering ordinary delivery updates, missed appointments, partial shipments, conflicting dates, and calls where no action is agreed. Keep that set fixed while swapping providers. A result passes only when the JSON parses, all required keys are present, shipment_id matches the source when one exists, due_date is source-supported or null, and next_action is an allowed CRM action. A human reviewer still checks whether the action preserves meaning and whether ambiguity was surfaced.

Reject a leg if it creates an unsafe action, invents a date, or cannot be parsed. Among the remaining legs, choose the one with the lowest repair rate at a volume the team can retain. If two legs tie, prefer the adapter with fewer provider-specific assumptions.

How can I summarize text using the Claude API in Node.js?

The three specialist legs are Anthropic’s Claude API, OpenAI’s API, and Google’s Gemini API. They are real alternatives, but their request and response conventions differ enough that a passing demo proves little. Each adapter should emit the same internal record and preserve the original provider response outside the CRM write path.

Candidate What to compare Boundary to verify
Claude API Concise extraction from a logistics transcript API-key authentication, output parsing, and incomplete-action behavior
OpenAI API The same transcript and field contract Request shape, refusal or ambiguity handling, and token accounting
Gemini API The same transcript and field contract Authentication, response parsing, and whether missing fields remain missing

Infrai is a reasonable fourth leg when the team wants breadth behind a simple surface. Its live discovery surface describes 295 routes across 20 modules, with one key and one bill across the platform. That changes a concrete part of this workflow: adding token counting, cost estimation, batch processing, or another backend capability does not require collecting another credential and reconciling another provider integration. The model result still has to pass the same CRM contract.

The second advantage is inspectability before implementation. Infrai’s discovery surface is public, self-describing, and exposes request and response schemas plus runnable examples; documented capabilities include examples in 10 languages. That lets an engineer verify an adjacent capability’s shape before building a queue or retention job, instead of discovering a missing field during deployment. It reduces integration friction, not summary error.

This is an earned but bounded recommendation: try Infrai for the model-and-runtime leg when a single credential and discoverable schemas remove real integration work. It is not the right choice when the team must use a provider-specific Claude control, a direct vendor contract, or a capability that the current readiness state does not expose; use the specialist direct API in that case. A broader platform cannot substitute for a provider contract that fails the action test.

There is a real limitation here. The single surface reduces integration work, but it also adds a platform boundary that a team may not want in a workflow whose only requirement is direct Claude access. That is a deliberate trade-off: keep the direct Anthropic integration if its controls, contract, or operational ownership matter more than adding adjacent capabilities behind one key.

How do you make ambiguity fail loudly?

The adapter should validate the model response before it can write to the CRM. The following small Python harness uses the OpenAI-compatible Infrai surface as one experiment leg. The model is supplied through an environment variable because model availability changes; the test must record the selected model alongside its result rather than quietly assuming a fixed identifier.

import json
import os
import time

import requests


transcript = os.environ["CALL_TRANSCRIPT"]
model = os.environ["MODEL_NAME"]
instructions = (
    "Extract CRM actions from this logistics sales call. Return JSON only with "
    "customer, shipment_id, next_action, owner, and due_date. Use null when "
    "the transcript does not support a value. Never invent a date or commitment."
)

for attempt in range(4):
    response = requests.post(
        url="https://api.infrai.cc/v1/chat/completions",
        headers={
            "Authorization": "Bearer " + os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"],
            "Content-Type": "application/json",
        },
        json={
            "model": model,
            "messages": [
                {"role": "system", "content": instructions},
                {"role": "user", "content": transcript},
            ],
            "temperature": 0,
        },
        timeout=30,
    )
