    # Equivalent copyable call: curl --request POST --url https://api.infrai.cc/v1/chat/completions --header "Authorization: Bearer $INFRAI_API_KEY" --header "Content-Type: application/json" --data '{"model":"'"$MODEL_NAME"'","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"'"$CALL_TRANSCRIPT"'"}]}'
    if response.status_code == 429:
        retry_after = response.headers.get("Retry-After")
        time.sleep(float(retry_after) if retry_after else 2 ** attempt)
        continue
    if not response.ok:
        raise SystemExit(
            f"summary request failed ({response.status_code}): {response.text}"
        )
    try:
        record = json.loads(response.json()["choices"][0]["message"]["content"])
    except (KeyError, TypeError, ValueError, json.JSONDecodeError) as error:
        raise SystemExit(f"summary rejected: invalid response: {error}") from error
    required = {"customer", "shipment_id", "next_action", "owner", "due_date"}
    missing = required.difference(record)
    if missing:
        raise SystemExit(f"summary rejected: missing fields: {sorted(missing)}")
    print(json.dumps(record, ensure_ascii=True))
    break
else:
    raise SystemExit("summary rejected after rate-limit retries")

The retry loop is for rate limiting, not for hiding bad data. A CRM write belongs after validation and should carry a client-generated idempotency key, so a retry cannot duplicate an action. This example stops at the provider boundary because the response contract is what the experiment measures.

What should the retention policy keep?

The bill is made primarily from tokens sent and generated per call, multiplied by the number of calls retained for reprocessing. The input is usually the transcript plus instructions; the output is a short action object. Count tokens before sending when possible, set a maximum output budget, and split unusually long transcripts into sections. Record the provider’s returned usage where available. An estimate is a control signal, not a savings claim.

Retain the final structured action, provider and model identifiers, request identifier, validation result, and a bounded excerpt or hash that lets an operator find the source. Keep raw transcripts under the logistics team’s access policy, with a shorter default retention than the derived CRM action where the business process allows it.

What should stop being retained by default is every full prompt and response. That makes a shipment dispute harder to reconstruct, so define a documented exception for disputes rather than treating indefinite storage as an audit strategy. The retention decision belongs in the experiment record alongside parse failures and human repair.

Keep it bounded.

For example, if a consignee challenges a delivery commitment two weeks after the call, the useful audit trail is the structured action, the model and provider, the validation outcome, and a pointer to the source transcript under the team’s access policy. It is not necessarily a permanent copy of every intermediate prompt, retry, and malformed response. If the source transcript has already expired, the pointer should resolve to an explicit “unavailable” state rather than encouraging an operator to trust a reconstructed summary. If the case is placed into a dispute workflow before expiry, retain the source for that exception and record who authorized the extension. This gives the CRM team a way to explain why a date was written, while keeping routine calls from becoming an unbounded archive. The trade-off is visible: shorter retention reduces exposure and storage work, but it removes evidence that may be needed for a later dispute. The experiment should therefore report how many records would have required an exception, not quietly assume that the default policy covers every operational question.

The experiment succeeds when it produces a defensible decision, not when every call receives a confident paragraph. Infrai fits the workflow when its one-key breadth and public schemas remove integration work while the output still passes the same safety checks; a specialist direct API is better when its provider-specific controls or evaluation results matter more. If this boundary fits your system, start with the text summarization API guide.

Further reading

  • Anthropic API documentation
  • OpenAI API documentation
  • Google Gemini API documentation
  • OpenAI Embeddings guide

title: Checking a WAV file before it goes on a USB drive: a tiny Python validator
description:
Some devices are strict about the audio files they accept. A car that plays a custom lock sound is a good example: it wants one file, with an exact name, in a specific format, under a size limit. When the file is wrong, you usually get no error message, just silence. So I wrote a small Python script that checks a file before it ever reaches the USB drive.

The rules I check

For a Tesla custom lock sound, the requirements are well documented:

  • the file is named exactly LockChime.wav
  • it is a real WAV container with uncompressed PCM audio
  • it is smaller than 1 MB
  • it sits in the root of the drive

The standard library's wave module handles most of this. It only opens PCM WAV files, which is exactly the check we want.

The script 

import os, sys, wave

def check(path):
    problems = []
    name = os.path.basename(path)
    if name != "LockChime.wav":
        problems.append(f"name is {name!r}, expected 'LockChime.wav'")
    size = os.path.getsize(path)
    if size >= 1_000_000:
        problems.append(f"size is {size} bytes, must be under 1 MB")
    try:
        with wave.open(path, "rb") as w:
            ch, width, rate, frames = w.getnchannels(), w.getsampwidth(), w.getframerate(), w.getnframes()
            print(f"{ch} ch, {width*8}-bit, {rate} Hz, {frames/rate:.2f} s")
            if ch != 1:
                problems.append("stereo file: mono is smaller and plays the same on one speaker")
    except wave.Error as e:
        problems.append(f"not a PCM WAV ({e}); was an MP3 renamed?")
    return problems

if __name__ == "__main__":
    issues = check(sys.argv[1])
    print("OK" if not issues else "\n".join("- " + i for i in issues))

Why each check matters

The name check catches the classic LockChime.wav.wav problem that hidden extensions cause on Windows and macOS. The wave module raises an error for compressed or non-WAV data, which catches renamed MP3s. The size check is simple arithmetic: 16-bit mono at 44.1 kHz is about 88 KB per second, so anything longer than roughly 11 seconds will not fit.

Checking the drive itself

You can extend the script to take a mount point instead of a file, then confirm LockChime.wav is in the root and that there is only one. Checking the file system type is platform-specific; on Linux, reading /proc/mounts works, and you are looking for vfat, exfat, ext3 or ext4 rather than ntfs.

Where this came from

I help run Tesla Lock Sounds, a free library where every download is already a PCM WAV under 1 MB named LockChime.wav. Even with consistent files, the most common support question is still "why doesn't my car see it?", and nearly every answer is one of the checks above. The car side matters too: custom lock sounds need the external pedestrian warning speaker and supported software, which no script can fix.

title: ISR Isn't Dead, It Just Moved Into The Components
description:
@Kamalakannan

The question I keep getting

Lately I keep hearing some version of this from friends, colleagues, and teams at my current organization: "We're rebuilding our customer-facing site. It needs to be fast, it needs SEO, and someone said ISR and PPR. What's the actual architecture in 2026?"

For years the honest answer was "it depends, pick a rendering mode per page and pray." A product page was either static (fast, but stale prices) or server-rendered (fresh, but we pay for it on every request). we picked one and lived with the tradeoffs.

That choice mostly went away this year. ISR and PPR didn't die. They just stopped being route-level switches and became two halves of one model that lives inside our components. This post is my attempt to explain that model the way I wish someone had explained it to me, plus the architecture I'd actually ship for an enterprise site today.

What actually changed

Quick timeline, because the naming churn is half the confusion:

  • Next.js 16 (Oct 2025) shipped Cache Components. The "use cache" directive, cacheLife() and cacheTag() became the way to cache things, and the old experimental.ppr flag was removed. PPR didn't go away, it got folded in.
  • Next.js 16.3 (Aug 2026) added Instant Navigations: Partial Prefetching and App Shells, so client-side navigation feels like an SPA while the server still does the rendering.
  • Next.js 16.4 (Oct 2026) is the one that made me write this. The team now recommends Cache Components for every app, and create-next-app turns it on by default.

The philosophy shift matters more than any single API. Caching is opt-in now. Everything runs at request time unless we explicitly say "cache this." If we lived through the Next 13/14 era of "why is this page stale and where is that cache even coming from," we will appreciate how much calmer this is.

PPR and ISR are two halves of one idea

Here's the mental model that finally made it click for me:

  • PPR answers "where does this render?" Our page becomes a prerendered static shell with dynamic holes punched in it. Anything wrapped in <Suspense> that reads request data (cookies, headers, live prices) is a hole.
  • ISR answers "how long is this fresh?" Except now we set it per component or per data function with cacheLife(), and we refresh it on demand with cacheTag() + revalidateTag().

Picture a product page:

+--------------------------- /p/[slug] ---------------------------+
|                                                                 |
|  STATIC SHELL (cached, indexed)    DYNAMIC HOLES (per request)  |
|  +---------------------------+     +-------------------------+  |
|  | Header + nav              |     | Price + stock           |  |
|  | cacheLife('days')         |     | <Suspense>              |  |
|  +---------------------------+     +-------------------------+  |
|  | Title, copy, images,      |     | Recommendations         |  |
|  | JSON-LD                   |     | reads cookies()         |  |
|  | cacheTag('product:123')   |     +-------------------------+  |
|  +---------------------------+     | Cart badge              |  |
|  | Reviews summary           |     | per user                |  |
|  | cacheLife('hours')        |     +-------------------------+  |
|  +---------------------------+                                  |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------+

The left column ships instantly from the CDN and is what Googlebot reads. The right column streams in a few hundred milliseconds later. Nobody had to choose "static or dynamic" for the whole URL.

If we are mapping old habits to new APIs:

we used to write Now we write
export const revalidate = 3600 "use cache" + cacheLife('hours') on the function
revalidateTag('x') from a webhook cacheTag('x') on the data, then revalidateTag('x', 'max')
Read-our-own-writes after a form post updateTag() inside a Server Action
experimental.ppr Gone. It's automatic with cacheComponents: true
generateStaticParams Still here. Prebuild shells for our top URLs, the rest build on first hit

The architecture i had ship

Boring layers, each with one job:

              Users + crawlers
                     |
        +------------+-------------+
        |  CDN edge cache          |---->  proxy.ts
        |  static shells, assets   |       (A/B, geo, i18n)
        +------------+-------------+
                     |
   +-----------------+------------------------------+
   |  Next.js 16.4 app (Node runtime, App Router)   |
   |                                                |
   |  [Static shell]  [Dynamic holes]  [SEO layer]  |
   |   use cache       <Suspense>       metadata,   |
   |   cacheTag        price, stock     JSON-LD     |
   +--------+------------------------------+--------+
            |                              |
   +--------+---------+         +----------+---------+
   | Shared cache     |         | Data / BFF layer   |
   | Redis / Valkey   |         | typed + tagged     |
   +------------------+         +----------+---------+
                                           |
           +-----------+-----------+-------+-------+
           |           |           |               |
       Headless    Commerce      Search      Auth / profile
         CMS        / PIM

A few opinions baked into that picture:

  • Node runtime, not edge. The 16.3 release started deprecating the Edge Runtime. I'd keep personalization logic in proxy.ts light and do real work in Node.
  • Tags live in the data layer, not the page. If getProduct() carries cacheTag('product:123'), then one CMS update refreshes the PDP, every category grid showing it, and the landing page that features it. We don't hunt down paths.
  • A shared cache handler if we self-host. Run three pods without one and we have three separate ISR caches that disagree with each other. Ask me how I know. (Actually, don't.)
  • Tiny client components. "use client" goes on the cart drawer and the filter panel, not on the layout. The React Compiler is stable now, so stop hand-writing useMemo.

Show me the code

Turn it on first. On a fresh 16.4 app it's already there:

// next.config.ts
import type { NextConfig } from 'next'

const nextConfig: NextConfig = {
  cacheComponents: true,
}

export default nextConfig

The data layer is where caching actually happens:

// lib/products.ts
import { cacheLife, cacheTag } from 'next/cache'

export async function getProduct(slug: string) {
  'use cache'
  cacheLife('hours')            // the "ISR" part
  cacheTag(`product:${slug}`)   // so we can invalidate it later

  const res = await fetch(`${process.env.API_URL}/products/${slug}`)
  return res.json()
}

The page composes cached and dynamic pieces. Notice there's no revalidate export and no dynamic = 'force-dynamic' anywhere:

// app/p/[slug]/page.tsx
import { Suspense } from 'react'
import { getProduct } from '@/lib/products'
import { ProductInfo } from './product-info'
import { LivePrice, PriceSkeleton } from './live-price'

export default async function ProductPage({
  params,
}: {
  params: Promise<{ slug: string }>
}) {
  const { slug } = await params
  const product = await getProduct(slug)

  return (
    <>
      {/* static shell: crawlable, cached */}
      <ProductInfo product={product} />

      {/* dynamic hole: fresh on every request */}
      <Suspense fallback={<PriceSkeleton />}>
        <LivePrice slug={slug} />
      </Suspense>
    </>
  )
}

And the webhook our CMS calls when an editor hits publish:

// app/api/revalidate/route.ts
import { revalidateTag } from 'next/cache'

export async function POST(req: Request) {
  // verify the CMS signature here. Seriously, don't skip this.
  const { slug, categories = [] } = await req.json()

  revalidateTag(`product:${slug}`, 'max')
  for (const c of categories) revalidateTag(`category:${c}`, 'max')

  return Response.json({ ok: true })
}

That 'max' profile means stale-while-revalidate: nobody waits on a rebuild. The next visitor gets the old version once while the new one renders in the background.

What happens when an editor hits publish

This is the part people get wrong in production, so here's the whole loop:

1. Editor publishes product         (CMS)
           |
2. POST /api/revalidate             (verify signature, map to tags)
           |
3. revalidateTag('product:123', 'max')
   -> entries marked stale in the SHARED cache
           |
4. Next request arrives
   -> old shell served instantly, new one renders in background
           |
5. Fresh shell cached
   -> CDN purged by tag, or its short TTL expires

Gotchas worth knowing before we ship

The build will yell at us, and that's a feature. Read cookies(), headers(), searchParams or an un-cached fetch outside a <Suspense> boundary and the build fails. It feels annoying for about a day. Then we realize it's forcing us to decide, file by file, what belongs in the shell.

Don't hide SEO content in a hole. Anything inside Suspense streams in after the shell. Titles, body copy, internal links and JSON-LD belong in the cached part. Price inside Product schema is the classic trap: either cache price with a short cacheLife so it lands in the shell, or accept that the schema price is the cached one.

Fan out our tags. A product edit should invalidate product:123, its category:* tags and any collection:* it belongs to. Put that mapping in one function next to our data layer, not scattered across webhooks.

Webhooks get lost. Return a non-2xx when invalidation fails so the CMS retries, and set a sane cacheLife on everything anyway. Worst case, content goes stale for hours, not forever.

Stay patched. Next.js has had several security releases this fall, including fixes for cache poisoning in SSG and ISR. If we are running a cache that serves thousands of users from one render, that's not a release we skip.

Pages Router still works. getStaticProps with revalidate isn't going anywhere today. We can migrate one route at a time.

When I wouldn't reach for Next.js

  • Mostly content, barely interactive (docs, publishing, marketing): Astro. Zero JS by default is hard to beat.
  • React team that finds RSC more trouble than it's worth: React Router v7, the framework formerly known as Remix. Loaders and actions map cleanly to HTTP.
  • Vue shop: Nuxt 4. Same ideas, different ecosystem.

But for a big customer-facing site where SEO pays the bills and personalization pays the rest, Next.js 16 with Cache Components is the most complete answer I have seen. The best part is that the model finally matches how pages actually work: mostly the same for everyone, with a few bits that are about us.

If we are migrated a real app to Cache Components, I'd love to hear what bit you. Drop it in the comments.

Further reading

  • Next.js 16 release post
  • Next.js 16.3: Instant Navigations
  • Next.js 16.4 release post
  • Next.js blog (security releases)
  • Next.js alternatives in 2026 (OpenReplay)

title: GraphQL Isn't Magic: How ASTs, Resolvers, and DataLoaders Actually Work Under the Hood
description:
Ask almost any frontend developer why they love GraphQL, and you will hear a familiar promise:

"You just ask for the exact fields you need, and the server returns exactly what you asked for. No over-fetching, no under-fetching, no multiple roundtrips."

It sounds like pure sorcery. You write a neat JSON-like query in your frontend codebase:

query GetUserProfile {
  user(id: "usr_42") {
    name
    email
    posts {
      title
      comments {
        text
        author {
          name
        }
      }
    }
  }
}

You hit send. In a single network request, you get back users, their posts, their comments, and the comment authors, all perfectly nested in a clean JSON object.

Because it feels so seamless from the client side, many developers develop an intuitive mental model: they assume GraphQL is a smart query planner, something like an intelligent SQL optimizer that inspects the request, constructs a series of database joins, and returns the result.

Then the application goes into production.

Traffic ramps up. Suddenly, database CPU spikes to 100 percent. The connection pool runs dry. A single client query requesting twenty posts and their authors quietly fires seventy-one distinct SQL queries to PostgreSQL in less than ten milliseconds. Latency surges from fifty milliseconds to four seconds. The backend team scrambles to figure out why a simple profile page brought down the database server.

GraphQL is not an automated query planner. It is not an ORM, and it knows absolutely nothing about your database tables, foreign keys, or indexes.

GraphQL is a runtime specification and execution engine that recursively evaluates an Abstract Syntax Tree by invoking isolated resolver functions.

Once you understand what happens beneath the syntax, you can predict performance bottlenecks before they happen, write clean server architectures, and stop treating GraphQL like a black box.

Here is how the engine actually works under the hood.

Phase 1: From Raw String to AST (The Ingestion Pipeline)

When a client sends a GraphQL request, it arrives at your server as an ordinary HTTP POST request with a JSON payload:

{
  "query": "query GetUser { user(id: \"42\") { name email } }",
  "variables": {}
}

Notice that the query is simply a plain text string. Your server cannot execute a string directly. Before any business logic runs, the GraphQL engine pushes that string through three strict phases: Lexing, Parsing, and Validation.

[ Incoming HTTP POST Request ]
              │
              ▼
    1. Lexing (Tokenizing)
              │
              ▼
    2. Parsing (AST Generation)
              │
              ▼
    3. Schema Validation (Type Checking)
              │
              ▼
    4. Execution Phase (Resolver Tree)

1. Lexical Analysis (Lexing)

The lexer scans the raw query string character by character and groups them into lexical tokens: keywords, names, punctuation marks (such as curly braces and colons), and literal values.

For example, { user(id: "42") } is converted into an array of distinct tokens:

  • PUNCTUATOR: {
  • NAME: user
  • PUNCTUATOR: (
  • NAME: id
  • PUNCTUATOR: :
  • STRING: "42"
  • PUNCTUATOR: )
  • PUNCTUATOR: }

2. Syntactic Parsing (Building the AST)

Next, the parser takes the stream of tokens and constructs an Abstract Syntax Tree (AST). An AST is a deeply nested JavaScript object that represents the grammatical structure of your query.

Here is a simplified view of what { user { name } } looks like as an AST:

{
  kind: "Document",
  definitions: [
    {
      kind: "OperationDefinition",
      operation: "query",
      selectionSet: {
        kind: "SelectionSet",
        selections: [
          {
            kind: "Field",
            name: { kind: "Name", value: "user" },
            selectionSet: {
              kind: "SelectionSet",
              selections: [
                {
                  kind: "Field",
                  name: { kind: "Name", value: "name" }
                }
              ]
            }
          }
        ]
      }
    }
  ]
}

This tree structure is crucial: the execution engine does not care about the text formatting, tabs, or whitespace of the original query. It only navigates this hierarchical AST.

3. Schema Validation

Before executing a single line of backend code, the engine validates the AST against your defined GraphQL Schema (the Type System).

It answers critical questions statically:

  • Does the user field exist on the root Query type?
  • Does the user field accept an id argument?
  • Is the provided argument type valid (e.g. String instead of Int)?
  • Does the User object actually have a field named name?

If a client requests a field that does not exist in the schema, the engine halts immediately during validation. It never touches your database, never runs your authentication middleware, and never invokes a resolver. It returns an HTTP 200 response with a top-level errors array explaining the exact syntax or validation mismatch.

Phase 2: Resolvers (How Execution Actually Works)

Once the query passes validation, the engine begins the Execution Phase. This is where your custom application code runs.

In GraphQL, every single field in your query corresponds to an underlying function called a Resolver.

The Anatomy of a Resolver

A resolver function always receives four arguments, regardless of language or framework:

const userResolver = (parent, args, context, info) => {
  // your custom fetching logic
};

Let's demystify these four parameters:

  1. parent (or root): The resolved value returned by this field's immediate parent resolver. For top-level query fields, this is usually undefined. For nested fields, it is the parent object.
  2. args: An object containing all arguments passed to this field in the query (for example, { id: "42" }).
  3. context: A shared object passed across every single resolver during a single request. This is where you store database connections, current authenticated user sessions, and caching instances.
  4. info: A low-level object containing AST metadata about the current field, path, and incoming query structure.

Depth-First Recursive Execution

How does the engine traverse the AST? It uses a Depth-First Search (DFS) algorithm.

Consider this query:

query {
  user(id: "42") {
    name
    profile {
      bio
    }
  }
}

Here is the exact step-by-step sequence the engine executes:

Step 1: Execute Query.user(parent=undefined, args={ id: "42" })
         │
         ▼ Returns: { id: "42", name: "Sarah Connor", profileId: "prof_99" }
         │
Step 2: Concurrently resolve fields inside User selection set:
         ├─► Execute User.name(parent={ id: "42", name: "Sarah Connor", ... })
         │    └─► Returns: "Sarah Connor"
         │
         └─► Execute User.profile(parent={ id: "42", name: "Sarah Connor", ... })
              └─► Returns: { id: "prof_99", bio: "Protecting the future." }
                   │
                   ▼
Step 3: Execute Profile.bio(parent={ id: "prof_99", bio: "..." })
         └─► Returns: "Protecting the future."

The Default Resolver

You might wonder: "Do I have to write a resolver for every scalar field like name, email, and bio?"

No, because GraphQL engines provide a Default Resolver for any field you do not explicitly define. If you do not provide a resolver for name, the engine uses an internal fallback that behaves like this:

function defaultFieldResolver(parent, args, context, info) {
  if (typeof parent === "object" && parent !== null) {
    const property = parent[info.fieldName];
    if (typeof property === "function") {
      return property.call(parent, args, context, info);
    }
    return property;
  }
  return null;
}

If the parent object already has a property matching the field name, it just extracts it. If not, it returns null.

This recursive tree execution model is clean, elegant, and modular. But it hides an architectural landmine.

Phase 3: The Fatal Trap (The N+1 Query Problem)

Because each resolver is an isolated function responsible only for its own field, resolvers have zero awareness of what their sibling resolvers or parent resolvers are doing.

This architectural isolation leads directly to the single most notorious performance flaw in GraphQL: The N+1 Query Problem.

How the Trap Springs

Imagine an e-commerce platform displaying a list of twenty recent orders, along with the customer details for each order:

query GetRecentOrders {
  recentOrders(limit: 20) {
    id
    totalAmount
    customer {
      id
      name
      email
    }
  }
}

Now look at how a typical beginner writes the resolver schema:

const resolvers = {
  Query: {
    recentOrders: async (parent, args, context) => {
      // 1 Database Query: Fetch 20 orders
      return await context.db.query("SELECT * FROM orders ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT $1", [args.limit]);
    }
  },
  Order: {
    customer: async (order, args, context) => {
      // Runs once FOR EVERY SINGLE ORDER!
      return await context.db.query("SELECT * FROM customers WHERE id = $1", [order.customerId]);
    }
  }
};

Let's count what happens in your database:

  1. The Query.recentOrders resolver fires 1 query: SELECT * FROM orders ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20; It returns an array of 20 order rows.
  2. The engine iterates over the 20 orders and invokes the Order.customer resolver for each item.
  3. The server fires 20 individual database queries:
    • SELECT * FROM customers WHERE id = 101;
    • SELECT * FROM customers WHERE id = 102;
    • SELECT * FROM customers WHERE id = 103;
    • ...and so on, 20 times in a row.

Total database roundtrips: 1 + 20 = 21 queries.

If you change the limit to 100 orders, you trigger 101 queries. If each customer has a nested addresses field, you trigger another 100 queries. Before you realize it, a single HTTP request generates hundreds of database queries, choking your connection pool and dragging server throughput to a halt.

Phase 4: How DataLoader Saves the Day (Event Loop Magic)

To solve the N+1 problem without destroying the modular nature of resolvers, Facebook created a utility called DataLoader.

Most developers know that DataLoader "batches and caches" database requests. But very few understand the mechanical trick that makes it possible: JavaScript Event Loop Microtask Batching.

The Architectural Problem

Resolvers run asynchronously. How can individual resolvers, running on separate array items, know what other resolvers are about to request so they can combine their queries into a single SELECT * FROM customers WHERE id IN (...)?

If resolver 1 runs, how can it pause and wait for resolver 20 to declare its needs before making the database call?

The Microtask Queue Mechanism

DataLoader takes advantage of the fact that Node.js processes JavaScript execution in distinct ticks and microtask queues.

When a resolver asks DataLoader for an item:

customerLoader.load(order.customerId);

DataLoader does not immediately fire a database query. Instead, it does three things:

  1. It records the requested ID in an internal memory array ([101]).
  2. It creates and returns a pending JavaScript Promise to that specific resolver.
  3. It schedules a batch-clearing function to run on the next tick of the event loop using process.nextTick() or microtask queues.

Because JavaScript runs synchronously within the current tick of the event loop, all twenty Order.customer resolvers execute their synchronous parts in the exact same event loop turn!

Tick 0 (Current Synchronous Call Stack):
  Resolver 1 calls customerLoader.load(101)  --> ID stored, Promise 1 returned
  Resolver 2 calls customerLoader.load(102)  --> ID stored, Promise 2 returned
  Resolver 3 calls customerLoader.load(101)  --> Deduplicated! Returns Promise 1
  ...
  Resolver 20 calls customerLoader.load(120) --> ID stored, Promise 20 returned

Tick 1 (Microtask Phase - Call Stack Cleared):
  DataLoader batch function fires:
  "SELECT * FROM customers WHERE id IN (101, 102, ..., 120);"

  Single SQL response arrives:
  DataLoader matches returned rows to pending Promises and resolves each one!

Implementing a Real DataLoader

Here is what setting up a DataLoader looks like in practice:

import DataLoader from "dataloader";

// Define the batch function: receives an array of keys, must return an array of values in matching order
const batchGetCustomers = async (customerIds, db) => {
  // customerIds = [101, 102, 120, ...]
  const rows = await db.query(
    "SELECT * FROM customers WHERE id = ANY($1)",
    [customerIds]
  );

  // CRITICAL: DataLoader requires results to be returned in the EXACT same order as keys
  const customerMap = new Map(rows.map(row => [row.id, row]));
  return customerIds.map(id => customerMap.get(id) || null);
};

// Instantiated per request inside context!
export function createLoaders(db) {
  return {
    customerLoader: new DataLoader(ids => batchGetCustomers(ids, db))
  };
}

Now, your resolver becomes clean and fast:

const resolvers = {
  Order: {
    customer: (order, args, context) => {
      // Returns a promise that DataLoader resolves in a single batch query!
      return context.loaders.customerLoader.load(order.customerId);
    }
  }
};

Instead of 21 queries, your server executes exactly 2 queries: one for the orders, and one batched lookup for all customers.

Important Rule: Always instantiate DataLoaders inside your request context, never as global singletons. If you create a global DataLoader, it will cache database records across different users indefinitely, leading to massive memory leaks and critical security vulnerabilities where User A reads cached data belonging to User B.

Phase 5: The Security Dilemma (Circular Depth Attacks)

Because GraphQL gives clients the freedom to ask for whatever structure they want, it introduces a severe security vulnerability that does not exist in traditional REST APIs: Unbounded Query Depth.

If your schema allows users to query their friends, and each friend has friends, a malicious actor or buggy client can send this query:

query MaliciousDepthAttack {
  user(id: "1") {
    friends {
      friends {
        friends {
          friends {
            friends {
              friends {
                name
              }
            }
          }
        }
      }
    }
  }
}

If left unprotected, your GraphQL engine will happily recurse down all seven levels, expanding exponentially. If each user has 50 friends, level 6 evaluates millions of resolver calls, instantly consuming server memory and CPU until the process crashes.

Production GraphQL servers defend against this using two complementary techniques:

1. Query Depth Limiting

Before allowing an AST to enter the execution phase, a depth-limiting validator traverses the AST and counts how many levels of nested selection sets exist. If the depth exceeds a safe threshold (typically 5 to 7 levels), the engine rejects the query during validation with an immediate error:

import depthLimit from "graphql-depth-limit";
import { createYoga } from "graphql-yoga";

const yoga = createYoga({
  schema,
  validationRules: [
    depthLimit(5) // Rejects queries nested deeper than 5 levels
  ]
});

2. Query Cost Analysis

Depth alone is not enough. A query with a depth of only two levels could still ask for recentUsers(limit: 10000) { expensiveCalculatedField }, which is cheap in depth but catastrophic in computation cost.

Query Cost Analysis assigns a numeric weight to each field:

  • Simple scalar fields (name, email): Cost = 1 point.
  • Relational fields with pagination (posts(limit: 50)): Cost = 50 * inner field costs.

The engine computes the total query score before execution. If the cost exceeds a predefined budget (for example, 500 points per request), the query is rejected immediately.

Phase 6: The Caching Conundrum (REST vs GraphQL)

In a conventional REST API, caching is built directly into the foundational fabric of the internet: the HTTP specification.

If you make an HTTP GET /api/users/42:

  • Web browsers cache the response.
  • Edge CDNs (Cloudflare, Fastly, CloudFront) cache the response based on Cache-Control headers.
  • Reverse proxies return 304 Not Modified using ETag validation without touching application servers.

In GraphQL, almost everything breaks that paradigm:

  1. Every request is an HTTP POST: Standard web infrastructure and CDNs do not cache POST requests because POST is defined as non-idempotent by the HTTP specification.
  2. Every request hits the same endpoint: Requests go to /graphql. You cannot cache by URL path.
  3. HTTP Status Code 200 for Errors: Even if half your query fails due to a database exception, GraphQL returns HTTP 200 OK with a payload containing partial data and an errors array.

How do production GraphQL architectures solve caching? Through two distinct layers: Persisted Queries at the Edge and Normalized Caches on the Client.

[ Edge Caching Strategy: Automatic Persisted Queries (APQ) ]
Client sends SHA256 Hash of Query via HTTP GET /graphql?hash=a7b3...
               │
               ├─► CDN Cache Hit: Returns cached JSON immediately!
               │
               └─► CDN Cache Miss: Server executes query, stores in CDN, returns JSON.

[ Client-Side Caching Strategy: Normalized In-Memory Cache ]
Response JSON arrives with __typename and id:
  User:usr_42   --> { name: "Sarah Connor" }
  Post:post_88  --> { title: "Liquid Metal", authorRef: "User:usr_42" }
Graph is flattened into relational relational key-value store!

1. Automatic Persisted Queries (APQ)

To re-enable CDN caching, modern architectures use Persisted Queries:

  1. During the build step or initial request, the client computes a SHA-256 hash of the query string.
  2. The client sends a lightweight GET /graphql?id=<hash> request instead of a bulky POST body.
  3. Because it is a standard HTTP GET request with a deterministic hash query parameter, edge CDNs can cache the entire response payload based on standard Cache-Control headers!

2. Normalized Client Caches

On the client side (using Apollo Client, Urql, or Relay), the cache does not store raw server responses as arbitrary JSON blobs.

Instead, the client cache performs Normalization:

  • It inspects every object in the returned JSON.
  • It extracts the __typename and id (e.g. User:42).
  • It flattens the nested graph into a relational dictionary of unique entity keys.

If a profile update mutation updates User:42's name, every component across your entire application displaying User:42 automatically updates instantly, without needing a full refetch.

Phase 7: Building a Mini GraphQL Engine from Scratch

The best way to solidify your mental model of GraphQL is to build a stripped-down resolver engine yourself.

Here is a complete, runnable resolver evaluator in approximately thirty lines of vanilla JavaScript:

// A minimal schema with types and field resolvers
const schema = {
  Query: {
    user: (parent, args) => ({ id: args.id, name: "Sarah", role: "Engineer" })
  },
  User: {
    company: (parent) => ({ name: "Skynet", domain: "defense.ai" })
  }
};

// Simplified query AST representation
const queryAST = {
  field: "user",
  args: { id: "42" },
  selectionSet: [
    { field: "name" },
    { 
      field: "company", 
      selectionSet: [{ field: "domain" }] 
    }
  ]
};

// The recursive execution engine
async function executeQuery(ast, typeName, parentData = null) {
  const typeResolvers = schema[typeName] || {};
  const resolver = typeResolvers[ast.field] || ((parent) => parent?.[ast.field]);

  // Resolve the current field
  const resolvedValue = await resolver(parentData, ast.args);

  // If there are no nested fields, return the scalar value
  if (!ast.selectionSet || ast.selectionSet.length === 0) {
    return resolvedValue;
  }

  // Determine the child type name (for demo purposes, capitalized field name)
  const childTypeName = ast.field.charAt(0).toUpperCase() + ast.field.slice(1);
  const result = {};

  // Concurrently resolve all fields in the selection set
  await Promise.all(
    ast.selectionSet.map(async (childAST) => {
      result[childAST.field] = await executeQuery(childAST, childTypeName, resolvedValue);
    })
  );

  return result;
}

// Run it!
executeQuery(queryAST, "Query").then((output) => {
  console.log("Resolved GraphQL Output:", JSON.stringify(output, null, 2));
});

Run that script with node mini-graphql.js and you will see:

{
  "name": "Sarah",
  "company": {
    "domain": "defense.ai"
  }
}

Look closely at what those thirty lines do:

  • They recursively walk the tree.
  • They invoke resolvers with the parent data.
  • They fall back to default property accessors when no custom resolver is declared.
  • They resolve children concurrently using Promise.all.

There is no magic, no secret database connection, and no compiler sorcery. GraphQL is simply a structured recursive function evaluator that traverses a tree.

The Architectural Decision Matrix: When to Use GraphQL vs REST

GraphQL is a powerful tool, but it is not a silver bullet that should replace REST in every project. Choosing the wrong tool for your use case creates unnecessary operational overhead.

Here is an architectural comparison to help you choose the right paradigm:

Architectural Dimension Traditional REST API GraphQL Architecture
Data Fetching Precision Fixed endpoints; risk of over-fetching or under-fetching Client requests exact fields; eliminates payload bloat
Network Roundtrips Often requires multiple waterfall requests for related data Single roundtrip retrieves nested relational trees
HTTP Caching Native, effortless caching via URLs, CDNs, and browser caches Requires Automatic Persisted Queries (APQ) or client normalization
Database Performance Predictable query patterns; easy to optimize with SQL joins Prone to N+1 problem unless mitigated by DataLoaders
API Versioning Explicit versioning in URL (/v1/, /v2/) Continuous evolution; deprecated field directives
Security & DoS Protection Standard rate limiting by IP and endpoint path Requires Query Depth Limiting and Cost Complexity Analysis
File Uploads Simple, native multipart/form-data support Awkward workarounds or separate upload endpoints required
Best Used For Microservice-to-microservice RPC, simple CRUD, public APIs Complex frontend apps, mobile clients with low bandwidth, rapidly evolving UIs

The Complete GraphQL Mental Model Cheat Sheet

Keep these core principles in mind whenever you design or debug a GraphQL system:

  1. GraphQL executes strings through an AST: Lexing tokenizes the string, parsing builds the syntax tree, and validation checks the tree against your schema before execution begins.
  2. Every field is a resolver: If you do not provide a resolver, the default resolver reads the property directly off the parent object.
  3. Resolvers are isolated by design: Because resolvers do not know what their peers are doing, nested queries naturally cause the N+1 database problem.
  4. DataLoader uses event loop ticks: It queues IDs synchronously during Tick 0, yields to the microtask queue, and dispatches a single batched database query in Tick 1.
  5. Always limit query depth and calculate cost: Never expose an unhardened GraphQL endpoint to the public internet without depth limiting and complexity budgeting.
  6. Cache at the edge with APQ and normalize on the client: Use SHA-256 persisted queries to regain CDN caching, and let client libraries flatten your graph using __typename:id.

Once you stop viewing GraphQL as a magical database client and start treating it as a recursive tree execution engine, the mysterious performance drops disappear. You know exactly when to reach for a DataLoader, how to protect your server from abusive queries, and how to build backends that remain fast, stable, and predictable under heavy production load.

If you have worked with GraphQL in production, you have almost certainly encountered a moment where a nested query brought your database or memory usage to its knees. How do you usually handle relational fetching in your team: do you rely strictly on DataLoaders, use query lookahead engines, or build purpose-built REST endpoints for high-throughput views? I would love to hear your experiences and architectural trade-offs in the comments below.

title: 360 green runs, and one test that would pass with the server down
description:
I gave an AI a Playwright + TypeScript repo and ten test scenarios. It wrote 13 tests. I ran every test in the repo 20 times with retries off: 360 runs, 360 passed.

Then I read the tests. One of them would still pass if the server were down.

This article covers:

  • the project structure the AI worked in, and why each piece is there
  • how I measured the tests instead of trusting the green
  • where the AI got it right, and where it went wrong
  • a four-question checklist for reviewing AI-generated tests

Everything is in a public repo: flakelab-dev/playwright-structure. The AI's raw output is committed before any fix, so you can check every claim here.

TL;DR

  • Stable is not the same as correct. 360/360 proved the tests don't flake. It didn't prove they check the right thing.
  • The AI wrote good code and followed the structure. Its mistakes were about what to check, not how to write it.
  • It loosened an assertion to fit a bug, and it copied a gap from my own tests.
  • Without a spec, the AI turns current behavior into expected behavior. So do we, when we're in a hurry.
  • Seeded bugs told me more than 360 green runs.

The structure

Two public demo apps: SauceDemo for UI and Restful Booker for API.

config/environments.ts   URLs per environment, picked with TEST_ENV
src/
  pages/                 Page objects: locators and actions, no business assertions
  api/                   Typed API client + Zod schemas
  fixtures/              Wires pages, clients and auth together
  data/                  Test data builders
tests/
  ui/                    SauceDemo tests
  api/                   Restful Booker tests
playwright.config.ts     Two projects, "ui" and "api"; retries off

Four decisions matter most.

1. Fixtures do the setup. Tests only declare what they need. A test that asks for loggedInPage gets a browser that is already logged in:

test('adding a product updates the cart badge', async ({ loggedInPage }) => {
  await loggedInPage.addToCart('Sauce Labs Backpack');
  await expect(loggedInPage.cartBadge).toHaveText('1');
});

2. The API client checks every response. Methods like createBooking() validate the body with a Zod schema, and a failed call reports the URL, status and body:

async function jsonOrThrow(response: APIResponse): Promise<unknown> {
  if (!response.ok()) {
    throw new Error(`${response.url()} returned ${response.status()}: ${await response.text()}`);
  }
  return response.json();
}

Methods ending in Raw return the response untouched, for tests about status codes.

3. Test data is unique per run. buildBooking() adds a random suffix to the last name, so parallel tests can't collide on a shared public API.

4. Retries are off. Retries hide flakiness, and measuring flakiness is the point. The CI workflow can repeat the whole suite from the Actions tab.

One more thing about structure: it is also what you give the AI. The AI doesn't read your mind, it reads your repo. Keep that in mind for later.

The experiment

  1. The prompt was written and committed before generating. (prompt.md)
  2. Fresh session: Claude Opus 5.5 in Claude Code, with only the repo and the prompt.
  3. The output was committed exactly as produced, before running or reviewing it. (raw output)
  4. Every test ran 20 times, retries off.
  5. I reviewed every test by hand against the code and the API docs.
  6. I ran the UI tests against users with deliberate bugs.

The prompt listed five UI scenarios (sorting, cart, checkout, form errors, logout) and five API scenarios (PUT, PATCH, filter, invalid payload, wrong credentials). It ended with:

Rules: no hard waits, no retries, each test independent.
Do not run the tests; only write them.

Why "do not run"? If the AI runs its tests, it fixes them until they pass, and I lose the first draft. I wanted to measure that draft.

Result 1: 360 out of 360 

npx playwright test --repeat-each=20

The 13 generated tests plus the 5 already in the repo, 20 times each: 360 runs, 360 passed.

That proves the tests are stable. It doesn't prove they are useful. A test that never fails might simply be unable to fail.

Result 2: seeding bugs

SauceDemo has demo users with deliberate bugs. The loggedInPage fixture reads the user from an environment variable, so I ran the same 7 UI tests as each user, 3 times each:

UI_USER=problem_user npx playwright test tests/ui/ai- --project=ui --repeat-each=3
User Passed What failed
standard_user 21/21 Nothing (control)
problem_user 9/21 Sorting doesn't sort; the last name field ignores input, so checkout breaks
error_user 12/21 Sorting doesn't sort; checkout can't finish; a missing last name isn't reported
visual_user 18/21 The prices shown after sorting are not the prices shown before
performance_glitch_user 17/21 Not a bug in the app's logic: login is slow (see below)

I checked every failure: each one came from the seeded bug, not from a mistake in the test. The tests that stayed green did so because the bug wasn't on their path (logout works for every user).

This is the result I trust more than 360/360. The generated UI tests catch real bugs.

A side lesson on flakiness

performance_glitch_user takes over 5 seconds to log in. Look at what that did:

Test Passed
Sorting 0/3
Logout 2/3
Cart and checkout (5) 15/15

Same slowness, three different outcomes. The difference is the first step after login:

  • Sorting and logout start with an assertion: expect(loggedInPage.title).toHaveText('Products'). Assertions give up after 5 seconds by default.
  • Cart and checkout start with an action: addToCart(). Actions have no timeout of their own by default, so they keep waiting.

Logout passed 2 times out of 3. That's what a flaky test looks like the first time you meet it. With retries on, it would have been green and the slow login would have gone unnoticed.

Where the AI got it right

Before the mistakes, credit where it's due. Some of these I didn't ask for.

  • It followed the structure. It used the fixtures, page objects and client. It added new page objects and client methods using the existing Raw naming, and a data builder like the one already there.
  • It used unique data. The filter test searches for a first name like Flake-3f9a1c2e, so other bookings on the shared public API can't match.
  • It guarded the sorting test. If the products already loaded in ascending order, the test would pass even with a broken sort button. The AI checked for that first: 
// Guard: if the default order were already ascending, the test would prove nothing.
expect(pricesBefore.length).toBeGreaterThan(1);
expect(pricesBefore).not.toEqual(expected);
  • It declared its assumptions. Its report listed four, like "Restful Booker returns 500 for an incomplete booking payload". All four are true today. None of them is documented.

Where the AI went wrong

1. It loosened an assertion to fit a bug

Scenario: "Creating a booking with an invalid payload is rejected."

Restful Booker answers a booking with missing fields with 500. A validation error should be 400; a 500 means the server failed. The AI knew this, and wrote:

// Restful Booker answers 500 here rather than 400; the test checks rejection, not the code.
expect(response.ok(), `expected rejection, got ${response.status()}`).toBe(false);
expect(response.status()).toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(400);

This passes with 400, with 500, and with 503 Service Unavailable. If the service were down, this test would still pass. That's the test in the title.

The AI didn't hide the bug, since it left a comment. But it wrote the assertion so the bug fits, and the test can no longer fail for the reason that matters.

2. An error check that accepts any error

Scenario: "Authenticating with wrong credentials fails."

await expect(bookingClient.getToken(apiAdmin.username, 'wrong-password')).rejects.toThrow();

toThrow() with no message accepts any error: a network failure, a timeout, a typo in the URL.

And here's why it passed. Restful Booker answers wrong credentials with 200 and {"reason":"Bad credentials"}. The client tried to read a token from that body, the schema check failed, and that error made the test pass. It passed because of a parsing error, not because the API rejected the login.

3. It copied my gap

The PUT, PATCH and filter tests create bookings and never delete them. That's about 60 abandoned bookings per 20-run session, on a public service that other people use.

The test I wrote by hand had the same gap. The AI followed the pattern it was given, including the bad part.

That's the lesson I keep from this experiment: AI multiplies your repo's conventions, good and bad. Fix the base before you generate on top of it.

4. Minor: duplication

The same locators (page title, item names, cart badge) are defined in three page objects, and four checkout tests repeat the same setup. They aren't bugs, so I left them for a later refactor.

The bigger problem: there was no spec

SauceDemo has no documentation. Every expected value in the UI tests (the error messages, the empty cart after checkout, the text after logout) came from what the app does today.

When I reviewed them, I got stuck on one question: if the app has a bug today, should the test adapt to it, or fail? And based on what?

Without a spec, these tests are characterization tests: they detect change, not correctness. That's still useful (the seeded bugs prove it), but it's worth naming. I marked all 7 UI tests "⚠️ Oracle": the expected behavior isn't backed by a specification.

The API has docs, so the review was clearer. PUT, PATCH and filter match the docs. The wrong-credentials response (200 with a reason) isn't described in the docs at all, and the test treats it as correct.

Final count for the 13 tests:

Verdict Tests
✅ Good as is 3
⚠️ Oracle: expected value not backed by a spec 8
⚠️ Weak: wouldn't catch the failure 1
❌ Wrong 1

The AI did what we all do in a hurry: it looked at current behavior and wrote it down as expected behavior. At least it listed its assumptions. Read that list: it's where the oracle problems are.

The fixes

Each fix is a separate commit on top of the AI's output, so you can compare before and after.

Invalid payload (bed0c5d): assert the exact status and record the bug.

test.info().annotations.push({
  type: 'known bug',
  description: 'Returns 500 instead of 400 for missing fields',
});
expect(response.status()).toBe(500);

Now the test fails if the service is down (503), and it fails if the bug gets fixed (400), which is exactly when you want to update it. The annotation shows up in the HTML report, so the bug stays visible.

I considered test.fail() and rejected it: it treats any failure as expected, including an outage. Same problem as before.

Wrong credentials (c272114): the client now throws Authentication failed: <reason> when the API rejects the login, and the test asserts that exact message.

Cleanup (5b5ce0b): the bookingClient fixture deletes every booking the test created, after the test ends. To check it, a temporary test created a booking; after the run, a GET for that booking returned 404.

A checklist for AI-generated tests

Ask these four questions about every test:

  1. Oracle: where does each expected value come from: a spec, or what the app does today?
  2. Sensitivity: if the feature broke, would this test fail? Better than guessing: break it and see.
  3. Isolation: does it depend on data it doesn't control, or leave data behind?
  4. Structure: does it use the fixtures, page objects and client, or bypass them?

In this experiment, questions 1 and 2 found every real problem. Question 4 is the one the AI already handles well.

One tip from my own review: read the support code before judging a test. I flagged a missing status check in the API tests, and it was already there, in the client.

Try it yourself 

git clone https://github.com/flakelab-dev/playwright-structure
cd playwright-structure
npm ci
npx playwright install chromium
npm test
  • Full review sheet with every verdict and note
  • The prompt
  • The AI's raw output, before any fix

Run npm run test:repeat to measure it yourself, or set UI_USER to one of the broken users and watch the tests catch the bugs.

How do you review AI-generated tests today? I'd like to hear what you check first.

I publish one measured experiment like this at a time. If you want the next one by email: flakelab.dev/subscribe

title: DORA and NIS2 as Code: Policy-as-Code Compliance Evidence for Spring Boot on Kubernetes
description:
Compliance work tends to stall in the same place. A requirement gets filed on the security team's board, and the people who could actually change the payments service never see it. Three quarters later an auditor asks for proof, and the team learns that "we do this" and "we can show this" are two separate claims.

I write Java for systems that move money. My background includes high-traffic airline platforms, OpenBanking PSD2 integrations and a startup I co-founded. I should be plain about one thing: those were not DORA or NIS2 audits. What carried over from them was a habit. Checks that run on every deploy keep working, and checks that live in a document drift. This post applies that habit to the two EU regulations, from the point of view of the person who has to write the YAML and the Java.

A boundary before anything else. This is an engineering pattern, not legal advice and not an official compliance mapping. The regulation text, the technical standards and your supervisor's reading decide what you owe, and your compliance and legal colleagues own that reading. I only cover what an engineer can do once a requirement arrives: what to ship so a pipeline run can demonstrate it.

What a pipeline can prove, and what it cannot

A rule of thumb I use: for any control that is technical in nature, I want a pipeline run to be able to produce evidence of it. A wiki sentence saying "all images are scanned" is a statement of intent. A signed scan report tied to the exact commit, with a timestamp, sitting in a bucket nobody on the team can edit, is something an auditor can examine.

That rule has limits, and pretending otherwise would be dishonest. Management-body accountability, staff training, contract clauses with ICT providers, exit strategies and the governance of the whole risk framework are not provable by a build. Auditors also separate design effectiveness (is the control sensibly built?) from operating effectiveness (did it actually run, consistently, over the period?). A green pipeline speaks mainly to the second one, and only for the checks it contains. Treat everything below as the machine-checkable slice of a larger programme.

For that slice, I describe each control with three parts:

  1. Mechanism: the thing that enforces or measures (an admission policy, a circuit breaker, a probe).
  2. Artifact: what the mechanism leaves behind (a policy report, an SBOM, an audit event, a drill result).
  3. Retention: where the artifact lives, for how long, and how it connects to one specific deploy.

Here is how those parts line up for the areas I work on. The areas are my reading of the texts, not legal citations.

Area Mechanism Artifact Where it stops
Change and configuration safety on production workloads Admission policies (Kyverno or Gatekeeper) Policy report per deploy Says nothing about governance or risk appetite
Supply chain and third-party software Signed images, CycloneDX SBOM, scan attestation Cosign signature, SBOM, scan result A snapshot at build time, not ongoing monitoring
Resilience testing Resilience4j fault drills, probes, staging chaos Drill result JSON per release Not a substitute for a full testing programme
Logging and detection Actuator audit events, OpenTelemetry traces Queryable trail with trace IDs Needs a human process to review it
Backup and recovery Scheduled restore drills with measured RTO/RPO Drill report against targets Covers the data tier, not the whole recovery chain
Incident clocks Timestamped alert classification Incident timeline Classification criteria come from compliance

Before any of that, though, there is a prerequisite I skipped for years: an inventory. DORA is built around knowing your ICT assets and how critical each is, and a policy has to be scoped to something. I keep a small register listing each service, its owner team, and a criticality tier agreed with the business. The payments namespace in the examples below is only the first entry on that list, and the tier decides how strict the policies and drills are for each service.

Admission control: the policy that says no

Kubernetes admission is the point where "we require X" turns into "the cluster refuses without X". I have used both Kyverno and OPA Gatekeeper. Kyverno expresses policy in the same YAML dialect as the rest of your manifests, which lowers the barrier for service teams reviewing a change. Gatekeeper makes sense if people on your platform team already write Rego or you share constraint templates across many clusters. Choose one per platform; running two means two sets of reports to explain.

The policy below blocks pods in payments unless the image was signed by our CI identity and carries a CycloneDX SBOM attestation:

apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
  name: payments-require-signed-image-with-sbom
  annotations:
    policies.kyverno.io/title: Signed images with SBOM for payment workloads
    compliance.internal/control-id: SUPPLY-001
spec:
  validationFailureAction: Enforce
  webhookTimeoutSeconds: 15
  failurePolicy: Fail
  rules:
    - name: verify-signature-and-sbom
      match:
        any:
          - resources:
              kinds: [Pod]
              namespaces: [payments]
      verifyImages:
        - imageReferences:
            - "registry.example.eu/payments/*"
          attestors:
            - entries:
                - keyless:
                    subject: "https://github.com/example-org/*"
                    issuer: "https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com"
                    rekor:
                      url: https://rekor.sigstore.dev
          attestations:
            - type: https://cyclonedx.org/bom

The control-id annotation is just a string, but it is the join key between the cluster and the control register. When someone asks which control covers supply chain integrity, I answer SUPPLY-001, and the policy report for each deploy carries the same ID.

Rollout: Audit first, and read the output

Never start in Enforce. Run the policy in Audit on a staging cluster and read the reports. In my experience the first reading is humbling, because policies written from a checklist collide with workloads nobody remembered: an init container pulling an unsigned utility image, a vendor sidecar on a latest tag, a CronJob owned by a team that left. Count the violations by rule, fix the real ones, and write exceptions for the legitimate leftovers. Only then switch to Enforce, and do it namespace by namespace. Turning it on everywhere on day one is how a compliance project becomes the cause of a payments outage.

Beyond signatures, the baseline rules I apply to a regulated namespace come mostly from the Kubernetes Pod Security Standards. The ones I check hardest are pinned image digests instead of floating tags, runAsNonRoot, no privileged containers, and an owner label that names a team rather than a person. Resource limits belong on the list as well, for a more practical reason: a pod with no memory limit can starve its neighbours.

The admission controller is production infrastructure too

An admission webhook sits in the path of every deploy and every pod restart that matches it, so its own availability needs thought:

  • Replicas. Run the Kyverno admission controller with at least three replicas across zones and a PodDisruptionBudget. A single replica means any node drain can freeze deployments.
  • Failure policy. failurePolicy: Fail is the safer choice for security but turns an unreachable webhook into a blocked cluster. Ignore keeps the cluster moving but silently disables the control. I use Fail for the payments namespace and make sure the webhook is healthy through alerting, and I accept Ignore only where the control is advisory.
  • Scope. Exclude kube-system and the Kyverno namespace itself with namespace selectors. Otherwise a policy can block the very pods that make the policy engine run, and recovery becomes a manual job with kubectl and the webhook configuration.
  • Latency. Signature verification calls out to the registry and transparency log. Keep webhookTimeoutSeconds low enough that a slow Rekor lookup fails fast, and cache verification results. If the transparency log is unreachable during a scale-up event, new pods cannot start, so decide in advance whether that dependency is acceptable or whether you verify against a mirrored log.

Exceptions and break-glass

The first thing a good auditor asks about is exceptions. A policy engine with no sanctioned bypass invites people to disable it at 3 AM. Two paths cover most cases.

For planned, long-lived exceptions, use a Kyverno PolicyException, kept in Git, reviewed like any other change, and carrying an expiry date and an owner in its annotations:

apiVersion: kyverno.io/v2
kind: PolicyException
metadata:
  name: legacy-reporting-unsigned-image
  namespace: payments
  annotations:
    compliance.internal/approved-by: platform-lead
    compliance.internal/expires: "2027-01-31"
spec:
  exceptions:
    - policyName: payments-require-signed-image-with-sbom
      ruleNames: [verify-signature-and-sbom]
  match:
    any:
      - resources:
          kinds: [Pod]
          namespaces: [payments]
          names: ["legacy-reporting-*"]

For emergencies, the break-glass route is a documented, access-controlled procedure: a named on-call role applies a short-lived exception, an alert fires to the security channel the moment it is created, and a follow-up ticket is mandatory. The evidence an auditor wants is that the bypass was rare, approved, logged and removed. A scheduled job that lists expired or orphaned exceptions and opens tickets for them closes the loop.

Signed images and SBOMs: knowing what you run

Third-party risk in DORA reaches past the vendors you hold contracts with. Your Maven dependency tree is also a supplier list, and each entry in it is a party whose code runs inside your payment path.

On the Java side, the CycloneDX Maven plugin produces the SBOM during the build. In the pipeline, the image is pushed, Cosign signs its digest (a tag can be moved; a digest cannot), and the SBOM is attached as an attestation. A scanner such as Grype or Trivy reads the SBOM, and its result becomes an attestation too, so the admission policy above can later require it.

Once SBOMs are stored per release, a question like "which production images ship jackson-databind below a given version?" turns into a query rather than a round of messages to every team. That speed is the practical payoff, and it is what makes upgrade campaigns tractable. I wrote about one such case in Spring Boot 4.1 SSRF mitigation and gRPC auto-configuration, where knowing exactly which services were affected decided the order of work.

One limit deserves emphasis. A signed attestation proves who built the image and what the scanner reported at build time. Vulnerability data changes daily, so a clean scan from last month says little about today. Load stored SBOMs into a continuous monitor such as OWASP Dependency-Track, which re-evaluates them against fresh advisories and alerts when a component you already deployed becomes vulnerable. The build-time gate stops new problems; the monitor catches the old ones that age badly.

Resilience testing: prove the fallback fires

DORA expects regular testing of operational resilience, with deeper exercises for the more critical entities. A circuit breaker configuration is nowhere near a testing programme, and I would not present it as one. The building blocks, however, are code, and code can be exercised on every release.

First, the configuration should state its failure behaviour explicitly instead of inheriting defaults:

@Configuration
class PaymentGatewayResilienceConfig {

    @Bean
    CircuitBreakerConfig cardNetworkBreakerConfig() {
        return CircuitBreakerConfig.custom()
            .slidingWindowType(SlidingWindowType.TIME_BASED)
            .slidingWindowSize(30)
            .minimumNumberOfCalls(20)
            .failureRateThreshold(40f)
            .slowCallDurationThreshold(Duration.ofMillis(1200))
            .slowCallRateThreshold(60f)
            .waitDurationInOpenState(Duration.ofSeconds(20))
            .permittedNumberOfCallsInHalfOpenState(5)
            .recordExceptions(IOException.class, TimeoutException.class)
            .ignoreExceptions(CardDeclinedException.class)
            .build();
    }

    @Bean
    CircuitBreakerRegistry breakerRegistry(CircuitBreakerConfig cardNetworkBreakerConfig,
                                           ResilienceEvidenceRecorder recorder) {
        CircuitBreakerRegistry registry = CircuitBreakerRegistry.of(cardNetworkBreakerConfig);
        registry.getEventPublisher().onEntryAdded(added ->
            added.getAddedEntry().getEventPublisher()
                .onStateTransition(recorder::recordTransition));
        return registry;
    }
}

Look at ignoreExceptions(CardDeclinedException.class). A declined card is a legitimate business outcome. If it counts as a downstream failure, an ordinary evening of customers with empty accounts can open the breaker and take down a healthy path. It is an easy mistake to make when exception types are shared across layers.

Second, the drill. A test in the release pipeline starts a stub of the downstream service (WireMock handles this well), injects latency and errors, and asserts what an operator would observe: the breaker opens within the expected window, the fallback queues the payment rather than dropping it, and the readiness probe reports the degraded state truthfully. The test writes a JSON file with the scenario, thresholds, observed time-to-open and fallback outcome, and the pipeline archives it.

Probes matter here more than they get credit for. A liveness probe that restarts a pod because a dependency is slow converts a degraded service into a restart storm. I keep liveness shallow (the JVM responds), tie readiness to the ability to serve, including breaker state for hard dependencies, and add a startup probe so a slow Spring context start is not killed halfway. Setting management.endpoint.health.probes.enabled=true gives you separate liveness and readiness groups.

Staging chaos experiments, such as killing pods and adding network delay, cover what a stub cannot. Schedule them so they run regardless of anyone's goodwill; the scheduled run's output is the evidence.

Audit trails: Actuator events and OpenTelemetry

Logging requirements boil down to one question: after an incident, can you reconstruct who did what, when, and which systems were involved? Free-form application logs rarely manage it. Structured audit events with trace correlation do.

Spring Boot Actuator already includes an audit event model. I publish domain-significant actions through it and stamp each with the current trace ID, so an audit record leads straight to the distributed trace:

@Component
class PaymentAuditPublisher {

    private final ApplicationEventPublisher publisher;
    private final Tracer tracer;

    PaymentAuditPublisher(ApplicationEventPublisher publisher, Tracer tracer) {
        this.publisher = publisher;
        this.tracer = tracer;
    }

    void paymentLimitOverridden(String operatorId, String accountRef, BigDecimal newLimit) {
        Span current = tracer.currentSpan();
        String traceId = current != null ? current.context().traceId() : "no-active-trace";

        Map<String, Object> details = Map.of(
            "accountRef", accountRef,
            "newLimit", newLimit.toPlainString(),
            "traceId", traceId,
            "controlId", "ACCESS-014"
        );
        publisher.publishEvent(
            new AuditApplicationEvent(operatorId, "PAYMENT_LIMIT_OVERRIDE", details));
    }
}

Two choices in that snippet matter more than the syntax. accountRef is an opaque reference, never an IBAN or a name, because audit logs get copied into tools and tickets, and personal data in them becomes a separate compliance problem. And controlId links the event back to the register, the same trick as the Kyverno annotation.

Back the AuditEventRepository with durable, append-only storage; the default in-memory one forgets everything on restart. Ship events to storage with retention locks. Traces flow through OpenTelemetry to your backend, and my post on distributed tracing with OpenTelemetry in Spring Boot covers the propagation details, while the observability guardrails post covers what to redact before telemetry leaves the process.

Both regimes also put clocks on incident reporting. As I read them, DORA's major-incident flow has an initial notification, an intermediate report and a final report, and NIS2 has an early warning, an incident notification and a final report, all with short deadlines. Confirm exact deadlines and classification criteria with your compliance team. The engineering contribution is modest but real: timestamps. The moment an alert is classified as a potential major incident has to be recorded automatically, since every deadline counts from a moment someone will later need to prove.

Backups: an untested backup is a rumour

Almost every team has backups. Far fewer know how long a restore takes or how much data it would cost them. Recovery time objective (RTO) is how long you can be down, and recovery point objective (RPO) is how much data you can lose. The business agrees to both numbers, and engineering should measure them rather than assert them.

I schedule a restore drill against a scratch database that fails the job if either number misses its target:

@Component
class RestoreDrillRunner {

    private static final Duration RTO_TARGET = Duration.ofMinutes(45);
    private static final Duration RPO_TARGET = Duration.ofMinutes(5);

    private final BackupCatalog catalog;
    private final JdbcTemplate scratchDb;
    private final DrillReportWriter reportWriter;

    RestoreDrillResult runDrill() throws IOException, InterruptedException {
        Instant drillStart = Instant.now();
        BackupSet latest = catalog.latestVerifiedBackup();

        Process restore = new ProcessBuilder(
            "pg_restore", "--clean", "--if-exists", "--no-owner",
            "--dbname", scratchDb.getDataSource().getConnection().getMetaData().getURL(),
            latest.location().toString())
            .inheritIO()
            .start();
        if (restore.waitFor() != 0) {
            throw new IllegalStateException("pg_restore failed for backup " + latest.id());
        }

        Instant newestRestoredRow = scratchDb.queryForObject(
            "SELECT max(created_at) FROM payment_ledger", Instant.class);
        Instant liveCutoff = latest.captureCompletedAt();

        Duration measuredRto = Duration.between(drillStart, Instant.now());
        Duration measuredRpo = Duration.between(newestRestoredRow, liveCutoff.plus(catalog.walLagFor(latest)));

        RestoreDrillResult result = new RestoreDrillResult(
            latest.id(), measuredRto, measuredRpo,
            measuredRto.compareTo(RTO_TARGET) <= 0,
            measuredRpo.compareTo(RPO_TARGET) <= 0);
        reportWriter.write(result);
        return result;
    }
}

Be clear about what that number represents. It times the restore step on a database sized like production. A real recovery also includes failover, DNS, cache warm-up and verification, so add those to the drill as you automate them. Use representative data volume, because restoring an empty schema proves nothing. Reports go to the same evidence store as everything else, and a missed target opens a ticket. Pair this with the discipline from zero-downtime database migrations with Flyway, because a restore that lands on a schema your current code cannot read counts as a failed drill too.

The pipeline: evidence on every deploy

Now the pieces connect. This condensed GitHub Actions job shows the shape; adapt it to your own CI:

jobs:
  build-and-evidence:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      id-token: write
      contents: read
      packages: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Build, test, generate SBOM
        run: ./mvnw -B verify org.cyclonedx:cyclonedx-maven-plugin:makeAggregateBom
      - name: Build and push image
        run: |
          docker build -t "$IMAGE:$GITHUB_SHA" .
          docker push "$IMAGE:$GITHUB_SHA"
          echo "DIGEST=$(docker inspect --format='{{index .RepoDigests 0}}' $IMAGE:$GITHUB_SHA)" >> "$GITHUB_ENV"
      - name: Sign image and attach SBOM attestation
        run: |
          cosign sign --yes "$DIGEST"
          cosign attest --yes --type cyclonedx --predicate target/bom.json "$DIGEST"
      - name: Vulnerability scan (fails on critical)
        run: grype sbom:target/bom.json --fail-on critical -o json > evidence/vuln-scan.json
      - name: Admission policy dry run
        run: kyverno test policies/ --detailed-results > evidence/policy-test.txt
      - name: Resilience drill
        run: ./mvnw -B -Pdrill verify -Ddrill.output=evidence/resilience-drill.json
      - name: Bundle and store evidence
        run: |
          tar czf "evidence-$GITHUB_SHA.tgz" evidence/ target/bom.json
          aws s3 cp "evidence-$GITHUB_SHA.tgz" "s3://$EVIDENCE_BUCKET/$GITHUB_SHA/"

"Immutable bucket" is easy to say and easy to get wrong, so here is what I would specify. Enable S3 Object Lock in compliance mode, not governance mode, because governance mode lets a privileged user lift the lock. Set the retention period to whatever your record-keeping obligations require; that number comes from compliance, not from engineering. Give the CI role write-only access, give a small audit role read access, and let nobody hold delete rights. Link each object to its deploy by keying it on the commit SHA and recording the image digest inside the bundle, so one path leads from a running pod back to the evidence. The restore drill runs on its own schedule and writes to the same bucket under a dated prefix.

Last comes the unglamorous piece that decides whether any of this works: a single page indexing controls to evidence. Control ID, requirement area, mechanism, artifact location, owner. If a control has no row pointing at a bucket path, treat that as a defect and put it on the backlog.

A RACI that fits in sprint planning

Compliance RACIs usually fail by being drawn for an org chart instead of a sprint. This one is drawn for a sprint board, one line per type of work:

Work item Responsible Accountable Consulted Informed
Admission policy change Platform engineer Platform lead Security, service teams Compliance
Policy exception approval Platform engineer Platform lead Service owner, security Compliance
Service audit events and trace fields Backend engineer on the service Service tech lead Security, data protection Compliance
Resilience drill scenarios Backend engineer, SRE Engineering manager Business owner of the payment flow Risk
Restore drill and RTO/RPO targets SRE, DBA Head of engineering Business owner, compliance Risk, audit
Asset register and criticality tiers Service owners Head of engineering Risk, compliance Audit
Control register and evidence index Compliance engineer Compliance lead Platform, backend Audit
Interpretation of regulatory text Legal and compliance Chief compliance officer Engineering Everyone

The last row matters most. Engineers implement the control as written by the people who interpret the regulation; they do not interpret it themselves. The sprint rule I push is that every control change is a ticket whose acceptance criterion is phrased as evidence: "done" means the pipeline produces artifact Y and the index row points at it, not "we configured it."

Start here this week

Pick one service in your payments namespace and do three things before the next sprint review. Write a single Kyverno or Gatekeeper policy that checks image signatures, and run it in audit mode. Add the CycloneDX plugin and store the SBOM against the deploy commit. Create the control index with exactly two rows, each pointing at a real bucket path. Two controls with genuine evidence are worth more than forty in a spreadsheet, and the third one gets easier. For regulated integrations seen from the code level, my PSD2 API development notes are a useful companion, and if you want to compare setups, my details are in the contact section.

Related Articles

  • Distributed Tracing with OpenTelemetry in Spring Boot
  • Transactional Outbox and Idempotent Consumers for Payment Systems
  • OpenBanking PSD2 API Development

title: Your On-Device Model Is a Deploy Artifact, Not a Library
description:
