title: Building a small web app to last: the future of CountMyDays
description:
Over the last few posts I've written about the unglamorous parts of building CountMyDays: counting days without off-by-one bugs, streak counters that survive midnight and DST, and "tomorrow" vs "in 2 days" labels that respect the reader's time zone. This one is different. It's less about code and more about intent: what this little app is for, and how I want it to age.

What CountMyDays is

CountMyDays is a free web app for two simple questions:

  • How long until something? A wedding, a trip, an exam, a birthday.
  • How long since something? A new habit, a quit date, an anniversary.

You type a name and a date, and you get a countdown or a count-up with a progress bar. You can share it with one link, add it to your calendar, put it in fullscreen on a big screen, or install it to your home screen like an app. There are no ads, and you don't need an account to start. If you want your countdowns on more than one device, you can sign in with a passwordless magic link.

It's built by one developer in Iceland on React 19, Supabase and Vercel. That's the whole team.

Why "futureproof" matters for a countdown app

A countdown is a promise about the future. Someone creates one for a wedding that's 400 days away and sends the link to their family. That link has to still work, and still show the right number, on day 1 and on day 400.

That's a higher bar than it sounds. Most small web apps are judged on day one: does it look nice, is it fast? A countdown is judged on the day the event arrives. So the question I keep asking is not "what can I add?" but "what will still be true in two years?"

Here are the principles I want CountMyDays to keep, whatever else changes.

1. The core stays free and needs no account

Creating a countdown, sharing it and counting days since something should never sit behind a sign-up or a paywall. Guest mode isn't a trial; it's the product. Accounts exist for convenience (sync across devices), not as a gate.

This also keeps the app honest. If the basic thing works without me knowing who you are, there's less to go wrong and less to protect.

2. Your data is yours

A countdown is personal. You should be able to take your data with you. Today the app has a backup code and a downloadable text archive with one-click restore. I want that kind of exit door to stay a first-class feature: plain, readable formats over clever ones, and no lock-in.

3. Links that keep working

A shared link is a small contract. The direction is simple:

  • Share URLs should be stable. If the app changes shape, old links should still land somewhere sensible.
  • The number on the page has to be computed in the viewer's time zone, using calendar days, not raw milliseconds. (That's what the earlier posts in this series were really about.)
  • A finished countdown shouldn't just break. It should move into a "passed" state and become a memory rather than an error page.

4. Boring, standard web tech

I'd rather lean on the platform than on a pile of dependencies. A few examples from this series:

// Wording comes from the platform, in any locale the browser supports
new Intl.RelativeTimeFormat('pl', { numeric: 'auto' }).format(1, 'day');
// "jutro"

// Calendar-day maths in UTC, where every day is exactly 24 hours
const dayIndex = (y, m, d) => Date.UTC(y, m - 1, d) / 86400000;

Intl, Date.UTC, localStorage, .ics calendar files, service workers and web app manifests are standards. They'll still be here long after today's favourite library has a new major version. When the Temporal API is widely available, the date code can get even simpler without changing what users see.

The stack is deliberately small: a React front end, a Postgres database with row-level security, and static hosting with a few server routes. Small enough for one person to understand completely, which matters more than any single feature.

5. Offline and installable, as a habit of thought

A countdown is something you glance at, often on your phone, sometimes on bad Wi-Fi. Thinking "what happens with no network?" early makes the whole app better: local-first data for guests, cached assets, and sync as a bonus rather than a requirement. Progressive Web App support is part of that, and keeping it working well is ongoing work rather than a box I ticked once.

6. Accessible and calm

No ads, no pop-ups, no dark patterns. Big, readable numbers. A compact view for people with many countdowns and a spacious one for people with a single important date. Accessibility is never "done", and I'd like it to keep improving with every change rather than in one big push.

Resilience: fixing things in public

Here's my favourite part of writing on dev.to. After my first post about the app's architecture, a reader left a thoughtful comment pointing out a weakness in how the live-updating shared view used Supabase Realtime broadcasts. In short: on a public channel, the app trusted the content of broadcast messages a bit too much.

They were right. Nothing in the database could be changed or lost, but it's worth fixing properly, and that fix is underway. The idea behind it is a good general lesson, so here it is:

Treat a realtime message as a signal, not as data. When something says "this changed", go and fetch the real state from the database, where access rules apply.

channel.on('broadcast', { event: '*' }, () => {
  // Don't render the payload. Just refetch the source of truth.
  refetchSharedItem();
});

With that change, viewers still see updates live, but nothing on screen comes from an untrusted message. Tighter channel permissions are a possible next step after that.

So, a sincere thank you to that reader, and to everyone who has read, commented on or shared these posts. A small app gets more resilient when the community is generous enough to point out its weak spots.

What's next

I won't give you a roadmap with dates, because roadmaps for one-person projects are mostly fiction. What I can promise is a direction:

  • keep the free, no-account core
  • keep shared links working and numbers correct
  • keep the stack small and standard
  • keep improving offline support, accessibility and privacy
  • keep fixing things openly when people find problems

If any of that sounds useful, try it: create a countdown to something you're looking forward to, or a "days since" for a habit you're proud of, at countmydays.to. If you find a bug or have an idea, I'd genuinely love to hear it in the comments or on X at @countmydays_to.

Thanks for reading, and for counting along.

title: TIL: Map the Node Roles Before Installing GBase Database
description:
When reviewing a GBase Database(GBase 8a) cluster installation, I once saw three host lists that looked like unrelated inventories: three scheduling nodes, four data nodes, and three GCware nodes.

The problem wasn't necessarily the number of machines. It was the assumption that each list represented a completely separate group of servers.

With GBase Database(GBase 8a MPP Cluster), the first step in a cluster deployment should be to map the node roles before running the installer.

1. Understand the Three Host Lists in demo.options

The host lists in demo.options describe different cluster roles. They are not necessarily three independent pools of machines.

  • coordinateHost: Hosts running GCluster, which handles SQL requests and coordinates distributed query execution.
  • dataHost: Hosts running GNode, which provides data storage and query execution.
  • gcwareHost: Hosts running GCware, which manages cluster metadata, topology, and consistency-related coordination.

Depending on the deployment architecture, one machine may serve multiple roles. The actual role assignment must follow the requirements of the target GBase Database release and cluster design.

Here is an illustrative configuration:

installPrefix = /opt
coordinateHost = 192.168.146.20,192.168.146.21,192.168.146.22
coordinateHostNodeID = 20,21,22
dataHost = 192.168.146.20,192.168.146.21,192.168.146.22,192.168.146.23
gcwareHost = 192.168.146.20,192.168.146.21,192.168.146.22
gcwareHostNodeID = 20,21,22
dbaUser = gbase
dbaGroup = gbase

This example shows three hosts assigned both coordinator and GCware roles, with four hosts listed for data services. It is an example of role mapping, not a universal production topology.

Before copying it into your environment, confirm the required host-list format and NodeID rules in the documentation for your specific GBase Database version.

2. Check IP Addresses, Hostnames, and NodeIDs

A role map is only useful when its entries correspond to real, reachable machines.

If the configuration uses IP addresses, verify that each address belongs to the intended host and that the required network connections work.

If it uses hostnames, check name resolution on every relevant node. The hostnames must resolve consistently to the intended addresses, and SSH connectivity must work wherever the installer requires remote access.

NodeID handling also deserves attention. Some configurations derive or assign IDs according to release-specific rules, but you should not assume that an IP address's last octet is always the correct NodeID. Check the target release's demo.options example and installation manual.

Two common configuration mistakes are:

  • A host appears in dataHost, but the associated role or NodeID configuration does not match the intended cluster topology.
  • An IP address changes while a related node identifier or other configuration entry remains unchanged.

Either can cause problems during installation or cluster registration, depending on the release and deployment state.

3. Validate the Role Map Before Installation

Before starting a GBase Database cluster installation, create a simple table:

Host or IP GCluster GNode GCware
192.168.146.20 Yes Yes Yes
192.168.146.21 Yes Yes Yes
192.168.146.22 Yes Yes Yes
192.168.146.23 No Yes No

Treat this as a planning worksheet, not a recommended topology for every production system.

Then verify three things:

  1. Role consistency: The entries in coordinateHost, dataHost, and gcwareHost match the intended deployment.
  2. Network reachability: Each listed host exists, resolves correctly where hostnames are used, and is reachable through the required network paths.
  3. Remote access: SSH authentication and permissions meet the installer's requirements for the relevant accounts.

A single-node or small test deployment can help validate installation parameters, but it does not prove that a multi-node production topology, network configuration, or high-availability design is correct.

4. Diagnose Failures by Installation Stage

When a GBase Database installation fails, identify the stage before changing configuration.

  • Configuration validation: Check host-list syntax, required fields, and NodeID definitions.
  • Remote distribution or login: Check SSH access, name resolution, account permissions, and connectivity.
  • Cluster registration: Compare the configured roles with the nodes already installed and the cluster's actual state.

The key is not to assume that every failure comes from a mismatch between the three lists. Review the installer output and the relevant node logs to identify the actual cause.

5. What If the Cluster Is Already Partially Installed?

If the installation has already progressed partway, editing demo.options alone may not resolve the problem. The configuration file may no longer describe the state of the nodes already installed or registered.

First, document:

  • Which nodes have been installed successfully
  • Which services and roles are present on each node
  • Which nodes failed and at what stage
  • Whether the cluster has already registered those nodes

Then determine whether the appropriate recovery path is to rerun the installation or add nodes to the existing cluster. For a supported node-add operation, follow the release-specific procedure and configuration format, including gcChangeInfo.xml where required.

Avoid rebuilding the entire cluster or modifying registration settings until you understand the existing state and the supported recovery procedure.

Final Takeaway

For GBase Database(GBase 8a MPP Cluster), demo.options is more than an installation parameter file. It describes how hosts are assigned to cluster roles.

Map the hosts first, validate connectivity and identifiers, and only then start the installation. A few minutes spent checking the role map can prevent much more expensive troubleshooting later.

Always confirm the exact configuration rules against the documentation for your GBase Database release.

title: GBase Database Installation Errors: 5 Package and License Problems and How to Fix Them
description:
Summary: Troubleshooting GBase Database(GBase 8a) installation failures starts with identifying the failing layer. This guide covers five common problems involving CPU architecture, operating system validation, License loading, License binding, and Python interpreter compatibility, with practical commands to help narrow down the cause.

When a GBase Database(GBase 8a) installation fails, the instinct is often to download another package and rerun the installer. But repeated attempts rarely help when the underlying problem has not been identified.

Package compatibility, operating system checks, License authorization, and Python runtime errors belong to different troubleshooting layers. Identifying the correct layer is usually faster than guessing.

Here are five common GBase Database installation problems, how to investigate them, and what to verify before trying again.

1. Cannot execute binary file: Check CPU Architecture

This error often indicates that the executable does not match the target system's CPU architecture.

For example, an x86_64 package may have been selected for an aarch64 server, or vice versa.

Start by checking the host architecture and the available installation package:

uname -m
ls /opt/GBase8a_MPP_Cluster-*.tar.bz2

Common platform mappings include:

  • Intel, Hygon, and Zhaoxin: generally x86_64
  • Kunpeng and Phytium: generally aarch64
  • Loongson and Sunway: confirm the required package through the appropriate vendor channel

Compare the architecture reported by uname -m with the architecture specified in the package name and release documentation.

The fix: Obtain the correct package for the target architecture. Installer flags cannot make a binary built for an incompatible instruction set run natively.

2. operating system is 'xxx', must be centos7: Check OS Validation

An operating system validation error means that the installer rejected the detected platform. It does not automatically prove that the underlying kernel is incompatible.

Start by inspecting the kernel version:

uname -r

Then verify the operating system release and the compatibility requirements of the selected GBase Database package.

Some distributions may have a kernel environment similar to a supported platform but report a different operating system identity. In that situation, the installer may reject the OS during its validation step.

For releases that document -i as an option to skip the relevant operating system check, the installation command may look like this:

./gcinstall.py -i --silent=demo.options

Use this option only after confirming that the target environment is genuinely compatible and that bypassing the check is supported.

If the kernel or platform is actually incompatible, select the correct package family, such as the appropriate redhat7 or redhat8 build, according to the release compatibility matrix.

Important: Skipping an OS identity check does not change binary compatibility or make an unsupported environment supported.

3. gcadmin Shows close: Verify License Loading

A GBase Database cluster may have installed its binaries and started services without completing the required License authorization.

If gcadmin reports close and the application cannot connect, check the License before assuming that the network or installation package is the cause.

Where supported by the installed release, run:

chkLicense -n 10.10.10.1,10.10.10.2 -u gbase -p '<DBA_PASSWORD>'
gcadmin

Replace the example addresses and credentials with the actual values. Avoid placing real passwords in shell history or shared logs.

Review the following License fields:

  • is_exist: Indicates whether the License file exists.
  • version: Reports the License category, such as business or trial.
  • is_valid: Indicates whether the License is valid.

A file can exist without being valid, so is_exist alone is not sufficient.

Also check whether the commercial License was passed during installation using --license_file, if that parameter applies to your release.

If the License was not loaded, follow the documented loading procedure for the installed version. Restart services only when required by that procedure, then verify the License and cluster state again.

The fix: Establish whether the issue is a missing License, an invalid License, or another cluster-state problem before deciding on the next action.

4. is_valid: no After a Node Replacement: Check License Binding

A License that was previously valid may become invalid after a node replacement or another infrastructure change.

For the relevant GBase Database(GBase 8a) releases, License authorization can be associated with the ESN and SSH private key of the GCware node. Changes to the machine, key material, or operating system may therefore affect the existing authorization.

Before applying for a replacement License, confirm:

  1. The target GBase Database version.
  2. The current GCware node IP address and ESN.
  3. The required SSH key information.
  4. The License requirements documented for that release.

If reissuance is required, submit the correct node information through the approved License process. Do not assume that copying a License file from another cluster will work.

The fix: Treat node replacement as a potential License-impacting change and verify authorization before returning the cluster to service.

5. Python SyntaxError: Check the Interpreter

A Python syntax error during installation can indicate that the script is being executed with the wrong interpreter.

For example, a script written for Python 2 may fail when invoked through Python 3. The fact that Python 2 is installed does not prove that the installer is actually using it.

Check the default interpreter:

which python
python -V

Then check the environment used by the database installation account:

su - gbase -c 'which python; python -V'

Compare the results with the requirements for the specific GBase Database release and installation package.

If the installer requires Python 2 but python resolves to Python 3, correct the runtime configuration according to the supported installation procedure.

Do not assume that invoking python2 gcinstall.py is equivalent to running the documented entry point. Some installation workflows depend on environment preparation performed by the expected command or launcher.

On CentOS 8 and RHEL 8 environments, also verify any required Python packages and dependencies against the release-specific installation guide.

The fix: Confirm the interpreter, runtime dependencies, and supported installer entry point before rerunning the installation.

A Repeatable GBase Database Troubleshooting Workflow

The fastest way to troubleshoot GBase Database installation problems is to identify the failing layer before making another change.

Use this sequence:

  1. CPU architecture: Does the package match the target instruction set?
  2. OS compatibility: Does the platform meet the package requirements, and is the installer rejecting only the OS identity?
  3. License authorization: Was the License loaded, and is it valid for the target environment?
  4. Python runtime: Is the installer using the expected interpreter and dependencies?
  5. Verification: After correcting the cause, rerun the appropriate step and verify the result.

Keep a record of the original error, the confirmed root cause, the change made, and the final verification result. These notes help prevent the same problem from recurring during future installations or cluster expansions.

Conclusion

GBase Database installation failures can look unrelated, but many can be traced to a small number of compatibility and authorization checks.

For GBase Database(GBase 8a), start with the CPU architecture, verify the operating system, inspect License status, and confirm the Python runtime. Apply one correction at a time, and validate the result before proceeding.

The goal is not simply to make the installer finish. It is to establish a compatible, authorized, and supportable database environment.

For version-dependent parameters and recovery procedures, always consult the installation manual for the exact release you are deploying.

title: What are cheaper alternatives to AWS for GPU training?
description:
The cheaper alternatives to AWS for GPU training are platforms that list H100 hours well below the $6.88 an H100 costs inside an on-demand AWS p5.48xlarge: Nodus at $2.60, Modal at $3.95, and Lambda and RunPod Secure Cloud at $3.99. Nodus can also connect your AWS account and, in Beta, run your jobs there first, so you spend AWS credits before you spend cash.

If you hold AWS credits, a Reserved Instance or a Savings Plan, or terabytes of data in S3, staying on AWS can still be right. The sections below show where the line falls.

Is AWS actually expensive for GPU training?

At on-demand list price, yes. We read the official AWS price list for us-east-1 on October 26, 2026: p5.48xlarge (8 x NVIDIA H100) is $55.04 per hour, which is $6.88 per H100-hour. p5en.48xlarge (8 x NVIDIA H200) is $63.296 per hour, or $7.912 per H200-hour. The A100 machines are p4d.24xlarge at $21.9576 per hour and p4de.24xlarge at $27.44705.

Those rates come from the EC2 on-demand pricing page and its public price list. Hardware details are on the P5 and P4 pages.


At list prices, an H100 hour costs 42 to 62 percent less outside AWS.

List price is not what everyone pays. Teams with Reserved Instances, Savings Plans or a negotiated discount pay less per hour, and the gaps below shrink for them.

Which platforms are cheaper than AWS per H100 hour?

Four alternatives publish lower H100 rates than AWS on-demand:

Platform H100 (per GPU-hr, list) How it bills After the work finishes Source
AWS p5.48xlarge, us-east-1 $6.88 per instance-hour, 8 GPUs billed until you stop it EC2 on-demand pricing
Nodus H100 SXM $2.60 while the Job runs the Job ends when your command exits Nodus pricing
Modal H100 $3.95 per second no charge between function calls Modal pricing
Lambda 8x H100 SXM $3.99 one-minute increments billed until you terminate it Lambda pricing, Lambda billing
RunPod Secure Cloud H100 SXM $3.99 per second billed until the Pod stops RunPod pricing, RunPod Pod pricing

Prices checked October 26, 2026. Nodus is listed at $2.60/hr on the Nodus pricing page; Modal's per-second H100 rate multiplies out to $3.949/hr.

RunPod also lists a cheaper Community Cloud tier on the same page. We use Secure Cloud here because it is the closer match to AWS on-demand for a long run.

The worked example is the one most teams ask about: 8 x H100 for 10 hours, rate times 8 GPUs times 10 hours, nothing else added.

Platform 8 x H100, 10 h at list
AWS p5.48xlarge $550.40
Lambda $319.20
RunPod Secure Cloud $319.20
Modal $316.00
Nodus $208.00


The same 80 GPU-hours cost $342.40 less on Nodus than on an on-demand p5 at list.

Storage, data transfer and idle time come on top. Our cost per finished job breakdown adds those to the same 8 x H100 run.

Should you spend your AWS credits before switching?

Yes. Credits you already hold cost nothing at the margin, so moving work elsewhere while they expire is paying twice. The useful question is what to do with the work that does not fit inside them.

Nodus answers that with a connected account. The read-only connection is an IAM role that only Nodus can assume, with an external id unique to your connection, limited to listing instances, daily spend, credits left and GPU quota. It never creates anything. The run work in your own account Beta adds a second role that can launch and terminate only machines Nodus tags as its own.

With both roles in place, the flow is short:

  1. Set a monthly credit limit on the account in the Nodus console.
  2. Submit Jobs and Workspaces as usual. Single-node work goes to your AWS account first, up to the limit.
  3. When the account is full or out of credit, work moves to Nodus capacity, or waits for your approval if you chose that.

Sandboxes and multi-node runs always use Nodus capacity, so plan large distributed jobs as cash, not credit. The cloud-accounts docs list every permission both roles ask for.


$10,000 buys 181.7 hours of 8 x H100 on an on-demand p5 and 480.8 hours on Nodus.

The chart is $10,000 divided by each 8-GPU hourly rate. It shows why the order matters: once credit runs out, every overflow hour on AWS costs more than 2.6 times what it costs on Nodus at list.

Why are teams moving GPU training off AWS?

Sticker price is the obvious reason, but three others show up in the bill and the calendar.

GPU quota is the first. AWS limits how much of each GPU machine family an account can run per region, and more needs a request through AWS Service Quotas. When a connected account hits its quota, Nodus skips that machine family in that region for an hour and runs the work elsewhere, so a quota wall stops being a blocked job.

Idle time is the second. Instance-style billing, which covers AWS, Lambda instances and RunPod Pods, charges until someone stops the machine. Lambda's billing docs say instances are billed "for as long as they're running, regardless if they're actively being used." On an 8-GPU machine, one forgotten hour is 8 GPU-hours. Job-style billing ends when the work does.

Interruptions are the third. EC2 Spot is cheaper than on-demand, but when AWS reclaims the machine you build the save, replace and restore steps yourself. On Nodus, a reclaimed interruptible machine restarts elsewhere with its /nodus/state directory restored, as our spot preemption guide walks through.

If your real question is the managed platform rather than raw compute, read Nodus vs AWS SageMaker instead.

When is AWS still the better choice?

Pick AWS if you hold credits that will expire. Spend them first, then send the overflow somewhere cheaper. Connecting the account to Nodus lets you do both without changing how you submit work.

Pick AWS if a large dataset already lives there and you train on it repeatedly. Data transfer out of AWS to the internet is $0.09 per GB for the first 10 TB a month and $0.085 per GB for the next 40 TB, per the EC2 on-demand pricing page. Pulling a 20 TB dataset out once is 10,240 GB at $0.09 plus 10,240 GB at $0.085, about $1,792. Copy it once and that is a one-time cost; pull it every run and it adds up fast.

Pick AWS if you already pay for a Reserved Instance or Savings Plan on p5. That commitment lowers your effective rate below the $6.88 list, and you pay for it whether you use it or not.

Pick AWS if your team builds on SageMaker features such as managed hyperparameter tuning, Pipelines or Model Monitor. Those are products, not just compute, and the switching cost is real.

Pick AWS if you need a large H100 cluster for fixed dates. EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML let you reserve GPU capacity for a set window in advance.

How do you add Nodus without leaving AWS?

Keep AWS as it is and connect it, then send new jobs through Nodus. These commands are copied from the install, cloud-accounts and quickstart docs:

pip install nodus-compute
nodus login
nodus create cloudaccount aws-main --provider aws --account-id 123456789012
# after the read-only and execute CloudFormation stacks show CREATE_COMPLETE:
nodus cloud connect aws aws-main --credit-limit 500
nodus run --name first-train --gpu H100 --image nodus/pytorch \
  --max-cost 300 -- python train.py

--max-cost 300 puts a hard $300 limit on that Job. With the account connected, the Job runs in AWS while the $500 monthly limit lasts and on Nodus capacity after that. Full rates are on the Nodus pricing page, and our RunPod alternatives guide compares the other options.

FAQ

Does moving training off AWS add data transfer fees on the other side?

Not for getting data in. AWS lists data transfer in at $0.00 per GB, and RunPod's Pod pricing docs say Pods carry no ingress or egress fees. The fee that matters is AWS's charge to move data out, so copy a dataset once rather than streaming it every run.

How is the AWS credit limit counted in Nodus?

Nodus spends the limit at its own list estimate for each machine, which can differ from what AWS bills you, so set it a little below the credit you hold. The default period renews each calendar month in UTC; a Total period spends it once.

Which AWS regions can Nodus run work in?

The execute role launches machines in the stack's region, which must be us-east-1, us-east-2 or us-west-2. Sandboxes and multi-node runs use Nodus capacity either way.

What happens to my machines if I disconnect the account?

Disconnect in Nodus first. Nodus stops placing work there, moves running work to the next source and terminates the machines it started. Then delete the execute stack in AWS.

Originally published on the Nodus blog.

title: GBase Database Commercial Installation: A Step-by-Step Guide to License Loading
description:
Summary: Installing GBase Database(GBase 8a) commercial edition requires more than extracting a package and starting services. This guide covers package compatibility checks, license preparation, cluster installation, license validation, and post-installation verification to help prevent avoidable deployment delays.

A commercial installation of GBase Database(GBase 8a) is not necessarily difficult. The real challenge is coordinating the installation package, target environment, node information, and License authorization before deployment begins.

For clusters with three or more nodes, a clear installation sequence can prevent a common problem: the software is installed, but the cluster is not ready for production because the License has not been loaded or validated correctly.

The recommended approach is to confirm compatibility first, prepare the License against the intended environment, install the cluster, and verify the final state before handover.

Step 1: Request the Commercial License Before Installation

Start with the License application process.

For the relevant GBase Database(GBase 8a) releases, commercial License authorization may be associated with the ESN and SSH private key of the GCware node. Confirm the exact requirements for your target release and provide the correct node information when requesting the License.

Applying too late can delay the project. If a relevant node or key changes during deployment, the existing License may need to be reissued.

Store the License file in an appropriate location, such as /opt, and ensure that the installation user can access it without exposing it to unauthorized users.

Before proceeding, record:

  • Target GBase Database version
  • Intended GCware node information
  • Required License type
  • License file location
  • License validity period, where applicable

Step 2: Check CPU Architecture, Operating System, and Python

Before extracting the package, verify three compatibility dimensions: processor architecture, operating system, and Python runtime.

Run the following commands on the target host:

uname -m
grep -E '^(NAME|VERSION_ID)=' /etc/os-release
python -V

Interpret the results against the compatibility matrix for the exact GBase Database release.

CPU architecture

  • Intel, Hygon, and Zhaoxin platforms generally use x86_64.
  • Kunpeng and Phytium platforms generally use aarch64.
  • Loongson and Sunway platforms may require separately confirmed packages.

Operating system

Package selection depends on the supported operating system release and kernel environment. For example, certain CentOS 8, openEuler, and Kylin V10 environments may use a redhat8 package family, while certain CentOS 7 environments use redhat7.

Do not assume that similarly named distributions are interchangeable. Confirm the exact supported combinations before installation.

Python runtime

The required Python interpreter depends on the installer and commercial package edition. The FREE edition and commercial builds may have different runtime requirements, and Python 3 builds may require separate licensing.

Verify the Python version on every node, not just the Coordinator. A runtime mismatch can cause deployment scripts to fail even when the binary package itself is correct.

Step 3: Extract the Installation Package

Copy the installation archive to /opt and extract it using the installation account and directory permissions required by your deployment procedure.

For example:

cp /tmp/GBase8a_MPP_Cluster-*.tar.bz2 /opt
cd /opt
tar -jxvf GBase8a_MPP_Cluster-*.tar.bz2
cd gcinstall

Confirm that the archive matches the target architecture, operating system, and release. If multiple package archives exist in the directory, identify the intended package explicitly rather than relying on a wildcard.

Step 4: Prepare the Installation Environment and Configuration

Use the environment preparation script supplied with the package when required by the release.

For example:

python SetSysEnv.py --dbaUser=gbase --installPrefix=/opt/gbase

Confirm the supported interpreter and script parameters in the package documentation before execution.

Next, prepare demo.options. The following is an illustrative configuration based on the fields in this deployment workflow:

installPrefix=/opt/gbase
dbaUser=gbase
dbaPwd=<DBA_PASSWORD>
sshPort=22
rootPwd=<ROOT_PASSWORD>

Replace the placeholders with the required credentials. Do not store real passwords in published documentation, shared scripts, or unrestricted configuration files.

The actual required fields and their names must match the demo.options format for your installed release. Configure the SSH port to match the target hosts; if the hosts use a non-default port, do not leave it set to 22.

Also verify SSH connectivity and authentication before starting a multi-node installation. Password parsing and special-character handling depend on the installer and configuration mechanism. Rather than weakening credentials, follow the supported escaping or credential-handling procedure for the target version.

Step 5: Load the License During Commercial Installation

For releases that support this syntax, specify the commercial License file with --license_file:

./gcinstall.py --license_file=/opt/gbase.lic --silent=demo.options

In this example:

  • --license_file specifies the License file.
  • --silent specifies the installation parameter file.

Check the exact command syntax and License loading behavior in the manual for your target GBase Database release.

The important principle is to plan License authorization as part of installation rather than assuming it can be added later without further checks. If the License was not loaded, determine the supported recovery procedure before considering a reinstall.

Step 6: Verify Services, License Status, and Cluster State

After installation, verify the environment in a controlled sequence.

If the relevant profile and service-management commands apply to your release, the workflow may resemble the following:

source ~/.gbase_profile
gcware_services all start
gcluster_services all start

Only start or restart services when required by the documented installation procedure and the current cluster state.

Next, check License status. For versions that support the following command syntax:

chkLicense -n 10.10.10.1,10.10.10.2 -u gbase -p '<DBA_PASSWORD>'

Use the actual node IP addresses and supported authentication options for your environment. Avoid placing real passwords directly in shell commands where they could be exposed through shell history or process inspection.

Review these fields in the output:

  • is_exist — Whether the License file exists.
  • version — The reported License category, such as business or trial.
  • is_valid — Whether the License is valid.

For a commercial deployment, confirm that the reported License category and validity match the intended authorization.

Finally, inspect the cluster with:

gcadmin

Use the status definitions for your installed release to interpret the result. If the cluster remains close, do not immediately reinstall. Check whether the License was loaded, whether authorization is valid, and whether the services and node configuration are correct.

A License file's existence alone does not prove that authorization is working. Similarly, a cluster status should be evaluated alongside the relevant service and License checks.

For multi-node environments, verify all relevant nodes rather than assuming that a successful check against one machine proves the entire cluster is ready.

Step 7: Document the Installation for Handover

A deployment is not complete until the operations team can verify what was installed and maintain it afterward.

Record the following information in the handover document:

  • GBase Database version and package filename
  • CPU architecture, operating system, and Python version
  • Node IP addresses and relevant ESN information
  • GCware node and cluster role assignments
  • License type, validation result, and expiry date where applicable
  • Location of protected key backups and recovery documentation
  • Final service and cluster-status verification results

Changes to relevant nodes or keys may affect License authorization. Assess these impacts before a node replacement, operating system reinstall, or other significant infrastructure change.

A complete handover record reduces uncertainty during maintenance, expansion, and future troubleshooting.

Important Version Note: GBase Database 9.5.3.27

The License system and related installation procedures differ around the 9.5.3.27 release boundary.

License formats, command parameters, loading behavior, and activation procedures may vary. Do not copy commands from another environment without confirming the target version and its documentation.

This is also why package selection, runtime verification, and License preparation should be completed before the installation window begins.

Conclusion

A successful GBase Database(GBase 8a) commercial installation starts before the first command is executed.

Confirm the package against the target CPU architecture and operating system. Verify the Python runtime across all nodes. Request and prepare the appropriate License. Load it using the supported installation procedure, then validate License status and cluster readiness before handover.

The key lesson is simple: installation completion, License validity, and production readiness are three separate checkpoints.

Treating them as one documented workflow helps reduce avoidable delays and makes future cluster maintenance more predictable.

title: Your Website's Video Is Probably Killing Your LCP. Here's a Checklist
description:
A full-width hero video looks great in the design file. In production, it's often the heaviest thing on the page, and it quietly drags down your performance score.
This is a checklist I use whenever video shows up in a frontend project. Each item is small, but together they make a big difference.
First, measure
Before changing anything, find out whether video is actually your problem:

  1. Run Lighthouse or PageSpeed Insights on the page.
  2. In Chrome DevTools, open the Network tab, filter by Media, and sort by size.
  3. In the Performance panel, check what element is reported as your LCP. If your LCP element is a video poster or a frame, or if the video request competes with your critical resources on a slow connection, keep reading. The checklist
  4. Compress the source file first Most videos exported from editors or screen recorders are far heavier than they need to be. A sensible web-friendly baseline with FFmpeg: ffmpeg -i input.mp4 \ -c:v libx264 -crf 26 -preset slow -pix_fmt yuv420p \ -c:a aac -b:a 96k \ -movflags +faststart \ output.mp4

If you'd rather not touch the command line, an online tool such as VideoBee's video compressor does the same job in the browser. (Disclosure: I work on VideoBee.)

  1. Use the right resolution A background video behind a headline rarely needs 4K. Match the video to how it's displayed: ffmpeg -i input.mp4 -vf "scale=-2:720,fps=30" -c:v libx264 -crf 26 -an hero-720.mp4

For decorative background video, 720p (or even lower) is often enough.

  1. Drop the audio track when it's not used Muted autoplay backgrounds don't need audio at all. -an removes it and saves bytes.
  2. Keep it short

A 6 to 10 second loop is usually all a hero needs. If you have a longer source, trim it. A browser-based video cutter is handy for quick trims, or use FFmpeg:
ffmpeg -ss 00:00:03 -to 00:00:11 -i input.mp4 -c:v libx264 -crf 26 -an loop.mp4

  1. Provide modern formats with a fallback WebM (VP9) and AV1 can be smaller than H.264 at similar quality. Offer them first and keep MP4 as the universal fallback:

Create the WebM version:
ffmpeg -i hero.mp4 -c:v libvpx-vp9 -crf 33 -b:v 0 -an hero.webm

Need to convert between formats without installing anything? A video converter works for one-off jobs.
Browsers pick the first  they can play, so order matters: most efficient format first, safest format last.

  1. Always set a poster image The poster shows immediately while the video loads, so users never see an empty box. Generate one from a frame: ffmpeg -i hero.mp4 -frames:v 1 -q:v 3 hero-poster.jpg

Optimize the poster too (modern formats like WebP or AVIF work), because in many cases it becomes the element that determines your LCP.

  1. Control preloading The preload attribute tells the browser how aggressively to fetch the video: ● preload="none": don't download anything until the user interacts (good for below-the-fold videos). ● preload="metadata": fetch only duration and dimensions. ● preload="auto": let the browser decide (can be expensive on mobile). For non-critical videos, none or metadata is usually the right call.
  2. Lazy-load videos below the fold Don't load videos the user hasn't scrolled to. A small IntersectionObserver does the job:

const observer = new IntersectionObserver((entries, obs) => {
entries.forEach((entry) => {
if (!entry.isIntersecting) return;
const video = entry.target;
video.src = video.dataset.src;
video.load();
video.play().catch(() => {});
obs.unobserve(video);
});
});

document.querySelectorAll("video[data-src]").forEach((v) => observer.observe(v));

  1. Make sure the server supports range requests and caching Browsers fetch video in chunks using HTTP range requests. Check that your server or CDN returns Accept-Ranges: bytesand sets sensible Cache-Control headers for video files. Putting videos behind a CDN also helps users far from your origin.
  2. Use +faststart for MP4 Moving the MP4 metadata (the moov atom) to the beginning of the file lets playback start before the entire file is downloaded. It's a single flag: -movflags +faststart.
  3. Consider not autoplaying at all For longer product demos, a poster with a play button (and the video loaded on click) is much lighter than an autoplaying video. Reserve autoplay for short, muted loops.
  4. Respect user preferences Some users ask their OS to reduce motion or save data. You can honor that: @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) { .hero-video { display: none; } }

Show the poster image instead.
Before and after
Measure the same page before and after applying the checklist, and record:
Metric
Before
After
Video file size
measure
measure

measure
measure
Total page weight
measure
measure
[Add your own numbers and a Lighthouse screenshot here. Real before/after data is far more convincing than generic claims.]
The short version (save this)
● [ ] Compress the source (CRF 24 to 28 for web)
● [ ] Reduce resolution and frame rate to what the layout needs
● [ ] Remove audio if the video is muted
● [ ] Trim to the shortest useful loop
● [ ] Offer WebM/AV1 plus an MP4 fallback
● [ ] Set an optimized poster
● [ ] Use preload="none" or "metadata" where possible
● [ ] Lazy-load below-the-fold videos
● [ ] Enable range requests, caching, and a CDN
● [ ] Add -movflags +faststart to MP4s
● [ ] Don't autoplay long videos
● [ ] Respect prefers-reduced-motion
What's the worst video-related performance problem you've found in the wild? Tell me in the comments.

title: TIL: GBase Database Cluster Shows `close` After Installation? Check the License First
description:
Summary: If GBase Database(GBase 8a) finishes installing but gcadmin still reports close, check the License status before reinstalling the cluster. This guide explains how to verify License validity, identify version-related differences, and avoid common post-installation failures.

Yesterday, a cluster installation completed successfully. The services appeared to be running, but gcadmin reported close, and the business application could not connect.

The first suggestion was to reinstall everything. But the actual problem was simpler: the License for GBase Database(GBase 8a) had not been loaded correctly during installation.

The binaries were in place. The authorization state was not ready.

This is an important distinction in GBase Database troubleshooting: a completed installation does not necessarily mean the cluster is ready for business traffic.

1. Why Does GBase Database Show close After Installation?

When a GBase Database cluster remains in close after installation, do not immediately assume that the network, firewall, or database binaries are responsible.

License configuration is one of the checks worth performing early.

For the relevant GBase Database(GBase 8a) deployments, License authorization is associated with the ESN and SSH private key of the GCware node. Changes to the node, key material, or operating system can affect the existing authorization, depending on the release and licensing mechanism.

This explains a frustrating situation: the License file still exists, but the authorization is no longer valid for the current environment.

A safer workflow is:

  1. Confirm the exact GBase Database release.
  2. Verify the required License and target environment information.
  3. Load the License using the procedure supported by that release.
  4. Check the License status after installation.
  5. Confirm the cluster state before handing the environment over to the application team.

2. Load the License During Installation

For releases that support the following installation syntax, the License file can be specified with --license_file:

./gcinstall.py --license_file=/opt/gbase.lic --silent=demo.options

Confirm the exact parameter syntax and response-file requirements in the installation manual for your target GBase Database release before running the command.

If the cluster has already been installed, first determine which licensing mechanism the release uses and whether the License can be loaded or replaced without reinstalling the cluster.

Reinstallation should not be the default response to a License problem.

3. Verify the License with chkLicense

Where supported by the installed release, chkLicense can be used to inspect License status across multiple nodes.

For example:

chkLicense -n 10.10.10.1,10.10.10.2 -u gbase -p '******'

Replace the example IP addresses and credentials with the values appropriate for your environment. Avoid exposing real passwords in shell history, shared terminal recordings, or troubleshooting logs.

Focus on three fields in the output:

  • is_exist — Indicates whether the License file exists.
  • version — Identifies the reported License category, such as business or trial.
  • is_valid — Indicates whether the License is currently valid.

These fields answer different questions. A License file can exist without being valid, and a trial License may expire even when the file remains in place.

Do not treat is_exist alone as proof that authorization is working.

For a commercial deployment, confirm that the reported category matches the intended License type and that the validity check succeeds. Also verify the cluster status using the tools and status definitions documented for your release.

4. Check Every Relevant Node

In a multi-node GBase Database cluster, do not assume that checking a single machine provides sufficient evidence for the whole environment.

The -n option in the example accepts a comma-separated list of node IP addresses. Some versions also support options such as --hosts for reading a node list from a file and -f for writing results to a file.

Check the supported options with the documentation or help output for the installed version.

For larger clusters, a node list file and a saved verification report make the process easier to repeat and audit.

The handover record should include the relevant License status, target release, authorized node information, and expiry date when applicable.

5. License Replacement Requires a Controlled Procedure

If the License needs to be replaced, avoid uploading a new file and restarting services without first confirming the release-specific procedure.

A controlled replacement workflow generally includes:

  1. Back up the existing License file and relevant configuration.
  2. Confirm the new License matches the target environment and release.
  3. Upload the new file to the documented location.
  4. Apply the required ownership and permissions.
  5. Follow the documented loading or service-restart procedure, if required.
  6. Run the License verification again and confirm the resulting cluster state.

The exact sequence matters because License loading and activation behavior can differ between releases. Do not assume that every version requires the same restart procedure.

A backup also provides a recovery reference if the replacement does not work as expected.

6. Watch the GBase Database 9.5.3.27 Version Boundary

One important compatibility point is the change in the License system around GBase Database 9.5.3.27.

License formats, installation parameters, validation commands, and activation procedures may differ across the relevant releases. A command that works in one environment should not automatically be copied into another.

Before troubleshooting, record the exact software version and consult the corresponding installation and License manuals. This is also why package selection and version confirmation belong in the pre-installation checklist.

7. Include License Details in the Handover Checklist

A successful installation is not the end of the deployment process.

For GBase Database(GBase 8a), include the following information in the handover record:

  • Installed software version and package details
  • License type and validation results
  • Relevant GCware node ESN information
  • Required key-backup and recovery arrangements
  • Trial License expiry date, where applicable
  • Results of the final cluster-status check
  • The approved procedure for node replacement and License revalidation

Before changing a node, regenerating relevant keys, or reinstalling an operating system, assess the potential impact on License authorization.

This helps avoid discovering an authorization problem during a planned maintenance window.

Conclusion

When GBase Database shows close after installation, reinstalling the cluster is not necessarily the right first move. Check the License, confirm the exact release, and verify authorization across the relevant nodes before moving on to more disruptive troubleshooting.

For GBase Database(GBase 8a), the key lesson is simple: installation completion, License validity, and cluster readiness are separate checks.

A reliable deployment process requests the correct License before installation, loads it using the supported procedure, verifies the result afterward, and documents the evidence for handover.

Have you encountered a GBase Database cluster that installed successfully but remained in close? What was the root cause in your environment?

title: Converting PDF pages to JPG entirely in the browser: PDF.js, DPI math and the iOS canvas limit
description:
I'm the developer of MakeQuickWork, a small collection of free browser tools. This post is about how one of them, PDF to JPG, works under the hood.

Most "PDF to JPG" sites follow the same pattern: you upload the file, a server renders it, and you download a ZIP a few seconds later. That works, but it means a contract, a payslip or a medical letter sits on someone else's server for a while. I wanted a version where the PDF never leaves the browser tab. It turned out to be a nice little exercise in canvas, DPI math and browser quirks.

The tool is live at https://makequickwork.com/pdf/pdf-to-jpg/ if you want to follow along with DevTools open.

The pipeline

The whole thing is four steps, all client side:

  1. Read the File the user picked into an ArrayBuffer.
  2. Open it with PDF.js (Mozilla's PDF renderer).
  3. For each page, render to a <canvas> at the scale that matches the chosen DPI.
  4. Encode the canvas with canvas.toBlob() as JPEG or PNG, and if there are several pages, zip them with fflate.

One detail that matters for page speed: PDF.js is not small. The page itself is a static Astro page on Cloudflare Pages, and the PDF.js and fflate code is only downloaded after the user picks a file. Someone who lands on the page and leaves never pays for the library.

DPI to scale

PDF coordinates are in points, and a point is 1/72 inch. So a US Letter page reports a viewport of 612 × 792 at scale: 1. If you want an image at a given DPI, the scale factor is simply:

scale = dpi / 72

The tool offers three presets:

Preset DPI Scale Letter page size
Screen 72 1.0 612 × 792 px
Standard 150 ~2.08 ~1275 × 1650 px
High 300 ~4.17 ~2550 × 3300 px

Standard is the default. It's sharp enough for chat apps and slides, and the files stay reasonable. High is for printing or zooming into small text.

The canvas size wall

This is the part that bit me. Browsers cap how big a canvas can be, and the caps differ. iOS Safari is the strictest: a canvas above roughly 16.7 million pixels simply fails, often silently, and you get a blank image. A normal Letter page at 300 DPI is about 8.4M pixels, so that's fine. But PDFs contain all kinds of pages: posters, architectural drawings, A0 sheets, a page someone exported at 200 inches wide. At 300 DPI those blow straight past the limit.

So the scale is clamped by both a maximum side length and a maximum pixel count:

// iOS Safari refuses canvases above ~16.7M pixels; stay below that everywhere.
const MAX_PIXELS = 16_000_000;
const MAX_SIDE = 16_000;

async function pageScale(doc, n, dpi) {
  const page = await doc.getPage(n);
  const { width, height } = page.getViewport({ scale: 1 });
  let scale = dpi / 72;
  scale = Math.min(
    scale,
    MAX_SIDE / width,
    MAX_SIDE / height,
    Math.sqrt(MAX_PIXELS / (width * height)),
  );
  return scale;
}

The sqrt term is because pixel count grows with the square of the scale. I apply the same cap on every browser rather than sniffing for iOS. The trade-off is that a giant page comes out slightly smaller than the DPI you picked, and the tool page documents that, which beats producing a blank file.

White background, on purpose

PDF pages have no background by default. If you render to a fresh canvas and export PNG, you get transparent pixels wherever the page is "empty". That sounds nice until you open the PNG in a dark-mode chat app and your black text sits on a black background. JPEG doesn't support transparency at all, so transparent areas end up black or white depending on the encoder.

To keep JPG and PNG consistent, every page is rendered on white. PDF.js accepts a background option in page.render(), which saves a manual fillRect. It does mean the tool doesn't produce transparent PNGs, and I'd rather be upfront about that than surprise people.

Encoding and freeing memory

Encoding is just canvas.toBlob() wrapped in a promise. JPEG uses quality 0.92, PNG is lossless:

const canvas = await renderPage(doc, n, scale);
const blob = format === "jpg"
  ? await canvasToBlob(canvas, "image/jpeg", 0.92)
  : await canvasToBlob(canvas, "image/png");
// Free the bitmap right away; large PDFs would otherwise pile up memory.
canvas.width = canvas.height = 0;

That last line matters more than it looks. A 300 DPI page is a ~34 MB RGBA bitmap. If you keep canvases around while processing a 60-page document, mobile browsers will kill the tab. Setting the dimensions to zero lets the browser release the backing store immediately instead of waiting for GC.

Pages are also processed one after another, not in parallel. It's a bit slower on a fast laptop, but memory stays flat, which is what decides whether it works on a phone.

Zipping without compressing

For "Download all", the images go into a ZIP with fflate's zipSync at level: 0, which means store only, no deflate. JPEG and PNG are already compressed, so deflating them again saves maybe 1–2% and costs real CPU time on a phone. Store-only zipping is close to a memcpy.

File names get zero-padded page numbers (report-page-01.jpg ... report-page-12.jpg) so they sort correctly in every file manager.

Thumbnails and single pages

After the file opens, each page gets a low-resolution thumbnail and its own Download button. That's the common case: you need page 3 of a PDF as an image to drop into a chat, not all 40 pages. Thumbnails render at a small fixed size, and the full-resolution render only happens when you actually download.

How do you know nothing is uploaded?

You don't have to trust me. Open the Network tab, pick a PDF, and convert it. You'll see the library scripts load and, if you allowed analytics, a few small Google Analytics requests (the site uses GA4 for anonymous visit counts), but no upload and no request carrying your file. The site also has automated tests that fail if any tool sends a request to a third party (other than that analytics) or makes any POST while processing a file, or if an analytics event contains the file name.

Note that you still need a connection to open the page and load the code; it's not an offline app.

Known limitations

  • Password-protected PDFs aren't supported yet.
  • Very large pages are scaled down slightly to stay under the canvas limit.
  • Output is always on white, no transparent PNGs.

Wrapping up

None of this is novel on its own, but putting it together carefully (lazy loading, the scale clamp, freeing canvases, store-only ZIP) is the difference between a demo and something that works on a five-year-old phone.

If you want to try it or poke at it in DevTools: https://makequickwork.com/pdf/pdf-to-jpg/. There's also a PNG-focused page at https://makequickwork.com/pdf/pdf-to-png/. I'd be curious whether anyone has found a cleaner way to detect the real canvas limit per browser instead of hard-coding a conservative one.

title: SpaceX just delivered some very strange cargo to the International Space Station
description:
弱視(lazy eye)向けVRトレーニングにおける「左右独立提示」の実装メモ

きっかけ：宇宙で人工網膜を作るというニュース

SpaceXがISSへ届けた貨物に、宇宙で人工網膜を作るための技術が含まれていた——というニュースを読みました。視覚の研究が微小重力環境にまで広がっているのは素直に面白い。地上の実験室では重力が邪魔をする細胞の自己組織化を、軌道上で観察しようという発想自体が、視覚というテーマの射程の広さを感じさせます。

ただ、研究が臨床に届くまでのタイムラインは長い。研究室の成果がランダム化比較試験を経て標準治療になるまでには、数年から十年単位の時間がかかります。そこで今回は、その待ち時間のあいだにXRアプリ側で「今日できること」の実装論点を整理します。題材は弱視(lazy eye)向けのVRトレーニングです。

背景：ダイコプティック刺激とは

弱視の古典的介入は遮蔽(パッチ)。優位眼を物理的に隠し、弱い目を働かせます。ただしこれは両眼の統合そのものを練習する設計ではありません。片目を覆っているあいだ、脳は両眼の像を統合する処理を一度「使わない」わけです。

ダイコプティック(両眼視)アプローチは、左右の目に別々の刺激を提示し、優位眼を意図的に弱めながら、両目が協力して1つの知覚を作る状態へ導きます。パッチが「弱い目を鍛える」のに対し、こちらは「両眼の協調そのものを再学習させる」という違いがあります。

実装の3つの論点

1. 提示の分離

左右のディスプレイに独立した映像を描画できることが前提。片目にのみターゲットを出す、片方のレイヤーを減光・低コントラスト化する、といった制御が必要です。

// 概念的な擬似コード
if (stage === 1) {
  renderTargetOnlyTo(amblyopicEye);
}
if (stage === 2) {
  dimLayer(dominantEye, 0.7); // 抑制解除
}
if (stage === 4) {
  applyDisparity(bothEyes, withinPanumArea);
}

ここで最初にぶつかるのが、ステレオレンダリングのパイプラインをどう組むかという問題です。UnityであればXRSettingsのeye textureを、UnrealであればIStereoRenderingの実装を触ることになります。左右のカメラを個別に制御する以上、片目だけレイヤーを非表示にする・コントラストを下げるといった操作は、シェーダー側のuniformで切り替えるのが素直な設計です。フレームごとに左右で異なる描画パラメータを渡すため、CPU側のロジックとGPU側のステートを分離しておかないと、後からステージ遷移の条件を差し替えるときに辛くなります。

2. 融合制御

最終段階では、左右の像にわずかな視差(disparity)と輻輳(vergence)のオフセットを与え、Panumの融合領域内に収めます。ここを外すと二重像になり、トレーニングにならず負荷だけが増えます。Panumの融合領域は中心窩付近で狭く、周辺視野ほど広がるため、対象オブジェクトが視野のどこに置かれるかで許容できる視差量が変わります。画面中央に固定するのか、周辺を動かすのかで、パラメータのチューニング方針は変わってきます。

3. 進行のゲート

パフォーマンス指標でステージ遷移を制御します。AmblyoPunchの例では、直近10回の結果で70%以上、斜視プロファイルでは最終融合の前に80%以上が目安とされています。閾値の設計は、厳しすぎると離脱を招き、緩すぎると効果が薄まるというトレードオフになります。ローリングウィンドウで直近N回を見る方式は、単純な累積スコアより急な上達と急な不調の両方に反応しやすいという利点があります。

AmblyoPunchの構成

Meta Quest用の「AmblyoPunch」は、この設計をゲームとしてまとめた例です。

  • Gaborパターンのコインをパンチ、赤いスパイクを回避、ハート3つ
  • 進行：村→都市→宇宙→月→火星→金星。オブジェクトは高速化・小型化、スパイクは拡大
  • 自動モード4段階：片目ウォームアップ → 抑制解除 → 再バランス → 融合トレーニング
  • 設定：弱視の左右、重症度(軽度/中等度/重度)、斜視タイプ(内斜視/外斜視)。左右設定の誤りは効果を逆転させるため、初期設定に確認UIを挟むべき
  • カスタムモード：単眼/両眼/融合の手動トグル(上級者向け)

Gaborパッチをゲームオブジェクトにしたのは、視覚科学の文脈では定番の選択です。特定の空間周波数と方位に選択的な刺激は、コントラスト感度のトレーニングと相性がよく、パンチという単純な操作に落とし込むことで、認知負荷をゲームの操作ではなく視覚処理そのものに集中させられます。

気をつけること

  • セッションは短時間から。疲労・VR酔いを考慮した休憩設計を
  • 状態の永続化：左右の目、重症度、斜視タイプはセッション間で保持する
  • 表現の一貫性：本作は医療機器ではない。ストア説明、UI、マーケティング文言を「トレーニング/支援ゲーム」で統一する

状態の永続化は地味ですが、ダイコプティック系のアプリでは効いてきます。左右の目の設定を毎回入れ直すのはユーザー体験として悪いだけでなく、誤設定のリスクを毎セッションに持ち込むことになります。ローカルに保存するにせよアカウントに紐付けるにせよ、初回設定を正とし、変更時には確認を挟むのが無難です。

リンク

AmblyoPunch (Meta Quest): https://www.meta.com/en-gb/experiences/amblyopunch/1239507485902689/

※本記事は医療アドバイスではありません。本作は医療機器・治療・治癒ではなく、眼科専門家の指導を補完するものです。

title: Building a Wikipedia Trading Card Game: How We Built WikiMasters on TanStack Start & Cloudflare Edge
description:
Building an engaging web game is a journey of performance, gameplay balance, and real-time multiplayer synchronization. Today, we want to share the design and technical architecture behind WikiMasters (available to play at https://wikimasters.org), a bilingual Wikipedia Trading Card Game (TCG) where encyclopedic history, science, philosophy, and nature are transformed into collectible, strategic game cards.

1. The Vision: Knowledge as a Collectible Card Game

Digital trading card games often suffer from static card pools and repetitive meta cycles. We asked ourselves: What if every historical event, quantum physics theorem, ancient dynasty, and literary masterpiece in human history could be an evolving collectible card?

In WikiMasters:

  • Card Packs & Booster Openings: Players unbox themed boosters ranging from Ancient Roman Dynasties to Quantum Computing & Information Theory.
  • Live Quiz Duels: Battles are fought on contextual card placement and real-time knowledge trivia.
  • Global Card Market: Players trade, auction, and collect foil cards in a player-run economy.
  • Guild Collaborations: Guilds pool knowledge research points to unlock legendary historical archives.

2. High-Performance Serverless Stack

To provide instant load times, zero-latency transitions, and global low-latency multiplayer rooms, we architected the game on an edge-native stack:

  1. Framework: Full-stack React 19 + TanStack Start for server functions and SSR.
  2. Global Edge Execution: Cloudflare Workers serving compute across 300+ edge locations worldwide.
  3. Database & Persistence: Cloudflare D1 (distributed SQLite) for transactions, pack RNG generation, and card inventory.
  4. Asset Distribution: Cloudflare R2 for card art delivery with WebP/AVIF optimizations and edge caching.

3. Try It Out!

The game is open to play with zero installation required:

  • 🎮 Play WikiMasters Online: https://wikimasters.org
  • 📖 Official Project & Code Reference: WikiMasters Game on GitHub

We would love to hear feedback from fellow developers and game designers on our card-drafting mechanics and edge architecture!

title: Never Put a Pet on an AWS Spot Instance
description:
I got a task at my internship that sounded simple. Move one of our servers to a new AWS region, keep it the same as before, and spend as little money as possible.

That last part stuck with me. If you've spent any time reading about saving money on AWS, you've seen Spot instances everywhere. AWS says they can be up to 90% cheaper than normal on-demand instances. Ninety percent! I thought I'd found the easy win.

Then at standup, a teammate asked one question that killed the idea in about ten seconds:

"Where does this server keep its data?"

Here's what I learned, and the question I now ask before picking Spot for anything.

1. What a Spot Instance Actually Is

AWS has huge data centres full of servers, and not all of them are being used at any moment. Spot instances let you rent that spare capacity for a lot less money.

The catch is in the deal. AWS can take it back whenever it needs the capacity. You get a two minute warning, and then your instance is gone.

By default, an interrupted Spot instance is terminated, and unless you've set it up differently, the disk that came with it goes too.

Two minutes is enough to save a bit of work. It's not enough to save a server's whole memory.

2. Our Server Couldn't Be Thrown Away

This is where the standup question came in.

The server I was moving keeps its context on its own disk. Everything it knows lives right there on that one machine. There's no separate database or storage holding a copy.

So if AWS took it back, we wouldn't just lose a running server. We'd lose everything it had built up and have to start from zero.

The cheap option could have ended up being the most expensive one.

3. Pets vs Cattle

There's an old saying in DevOps that finally clicked for me after this.

Cattle are servers you don't get attached to. They're all the same, and if one dies, you replace it and nobody notices. Think of a web server behind a load balancer, where the real data lives in a database somewhere else.

Pets are servers you care about. They have their own name, their own data, and if one dies, you're having a bad day.

Spot instances are great for cattle. They're risky for pets.

Our server was very much a pet

4. The Question I Ask Now

Before choosing Spot for anything, I ask myself:

"If this server disappeared right now, what would we lose?"

If the answer is "nothing, we'd just start a new one", Spot is probably a great fit. Things like:

  • Batch jobs that can be restarted
  • CI runners
  • Test environments
  • Servers in an auto scaling group that keep their data somewhere else

If the answer is "a lot", stick with on-demand, at least until the data lives somewhere safer.

5. We Still Saved Money, Just Differently

The goal was still to keep costs down, so cheap wasn't off the table. It just had to be the right kind of cheap.

The plan is to run the server on an on/off schedule, so it only runs when it's needed. With on-demand, you don't pay for the compute while the instance is stopped, only a small amount for the disk. And because stopping an instance keeps its disk, nothing gets lost overnight.

Spot isn't ruled out forever either. Once the migration is done, we'll look at it again. If the data moves off the server, it stops being a pet, and Spot becomes an option.

Final Thoughts

I went in thinking the cheapest option was the smartest one. One question at standup showed me that cheap isn't cheap if it can lose your data.

Honestly, some of the best things I've learned in this internship didn't come from docs. They came from teammates asking simple questions I didn't think to ask. This is why I love working with people, you learn something new every day.

So I'm curious: what's a "cheap" decision that ended up costing you more?

title: I priced 33 VPS plans the way finance would: the same 2 vCPU / 4 GB server costs $4.54 or $29 a month
description:
The short version: I pulled 33 plans from 15 providers, and 26 of them have prices I verified on the provider's own page or API. For each one I added back what the sticker price leaves out: IPv4, backups and bandwidth overage. Here is what came out (as of 2026-10-26, at 2 TB of egress a month):

  • 2 vCPU / 4 GB: the cheapest verified plan is OVHcloud VPS-1 at $4.54/mo. The most expensive is Linode 4 GB at $29/mo. That is a $24.46/mo gap, or $294 a year, for the same headline specs.
  • 4 vCPU / 8 GB: the cheapest is OVHcloud VPS-2 at $8.50/mo. The most expensive is DreamHost Stack 16 at $34.99/mo. That gap is $26.49/mo, or $318 a year.
  • Renewal jumps: DreamHost Stack 16 goes up $12/mo at renewal (+52%). DreamHost Stack 4 goes up $7/mo (+78%). Hostinger KVM 2 goes up $6.20/mo (+71%) and Hostinger KVM 1 goes up $5.50/mo (+85%).
  • Largest hidden fee: Linode 4 GB has $5/mo in add-ons on top of its $24 list price.

You can run your own numbers in the calculator: https://vpsledger.pages.dev/calculator.html

Why the list price is misleading

A VPS pricing page shows you one number. The bill you actually pay usually includes some of these:

  1. IPv4. Some providers charge for the address separately.
  2. Backups. Usually a percentage of the plan price. Hetzner and Vultr both show about 20%.
  3. Bandwidth overage. Included transfer ranges from 0.5 TB to 20 TB. Past that, prices differ a lot. Hetzner charges €1 per extra TB (EU). Vultr charges $0.01/GB, which is $10 per TB.
  4. Promo pricing. Intro prices renew higher. The four renewal jumps listed above range from +52% to +85%.

Here is an example of how much transfer matters. Vultr's vc2-1c-0.5gb lists at $3.50. In the ledger its true cost is $9.20/mo at 1 TB of egress and $49.20/mo at 5 TB.

How I collected the data

  • Prices come only from official pricing pages or public APIs. Every price links to its source and shows the date it was checked.
  • Every plan is marked verified or unverified. A plan is unverified if I couldn't read its price or a fee on the check date, and it says why. Unverified plans are never ranked. That's why there are 26 verified plans out of 33.
  • EUR prices are converted at a dated rate (1.1188 USD/EUR on 2026-10-26).
  • The full method is here: https://vpsledger.pages.dev/methodology.html

Every provider has its own page with the fee breakdown, such as Hetzner and Linode. There are also head-to-head pages, such as DigitalOcean vs Hetzner.

The calculator in practice

Open the calculator, set 2 vCPU, 4 GB and 2 TB of egress, and turn backups on. You get the ranked list above, with each fee shown as a separate line and a source link for every number. Change the egress to 5 TB and the order changes, because providers with small transfer allowances start paying overage.

The data is open

The whole ledger is available as JSON under CC BY 4.0:

Free vs Pro

Everything above is free. VPSLedger Pro costs $9/mo. It adds price-drop and renewal alerts and CSV export. It's built for people who don't want to find out about a promo renewal from their invoice.

title: Stalwart email management program released in its first stable version 1.0
description:
Stalwart reaches v1.0, its first stable release in five years.

Built in Rust, the mail and collaboration server features SIMD/SWAR parser rewrites, a custom base64 library, and an overhauled search engine.

The program supports the basic protocols for sending, receiving, and storing email, as well as features for calendars, contacts, and file sharing.

Speed ​​and performance improvements

The new version brings significant changes for greater speed. The developers rewrote key parts of the code, while a new library for data processing was created from scratch. At the same time, database management was improved with more efficient transactions, fewer storage operations, and special compression for email. There were also adjustments for several popular data storage systems, while the redesigned in-memory storage method reduces the need to access the database for daily operations.

The text search engine has been completely redesigned to support advanced searches, predicate matching, and compressed indexes. According to the developers' tests, searching 250.000 messages takes less than four milliseconds.

READ ALSO

Noctalia version 5.4 released with new visual effects and options

In tests conducted on remote computers, Stalwart outperformed other well-known solutions in 35 out of 38 comparisons. For example, it was able to handle 5.445 incoming messages per second, compared to 723 messages for other systems.

New features and upgrades

Version 1.0 introduces content indexing for PDFs, document files, spreadsheets, presentations, and other file formats. Other additions include support for metadata, new digital signature formats that are resistant to future threats, and expanded connectivity capabilities.

The database structure has now been finalized, which promises easier upgrades in future releases. However, migrating existing installations to version 1.0 requires a separate migration process, as databases from older versions cannot be opened directly. A special tool allows for gradual data migration for installations running version 0.16.27, while the old server continues to operate.

title: How Databricks became worth $190 billion
description:
Databricks co-founder Arsalan Tavakoli-Shiraji discussed enterprise AI adoption, legacy system modernization using AI agents, and cloud partnerships at TechCrunch Disrupt.

Databricks is now a data storage and artificial intelligence giant, valued at $190 billion and with customers from over 70% of the Fortune 500 companies. Tavakoli-Shirazi spoke about these difficulties at the TechCrunch Disrupt conference, explaining how a new company can gain the trust of large customers.

Collaboration with larger companies

In its early years, Databricks unsuccessfully tried to secure a deal with Swiss bank UBS. The solution came when it partnered with Microsoft and became an Azure service partner.

This move helped the startup gain customer trust. Today, Databricks itself operates as a larger umbrella, selling the products of smaller companies, such as Hightouch, Addepar, and Tecton, under its own terms and security settings.

What worries big businesses?

When companies try to sell AI tools to large customers, they must address four key concerns, which Tavakoli-Shirazi calls the “four Cs”:

  • The context, i.e. the ability of artificial intelligence to understand the needs and data of the business.
  • Choice, that is, the freedom to switch between different models instead of being dependent on a single provider.
  • Cost, i.e. control of operating expenses.
  • Control, i.e. security controls and data protection.

The opportunity in old systems

According to him, 99% of the businesses he speaks to are still in the very early stages of AI. These companies still rely on expensive and legacy systems, such as old computers and decades-old programs, which are difficult to understand and update.
