title: Build a 'days since' streak counter in React with localStorage (that survives midnight, DST and bad data)
description:
"Days since I last smoked." "Days since the last production incident." "Days without sugar." A streak counter looks like the easiest widget in the world: store a start date and subtract. Then it shows 0 for two days after a clock change, crashes on the one user whose localStorage holds garbage, and stays on yesterday's number when the tab is left open overnight.

Here's the version I ended up with. It's plain JavaScript plus one React hook, with no libraries. All the logic below was run under Node 20 with TZ=Europe/Warsaw and TZ=America/New_York.

Rule 1: store calendar days, not timestamps

A streak is about days the user lived through, not milliseconds. If you store Date.now() and divide by 86,400,000, a 23-hour DST day or a trip across time zones will shift your count. So store a local day key, a plain YYYY-MM-DD string:

export function toDayKey(date = new Date()) {
  const y = date.getFullYear();
  const m = String(date.getMonth() + 1).padStart(2, "0");
  const d = String(date.getDate()).padStart(2, "0");
  return `${y}-${m}-${d}`;
}

Note the use of getFullYear/getMonth/getDate, which are local, not toISOString(). toISOString() is UTC, so in Warsaw shortly after midnight it would still say yesterday.

Rule 2: subtract day keys in UTC

To count the days between two keys, turn each into a UTC midnight. UTC has no DST, so every day there really is 86,400,000 ms long and Math.round handles the rest:

export function daysBetweenKeys(a, b) {
  const [y1, m1, d1] = a.split("-").map(Number);
  const [y2, m2, d2] = b.split("-").map(Number);
  return Math.round(
    (Date.UTC(y2, m2 - 1, d2) - Date.UTC(y1, m1 - 1, d1)) / 86400000
  );
}

export function daysSince(startKey, todayKey = toDayKey()) {
  return Math.max(0, daysBetweenKeys(startKey, todayKey));
}

Quick checks that used to bite me:

daysBetweenKeys("2026-03-28", "2026-03-30"); // 2  (EU DST weekend)
daysBetweenKeys("2026-10-24", "2026-10-26"); // 2  (EU DST ends)
daysBetweenKeys("2024-02-28", "2024-03-01"); // 2  (leap year)
daysSince("2026-11-01", "2026-10-26");       // 0  (future start never goes negative)

Math.max(0, …) matters more than it looks. Users change their device clock, and a negative streak is a bug report waiting to happen.

Rule 3: resetting should keep the record

People like seeing their best streak, and it makes a reset feel less painful. A reset is a pure function that takes the old state and returns the new one:

export function reset(state, todayKey = toDayKey()) {
  const current = daysSince(state.startKey, todayKey);
  return {
    startKey: todayKey,
    best: Math.max(state.best ?? 0, current),
    resets: (state.resets ?? 0) + 1,
  };
}

reset({ startKey: "2026-10-01", best: 10, resets: 0 }, "2026-10-26");
// { startKey: "2026-10-26", best: 25, resets: 1 }

Because todayKey is a parameter, it's trivial to test without mocking Date.

Rule 4: treat localStorage as hostile

localStorage can be missing (some private modes), full, or hold an old format from last year's version of your app. Wrap it so that the worst case is "start fresh", never a white screen:

export function load(storage, key, todayKey = toDayKey()) {
  try {
    const raw = storage.getItem(key);
    if (!raw) return { startKey: todayKey, best: 0, resets: 0 };
    const s = JSON.parse(raw);
    if (!/^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}$/.test(s.startKey)) throw new Error("bad data");
    return { best: 0, resets: 0, ...s };
  } catch {
    return { startKey: todayKey, best: 0, resets: 0 };
  }
}

export function save(storage, key, state) {
  try {
    storage.setItem(key, JSON.stringify(state));
  } catch {
    // quota exceeded or storage disabled: keep working in memory
  }
}

Passing storage in, instead of touching window.localStorage directly, lets you test it in Node with a five-line fake:

const mem = new Map();
const storage = {
  getItem: (k) => mem.get(k) ?? null,
  setItem: (k, v) => mem.set(k, v),
};
mem.set("streak", "{oops");
load(storage, "streak", "2026-10-27").startKey; // "2026-10-27", no crash

If you ever change the shape, add a version field now. Future you will thank you.

Rule 5: tick over at local midnight

The classic bug: the tab stays open overnight and still shows yesterday's number. You don't need a one-second interval. Schedule a single timeout for the next local midnight, and also refresh when the tab becomes visible again, because timers get throttled in background tabs and laptops go to sleep.

import { useEffect, useState, useCallback } from "react";
import { toDayKey, daysSince, reset, load, save } from "./streak";

function msUntilNextMidnight(now = new Date()) {
  const next = new Date(now);
  next.setHours(24, 0, 0, 0); // local midnight, DST-aware
  return next - now;
}

function useToday() {
  const [today, setToday] = useState(toDayKey);
  useEffect(() => {
    let timer;
    const refresh = () => setToday(toDayKey());
    const schedule = () => {
      timer = setTimeout(() => { refresh(); schedule(); }, msUntilNextMidnight() + 1000);
    };
    schedule();
    document.addEventListener("visibilitychange", refresh);
    return () => {
      clearTimeout(timer);
      document.removeEventListener("visibilitychange", refresh);
    };
  }, []);
  return today;
}

export function useStreak(key = "streak") {
  const today = useToday();
  const [state, setState] = useState(() =>
    typeof window === "undefined"
      ? { startKey: today, best: 0, resets: 0 }
      : load(window.localStorage, key, today)
  );

  useEffect(() => {
    save(window.localStorage, key, state);
  }, [key, state]);

  // keep several tabs in sync
  useEffect(() => {
    const onStorage = (e) => {
      if (e.key === key) setState(load(window.localStorage, key, toDayKey()));
    };
    window.addEventListener("storage", onStorage);
    return () => window.removeEventListener("storage", onStorage);
  }, [key]);

  const doReset = useCallback(() => setState((s) => reset(s, toDayKey())), []);

  return {
    days: daysSince(state.startKey, today),
    best: Math.max(state.best, daysSince(state.startKey, today)),
    resets: state.resets,
    reset: doReset,
  };
}

setHours(24, 0, 0, 0) asks the engine for "the next local midnight", so DST is handled for you. The extra second avoids landing at 23:59:59.999 because of timer jitter.

The component 

export function StreakCard({ label }) {
  const { days, best, reset } = useStreak(`streak:${label}`);
  return (
    <section aria-live="polite">
      <h2>{label}</h2>
      <p style={{ fontSize: "3rem", margin: 0 }}>{days}</p>
      <p>{days === 1 ? "day" : "days"} · best: {best}</p>
      <button onClick={() => confirm("Reset this streak?") && reset()}>
        Reset
      </button>
    </section>
  );
}

Two small UX details: aria-live so screen readers announce the new count at midnight, and a confirm step, because an accidental tap that wipes a 200-day streak is the fastest way to lose a user.

Server rendering note

If you render on the server (Next.js and friends), the server doesn't know the user's time zone or their localStorage. Render a neutral placeholder and fill in the number after hydration, or you'll get hydration mismatch warnings around midnight. The typeof window guard above covers the initial state.

Recap

  • Store local day keys (YYYY-MM-DD), not timestamps.
  • Subtract them in UTC, and clamp at zero.
  • Make reset a pure function that keeps the best streak.
  • Treat localStorage as unreliable: validate, catch and fall back.
  • Re-render at local midnight and on visibilitychange.

That's about 100 lines for a counter that behaves correctly on DST weekends, on leap days, and in tabs left open for a week.

If you'd rather not build it yourself, I made this into a free app with countdowns and "days since" trackers, no ads and no sign-up: CountMyDays.

title: How To Redesign Website Without Losing Seo
description:
Redesigning a Website Without Losing SEO: A Technical Breakdown

As a principal frontend engineer and conversion architect, I have witnessed numerous website redesigns that inadvertently compromise search engine optimization (SEO). The primary culprit behind this issue is the reliance on standard off-the-shelf templates and generic forms, which fail to account for the nuances of a website's existing SEO framework. These templates often lack the customization and adaptability required to preserve the site's search engine rankings, ultimately leading to a decline in online visibility and revenue.

The failure of generic templates can be attributed to several factors. Firstly, they rarely consider the website's historical content and link structure, which are crucial components of its SEO profile. Secondly, these templates often employ rigid and inflexible design patterns that hinder the implementation of optimized meta tags, header tags, and other essential SEO elements. Lastly, generic forms and templates frequently neglect the importance of mobile responsiveness, page speed, and user experience, all of which are vital ranking factors.

To mitigate these risks and ensure a successful website redesign without losing SEO, the following engineering takeaways are essential:

  1. Conduct a thorough SEO audit: Before initiating the redesign process, it is crucial to perform a comprehensive SEO audit to identify the website's existing strengths, weaknesses, and ranking factors. This audit should encompass technical SEO, on-page optimization, and link equity analysis.
  2. Implement a modular design architecture: A modular design approach enables the creation of flexible, reusable components that can be easily integrated into the new design. This architecture allows for the preservation of existing SEO elements, such as meta tags and header tags, while also facilitating the implementation of new optimization strategies.
  3. Prioritize technical SEO and performance optimization: The redesign process should prioritize technical SEO and performance optimization to ensure that the new website meets the latest search engine requirements. This includes optimizing images, minifying code, leveraging browser caching, and ensuring mobile responsiveness and fast page loading speeds.

By adhering to these principles and avoiding the pitfalls of generic templates, it is possible to redesign a website without compromising its SEO. Vareli breaks this down in the complete analysis:
https://vareli.info/blog/how-to-redesign-website-without-losing-seo

title: Anthropic begins the process of entering the stock market, leaving gaps in its financial data
description:
Anthropic filed its IPO prospectus (S-1), detailing massive multi-year infrastructure commitments and compute payment obligations approaching $808 billion while leaving recent quarterly revenue growth figures blank.

Specifically, the company did not include revenue figures for the quarter ended September 2026 in the prospectus. Michael Dabra, a professor at the University at Buffalo, notes that for a company of this size, closing the books takes time, and there is a need to scrutinize the numbers. U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission rules require Anthropic to update its third-quarter financials in its filing if it goes public after mid-November.

For her part, Erica Neumann, a professor at Youngstown State University, points out that it is not uncommon for confidential details to be removed from contract annexes, such as leases. In the same document, the company acknowledges that the cost of securing computing power is its largest operating expense and a serious business risk. Anthropic views the chips as a single, interchangeable pool of resources from partners that include Amazon, Google, Nvidia and AMD.

The huge financial obligations for infrastructure

The company has entered into contracts with total committed costs exceeding an amount that is not fully disclosed, primarily for computing power and infrastructure, based on contracts that extend through 2045. Specifically, as of December 31, 2025, Anthropic records future minimum payment obligations for computing power and infrastructure leases of approximately $417 billion, to which another $245 billion in infrastructure obligations has been added since June.

READ ALSO

SpaceX's mobile network will take four to six years and cost billions

Additionally, the company increased its uncommitted trade commitments by $125 billion to $150 billion, while short-term deals with minimum commitments that cannot be canceled added another $21 billion. In total, the company's estimated minimum commitments reach about $808 billion.

Professor Michael Dabra notes that companies that display gaps and omissions in their official documents are more likely to set a lower price for their shares when entering the stock market, in order to address potential investor distrust.

title: Counting days between two dates in JavaScript without off-by-one bugs
description:
"How many days until 24 December?" sounds like a one-liner. In JavaScript it's a small trap with three jaws: time zones, daylight saving time and the way Date parses strings. I ran into all three while building a countdown app, so here's what goes wrong and the small set of helpers I ended up trusting.

All snippets below were run in Node 20. The Temporal one uses the @js-temporal/polyfill package.

Pitfall 1: a day is not always 86,400,000 ms

The classic approach:

const a = new Date(2026, 2, 28); // 28 March 2026, local midnight
const b = new Date(2026, 2, 30); // 30 March 2026, local midnight
console.log((b - a) / 86400000);

In a European time zone (I ran it with TZ=Europe/Warsaw) this prints:

1.9583333333333333

Clocks went forward on 29 March, so that local "day" was only 23 hours long. Depending on whether you then use Math.floor, Math.ceil or nothing, you get 1, 2 or a fraction. In autumn you get the opposite: a 25-hour day and 1.04-ish.

The underlying problem: you're measuring elapsed time, but the question was about calendar days. Those are different things.

Pitfall 2: new Date('2026-03-29') is UTC, but new Date('2026-03-29T00:00') is local 

console.log(new Date('2026-03-29').toISOString());      // 2026-03-29T00:00:00.000Z
console.log(new Date('2026-03-29T00:00').getHours());   // 0 (local midnight)

A date-only ISO string is parsed as UTC midnight. Add a time and it becomes local. So for a user in New York, new Date('2026-03-29').getDate() returns 28, because UTC midnight is still the previous evening there. If you mix the two forms in one app (say, one from an <input type="date"> value and one from a database timestamp), you'll get off-by-one errors that only show up for some users.

Fix: compare calendar days, not milliseconds

The trick is to throw away the time of day and the time zone before subtracting. Take the year, month and day the user sees, and build a UTC midnight from them. UTC has no DST, so every day in it is exactly 86,400,000 ms.

function toUTCDay(d) {
  return Date.UTC(d.getFullYear(), d.getMonth(), d.getDate());
}

function daysBetween(start, end) {
  return Math.round((toUTCDay(end) - toUTCDay(start)) / 86400000);
}

// 23:30 on the 28th to 00:05 on the 30th, across the DST change:
console.log(daysBetween(new Date(2026, 2, 28, 23, 30), new Date(2026, 2, 30, 0, 5))); // 2

Math.round is a belt-and-braces guard; with both sides at UTC midnight the division is already an integer.

If your dates arrive as YYYY-MM-DD strings (date inputs, a date column in Postgres), don't hand them to new Date() at all. Parse the parts yourself:

function parseDateOnly(str) {
  const [y, m, d] = str.split('-').map(Number);
  return Date.UTC(y, m - 1, d);
}

const diff = (parseDateOnly('2026-12-24') - parseDateOnly('2026-10-27')) / 86400000;
console.log(diff); // 58

Treat date-only values as labels for a calendar day, not as instants. That one mental rule removes most of these bugs.

"Today" depends on where you are

Countdowns need "today", and "today" is a time-zone question. At 23:30 UTC on 26 October it's already the 27th in Tokyo. Intl.DateTimeFormat can tell you the calendar date in any zone without a library. The en-CA locale happens to format as YYYY-MM-DD, which plugs straight into parseDateOnly:

function todayIn(timeZone, now = new Date()) {
  return new Intl.DateTimeFormat('en-CA', {
    timeZone, year: 'numeric', month: '2-digit', day: '2-digit',
  }).format(now);
}

const now = new Date(Date.UTC(2026, 9, 26, 23, 30));
console.log(todayIn('Atlantic/Reykjavik', now));  // 2026-10-26
console.log(todayIn('Asia/Tokyo', now));          // 2026-10-27
console.log(todayIn('America/Los_Angeles', now)); // 2026-10-26

For anything shown to a user, compute "today" in their zone (the default when you omit timeZone), not the server's. A server-rendered "3 days left" from a server in UTC can easily be wrong for half your users.

"Days since": decide whether day one is 0 or 1

Counting up has its own off-by-one, and it isn't a bug in the code, it's a product decision. If I start a habit today, is that "0 days" or "day 1"?

function daysSince(startStr, todayStr) {
  return (parseDateOnly(todayStr) - parseDateOnly(startStr)) / 86400000;
}

console.log(daysSince('2026-10-26', '2026-10-26')); // 0
console.log(daysSince('2026-10-26', '2026-10-27')); // 1

"Days since" (elapsed) naturally starts at 0. "Day N of a streak" starts at 1, so it's daysSince(...) + 1. Pick one, name the function after it, and don't let the + 1 drift around the codebase.

For display, Intl.RelativeTimeFormat handles the wording and pluralisation in any language:

const rtf = new Intl.RelativeTimeFormat('en', { numeric: 'auto' });
console.log(rtf.format(-1, 'day')); // yesterday
console.log(rtf.format(58, 'day')); // in 58 days

Temporal: the real fix (when you can use it)

The Temporal API was designed for exactly this. It has a PlainDate type, a calendar date with no time and no zone, so the whole class of bugs above can't happen:

import { Temporal } from '@js-temporal/polyfill';

const start = Temporal.PlainDate.from('2026-10-27');
const end = Temporal.PlainDate.from('2026-12-24');
console.log(start.until(end, { largestUnit: 'day' }).days); // 58

const today = Temporal.Now.plainDateISO('Atlantic/Reykjavik'); // today in that zone

Native support is still arriving across browsers and runtimes, so check support for your targets or ship the polyfill. The toUTCDay approach above is a good bridge until then, and it maps cleanly onto PlainDate later.

Live countdowns are a different problem

Everything above is about whole days. A ticking "2d 4h 13m 09s" timer is about elapsed time, and there the millisecond difference is the right tool, as long as you always derive it from the clock instead of accumulating ticks. setInterval(tick, 1000) drifts and fires slightly late. Recomputing from Date.now() on each frame doesn't.

How CountMyDays handles it

CountMyDays is my side project for countdowns and "days since" trackers, built with React 19, Supabase and Vercel as an installable web app. A few of the choices in it come straight from the lessons above:

  • The timer is pure date math. Every frame it computes the difference from Date.now(), and a requestAnimationFrame loop only calls setState when the visible second changes. Because the value is always derived from the clock, there's no accumulated error. Background tabs pause rAF, so the hook switches to a 500 ms interval on visibilitychange and back again when the tab returns.
  • One function, four cases. When a countdown passes zero it flips to counting the time elapsed since the date, and a "days since" tracker with a future start date counts down until it starts. Keeping that in a single calculation function means the edge cases live in one place.
  • Normalise dates on the way in. Older data had targetDate, newer data target_date. The code accepts both and converts to ISO strings once, instead of letting two formats leak into the date math.

Cheat sheet

  • Days between dates: normalise both to UTC midnight (Date.UTC(y, m, d)), then divide.
  • Never pass YYYY-MM-DD to new Date() and then read local fields. Parse it yourself.
  • Compute "today" in the user's zone (Intl.DateTimeFormat with timeZone).
  • Decide whether "days since" starts at 0 or 1, and encode it in the function name.
  • Live timers: derive from the clock every frame, never count ticks.
  • Use Temporal.PlainDate where you can.

If you want to see these in practice, CountMyDays is free with no ads and no sign-up: countmydays.to. I'd love to hear about any date bugs that have bitten you in the comments.

title: AWS Skill Builder: The Free Official Platform to Start Your Cloud Journey
description:
When I started learning cloud, the hardest part wasn't the technology. It was knowing where to begin. There are endless YouTube playlists, paid courses, and blog posts, and it's easy to burn weeks just choosing what to study.

The best answer I found is also the official one: AWS Skill Builder. In this post I'll cover what it is, what you get for free, what the paid plans add, and how I'd use it as a beginner.

What is AWS Skill Builder?

AWS Skill Builder is Amazon's official online learning platform. It offers on-demand courses, learning plans organized by role and certification, exam preparation, digital badges, and hands-on practice. The content is written and maintained by AWS, so it tracks the real services and the real exams.

What you get for free

The free tier includes 600+ self-paced digital courses, learning plans, basic exam prep content, and digital badges. You don't need a credit card to start.

Highlights:

  • Digital courses from beginner to advanced: compute, storage, networking, security, databases, and more
  • Learning plans that group courses into a path so you don't have to guess the order
  • AWS Cloud Quest: Cloud Practitioner, a game-style way to learn by building solutions in a virtual city
  • Basic exam prep content and practice questions
  • Digital badges you can share on LinkedIn

What the paid plans add

Plan Who it's for What it adds
Free Beginners Courses, learning plans, basic exam prep, badges
Individual (from about $29/month) Learners preparing for certifications Builder Labs, full practice exams, AWS Jam challenge events
Team Organizations Admin dashboards, reporting, SSO support

Do you need to pay? For most beginners, no. The free tier plus your own AWS Free Tier account covers a lot. A subscription makes sense when you're preparing for several certifications or want guided labs and full-length practice exams. If you try it, subscribe for one month, finish the labs you wanted, and cancel.

Pricing and plan details change, so check the Skill Builder pricing page before deciding.

A beginner learning path

  1. Start with Cloud Practitioner Essentials. It teaches the core AWS vocabulary: Regions, IAM, EC2, S3, pricing, and the shared responsibility model.
  2. Play AWS Cloud Quest: Cloud Practitioner. It turns theory into practice, and finishing it earns a badge.
  3. Use the exam prep learning plan if you're aiming for the Cloud Practitioner certification (CLF-C02).
  4. Practice in your own account. Use the AWS Free Tier to repeat what you learned: create an IAM user, launch an EC2 instance, set up a billing alarm.
  5. Move to an Associate-level path such as Solutions Architect or Developer once the basics feel comfortable.

My experience

I earned the AWS Cloud Quest: Cloud Practitioner (Trained) badge through Skill Builder, and it did more for my understanding than passive video watching. Building a solution inside the game, then recreating it in my own AWS account, made the concepts stick. You can see the badge on Credly.

Tips to get the most out of it

  • Follow a learning plan instead of picking random courses
  • Take notes in your own words, then turn them into blog posts
  • Pair every course with a small hands-on task in the Free Tier
  • Set a billing alarm first so practice never surprises you with a bill
  • Share your badges on LinkedIn to document your progress
  • Be consistent. Thirty focused minutes a day beats a six-hour weekend binge

Free tier limits to know about

The free tier is generous but not unlimited. Guided hands-on labs and full practice exams are mostly part of the paid plan, and free courses don't give you a completion certificate like an official certification does. Badges show learning progress. They don't replace a certification exam.

Wrapping up

If you're starting with AWS, Skill Builder is the best first stop: official, structured, and largely free. Pick a learning plan, practice in your own account, and share what you learn. That combination is what turns courses into real skills.

What's your favorite Skill Builder course so far? Let me know in the comments.

Connect with me

  • LinkedIn: vishalpatil-devops-aws
  • dev.to: @vishal_patil_aws
  • GitHub: VishalPatil-DevOps-AWS

title: I rebuilt my AI coding agent workspace in Rust. It uses 1/15 the memory of the Electron app I replaced
description:
I run a lot of coding agents at the same time: Claude Code in one worktree, Codex in another, a dev server, a couple of shells. The agent workspace I was using did the job, but it was an Electron app, and with a dozen terminals open it had quietly become the heaviest thing on my Mac.

So I built Krill: the same parallel-agent workflow in pure Rust. This post is about the architecture, and about a benchmark I ran to check whether the rewrite was actually worth it.

What it does

  • Each task gets its own Git worktree and terminal, so agents don't trip over each other.
  • It works with any CLI agent (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor CLI, OpenCode, Antigravity) or a plain shell.
  • Agent status hooks (working, waiting, done, blocked...) feed a Needs You queue, so the agent waiting on your approval floats to the top.
  • Sessions outlive the app. Quit it, crash it, update it: the agents keep running and you reconnect to the same session IDs.
  • A headless krill CLI drives everything without the GUI (krill new, send, read, wait, attach).

Three processes, not one

The "sessions survive the app" part drove most of the design.

krill-app      gpui UI. Renders only the panes you can see.
   │  IPC
krilld         session daemon: terminal state (alacritty_terminal),
   │           1,000 hot rows + zstd-compressed cold scrollback,
   │           hooks, git watching, mobile gateway
krill-holder   tiny PTY parent. Owns the file descriptors. Never panics.
  • krill-holder is the only process that owns PTYs. It is deliberately small (the macOS build has a 1,300-line budget) and panics are banned there. If it dies, krilld still holds the fds.
  • krilld keeps the terminal state and is the only thing that answers terminal queries. Session work runs under catch_unwind, so one bad session doesn't take down the others. If krilld crashes, the agents survive because the holder keeps the PTYs. Output that krilld had read but not yet written to a segment can be lost, and the UI shows an explicit gap marker rather than pretending nothing happened.
  • krill-app can be killed at any time. On restart it restores the layout and reattaches to the same sessions.

Rebooting, or losing both holder and daemon at once, does end the processes. Krill then respawns shells in the last working directory and keeps the old scrollback above them, but it doesn't pretend the old process survived.

The benchmark

I wanted a number I could defend, so I measured Krill 0.2.2 against Orca 1.4.237 (an Electron agent workspace with a similar feature set) on the same machine:

  • Mac mini (Apple M6, 32 GB), macOS 27.0.1, release builds from /Applications, no tuning
  • fresh isolated profile per run, same 1200×760pt window
  • N login-shell tabs in the same git repo, one visible; each tab prints 20,000 lines (~2.8 MB of colored, wide, Unicode text)
  • every process the app spawns is counted (helpers, GPU, renderer, daemons); shells are excluded on both sides
  • 1, 10 and 20 terminals × 3 runs, alternating which app goes first; medians reported

At 10 terminals:

Metric Krill Orca
Memory (phys_footprint) 85.9 MiB 1,274.9 MiB 1/15
Idle CPU (30 s average) 1.1% 31.0% 1/27
CPU time to process the output 1.2 s 6.4 s 1/5
Install size 92 MiB 689 MiB 1/7

Most of the gap is the UI layer: 30 MiB for the Krill app versus about 994 MiB for Electron's main, GPU and renderer processes. The terminal daemons differ too (46.5 vs 256.3 MiB), mostly because Krill keeps 1,000 hot rows per terminal and compresses the rest.

Where Krill lost, and other caveats

  • Wall-clock output at 20 terminals: Krill took 7.5 s to finish the burst versus Orca's 4.0 s. Krill's runs varied a lot (1.9 to 7.9 s) and the machine was shared, so I can't yet say how much of that is load. It's a real result, though, and it's on my list.
  • Screen locked: all runs were recorded with the display locked. Even then, Orca's GPU process used ~22% CPU. I haven't measured the screen-on case yet, so I'm not claiming the 1/27 holds there.
  • Shared machine: other work (Rust builds) was running. Memory barely moves with load; CPU and timing can.
  • Agent processes themselves are excluded. Claude Code costs the same in either app.

Try it

Apple Silicon macOS is the main platform, and there's a Windows x64 preview. The macOS build isn't notarized yet; the installer verifies the checksum and signature before installing.

curl -fsSL https://krill.page/install.sh -o /tmp/krill-install.sh
# read it first
bash /tmp/krill-install.sh

It's Apache-2.0: github.com/craftowen/krill · krill.page

If you try it, the most useful feedback is which step blocked you first: install, opening a repo, starting an agent, creating a second worktree, or reconnecting after an app restart.

title: Databases on NEXUS AI: Managed, Portable, and Ready for AI-Built Apps
description:
Databases on NEXUS AI: Managed, Portable, and Ready for AI-Built Apps

Author: NEXUS AI Team

Category: Databases · Platform · AI Deployments

Reviewed: October 26, 2026

CLI syntax verified: NEXUS AI CLI 4.3.2

Reading time: 13 minutes

Most AI-built apps fail at the same point. The interface works, the demo impresses, and then someone asks where the data lives, who backs it up, and what happens when the AI agent runs a migration at 2 a.m.

Generating code got fast. Running the database underneath it did not get any easier.

NEXUS AI gives every app a database path that matches where it is in its life: a database that starts with the app, a standalone database you share between apps, the same database in your own AWS, Azure, or Google Cloud account, and a guarded way to connect databases you already run. One dashboard, one CLI, and one MCP server manage all of them.

This article explains what each option is, where to use it, how it looks from a management point of view, how portable your data stays, and why the design fits AI deployments in particular.

What NEXUS AI databases are

NEXUS AI databases are the data layer of the NEXUS AI deployment platform. There are four ways to use them:

Option What it is Engines Manage with
App database service A database that runs next to one app, created with the deploy PostgreSQL, MySQL, MongoDB, Redis nexus db
Managed database on NEXUS AI A standalone database you create once and attach to any app on NEXUS AI PostgreSQL, Redis nexus managed-db --local
Managed cloud database A standalone database on Amazon RDS, Google Cloud SQL, or Azure Database, in the platform account or yours PostgreSQL, MySQL nexus managed-db --provider
Connected external database A database you already run elsewhere, connected for schema inspection, guarded queries, and AI fix proposals PostgreSQL, MySQL Dashboard and MCP

All four sit behind the same organization, the same role-based permissions, and the same tools.

Where to use each option

App database service: for prototypes and single apps

Add a database when you deploy, and NEXUS AI runs it next to your app and injects the connection settings:

nexus deploy source --repo https://github.com/your-org/helpdesk --services postgres,redis

Use it when one app owns its data: a prototype, an internal tool, a side project, or the first version of a product. It is the fastest path from "generated code" to "working app with real data".

Each service gets backups you control:

nexus db services helpdesk                               # find the service ID
nexus db backup <service-id>                             # back up now
nexus db backup-schedule <service-id> --enable --retention 14   # daily, keep 14 days

Managed database on NEXUS AI: for data shared by several apps

When two apps need the same data (an API and a worker, or an app and its admin panel), the database should not belong to either one. Create it on its own:

nexus managed-db create orders-db --local --engine postgres
nexus managed-db attach orders-db --deployment orders-api
nexus managed-db attach orders-db --deployment orders-worker

Each app receives DATABASE_URL (or REDIS_URL for Redis) on its next deploy. Use --env-prefix to give a second database a different name, such as ANALYTICS_URL. Deleting an app no longer puts the data at risk, because the database has its own lifecycle.

Managed databases on NEXUS AI listen on the primary host's private Docker network, so they attach to apps deployed on NEXUS AI on that host.

Managed cloud database: for production and compliance

When the data needs a cloud provider's durability, encryption, and controls, create the database on Amazon RDS, Google Cloud SQL, or Azure Database for PostgreSQL and MySQL:

nexus managed-db create billing-db --provider AWS_RDS --engine postgres \
  --engine-version 17.10 --instance-class db.t3.micro --allocated-gb 20 --region us-east-1

Or let the deploy create it for you. On a cloud provider, --create-db provisions a managed database paired with the app:

nexus deploy source --repo https://github.com/your-org/billing --provider aws_app_runner --create-db postgres

Amazon RDS instances are created with storage encryption and seven days of automated backups. On AWS you can choose --network-mode vpc to keep the database private, reachable only from App Runner apps in the same account.

If you have added your own cloud credentials in Deployment Providers, new cloud databases are created in your AWS account or Azure subscription, not the platform's. See Bring Your Own Cloud Account.

Connected external database: for data you already have

Not every database should move. Connect an existing PostgreSQL or MySQL database in the dashboard, then inspect its schema, preview queries, and get AI-proposed fixes from your app's error logs, all with guardrails described below.

Quick decision guide

Your situation Start with
Prototype or demo with real data App database service
One app, small team, needs backups App database service with a backup schedule
Several apps share the same data Managed database on NEXUS AI
Production workload, customer data, uptime commitments Managed cloud database
Compliance requires data in your own account Managed cloud database with your own cloud provider
Data already lives somewhere else Connected external database

The management point of view

For the person responsible for the platform, databases are usually where tools sprawl: one console per cloud, scripts for backups, and a wiki page about who has the passwords. NEXUS AI keeps them in one place.

One inventory. Every database in the organization, whichever option and provider, appears in the dashboard and in nexus managed-db list and nexus db services.

Permissions by role. Reading data and changing it are separate permissions. A teammate with read access can run SELECT queries; write and schema-changing queries require the managed_databases.manage permission. Assign roles per person, and use scoped access tokens for CI.

Backups with a floor. Scheduled backups keep at least 7 days of history, and retention can be raised but never lowered below that. Expired automatic backups are pruned on schedule; backups you upload are never deleted automatically.

Recovery that does not overwrite. Managed database restores always create a new database from a snapshot:

nexus managed-db snapshot orders-db --notes "before v2 migration"
nexus managed-db restore orders-db --snapshot <snapshot-id> --new-name orders-db-check

You compare the restored copy with the original before you switch anything.

Safe sharing of backups. Instead of handing out credentials, create a signed download link that expires in 30 to 3,600 seconds:

nexus db backup-download <service-id> <backup-id> --share --ttl 900

Plan limits you can predict.

Plan Standalone managed databases
Free App database services only
Starter 2
Pro 10
Enterprise Unlimited

Portability: your data is never trapped

A database platform is only as good as your ability to leave it. NEXUS AI is built on that assumption.

Standard engines, no proprietary layer. PostgreSQL, MySQL, MongoDB, and Redis run as themselves. Your app connects with its normal driver and a normal connection URL. No SDK, no special query language.

Backups in native formats. PostgreSQL backups use pg_dump, MySQL uses mysqldump, and MongoDB uses mongodump. Download any backup and restore it with standard tools on any server:

nexus db backup-download <service-id> <backup-id> --out ./prod.dump
pg_restore -d "$TARGET_DATABASE_URL" --no-owner ./prod.dump

Move data between services. Copy production into staging without leaving the platform, as long as both use the same engine:

nexus db restore-to <staging-service-id> <backup-id> --yes

Or bring data in from outside with nexus db backup-upload.

Connection settings, not code changes. Apps read their database from environment variables. Detach one database and attach another, redeploy, and the app follows. Moving from a database on NEXUS AI to Amazon RDS is a data copy and an attach, not a rewrite.

Your cloud account, your resources. Cloud databases created with your own provider credentials live in your account. If you stop using NEXUS AI, they keep running where they are.

Flexibility: one workflow, many shapes

  • Four engines for different jobs: relational data in PostgreSQL or MySQL, documents in MongoDB, caches and queues in Redis.
  • Four homes for standalone databases: NEXUS AI, Amazon RDS, Google Cloud SQL, and Azure Database.
  • Public or private networking on AWS: public endpoints restricted to allowed address ranges, or VPC mode with no public endpoint.
  • Several databases per app, each under its own environment variable prefix.
  • Three ways in: the dashboard for people, the CLI for scripts and CI, and the MCP server for AI assistants.

Who it is for

Founders and solo builders who generated an app with AI and need real data, backups, and a URL today, without learning a cloud console.

Product and agency teams shipping many small apps, who need each one to have a database that is backed up, separated, and easy to hand over.

Platform and DevOps leads who want one inventory, consistent backups, and role-based access across every database their teams create.

Regulated and enterprise teams who need the data in their own cloud account, encrypted, with their own audit trail, while developers keep a simple workflow.

Why NEXUS AI is a strong fit for AI deployments

AI changes who touches the database. An agent in Claude, Cursor, or Codex can now create a schema, write a migration, and run it, often faster than a person can review it. That is useful, and it needs guardrails that do not depend on the agent behaving perfectly.

AI assistants get real database tools. The NEXUS AI MCP server exposes database operations directly to AI assistants: listing services, taking and restoring backups, creating and attaching managed databases, taking snapshots, inspecting schemas, and running queries. An agent can deploy an app with a database and back it up before a migration in the same conversation.

Every query is classified before it runs. Queries are sorted into reads, data changes, schema changes, and blocked operations. Statements such as DROP DATABASE, role changes, extension installs, and server file access are refused outright.

Preview before execute. On connected databases, a preview runs read queries with EXPLAIN and does not apply changes, so the agent (and you) can see what a statement would do first. Execution runs with a statement timeout and returns at most 1,000 rows by default.

Permissions apply to agents too. An assistant acts with the permissions of the person or token it uses. Give an agent a read-only role and it cannot change data, whatever it is asked to do.

Fixes are proposals, not surprises. NEXUS AI can read an app's error logs and propose a schema fix, such as a missing column or index. The fix is stored as a proposal and is applied only when someone applies it.

Backups are one command away from any agent. The habit that saves teams most often is simple: snapshot before a migration. With MCP, asking the agent to "take a snapshot first" is all it takes, and restores never overwrite the original.

The database follows the app's lifecycle. AI-built apps change quickly: prototype on Monday, shared with a team on Wednesday, in production the next month. The path from app database service to managed database to your own cloud account uses the same commands and the same connection variables at every step.

What to know before you start

  • Managed databases on NEXUS AI support PostgreSQL and Redis; use a cloud provider for managed MySQL.
  • Managed databases on NEXUS AI attach only to apps running on the NEXUS AI primary host.
  • Private (VPC) cloud databases must be in the same cloud account as the app that uses them.
  • App database service restores replace the current data in place. Take a fresh backup first if you may want the current state back.
  • restore-to requires the source and target to use the same engine.

Frequently asked questions

What databases does NEXUS AI support?

PostgreSQL, MySQL, MongoDB, and Redis as app database services. PostgreSQL and Redis as managed databases on NEXUS AI. PostgreSQL and MySQL as managed cloud databases on Amazon RDS, Google Cloud SQL, and Azure Database.

Can I export my data and leave?

Yes. Backups use the engines' native dump formats, so you can download them and restore them anywhere with standard tools. Cloud databases created with your own credentials are already in your account.

Is it safe to let an AI agent run queries?

NEXUS AI classifies every query, blocks dangerous statements, separates read and write permissions, and offers a preview mode. Give agents the least access they need, and ask them to snapshot before migrations.

What is the difference between nexus db and nexus managed-db?

nexus db manages databases that run alongside one app, created with --services. nexus managed-db manages standalone databases that you create once and attach to any number of apps.

Can I move from a database on NEXUS AI to Amazon RDS later?

Yes. Create the RDS database, copy the data with a backup and restore, attach the new database to the app, and redeploy. The app keeps reading DATABASE_URL.

How long are backups kept?

Scheduled backups are kept for 7 days by default, and you can raise retention per service. Backups you upload are kept until you delete them.

Start with the database your app needs today

Deploy your next app with --services postgres, turn on a backup schedule, and connect your AI assistant to NEXUS AI through MCP. When the data outgrows one app, create a managed database and attach it. When it needs a cloud provider or your own account, move it there with the same tools.

title: Zero-downtime Postgres migration with logical replication: the checklist we actually used
description:
Most advice about moving a production database boils down to "schedule a maintenance window and run pg_dump". That works until customers use your product around the clock and six services write to the same database.

That was our situation. The database behind our own Console (every workspace, project and API key) lived on Amazon RDS, and we wanted it on Prisma Postgres, the managed Postgres we run for our users. We moved 83 tables and 74 GB without pausing writes, and we could have switched back to RDS for a full week afterwards without losing a row.

This is the checklist we'd hand a friend about to do the same thing, plus the SQL that mattered and the one thing that bit us.

Why logical replication and not dump/restore

A dump and restore is a snapshot. Anything written after the snapshot is lost unless you stop writes until the restore finishes. On 74 GB that's not a short pause.

Logical replication is built into Postgres and works differently. The old database publishes row changes, the new one subscribes. The subscriber copies each table once, then keeps applying inserts, updates and deletes as they happen. Your app keeps writing to the old database the whole time, and you switch over when the new one has caught up.

It has rules, though, and every gotcha we hit was one of them.

The pre-flight checklist

We went through each of these before creating anything. Skip one and the migration stalls.

1. Logical decoding is on at the source. Postgres needs wal_level = logical to publish row changes. On RDS you get there with the rds.logical_replication parameter. Ours was already set, but check it, because changing it needs a reboot.

2. Every table has a primary key. The subscriber uses it to find the row an update or delete applies to. This query should return nothing:

SELECT c.relname
FROM pg_class c
JOIN pg_namespace n ON n.oid = c.relnamespace
WHERE n.nspname = 'public' AND c.relkind = 'r'
  AND NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM pg_index i
    WHERE i.indrelid = c.oid AND i.indisprimary
  );

3. The target already has the schema. Replication copies rows, not tables. We let our normal CI pipeline run all 204 migrations against the new database, so both sides had identical schemas.

4. The target tables are empty, with one exception you need to plan for. Because CI had already migrated the new database, its migration history table was full. Copying the old one on top would fail on duplicate keys. So we published every table by name and left that one out. If you use any migration tool that tracks history in a table, you'll have the same issue.

5. The new database can reach the old one. The subscriber opens the connection, not the other way round. Our RDS security group blocked it. We added the inbound rule in a separate security group so we could delete it cleanly afterwards, then tested the path with dblink before going further.

6. The target stays awake. Ours pauses with no client connections, and a replication stream doesn't count, so a tiny service pinged it every few seconds during the copy.

7. You know where the bytes are. Two tables held about three quarters of the data. The biggest was a log of webhook deliveries with no retention policy. A 30-day retention job before the copy would have saved a lot of waiting. We added it afterwards, naturally.

The SQL that did the work

Here's the condensed version. Hostnames and passwords are placeholders.

On the source, create a dedicated replication login and a publication that lists tables explicitly:

CREATE ROLE migration_repl WITH LOGIN PASSWORD '<password>';
GRANT rds_replication TO migration_repl;
GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA public TO migration_repl;
GRANT SELECT ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA public TO migration_repl;

DO $$
DECLARE t text;
BEGIN
  SELECT string_agg(quote_ident(tablename), ', ')
    INTO t
  FROM pg_tables
  WHERE schemaname = 'public'
    AND tablename <> '_prisma_migrations';
  EXECUTE 'CREATE PUBLICATION app_migration FOR TABLE ' || t;
END $$;

On the target, subscribe. This creates the slot on the source and starts the initial copy:

CREATE SUBSCRIPTION app_migration
  CONNECTION 'host=<source> dbname=app user=migration_repl
              password=<password> sslmode=require'
  PUBLICATION app_migration
  WITH (copy_data = true, create_slot = true);

Then watch three things: per-table state on the target, error counters on the target, and how much WAL the slot is holding on the source.

-- target: r = ready
SELECT srsubstate, count(*) FROM pg_subscription_rel GROUP BY 1;
SELECT apply_error_count, sync_error_count FROM pg_stat_subscription_stats;

-- source
SELECT slot_name,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), restart_lsn))
FROM pg_replication_slots;

All 82 tables reached ready the same day, with both error counters at zero.

Verifying without fooling yourself

Run ANALYZE on the target first. The initial copy doesn't leave planner statistics behind, and your first real queries will plan badly without them.

Then we used two checks. First, one query (through dblink) counted rows in every table on both sides and returned only the tables that differ. An empty result is the signal you want, and it's much easier to trust than scrolling through 82 matching numbers.

Second, an md5 over full rows for a few tables:

SELECT md5(string_agg(x::text, '|' ORDER BY id)) FROM "Organization" x;

Hashes matched on slow-moving tables and differed on two tables touched on every login, simply because the two queries ran seconds apart. Expect that, and don't panic.

The cutover: one merge, every connection

Our rule was that every service, and every connection path inside each service, switches in the same deploy. If one path moves and another doesn't, a service can write a row to one database and then fail to read it from the other.

We made that boring on purpose:

  1. Days before, every service learned to read its connection string from a new secret name, falling back to the old one. No behavior change.
  2. Minutes before, we created the new secrets. Running services don't pick them up until redeployed, so still no change.
  3. We merged one pull request, and the deploy rolled every service onto the new database.

For a few minutes during the deploy, some services wrote to the old database and some to the new one. Forward replication kept carrying old-side writes across. A key collision would show up as an apply error (it stayed at zero). Two sides updating the same row would not show up anywhere, which is why we cared so much about keeping that window short. The last write to RDS landed seven minutes after the merge.

The rollback we kept for a week

This is the part we'd recommend most. After cutover, we turned replication around so the old database followed the new one:

  1. Minutes before the merge, create a logical replication slot on the new database. It retains every change from that moment, so the rollback covers the cutover itself. Don't create it days early: an unread slot was holding roughly a gigabyte of WAL per hour for us.
  2. Once the old side is quiet (we sampled its write counters for sixty seconds), drop the forward subscription.
  3. Subscribe the old database to the new one from that slot with copy_data = false, since it already has every row, and origin = none, so only the application's own writes flow back instead of echoing the replicated ones.

Going back would have meant reverting one commit. After a week of daily row count checks, we dropped the reverse subscription (outside a transaction block, since a slot was attached), snapshotted RDS and shut it down.

The thing that bit us

Logical replication does not replicate schema changes. No ALTER TABLE, no DDL at all. While replication runs in either direction, every migration has to run on both databases.

We knew that. We had one CI migration job per database. But one of our cutover changes accidentally pointed the old database's job at the new one. Fifty-two minutes after cutover, a migration added three columns on the new side only, and the reverse stream stopped at the first row that used them. We applied the same SQL to RDS by hand about fifteen minutes later, and the stream caught up with nothing lost.

The lesson is boring and real: before changing a connection setting, list everything that uses it, including CI jobs.

If we did it again

We'd keep: tables published by name, a dblink connectivity test before subscribing, mismatch-only verification queries, one deploy for every connection path, and a reverse replication rollback.

We'd change: audit who uses each connection string first, and add retention to noisy tables before copying.

We also paired with an AI coding agent: it drafted every query and read the results, and a human ran every statement that touched production. That split worked well.

We wrote up the full story, with every SQL file and a step-by-step timeline, here on our blog. And if you want somewhere to practice this on a real database, managed Postgres hosting from Prisma has a free plan with no card. It covers Prisma Postgres with 200,000 operations a month and 2 GB of storage, plus Prisma Compute with 1M requests, 360 GB-hours of memory, 4 active vCPU-hours and 10 GB of outbound bandwidth a month.

Questions about any step? Ask in the comments.

title: Beyond Code: Learning to Think Like a Software Engineer in the Age of AI
description:
AI can generate code, explain unfamiliar concepts, and help us build software faster. But as these tools become part of everyday development, I've been thinking about a more important question:

If AI can generate code, what should we focus on learning as software engineers?

A 30-minute office-hours conversation with Matthew Titmus, author of Cloud Native Go, gave me an opportunity to reflect on that question. It shifted my attention from which technology to learn next toward the judgment needed to build reliable, maintainable software.

Writing Code Is Only Part of the Job

It is tempting to measure progress by how quickly we can implement a feature. AI makes that especially easy: describe a requirement, receive an implementation, make a few changes, and move on.

But code that looks correct in a small example may behave very differently in production.

A solution can pass a happy-path test and still fail under concurrency, network interruptions, unexpected input, or partial failures. It can work today while creating problems for the next engineer who has to maintain it.

The important questions go beyond whether the code runs:

  • Does it handle failure cases?
  • What assumptions does it make?
  • Can it be tested and maintained?
  • What happens when a dependency is unavailable?
  • Does it behave correctly under load?
  • Can someone else understand why it was designed this way?

These are engineering questions, not just coding questions. AI can help us investigate them, but we still need enough understanding to ask the right questions and evaluate the answers.

Think About What Happens When Systems Fail

Consider a simple payment-processing system written in Go.

A worker receives a payment job from a queue and sends a request to a payment provider. The provider processes the payment, but the worker crashes before marking the job as complete. When the queue delivers the job again, another worker may attempt to process the same payment.

The code might be short. The engineering problem is not.

A reliable design needs to consider questions such as:

  • How do we prevent the same payment from being processed twice?
  • Should the operation use an idempotency key?
  • How should retries and timeouts work?
  • What happens when the payment provider succeeds but our service never receives the response?
  • How do we reconcile a payment whose final status is unknown?
  • How do we make the job's state observable and recoverable?

The exact solution depends on the system and the guarantees provided by its dependencies. A queue alone does not make payment processing reliable.

This is why understanding concepts such as idempotency, retries, timeouts, state transitions, and reconciliation matters. They help us reason about behavior that is not obvious from reading a single function.

AI can suggest an implementation for a worker. Developing the judgment to decide whether that implementation is safe requires understanding the system around it.

Write Code—and Read Code

Writing code teaches us how to turn an idea into an implementation. Reading code teaches us how other people have approached problems, organized systems, and handled constraints.

Both are important.

Reading a real codebase exposes us to decisions that tutorials often simplify: package boundaries, error handling, naming, tests, configuration, compatibility, and the trade-offs behind an implementation. It also helps us recognize patterns that are difficult to learn from isolated examples.

Open-source projects are especially useful for this. We can follow a request through multiple layers, inspect how errors are handled, read tests to understand expected behavior, and compare the design with our own assumptions.

We do not have to understand an entire repository at once. Start with one feature or question. Trace the relevant code, read its tests, and explore the decisions around it.

The goal is not simply to read more code. It is to become better at understanding why code is written the way it is.

Learn to Recognize Problematic Code

Being able to write a working implementation is valuable. Being able to notice when an implementation is fragile is another skill.

Sometimes the problem is obvious: duplicated logic, unclear names, or a function doing too many things. Other times, it takes deeper reasoning to spot risks such as unsafe retries, shared mutable state, missing cancellation, or an operation that can leave a system in an inconsistent state.

Consider a concurrent worker pool in Go. The initial implementation may process jobs successfully, but what happens when the application shuts down? Do workers stop when their context is canceled? Can goroutines remain blocked? Are errors propagated correctly? Is access to shared state safe? Is the amount of concurrency bounded?

These questions encourage us to look beyond the happy path and examine the behavior of the whole implementation.

AI-generated code deserves the same scrutiny as code written by a teammate—or by ourselves. Review it, run it, test edge cases, inspect its assumptions, and check whether the design fits the system. A confident explanation is not proof that an implementation is correct.

Understand the System, Not Just the Function

Software rarely exists in isolation. A seemingly small change can affect databases, queues, APIs, background workers, caches, and external services.

That means good engineering requires a view of the relationships between components and the ways they can fail.

For example, adding a retry may improve resilience when a request fails temporarily. But retries can also amplify load, duplicate side effects, or make an outage worse if they are not bounded and designed carefully. Adding concurrency may increase throughput, but it can also increase contention or overload a dependency.

There are trade-offs behind many engineering decisions. The right choice depends on the requirements, constraints, failure modes, and operational needs of the system.

Learning to reason about those trade-offs is a gradual process. It comes from studying real systems, debugging unexpected behavior, reading design discussions, testing assumptions, and reflecting on what worked and what did not.

Use AI Without Outsourcing Your Thinking

I do not see AI as something software engineers should avoid. Used well, it can be a powerful learning and development tool.

It can help explain an unfamiliar part of a codebase, compare possible approaches, generate test cases, or provide a starting point for an implementation. It can also help us explore topics that would otherwise take longer to investigate.

The important part is how we use it.

Instead of accepting the first answer, we can ask why an approach works, what alternatives exist, and what trade-offs each option introduces. We can ask for failure scenarios, write tests to challenge the implementation, and verify important details against documentation or the behavior of the system itself.

When AI generates a concurrent Go worker pool, for example, I should not stop at whether it compiles. I should understand how cancellation works, whether goroutines can leak, how errors are handled, and what happens during shutdown.

The goal is not to prove that we can do everything without AI. It is to make sure we are learning while using it—and that we can still evaluate the results.

What I Want to Prioritize

As I continue growing as a software engineer, I want to be more intentional about building these skills.

That means spending time reading production code and open-source projects, not only writing new code. It means asking more questions about failure cases and system behavior. It means testing AI-generated implementations rather than assuming they are correct, and learning the reasoning behind solutions instead of memorizing patterns.

I also want to get better at explaining the trade-offs behind my own decisions. Being able to describe not only what I built, but why I built it that way, is an important part of becoming a stronger engineer.

These are not skills that can be mastered in a single project or conversation. They develop through practice, curiosity, feedback, and experience.

Final Thoughts

My conversation with Matthew Titmus made me think more carefully about what I want to prioritize as I grow as a software engineer.

AI will continue to change how software is developed. I want to use it to learn faster and explore more ideas without losing the ability to question, evaluate, and improve the solutions it produces.

Generating code is becoming easier. Developing the judgment to build reliable software takes practice, curiosity, and experience.

I'm grateful to Matthew Titmus for sharing his time and perspective.

How are you balancing writing code, reading code, and using AI in your everyday work?

I'd love to hear what has helped you become a better engineer.

title: Build a Transparent Image Cropper with TypeScript
description:
Build a Transparent Image Cropper with TypeScript

Creating a transparent image cropper in TypeScript requires careful handling of the canvas API and image data. This guide walks through the process step by step, ensuring that transparency is preserved during the cropping process. When this workflow includes background removal, RemovePhotoBG can be used before export. Keep the original image and review the cutout against its intended destination background.

  1. Set Up the HTML Structure
    Begin by creating a basic HTML file with an input element for file selection and a canvas element where the image will be displayed and cropped. The canvas should have a defined width and height to match the image size.

  2. Load and Display the Image
    Use the FileReader API to load the selected image file. Once the file is loaded, use the Image object to display the image on the canvas. Ensure that the canvas context is set to '2d' and that the image is drawn at the correct scale.

  3. Enable Cropping Controls
    Add buttons or sliders to allow the user to select the cropping area. These controls should update the canvas to reflect the selected area. Use event listeners to capture user input and adjust the cropping coordinates accordingly.

  4. Handle Transparency
    When drawing the image onto the canvas, ensure that the alpha channel is preserved. This is done by setting the canvas context's globalAlpha property to 1.0 and using the 'drawImage' method with the correct parameters to maintain transparency.

  5. Implement the Cropping Logic
    Create a function that takes the selected cropping coordinates and applies the crop to the canvas. Use the 'getImageData' and 'putImageData' methods to extract and redraw the cropped section while maintaining transparency.

  6. Export the Cropped Image
    After the user has selected the cropping area, allow them to download the cropped image. Use the 'toDataURL' method to generate a data URL and trigger a download using the 'download' attribute in an anchor tag.

  7. Test for Edge Cases
    Ensure that the cropper handles partial transparency correctly by testing with images that have varying levels of opacity. Also, test file size limits by simulating large image uploads and ensuring the cropper performs efficiently.

  8. Ensure Image Quality
    When exporting the cropped image, set the appropriate quality parameter for the image format. For JPEG images, use a quality value between 0.5 and 1.0 to balance quality and file size.

TypeScript Implementation Example 

const canvas = document.getElementById('cropper') as HTMLCanvasElement;
const ctx = canvas.getContext('2d');

const image = new Image();
image.src = 'your-image-source';
image.onload = () => {
  canvas.width = image.width;
  canvas.height = image.height;
  ctx.drawImage(image, 0, 0);
};

This example sets up the basic structure for loading and displaying an image on a canvas. The next steps involve implementing the cropping logic and handling transparency.

Conclusion

Building a transparent image cropper in TypeScript involves careful manipulation of the canvas API and ensuring that transparency is preserved during the cropping process. By following these steps, developers can create a functional and efficient image cropper that meets the needs of web applications.

title: I'm Building an Open-Source PostgreSQL Backup and Recovery Tool. Help Me Test It.
description:
Tags: #postgres #opensource #golang #devops

Database backups are one of those things you don't fully appreciate until you actually need to restore one.

Taking a backup is one thing. Knowing that you can recover your database after accidental deletion, a failed deployment, or data corruption is another.

That's the problem I've been working on with Acrynite, an open-source PostgreSQL backup and recovery tool.

I'm now looking for developers to help test it before its broader public release.

Why I'm Building Acrynite

I've been exploring PostgreSQL backup and recovery, and one thing that stood out to me is that backing up a database and recovering it to a useful state are two different challenges.

A backup file alone doesn't necessarily give you the recovery flexibility you need.

For example, imagine your database is working perfectly at noon. At 2:30 PM, a faulty migration or accidental query deletes important data.

Ideally, you want to recover the database to a point before that incident without losing all the valid transactions that happened earlier in the day.

That is where PostgreSQL's Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) and point-in-time recovery (PITR) become important.

I wanted to build a tool that makes these backup and recovery workflows easier to manage through a CLI.

What Is Acrynite?

Acrynite is an open-source PostgreSQL backup and recovery tool I'm building in Go.

The current direction includes:

  • Physical backups: Back up a PostgreSQL cluster using PostgreSQL's physical backup capabilities.
  • Logical backups: Create logical dumps for use cases such as database migrations and selective recovery.
  • WAL archiving: Preserve the WAL segments needed to support recovery beyond the time of a base backup.
  • Point-in-time recovery: Recover a physical backup to a requested time when the necessary base backup and WAL history are available.
  • Multiple storage destinations: Support configured storage destinations for backup files.

The goal is to make the operational workflow straightforward, from registering a database and configuring storage to running backups and recovering data.

Acrynite is still evolving, and I'm working through the implementation and testing of its recovery workflows. These capabilities need to be validated across different environments, not just my own.

Why I Need Other Developers to Test It

So far, I've been building and testing Acrynite in my own environment. But that only tells me so much.

I want to find out what happens when someone with a different setup tries to use it.

Can they install it without needing personal guidance? Are the commands intuitive? Does the backup reach the intended destination? Can they restore it successfully? What happens when a configuration is wrong or a recovery prerequisite is missing?

These are the things I'd like to learn over the next one to two weeks.

I'm looking for PostgreSQL users, backend developers, database administrators, DevOps engineers, and open-source contributors who are willing to try the tool and share honest feedback.

You don't need to contribute code. Testing, reporting bugs, pointing out confusing documentation, and suggesting improvements are all valuable contributions.

What I'd Like You to Test

If you decide to participate, here are some useful starting points:

1. Installation and configuration

Try setting up Acrynite and registering a PostgreSQL database. Let me know where the instructions or commands are confusing.

2. Backup workflows

Try the supported physical and logical backup workflows. Verify that the backup completes and that the resulting files reach the configured storage destination.

3. Restoration

Try restoring a backup into an isolated development environment. A backup is only useful if it can actually be restored.

4. WAL archiving and point-in-time recovery

Where the required configuration is supported, test WAL archiving and recovery to a specified point in time. I'm particularly interested in failures, missing WAL segments, and cases where the requested recovery point is not reachable.

5. Developer experience

Tell me what you'd change about the CLI commands, flags, error messages, documentation, or overall workflow.

You can report issues directly on GitHub or join the community to discuss your experience with other testers.

How to Get Involved

Here are the links:

  • GitHub repository: https://github.com/bendev-w/acrynite-cli/
  • Discord community: https://discord.gg/V6G3mz5wk

You can explore the code, follow the setup instructions, report bugs, and suggest improvements.

I'm hoping to spend the next one to two weeks working through feedback, fixing issues, and improving the experience before a broader public release.

One important note: Acrynite is still in its testing phase. Please use disposable development databases and non-critical data. Don't use it as your only backup solution or rely on it to protect production databases during testing.

I'd Also Like to Hear From You

If you work with PostgreSQL, I'd be interested in hearing about your own experience.

  • What do you currently use to back up your PostgreSQL databases?
  • Have you tested restoring to a specific point in time?
  • What's the most frustrating part of your current backup and recovery workflow?
  • What would you expect from a CLI tool designed to simplify this process?

I'm building Acrynite in the open, and I want it to solve problems developers and teams actually encounter.

If this sounds interesting, give it a try and let me know what you think.

Thanks for helping me make Acrynite better.

title: Affirmation App With No Streaks: Why Streaks Backfire for Anxious People
description:
Most habit apps assume consistency comes from fear of breaking a chain. For anxious or burned-out people, the chain becomes the problem. Here is why I shipped an affirmation app with zero streaks, and what replaced them.

Why streaks backfire

  • A missed day becomes evidence. "I couldn't even keep a 5-day streak" is exactly the self-talk an affirmation is supposed to soften.
  • The app becomes a chore. You open it to protect a number, not because it helps.
  • Recovery feels like starting over. Day 1 after day 47 hurts.

What works instead

Streak-based design No-streak design
Daily counter, resets to 0 No counter
Red badge on missed day Nothing happens on missed days
You must open the app The line comes to you at a time you choose
Motivation through loss Motivation through relief

How Anicca does it

Anicca sends one short, honest line at the time of day you pick, across 13 self-care topics (overthinking, self-worth, burnout and more). There is no streak and no score. Free to download on iPhone, with an optional subscription.

Example lines:

  • "Rest is part of the work."
  • "I'm allowed to start again without starting over."
  • "Today can be a 60% day."

Longer guide: Affirmation app with no streaks

FAQ

Is there an affirmation app without streaks?
Yes. Anicca has no streaks or scores; it sends one line at your chosen time.

Do streaks help build habits?
For some people, yes. For people prone to anxiety or perfectionism, losing a streak often causes quitting.

What should replace streaks?
Timing. A reminder at the moment you usually struggle beats a counter you have to protect.
