title: Overcoming Challenges in Reading Technical Documentation for Java Spring Boot and Cloud Hosting
description:
Mastering Technical Documentation: Overcoming Challenges for Enhanced Productivity

Effectively reading and processing technical documentation is a cornerstone skill for programmers. Mastery in this area not only enhances productivity but also ensures success in both learning and professional environments. However, developers often face significant challenges when engaging with complex materials, such as Java Spring Boot and cloud hosting documentation. This article dissects these challenges, explores their underlying mechanisms, and provides actionable strategies to improve comprehension and retention. The stakes are high: without refining these skills, developers risk inefficiency, heightened frustration, and subpar project outcomes, which can impede career growth and confidence in tackling complex tasks.

Impact Chains: Understanding the Consequences of Poor Documentation Engagement

The process of reading technical documentation is fraught with pitfalls that can derail even the most motivated developers. These challenges manifest in distinct impact chains, each with its own internal processes and observable effects:

  • Impact: Overwhelm and frustration. Internal Process: Attempting to read and understand entire documentation at once. Observable Effect: Burnout and reduced motivation to continue learning. Analysis: This approach exceeds cognitive capacity, leading to mental exhaustion. Breaking documentation into manageable sections is essential to sustain focus and prevent burnout.
  • Impact: Poor retention and understanding. Internal Process: Passive reading without active engagement. Observable Effect: Difficulty recalling key details and applying concepts. Analysis: Passive reading fails to encode information effectively. Active engagement through note-taking and self-quizzing is critical for long-term retention.
  • Impact: Misalignment with assignment goals. Internal Process: Misprioritization of irrelevant details. Observable Effect: Incomplete or incorrect proposal and design documents. Analysis: Without a clear focus on key concepts, developers waste time on non-essential information, compromising the quality of their work.
  • Impact: Theoretical knowledge without practical understanding. Internal Process: Lack of practical application of learned concepts. Observable Effect: Inability to implement solutions effectively. Analysis: Theoretical knowledge remains abstract without hands-on practice. Bridging this gap is crucial for translating learning into actionable skills.

System Instabilities: Root Causes of Documentation Challenges

These impact chains are symptoms of deeper system instabilities that undermine effective documentation engagement:

  • Instability: Information overload. Mechanism: Complexity of Java Spring Boot and cloud hosting documentation exceeds cognitive load. Effect: Difficulty processing and retaining information. Analysis: The sheer volume and complexity of technical documentation overwhelm the brain’s processing capacity, necessitating strategies to reduce cognitive load.
  • Instability: Lack of structured approach. Mechanism: Absence of a clear reading plan or strategy. Effect: Inconsistent learning and progress. Analysis: Without a structured approach, learning becomes haphazard, leading to gaps in understanding and inefficient use of time.
  • Instability: Self-doubt and imposter syndrome. Mechanism: Negative self-perception affecting confidence and engagement. Effect: Reduced motivation and increased anxiety during learning. Analysis: Psychological barriers can paralyze progress. Building confidence through incremental achievements is vital for sustained engagement.

Mechanics of Processes: Strategies for Effective Documentation Engagement

To address these instabilities, developers can employ specific processes that enhance comprehension, retention, and application of technical documentation:

  • Process: Structured Reading Plan. Logic: Breaking documentation into sections reduces cognitive load and provides clear objectives. Effect: Improved focus and comprehension. Analysis: A structured plan transforms overwhelming content into manageable tasks, fostering a sense of progress and control.
  • Process: Active Learning Focus. Logic: Engaging with material through note-taking and self-quizzing enhances encoding and retrieval. Effect: Better retention and understanding. Analysis: Active learning transforms passive consumption into an interactive process, deepening understanding and memory retention.
  • Process: Information Prioritization. Logic: Focusing on key concepts aligns learning with assignment goals and reduces unnecessary effort. Effect: Efficient use of time and resources. Analysis: Prioritization ensures that effort is directed toward the most relevant information, maximizing productivity.
  • Process: Confidence Building. Logic: Starting with beginner-friendly resources reduces intimidation and builds familiarity. Effect: Increased confidence and willingness to tackle complex material. Analysis: Gradual exposure to complexity builds a foundation of confidence, making advanced topics more approachable.
  • Process: Practical Application Focus. Logic: Applying concepts through coding exercises reinforces understanding and retention. Effect: Bridging theoretical knowledge with practical skills. Analysis: Practical application transforms abstract concepts into tangible skills, enhancing both understanding and retention.
  • Process: Incremental Learning. Logic: Iterative review and revisiting documentation deepens understanding and connects new information with existing knowledge. Effect: Long-term retention and mastery of concepts. Analysis: Incremental learning builds a robust knowledge base, ensuring that new information is integrated into existing frameworks for lasting comprehension.

Constraints and Their Effects: Navigating Limitations for Optimal Outcomes

Several constraints further complicate the process of engaging with technical documentation. Understanding these constraints and their effects is crucial for developing effective strategies:
Constraint Effect on System
Time Constraints Requires prioritization and efficient reading strategies to meet externship deadlines.
Complexity of Material Increases cognitive load and risk of information overload.
Lack of Context Makes it difficult to understand how specific details fit into the broader system.
Memory Retention Necessitates active learning and practical application to reinforce understanding.

Conclusion: Mastering the art of reading technical documentation is not merely a skill but a necessity for developers aiming to excel in their careers. By understanding the impact chains, system instabilities, and mechanics of effective engagement, developers can transform challenges into opportunities for growth. Implementing structured strategies, prioritizing active learning, and addressing psychological barriers are essential steps toward achieving long-term success in both learning and professional environments.

The Critical Role of Documentation Mastery

The instability experienced by developers when reading technical documentation stems from a series of interconnected issues. Below is a detailed analysis of these impact chains, their internal processes, and observable effects:

Impact Internal Process Observable Effect
Cognitive Overload Attempting to process complex Java Spring Boot and cloud hosting documentation exceeds working memory capacity. Overwhelm, frustration, and burnout during reading sessions.
Passive Reading Absence of active engagement (e.g., note-taking, summarization) during reading. Poor retention and inability to recall key details when needed.

Intermediate Conclusion: These challenges create a vicious cycle where cognitive overload leads to passive reading, misprioritization exacerbates inefficiency, and the lack of practical application reinforces the theoretical-practical gap. Breaking this cycle requires targeted interventions that address each issue systematically.

The impact chains above manifest as specific instability points, each with profound consequences for developers:

To counteract the challenges outlined above, the following mechanisms stabilize the system by addressing the root causes of instability:

Mastering Technical Documentation: A Strategic Approach for Developers

Effectively reading and processing technical documentation is a cornerstone skill for programmers. Mastery in this area not only enhances productivity but also ensures success in both learning and professional environments. However, developers often face significant challenges when engaging with such materials, particularly in real-world scenarios like Java Spring Boot or cloud hosting platforms. This article dissects these challenges, offering actionable strategies to improve comprehension and retention, while highlighting the stakes of neglecting this critical skill.

Mechanisms of Effective Documentation Reading

The process of reading technical documentation can be optimized through several mechanisms, each addressing specific cognitive and practical barriers. These mechanisms are designed to reduce overwhelm, enhance retention, and ensure efficient application of knowledge.

  • Structured Reading Plan:

Breaking documentation into manageable sections with clear objectives reduces cognitive load by leveraging working memory capacity. This chunking of information makes complex material more digestible. Impact → Internal Process → Observable Effect: Overwhelm → Structured breakdown → Improved focus and comprehension. By systematically organizing content, developers can navigate documentation with greater ease, ensuring that no critical detail is overlooked.

  • Active Learning Focus:

Engaging with documentation through note-taking, summarization, and self-quizzing enhances encoding and retrieval via dual-coding and spaced repetition. Impact → Internal Process → Observable Effect: Passive reading → Active engagement → Enhanced retention and understanding. This approach transforms reading from a passive activity into an interactive learning experience, fostering deeper comprehension and long-term memory retention.

  • Information Prioritization:

Identifying and focusing on key concepts aligned with specific goals optimizes mental resource allocation. Impact → Internal Process → Observable Effect: Misprioritization → Targeted focus → Efficient time use and improved work relevance. By concentrating on the most pertinent information, developers can avoid the pitfalls of information overload and ensure that their efforts are directed toward achieving their objectives.

  • Practical Application Focus:

Immediate coding exercises bridge the gap between theory and practice by strengthening neural pathways. Impact → Internal Process → Observable Effect: Lack of application → Hands-on practice → Reinforced understanding. Applying concepts in real-world scenarios not only solidifies understanding but also builds confidence in using new technologies and frameworks.

  • Incremental Learning:

Iterative review and schema integration build long-term memory via the spacing effect. Impact → Internal Process → Observable Effect: Inconsistent learning → Progressive mastery → Reduced cognitive load over time. Regularly revisiting material ensures that knowledge is retained and integrated into a developer’s cognitive framework, facilitating smoother application in future projects.

Constraints and System Instability Points

Despite the effectiveness of these mechanisms, several constraints can hinder their implementation. Understanding these challenges is crucial for developing strategies to mitigate their impact.

  • Time Constraints:

Limited time necessitates prioritization and efficient strategies, increasing pressure on reading processes. Developers often find themselves juggling multiple tasks, leaving little time for thorough documentation review. This constraint underscores the importance of structured reading plans and information prioritization to maximize the utility of available time.

  • Complexity of Material:

Dense, specialized information elevates cognitive load, exacerbating overwhelm and burnout risks. Technical documentation is often written for experts, making it inaccessible to less experienced developers. This complexity highlights the need for active learning strategies and visual aids to simplify and clarify content.

  • Lack of Context:

Absence of prior experience hinders understanding of system-level relationships, leading to misprioritization. Without a foundational understanding of the subject matter, developers may struggle to discern which information is most relevant. Leveraging community resources and visual aids can provide the necessary context to overcome this barrier.

  • Memory Retention:

Without practical application or repetition, key details are poorly encoded, resulting in subpar outcomes. The human brain is not designed to retain information passively; active engagement and repetition are essential for long-term memory. This constraint emphasizes the importance of practical application focus and incremental learning in the documentation reading process.

System Instability Points and Their Mitigation

System instability points represent critical junctures where the reading process can break down. Addressing these points is essential for maintaining efficiency and effectiveness in documentation review.

  • Cognitive Overload:

Occurs when documentation complexity exceeds working memory capacity, triggering overwhelm and burnout. Physics/Logic: Limited cognitive resources are overwhelmed by unchunked information. Mitigation strategies include structured reading plans and the use of visual aids to break down complex information into manageable parts.

  • Passive Reading:

Lack of active engagement impairs memory encoding, leading to poor retention. Physics/Logic: Information is not effectively transferred to long-term memory without active processing. Active learning focus, such as note-taking and self-quizzing, ensures that information is processed deeply and retained effectively.

  • Misprioritization:

Focusing on irrelevant details wastes mental resources, compromising work quality. Physics/Logic: Misallocation of cognitive effort reduces efficiency. Information prioritization, guided by specific goals and assignment requirements, ensures that efforts are directed toward the most relevant content.

  • Lack of Application:

Theoretical knowledge remains abstract without practical use, creating a theory-practice gap. Physics/Logic: Neural pathways are not reinforced without hands-on experience. Practical application focus, through coding exercises and real-world projects, bridges this gap and reinforces understanding.

Expert Observations and Recommendations

To navigate these challenges effectively, developers can adopt several expert-recommended strategies. These strategies are designed to enhance comprehension, retention, and application of technical documentation.

  • Start Small:

Beginner-friendly resources reduce intimidation by gradually building familiarity. Mechanism: Confidence Building. Starting with simpler materials allows developers to build a foundation of knowledge and confidence before tackling more complex documentation.

  • Use Visual Aids:

Diagrams and mind maps clarify relationships, addressing lack of context. Mechanism: Structured Reading Plan. Visual aids provide a structured overview of complex systems, making it easier to understand how different components relate to one another.

  • Leverage Community Resources:

Supplemental materials provide alternative explanations, reducing complexity. Mechanism: Active Learning Focus. Community forums, tutorials, and videos offer diverse perspectives that can clarify difficult concepts and reinforce understanding.

  • Practice Retrieval:

Self-quizzing reinforces memory encoding, mitigating retention issues. Mechanism: Incremental Learning. Regularly testing oneself on key concepts ensures that information is retained and can be recalled when needed.

  • Iterative Review:

Repeated exposure deepens understanding, connecting new knowledge to existing schemas. Mechanism: Incremental Learning. Revisiting material at regular intervals strengthens memory and facilitates the integration of new knowledge into existing cognitive frameworks.

  • Focus on Goals:

Aligning reading with assignment requirements prevents misprioritization. Mechanism: Information Prioritization. Keeping specific goals in mind ensures that reading efforts are directed toward achieving tangible outcomes, enhancing both efficiency and effectiveness.

Conclusion

Mastering the art of reading technical documentation is a transformative skill for developers. By implementing structured reading plans, active learning strategies, and practical application focus, developers can overcome common challenges and enhance their productivity. The stakes are high: inefficiency, frustration, and subpar project outcomes can hinder career growth and confidence. However, with the right strategies, developers can turn technical documentation into a powerful tool for learning and professional advancement. By addressing constraints and system instability points, and by adopting expert recommendations, developers can ensure that they not only survive but thrive in their engagement with complex technical materials.

title: Two serious security vulnerabilities identified in Wasmtime software
description:
Two severe 9.9-rated flaws have been found in Wasmtime's Cranelift compiler.

CVE-2026-115889 impacts all architectures, while CVE-2026-115893 affects ARM64 systems.

Fixed versions are available across multiple release lines.

The problems lie in the internal part of the software that translates the code so that it can be executed by the computer. The first issue affects systems regardless of their processor type, while the second concerns only systems based on ARM64 processors. In order to exploit the gaps, someone needs to have control over the program that is currently running.

Who is most at risk?

The risk is greater for services that undertake to translate and run code originating from external users or customers, as is the case, for example, with the Fastly Compute service.

So far, the software creators have no reports of actual attacks exploiting these gaps, while the problems are not even included in the authorities' official lists of actively exploited vulnerabilities.

What should administrators do?

The developers released fixed versions on October 19 and 20. The safe versions include the 36.0.19, 48.0.7, 49.0.4, and 50.0.0 series or later.

Because this software is usually embedded within other programs, a simple file update is not enough. Every program that uses it must be rebuilt and recompiled from scratch with the new, corrected version.

title: Go 1.28 HTTP/2 Parking: Measuring Memory Savings
description:
While reading the draft Go 1.28 release notes, I noticed a change in the HTTP/2 server. With this change, the goroutine responsible for serving a connection can exit when there is no work to do, instead of waiting. A new goroutine takes over when needed. At first, it seemed like a small change, but I wondered how much memory it could save on a server with thousands of open connections.

I decided to measure it rather than guess. I wanted to see how it affected process memory usage, goroutine counts, and Go runtime memory metrics.

What is HTTP/2 parking?

An HTTP/2 connection can stay open even when it has no active streams. In the older server behavior, a goroutine runs the connection's serveLoop and waits there when nothing new is ready. The Go 1.28 development code adds an internal mechanism called parking. When serveLoop has no work ready to process, and the implementation's safety conditions are met, that goroutine can exit. When new work arrives, a new goroutine runs serveLoop again.

Parking is not limited to connections with no active streams. A handler can still be running while serveLoop has nothing immediate to process. If those safety conditions are met, the serving goroutine can be parked. That does not mean every active connection, or every running handler, can be parked.

The word parking comes from the Go implementation, including names such as tryPark and the temporary GODEBUG setting http2serveparking. It is not a public API, and the draft release notes do not use this name for the change. The change is how the server manages the goroutine for a connection, not how application code handles requests.

This also gave me a useful way to test the change. I could run the same Go 1.28 server binary with parking enabled and disabled, instead of relying only on a Go 1.27 versus Go 1.28 comparison.

How I tested it

I used the same benchmark code and machine for three configurations:

  1. Go 1.27.2, as an older-version reference.
  2. Go 1.28 development build, parking enabled, as the default behavior of the tested revision.
  3. The same Go 1.28 binary, parking disabled, using GODEBUG=http2serveparking=0.

The tested Go 1.28 revision was 5c51011e82ed754af072baaf4338ff35e76fe705. The benchmark source was pinned to commit 86753bd4d1f79621a4f3c6927c8239419e54bde2.

For each configuration, I measured the server with 0, 1,000, and 5,000 idle HTTP/2 connections. Each complete run used ten rounds for every case and connection count. I repeated the full experiment three times on the same Linux machine. The benchmark collected short sample windows after the connections had settled, and the published results use medians rather than a single sample.

The test machine used an Intel Core i7-1265U, Linux 6.18.56, and about 32 GiB of RAM. The benchmark configuration set GOMAXPROCS=12 and GOGC=100. I kept the natural garbage collection behavior rather than forcing a collection before each measurement.

I looked at four metrics. RSS measures resident memory for the server process as reported by Linux. Goroutines shows how many goroutines the Go runtime reports. StackInuse describes memory in use by goroutine stacks. HeapAlloc is the amount of allocated heap memory reported by the runtime. These values are related, but they do not measure the same thing.

RSS: the clearest change

The largest difference appeared at 5,000 idle connections. The table below shows median RSS from each complete run, in MiB:

Run Go 1.27.2 Go 1.28, parking off Go 1.28, parking on Saved by parking
1 249.89 218.28 129.19 89.08
2 247.18 223.73 131.11 92.62
3 245.60 217.94 133.25 84.70

Compared with the same Go 1.28 binary with parking disabled, enabling parking reduced RSS by 84.7 to 92.6 MiB, or about 38.9% to 41.4%, across the three runs. At 1,000 idle connections, the reduction was smaller but still clear, at about 15.7 to 16.6 MiB.

The zero-connection baseline stayed close to 8.5 to 8.7 MiB across the configurations. I also calculated baseline-adjusted RSS by subtracting each configuration's zero-connection median. That helps show the growth associated with idle connections, but the main comparison above uses the observed process RSS.

Fewer goroutines, less stack memory

The goroutine counts helped explain the shape of the result. With 5,000 idle connections, Go 1.28 reported about 10,007 goroutines with parking disabled and 5,007 with parking enabled. That is a difference of exactly 5,000 goroutines in this benchmark. At 1,000 idle connections, the difference was 1,000 goroutines.

The stack numbers moved in the same direction. At 5,000 connections, StackInuse was about 99 MiB with parking disabled and about 21 MiB with parking enabled. The reduction was close to 78 MiB in all three complete runs.

This does not mean that every byte saved in RSS came from stacks. RSS includes more than Go stacks, and changes in heap allocation, runtime state, and the operating system can affect it. It does show that the lower goroutine and stack counts are consistent with the parking mechanism.

HeapAlloc did not tell the same simple story

HeapAlloc was less consistent. In some runs, parking enabled used less heap than parking disabled. In another run, it used slightly more. This is a good reminder that one memory metric cannot stand in for another.

For this experiment, RSS, goroutine count, and StackInuse provide a clearer picture of the difference. I would not describe the change as a fixed heap saving or claim that a certain percentage of total memory always disappears.

Limits of this benchmark

These measurements come from one machine, one benchmark design, and a specific development revision of Go 1.28. They are not results from a final Go 1.28 release. I tested mostly idle connections, not a mix of real traffic, active streams, and application workloads.

The benchmark kept the Go 1.28 server binary the same when switching parking on and off. That makes the parking comparison more useful, but it still does not remove all system noise. The three full runs show a repeatable direction and a range, not a universal guarantee.

The GODEBUG=http2serveparking=0 setting I used for this comparison is temporary and undocumented. I would not treat it as a stable option for future releases.

I have kept the benchmark source at a fixed commit and the tested Go revision linked here so the details can be checked later.

Conclusion

In this benchmark, HTTP/2 parking made a clear difference in memory usage. With 5,000 idle connections, the same Go 1.28 server binary used around 85 to 93 MiB less RSS when parking was enabled. It also had 5,000 fewer goroutines and used about 78 MiB less stack memory.

What I found most interesting was how much memory an otherwise quiet connection can keep around. Changing what the server does while it waits can matter as much as optimizing the work it performs.

I would not apply these numbers to every Go service. Still, for servers that keep many idle HTTP/2 connections open, this is a change worth understanding and measuring with a real workload.

title: Building an AI-ready design system library: Code → Figma with MCP.
description:
In-System Design

A practical guide for designers: why my design system starts in code, and how I build, check and maintain the Figma library.

In-System Design: a three-part series.
Part 1: Building an AI-ready design system: Code → Figma (you are here)
Part 2: AI prototyping inside your design system (3 November 2026)
Part 3: From code to Figma and back (10 November 2026)

For designers who know Figma well and have never written production code, and for the design system teams around them. Every technical word is explained in the box at the end.

For most of my career, the work went one way. I designed in Figma, a developer turned it into code, and when something did not survive the trip, we sorted it out between us.

Then I handed that same route to an AI, and what came back was unsettling, mainly because it looked fine. It read my Figma file, translated it faithfully, and filled in everything the file did not say with whatever seemed plausible.

The code that comes out is mediocre, and that is the part everyone frets about. Fair enough, since code quality is at least the part you can read, review and complain about in a pull request.

What worries me more is what gets invented: the focus order, the error states, what a screen reader announces, what happens when a request fails, or when a list comes back empty. None of that shows up in a screenshot, so nobody catches it in review.

So I turned the direction around. My design system now starts in code, and I generate my Figma library from it. Code always wins, and Figma is a mirror, not a second truth.

That sounds like a demotion for Figma, and in practice my Figma file got busier. This article is why, how I build the library, and how I keep an existing one honest, including the parts that still need babysitting.

Why doesn’t Figma-to-code with AI work well?

Because your Figma file was always supposed to be an abstraction. Let me explain: I sat down one afternoon and compared what a React component can express with what a Figma component can express, because that is the kind of thing I do for fun now, apparently. The life and soul of the party, I am. My count came out at roughly 17% coverage. For CSS, it was better, around 45%, and still nowhere near complete.

Those are my own numbers from my own comparison, not an official statistic. Check them against your own stack before quoting them in a meeting.

Everything Figma cannot say used to be filled in by a developer who could walk over and ask a question.

That gap is not a Figma failure, and no, I do not want Figma to close it. If focus order, container behaviour and ARIA labels lived in the file, you would need to be a front-end developer to use your own library.

A developer also notices what is missing. An AI does not. It takes the file literally, as a complete instruction, fills the gaps with whatever it has seen most often, and carries on, so the old direction now produces a component that looks finished and is partly invented.

Turn the arrow around and the same literal-mindedness becomes a gift. Generating from code, “it reads exactly what is there” is precisely what you want, because what is there is the real thing: real props, real values, real defaults, real states.

Flip it: Code as the source of truth, Figma follows

Code is the source of truth. Figma mirrors it. Where they differ, Figma is wrong.

I know how that lands in a room full of designers. Designers still do not work in code, and I have no plans to write production code myself. Figma does not matter less either. I think best on a canvas; I design there, and I would fight anyone who tried to take it away, so hear me out.

Hands-on: from a repo to a Figma library, step by step:

This is the workflow I currently use and demo, with the prompts I actually use. You don’t need to be a developer for this. You do need to be comfortable opening a repo and reading what’s in it, and the AI will walk you through the rest. So yes, some new territory, but stay with me! It’s great fun!

What you need:
1. A design system in code you can access, with Storybook running on it
2. An empty Figma file
3. MCP connection. I use and recommend Figma Console MCP by Southleft for this because it reads and writes variables properly, which the basic connection does not.

1. Get access to the code as a designer

A branch, a sandbox, or a playground repo. Ask development for the smallest safe thing: a copy where nothing you do can reach production.

If you want to practise first, download any sample design system as a zip and point your AI at the folder. I hand out a sample file for trainings and sessions, but you can also make your own. Connect that folder or branch with your AI. I will use Claude Code for my example. Your developers will most likely use the terminal or an editor; I use the Claude desktop app and the Claude Code tab.

2. Check that Storybook is there

Once you are connected, ask Claude Code to open Storybook for you.

What you get is a local website: it runs on your own machine, at an address like localhost:6001. Only you can see it, nothing is published, and it is built from the code sitting in front of you. It shows every component, live and clickable.

Storybook does not keep its own copy of your system; it lives inside it. Next to each component sits a small stories file listing its examples, so the page you click through is built from the real code and you can see, understand and compare it as a designer. That is also the key to prototyping with AI and generating sensible output, and I will come back to it in another article.

It is so great to finally go through the real stuff visually as a designer; I cannot believe I didn’t use this earlier! You can look at the Storybook of one of my samples here.

No Storybook? You can still do everything in this article. What you lose is the view and the component list, which I personally need to understand and compare, and for some parity checks later on.

If you are in a playground environment, you can just ask Claude to add it to your own copy and play there. In a real repo, it is a developer’s call, because it brings dependencies somebody has to maintain, so ask rather than install. It also needs to be Storybook 10 or newer, with the components manifest switched on, before an agent can read that list (this is for parity checks and prototyping later).

3. Open an empty Figma file

Clean, empty, and destined to become the library. Not your existing library, which comes later. Then open the Console MCP inside it.

From here, Claude Code is the hub between the two: one arm in the real code, one in the open Figma file. I can ask in plain words for something to be read on one side and built on the other.

4. Tokens and styles first, always

Components use tokens, so the tokens and text styles have to exist before the components do.

First find out where the tokens live, and yes, you can just ask Claude. In my repo they are JSON: one layer of raw values, one of semantic roles. In yours they might be CSS custom properties, or a Tailwind config, in which case I am sorry. Figma then splits them into two: colours, spacing and radii become variables, typography becomes text styles bound to variables. Console MCP does this well; you still have to check it, and you still need to know your way around Figma properly.

My prompt for this step, roughly as I say it:

I want an exact mirror of this repo in Figma. The MCP is on and the file is empty. Let’s do this step by step. Transfer the tokens first. Always use the same naming as the code, so Figma and the code match. Set up collections that match the code, primitives and semantic. Alias them. Scope them. Where needed use modes (e.g. light and dark mode). Do the same for the text styles, using the naming from code, and use variables as in the code. Anything you cannot express, write into GAPS.md always. Then stop and tell me if you need anything.

You will need to adapt this to your setup; mine is React with tokens in JSON, two layers. Once done, check in Figma that everything is set up correctly and compare with Storybook (I ask it to display all of this on a page for me).

5. Build two components as a test

Not the whole system. Two, ideally one simple and one awkward. I use Button and Alert, or some sort of dropdown; it’s fun with Figma.

Now build the Alert and the Button component as a test, set up as in code, using my variables and styles. Anything you cannot express, write into GAPS.md always (GAPS.md I explain below; it’s the best part!).

Then I go and look properly: are the variants complete, are the properties named as in code, is auto layout set up, are the tokens bound and scoped, did it carry the description across.

That last part is where the real value sits. The two sides do not only look alike, they carry the same names and the same properties, down to the spelling. No danger on one side and error on the other, no Card that is secretly a Panel. Everything that comes later in an AI workflow stands on that: prototyping with real components, checking for drift, sending a screen back to code.

If the two come out right, I run the whole library. And yes, that costs time and tokens. However, only once. Staying in sync afterwards is a different job: a contract, or in my case a parity check comparing two JSON lists. More on that soon.

6. Know what you need! Context travels with each element, like a little parcel

You might have heard that context is key when working with AI design systems, especially later as we want to prototype with all of this stuff. Most of what gets called context is a markdown file: a DESIGN.md, a rules file, a page of guidelines. But most of the context is baked into the things themselves. Every token, every component, every style: think of each one as a little parcel carrying its own context.

What is in the parcel:

  • the component name, identical on both sides
  • each property with its allowed values and its default
  • each token name, what it points at, and where it is allowed to be used at all
  • the description written once in code and carried into the Figma component
  • the code syntax on a Figma variable, so the variable knows what it is called in CSS
  • a link back to that component’s page in Storybook
  • and the gaps file, for everything that could not make the trip

None of that was typed into a document by hand, and to be honest, by hand I wouldn’t even get close. Markdown is for the why and the when, the rules and the exceptions. Everything factual gets generated and attached, and then it cannot quietly disagree with the code. Oh, how I love my MCP!

7. Ask for the gaps, every single time via GAPS.md

You might have noticed that I ask for GAPS.md every single time. I ended up with this one by accident. I wanted to know what had happened to all the things Figma could not express, so I asked the AI to list them, and the list turned out to be more useful than the components it had just built.

Write a GAPS.md: everything you could not express in Figma, everything you were unsure about, and anything I should check by hand.

The gaps exist whether or not anyone writes them down, and written down they become reviewable. My own gaps file contains things like line heights that are unitless in code and have to become pixels in Figma, states that only exist in behaviour, and layout rules Figma has no equivalent for. Each one with a note on what I decided. I also include a list of items the AI was unsure about that need my revision.

A gaps file turns the imperfect mirror into a list you can take to a developer and work through, and you might come up with more creative ideas on how to use it.

8. Turn what you learned into a skill

By the third run you will notice you are typing the same corrections. That is the moment to make a skill: a packaged set of instructions your AI loads automatically for this kind of job.

Mine creates tokens and components, writes the gaps file, expects Storybook, then screenshots each generated component and compares it against the matching Storybook story, and compares manifests (a check I use later for parity). It exists because of my own mistakes, and I update it most weeks.

One safety note, because I am asked this every time: a skill can run code on your machine. Make your own as a team or install them, but only from people you trust; read them, or have a developer look first or at least ask Claude to run through it before installing. Installing a random skill because it sounded handy is the same move as opening the “you have won a million” attachment.

Keeping code and Figma parity

Generating the library once is the easy part. Keeping it true as the code changes week after week is the open problem, in my setup and in the industry generally.

So I built myself a little parity checker and keep it as a status page inside Storybook; you can check it out here on my sync status page. You don’t need a page; you need a check, but I am a designer, so I need to see things visually.

How it works, in three steps, quite unspectacular:

  1. Storybook can automatically write a component list. If you are using the Storybook MCP, it generates a file (JSON) called a manifest: every component, its properties, the allowed values and the defaults, straight out of the code. I only found it because of prototyping, where that short list is what makes AI prototyping work at all, since the agent reads the list instead of your whole repo. Which, by the way, is what got me into this whole setup in the first place, as I was so frustrated with the code output of AI builders when prototyping.
  2. So I asked Figma for the same thing. With the MCP open, I had Claude write me a matching list of what is really in my library: same components, same properties, same values. You can see the Figma JSON file I use here.
  3. Then I ran the two against each other. Name against name, property against property, default against default. Everything that matches turns green, anything that moved turns red. Easy!

Both lists are JSON, which is just a text file where every value has a label, so a machine can compare them without interpreting anything.

That comparison is deterministic, and that is exactly what we want: same input, same answer, every time, with no AI in it. The AI only kicks it off in my setup. The downside of mine is that I still have to trigger it by hand, and a real team would have a more sophisticated setup that runs automatically on every change. But very few teams have that right now.

However, building it taught me more than reading about it ever did. I now have a much better idea of what my developers mean when they talk about checks, and I can sit in that conversation and help shape the workflow with design needs in mind.

Side note: Right now it only checks the architecture, the names, properties, allowed values, and defaults. Not the visual side, no CSS. I am working on that.
Another side note: I initially called this a contract, but it isn’t. A contract sits above both sides and both get built from it. Mine compares two sides, and code wins every time, so the honest name is a parity check.

“But I already have a Figma library. Can I update it with MCP? ”

Most teams have one, often with years of work in it. The same connection can compare instead of create.

I take a component I know is out of step, and I ask:

In my open Figma file there is an Alert. Check it against the Alert in the code. This is a library file, so instances depend on it. Think it through with me: would a change list next to it be best, or should you generate a reference version from code next to it so I can compare, or do you want to propose a direct fix? Tell me here in the chat and add this as a visual note in Figma next to the component.

What comes back is usually a report plus a clean reference component sitting next to the old one, which is a very calm way to have an argument with your own library (and yes, I renamed my component to Pizza just to show you a fail):

The whole check runs through the MCP, and the answer is generated straight onto the canvas, next to the component it is about.

Three warnings:

  • Work on a copy. Never let an agent loose in a live library that other people’s files depend on. Duplicate first, test the workflow, then decide as a team.
  • Deleted variants do not come back. Every variant has a key underneath its name. Delete it and rebuild it identically, and the instances out in the wild still will not reconnect. Rename and repair, do not delete and recreate.
  • It still needs babysitting. On a real system with real history, this is assisted work, not magic. Go component by component, because the AI is quick and tireless and has no idea which differences matter. Once you are done, you can put a deterministic contract or other parity check on top that just checks whether things stay synced.

I use this technique for any sort of check, e.g. accessibility

Once you are aligned, you can do so much! Here’s an example: accessibility checks run in code, and then I get a little note like the one above in my Figma file next to the area with the issue and suggested solutions to discuss. Love it!

This is what becomes possible once Figma and code hold the same tokens and structure: Contrast measured against the real tokens, then laid out in Figma through the MCP

What if your product has more than one source?

Everything above assumes one. My sample is one design system in code and Figma on top, so that code wins and there is nothing to argue about. With two it still holds: pick one as the source, mirror it into Figma, keep the names matching on the other side. At three- iOS, Android and web- it falls apart, because each of them holds part of the truth and none of them is wrong.

You will not be the one deciding how that gets solved, and it decides what your Figma file can be, so it is worth knowing which one you are living in.

A library per platform. You do exactly what this article describes, once per platform. Each library mirrors its own codebase, like three small projects side by side. The drift then is not really between Figma and code any more, it moves into the structure: there is no single Button, there are three, and they slowly grow apart. That is the kind of thing a team ends up talking about as a whole, and it is good to see it coming.

Shared tokens, separate components. The one I see most often. Colours and spacing come from one source and land everywhere, while each platform keeps its own components, which is correct rather than sloppy, since a sheet is not a modal. You can mirror that split in Figma: one library for the variables and text styles, shared by everyone, and a component library per platform on top of it. The tokens are then safe to rely on, the component names are not.

One platform as the reference. Usually web. Then it is this article again, one mirrored library, and the others follow its names as far as they can. Worth knowing which platform that is, and if nobody can tell you, that is your answer.

Components defined as data. The one I find most promising comes from Nathan Curtis, whose talk about this idea I saw at SmashingConf Amsterdam in 2026 and really resonated with me. Instead of the definition living inside one codebase, every component is written down as data: its options, its allowed values, its defaults, in a plain file that sits above all the platforms. He calls it a contract (I wrote a longer article about contracts), and a schema says what a contract can contain. React, iOS, Android and Figma are all built from it and checked against it, so none of them is the original, and your Figma file stops being downstream of somebody else’s codebase.

Worth exploring, and not only for this. If you follow me a bit longer you will see JSON files and deterministic checks turning up everywhere, including in prototyping, which is where this way of thinking really pays off. So if you are working at that size, have a look at Curtis’s Spectacular (not a paid placement, as usual, just an honest recommendation), a Figma plugin and a command-line tool that read a component into schema-valid YAML or Markdown and render specs back into Figma.

The question to take back to your team is not which tool. It is which of these four you already are, and who is keeping it true.

What this does not solve

  • It needs a system worth mirroring. If the code is a mess, you get a beautifully generated mess. And the clean codebase you can happily generate from is rarer than any of us pretend. Mine behaves because it is a sample system I built myself. Real ones have two generations of components living side by side, props called type1, half the things undocumented, and a Storybook somebody set up in 2024 and stopped feeding. The honest version is that you do not need the whole system to be clean, only the component you are mirroring today, which is why I keep going one component at a time. And the first generated run is quite good at showing you exactly where the mess is. But yes it is work, a lot of work to get AI-ready.
  • Staying in sync is the open problem, and it’s tricky. My check tells me when the two have drifted; it does not stop them drifting, and I still trigger it by hand and in a playground. The state of the rest: Figma’s Code Connect links a component to its code but does not check whether they still agree, and it is on the larger plans only. Design system teams with engineers are building their own comparisons, which is the most common serious answer at the moment. Contracts are the most interesting direction and still early, closer to a proof of concept than something you install. And Figma’s own Code Sources (which they demoed at Config India in October 2026), which would point to the real system, is very promising, but still in closed beta. So if you feel behind on this, you are not. Almost nobody is doing it properly yet.
  • It only checks the structure. Names, properties, values, defaults. Not the visual side, no CSS. I am currently playing with this step; I will keep you updated. Contracts do not solve this either as far as I understand it: they can say which token a part must use, which catches most drift, and they cannot tell you whether the thing looks right when it renders. That is visual regression testing, a separate tool on the code side, and between Figma and code it is still me looking at two screenshots (the MCP compares them for me). There’s interesting work happening, but if I missed anything, let me know.
  • Library updates are hidden in Figma. This one caught me out properly. The library can be perfectly in sync and every designer still has to accept the update inside their own working file, and Figma buries that away in a corner. So half a team can be designing with last month’s Button, and nobody notices even though your setup is as polished as it gets.
  • It needs someone who can read both sides. Not write code. Read it, enough to notice when a translation went wrong. Still worth more right now than learning another tool.

Above all, this is also a human factor. All of this needs a change in workflow and mindset, on both sides. Designers have to read a codebase and to ask for access in the first place, which is the harder part. Developers have to prepare the system so it can be read, with typed props, descriptions and a clean manifest, and then be open about sharing it and inviting design in, which is the bigger ask. Nobody changes job, and reading code is worth more to a designer right now than another tool.

📖 Words in this article.

In-System Design (my term): designing with the system’s real components, on whichever surface suits the question, instead of next to the system in a tool that rebuilds it.

Props: the options a component accepts in code, like variant or size. Figma calls them component properties.

Token: a named design decision, likebackground-accent, instead of a raw colour value. Primitives are the raw values, semantic tokens give them meaning, and aliased means the semantic one points at the primitive.

Scoped (Figma): a variable is only offered where it belongs, so a text colour cannot be applied to a background.

Storybook: a website that shows every component of a codebase, live and clickable. It lives inside the codebase rather than keeping its own copy.

Story: one example of a component, written next to it in the code. The examples you click through in Storybook.

Manifest: the component as a list. Every prop, value and default, written once, generated from the code. Storybook can produce one, from version 10 with the components manifest switched on.

JSON: a plain text file where every value has a label, so a machine can read it without interpreting anything.

MCP (Model Context Protocol): a standard plug that lets an AI connect to a tool like Figma or Storybook and read from it or act in it. Figma Console MCP (by Southleft) is the one I use for variables and library work.

GAPS.md (my term): a file where the AI writes down everything it could not express, was unsure about, or faked.

Skill: a packaged set of instructions an AI loads automatically for a recurring job. Powerful, and worth vetting before you install one.

Deterministic check: a comparison with no AI in it. Same input, same answer, every time.

Parity check (what mine is): a deterministic comparison of two lists, code and Figma, where code wins.

Drift: when the design and the code slowly stop matching, one small difference at a time.

Component contract (Nathan Curtis and others): a component’s definition held as data, above any one platform, that code and Figma are both built from and checked against.

Schema: the model that says what a contract is allowed to express.

Code Connect (Figma): links a Figma component to its code so developers see the right snippet. It links, it does not check, and it is on the larger plans.

Visual regression testing: screenshots of the real rendered components, compared automatically on every change, so anything that shifts shows up as a difference.

Variant key (Figma): the invisible id under a variant’s name. Delete the variant and the key goes with it, which is why rebuilt variants do not reconnect to instances.

In-System Design: a three-part series.

  • Part 1: Building an AI-ready design system: Code → Figma (you are here)
  • Part 2: AI prototyping inside your design system (3 November 2026)
  • Part 3: From code to Figma and back (10 November 2026)

About the author: Christine Vallaure

I’m Christine Vallaure. I design, I teach, and I spend an unreasonable amount of my time on articles like this one. Through moonlearning.io I teach Figma, design systems and AI workflows to designers and teams. Along the way I speak at conferences like Figma Config and Smashing Conference, mostly about where design meets code, and I am a member of the Awwwards jury.

Currently, I offer these formats in these formats:

  • Build Scalable UI in Figma & AI: Design Systems Agents Can Actually Use · four-week, full Figma from the ground up, design system basics, and AI topics like these on top.
  • AI Design Systems & Prototyping for Designers · a two-week intensive that runs through exactly this workflow and the prototyping that follows it, for designers who already know their way around Figma and basic design system principles.
  • In-house team training · my favourite part. Get in touch if that sounds useful.

Please note: the on-demand video library on moonlearning.io does not cover these topics. I currently teach them only in live cohorts and in-house team training (October 2026).

I write these articles with an AI assistant, from my own notes, recordings and repositories. The thinking, the examples and the opinions are mine, and so is the final wording and tone.

title: Does Apple’s HomeView reduce effort, or ask for our attention?
description:
Truly useful domestic technology fades into the background. Too many smart home screens demand centre stage.

Apple’s latest foray into the home automation market is the HomeView, a 7 inch touch screen with integrated speaker designed to sit in a communal living space like the kitchen or dining area. It sounded pretty pedestrian, a competitor to Google’s Nest Hub or Amazon’s Echo Show, but something about it just felt a little off. Couldn’t the iPad already do most of this? My design brain kept asking, what problem is the HomeView solving?

The pitch: a shared screen at the kitchen table

I thought the best place to understand the intended use cases would be Apple’s ad for the HomeView. Light-hearted and cinematic, it takes the perspective of a family that places the HomeView literally at the centre of their kitchen counter/table, and their life unfolds around it at the pace of a manic start-up during a morning scrum.

This staging overlooks a real limitation that would typically relegate this device to one side of the room, wiring. The HomeView is a wired device and needs to be plugged-in to operate, this means having it sit neatly in the centre of a kitchen table or counter is less likely unless you have a kitchen conference table complete with grommets.

I understand an ad will always tidy up reality, but this tidies away where the device can live. Even if the cable were invisible, the premise itself surfaces a questionable design choice. The dining area is the one place families try to keep screen free, this is proposing we put one in the middle of it and make it a focal point.

It was here I reached for a quick test I use on any connected product, does this reduce effort, or does it ask for attention?

Good home automation disappears

Back in 1991, Mark Weiser a computer scientist at Xerox PARC introduced the concept of ubiquitous computing with a simple observation: “The most profound technologies are those that disappear. They weave themselves into the fabric of everyday life until they are indistinguishable from it.” [Weiser’s Scientific American article]

These ideas were developed further by cyborg anthropologist Amber Case, into the Calm Technology Principles, an approach for designing more human-centric technology. The first principle is that technology should require the smallest possible amount of attention. It echoes the test I use on any connected product. Against this standard, HomeView is working against itself, it falls into a classic design trap, assuming that visibility equals utility.

I’m not averse to a smart home, in a recent home refurbishment I installed a lot of ‘smart-tech’ from connected HVAC systems, lighting, CCTV, multi-room music and internet enabled appliances. All the ‘smart’ features are accessed through an Apple screen mounted discreetly on my wall, a 2018 iPad. Funnily enough with all this home automation, after the initial setup — most family interactions are largely limited to playing music and checking the doorbell camera.

Home automation is designed to be exactly that, automated not demanding constant interaction. It’s very much fire and forget, I want it all to just work for me. Once heating schedules are set up for the season I rarely have the need or urge to alter them, for more routine controls like lighting, I have pre-programmed physical switches and dials. By way of the attention test these reduce effort and ask nothing from me, whilst a dashboard in the middle of the room, inviting interaction does the exact opposite.

A centralised dashboard is very much a highlighted feature of the HomeView. In the Apple ecosystem the Home app consolidates all your smart home tech in one place, this unification is the key experience all these providers from Amazon to Google are seeking to deliver upon.

”…a classic design trap, assuming that visibility equals utility.”

In reality the experience is not as seamless, as third-party manufacturers typically provide limited functionality via their APIs to the Home app. The remainder of functions are then only available through their own app, resulting in a fractured two-tier experience. This can leave the Home app feeling more like a hobbled remote control rather than a fully featured control centre.

So an eight-year old iPad, using each manufacturer’s own apps can largely perform the home automation functions provided by the HomeView, which brings me back to that central question, what is the real problem being solved?

The real problem being solved

The HomeView is actually addressing two problems.

A manufactured problem

In 2022 Apple knee-capped the Home app features on the iPad such that it could no longer function as a home hub. Support for the old version ended in February 2026. Simply put, if you want to connect smart devices via Apple’s centralised Home app you’d now need some of their home hardware, specifically a HomePod or Apple TV, citing their new software architecture requires a device that’s always powered-on and fixed in the home.

This feature unbundling opened an opportunity for a single-purpose product like the HomeView, where previously a more than capable multi-purpose device like the iPad could have and did serve this need.

Missing out on the AI race problem

The other problem being addressed is Apple’s position in the AI race. They may not be competing for the frontier, but with no real horse in the race they are strategically positioned to act as the gateway for how households access third-party intelligence. The HomeView acts as a pervasive gateway, that deepens ecosystem tie-in all whilst delivering a series of revenue streams. A little investigation shows that accessing certain security camera recognition features requires an iCloud+ subscription.

A test for connected products

HomeView solves a number of strategic problems for Apple, just not that many real user ones. Herein lies the rub, a device that takes centre stage feels like it’s vying for my attention whilst not addressing that primary need of reducing effort.

“Home automation is designed to be exactly that, automated not demanding constant interaction”

Unobtrusive domestic user-centric experiences that borrow from the idea of ubiquitous computing are ones that fade into the background, and disappear into everyday life. These are the experiences that we can find most useful, demanding very little from us so we can focus our attention on things that matter more.

In a world filled with products craving our attention, we as designers can learn from the Calm Technology Principles and apply this mindful thinking to our own work, by starting with a simple honest question: does this reduce effort or does it ask for attention?

Further Reading

  • Designing with Tensions: Reframing Smart Home Ecosystem UX — ACM, 2026. Comparison of design frameworks used within Smart Home Tech.
  • Scaffolding a Design Process for Applying Calm Technology Design to Smart Toys — Interacting with Computers, 2026.
  • The Smart Home Agent Wars: A Five-Player Race Nobody Is Winning — Yahoo Finance, October 2026.

title: Our React App Worked Perfectly—Until Someone Closed Their Laptop
description:
What sleep/wake bugs taught us about Supabase, network recovery, and building reliable SaaS applications.

Imagine spending weeks building a React application.

Authentication works. Database queries work. Real-time updates work. Your dashboard loads quickly, and your end-to-end tests are passing.

You deploy it.

Everything looks great.

Then someone closes their laptop.

They return an hour later, open the lid, and continue working.

The application is still there. They're still logged in. The buttons are visible.

But something is wrong.

A request never finishes. A loading indicator keeps spinning. A piece of information disappears from the screen.

Refreshing the page fixes everything.

Sound familiar?

This became one of the most interesting reliability challenges we encountered while building Axon OSINT, a SaaS platform for digital investigations.

And the lesson was bigger than any particular library:

A web application that works after a fresh page load is not necessarily an application that survives real life.

1. The Bug That Didn't Look Like a Bug

One of the frustrating things about sleep/wake failures is that the application often doesn't crash.

There's no dramatic error screen.

No obvious exception.

No broken deployment.

Instead, the failure can be subtle.

A dashboard displays information from an earlier session. A request stays pending. An action appears to be running, but nothing happens.

During our work on Axon OSINT, we encountered variations of these problems across multiple areas, including investigation workspaces, account settings, and billing workflows.

The recurring pattern was particularly interesting.

A fresh reload could restore normal behavior.

But the application was supposed to keep working without asking users to refresh their browsers every time they returned to their desks.

That raised a question:

What exactly changes when a laptop sleeps, if the React application itself is still mounted?

2. Your JavaScript State Can Survive Longer Than Your Network State

When a browser tab goes into the background or a computer sleeps, several things can change.

JavaScript timers may be delayed.

Network connections may be interrupted.

Authentication credentials may approach expiration.

Real-time connections may disconnect.

An asynchronous operation that was started earlier may not complete when expected.

Meanwhile, React component state can remain in memory.

So after the user returns, the interface may still look exactly as it did before.

This creates a dangerous mismatch:

The UI remembers a healthy application, while the network may no longer be healthy.

Consider a basic loading pattern:

async function loadData() {
  setLoading(true);

  const { data, error } = await supabase
    .from("items")
    .select("*");

  if (error) {
    throw error;
  }

  setItems(data);
  setLoading(false);
}

This code has an immediate problem: if the operation throws, setLoading(false) is never reached.

We can improve that:

async function loadData() {
  setLoading(true);

  try {
    const { data, error } = await supabase
      .from("items")
      .select("*");

    if (error) throw error;

    setItems(data);
  } catch (error) {
    showError(error);
  } finally {
    setLoading(false);
  }
}

Better.

But there's still a problem.

What if the promise never settles within a reasonable amount of time?

The finally block won't execute until the awaited operation settles.

A loading indicator can remain visible indefinitely if nothing imposes a deadline.

This became one of our most important rules:

Every critical network action needs a predictable way to finish.

3. We Stopped Treating the SDK as the Only Transport

Axon OSINT uses React, TypeScript, Supabase, and Zustand.

Supabase provides a convenient SDK for database operations, authentication, and other backend functionality.

Under normal conditions, the SDK is exactly what we want.

But our post-wake engineering standard addresses a specific failure mode: after sleep or tab suspension, some SDK-dependent operations may stall even while the application still appears usable.

Our response was not to abandon Supabase.

Instead, we separated two concerns:

  1. What operation does the application need to perform?
  2. Which transport can safely perform it right now?

For critical operations, our architecture can use the SDK with a bounded timeout and an alternative direct HTTP route when appropriate.

Supabase exposes REST and RPC endpoints, so not every operation has to depend on the same client-side execution path.

A simplified read strategy looks like this:

User requests data
        |
        v
Is the SDK marked degraded?
        |
   +----+----+
   |         |
  Yes        No
   |         |
   v         v
Direct    Try SDK with
HTTP      a timeout
             |
        +----+----+
        |         |
      Success    Failure
        |         |
        v         v
      Return    Direct HTTP
      data      fallback

The distinction matters.

If we already know that the SDK has become unreliable in the current browser session, repeating the same problematic path can waste time.

Instead, eligible reads can use the alternative route immediately.

This is a resilience pattern, not a universal recommendation to bypass every SDK whenever something goes wrong.

The fallback still needs correct authentication, authorization, error handling, and data validation.

4. A Timeout Is a Deadline, Not a Recovery Strategy

A timeout is useful because it prevents the UI from waiting forever.

But a timeout alone doesn't solve the underlying problem.

Here's a simplified helper:

function withTimeout<T>(
  operation: PromiseLike<T>,
  timeoutMs: number
): Promise<T> {
  return Promise.race([
    Promise.resolve(operation),
    new Promise<never>((_, reject) => {
      setTimeout(() => {
        reject(new Error("Operation timed out"));
      }, timeoutMs);
    }),
  ]);
}

This illustration puts a deadline on waiting.

However, it doesn't actually cancel the underlying network request.

That's an important difference.

Promise.race() can stop your code from awaiting an operation, while the original request may still be running.

For cancellable direct HTTP requests, AbortController is a better tool for enforcing network deadlines.

For example:

async function fetchWithDeadline(
  url: string,
  init: RequestInit,
  timeoutMs = 8000
) {
  const controller = new AbortController();

  const timeout = setTimeout(() => {
    controller.abort();
  }, timeoutMs);

  try {
    const response = await fetch(url, {
      ...init,
      signal: controller.signal,
    });

    if (!response.ok) {
      throw new Error(`HTTP ${response.status}`);
    }

    return response;
  } finally {
    clearTimeout(timeout);
  }
}

The important design decision isn't whether to use 8, 10, or 15 seconds.

It's that the operation has an explicit boundary.

After that boundary, the application must make a decision.

Retry safely?

Use a different transport?

Display an error?

Preserve previously loaded data?

It cannot simply remain stuck.

One crucial caveat: a timed-out write may have succeeded on the server.

Blindly retrying a payment, record creation, or other non-idempotent action can introduce duplicate operations.

Writes need stronger safeguards, such as idempotency keys, reconciliation, or a status check before retrying.

5. We Introduced a Session-Level Degraded Mode

One useful decision in our architecture was to remember when a critical SDK operation had timed out.

Rather than repeatedly trying the same failing path, we introduced a session-level degraded state.

The concept is straightforward:

type SdkHealth = {
  degraded: boolean;
  reason?: string;
};

When a critical operation encounters a qualifying failure, the application can mark the SDK as degraded for the current browser session.

Then subsequent eligible actions can avoid unnecessary waits.

This isn't about declaring the entire backend offline.

The backend might be completely healthy.

The problem may exist in a particular browser-side request path.

It's an important distinction:

An unhealthy client connection does not necessarily mean an unhealthy server.

Our architecture deliberately keeps this degraded state until a hard page reload, rather than repeatedly switching back and forth using an automatic timer.

Why?

Because oscillating between healthy and degraded modes can create another category of problems.

One request works. Another hangs. The system retries. Then the user clicks again.

Suddenly one intermittent failure has become a cascade of activity.

Stability sometimes means choosing a conservative path and sticking to it for the session.

6. Authentication Recovery Must Not Depend on the Broken Path

There is another subtle failure mode.

Imagine you've detected an SDK problem and decided to use direct HTTP.

Before the fallback request, you try to retrieve the access token using another asynchronous SDK call.

What happens if that call depends on the same degraded client behavior?

Your fallback can hang too.

This is why our internal post-wake standard calls for using the application's already-maintained authentication state when appropriate.

In Axon OSINT, Zustand stores session information used by critical recovery flows.

The general principle is:

SDK request becomes unreliable
           |
           v
Use a verified, existing session token
           |
           v
Make the authorized fallback request
           |
           v
Handle success, expiration, or failure

This does not mean ignoring authentication expiration or inventing a token.

A cached token must still be valid for the request, and the server must enforce authorization on every path.

If no valid token is available, the application should follow a controlled authentication recovery flow.

A fallback is not a security bypass.

Resilience and authorization must work together.

7. Recovering Every Component at Once Can Make Things Worse

At first, it might seem that the solution to wake-related bugs is simple:

Whenever the browser tab becomes visible, refetch everything.

Unfortunately, this can introduce an entirely new problem.

Imagine your application has:

  • An investigations list.
  • A graph workspace.
  • A notification panel.
  • Account settings.
  • A billing summary.
  • Several background queries.

If every component independently reacts to a focus or visibilitychange event, returning to the tab can trigger many simultaneous requests.

Some may overlap.

Others may compete for state updates.

A few might fail while the others recover.

We've had to consider this problem in Axon OSINT as well.

Our recovery architecture tracks wake cycles and avoids treating every focus event as a completely new recovery operation.

It also distinguishes between ordinary tab focus and a situation that actually requires recovery.

The key lesson:

Recover the application, not every component independently.

One coordinated recovery process is easier to reason about than a dozen unrelated event listeners.

8. The UI Must Be Honest About What It Knows

Here's a particularly dangerous response to network failure:

try {
  return await loadSubscription();
} catch {
  return null;
}

At first glance, it looks harmless.

But what does null mean?

Does the user have no subscription?

Or did the network fail?

Those are completely different states.

If the application treats a transport failure as an absence of business data, it may hide information that still exists on the server.

The same issue applies to returning an empty array when a request fails.

An empty list might mean there are no investigations.

Or it might mean the application couldn't load them.

A reliable interface should distinguish these cases.

For example:

type LoadResult<T> =
  | { status: "success"; data: T }
  | { status: "stale"; data: T }
  | { status: "error"; message: string };

Now the application can display previously confirmed information without pretending that a failed network request returned an empty result.

But cached information must be clearly understood as potentially outdated.

And sensitive actions should still require fresh, authorized server confirmation.

This distinction became especially important for workflows involving account status, permissions, and billing.

A network error is not a business decision.

9. We Learned That Background Writes Need Their Own Rules

Our investigation workspace includes graph-based interactions.

Users may move entities around, organize relationships, and update layouts.

Some of these operations generate background writes.

Imagine moving dozens of nodes, then returning from sleep while the application attempts to persist every position at once.

A naive implementation might look like:

await Promise.all(
  nodes.map((node) => savePosition(node))
);

For a large graph, this can create a burst of network requests.

If the network is degraded, the application may produce multiple timeouts and errors, even though saving node positions is not the user's most important task.

Our engineering guidelines therefore distinguish between critical actions and non-critical persistence.

For position updates and similar background operations, we favor concepts such as:

  • Queuing.
  • Deduplication.
  • Debouncing.
  • Bounded concurrency.
  • Summarized failures.

The user should be able to continue interacting with the graph without a non-critical persistence problem freezing the entire interface.

But the application must also avoid pretending that unsaved changes were successfully persisted.

The right trade-off depends on the operation.

A graph position and a financial transaction should never share the same retry policy.

10. The Tests That Matter Happen After the Happy Path

A typical frontend test might do this:

Open the page
Click a button
Verify the result
Done

That's useful.

But it doesn't cover the conditions that exposed our reliability problems.

Our sleep/wake test scenarios also consider situations such as:

Open the application
Authenticate
Open an investigation
Put the laptop to sleep
Wake it
Try to create an entity
Switch between graph and table
Verify the UI reaches a terminal state

Other scenarios cover network interruption, security settings, account sessions, and post-wake actions.

The desired result isn't always that every request succeeds.

Sometimes the network genuinely isn't available.

What matters is that the application behaves predictably.

No infinite loading.

No blank screen.

No uncontrolled request storm.

No misleading empty data.

No duplicate writes caused by unsafe retries.

And no action that leaves the user wondering whether it happened.

That final point matters more than it might sound.

For users, uncertainty about whether an action succeeded can be worse than a clear error message.

11. Our Reliability Checklist Changed

After working through these issues, we began asking different questions during development.

Not just:

"Does this action work?"

But:

Does it work after the browser has been suspended?

What happens if the SDK request stalls?

Can the user recover without refreshing the entire page?

Will a timeout leave an action stuck in loading state?

Could retrying this operation create duplicate data?

Does an empty response mean no records exist, or that something failed?

Will multiple components initiate recovery simultaneously?

Does the fallback preserve the same authorization boundaries?

These questions are now part of how we approach critical workflows.

And there is an important qualification: architecture standards don't automatically eliminate every regression.

New features can still introduce bugs if they don't follow the same rules.

Reliability is a property that has to be maintained, not a checkbox that can be completed once.

The Most Important Lesson

When we started building Axon OSINT, our attention was naturally focused on features.

Investigations. Entities. Relationships. Collaboration. Billing. AI-assisted workflows.

All of those are important.

But real users don't always interact with applications under ideal conditions.

They close their laptops.

They switch between tabs.

Their internet connection drops.

Their session changes while the application is in the background.

They return to something they started earlier and expect to continue.

That is normal behavior.

And a well-designed SaaS application must treat it as normal.

The real test of a web application isn't only whether it works when everything goes right. It's whether it remains understandable, secure, and recoverable when something goes wrong.

That's one of the biggest engineering lessons we've learned while building Axon OSINT.

And we're still learning.

Let's Discuss

Have you experienced bugs that only appear after laptop sleep, browser suspension, or network reconnection?

How do you handle stalled requests, background recovery, and duplicate-action prevention in your React applications?

I'd love to hear what has worked for you.

We're building Axon OSINT, a platform for digital investigations, OSINT research, and collaborative evidence analysis.

This article is part of our **Building Axon OSINT* engineering series. The code snippets are simplified educational illustrations, not verbatim production code.*
